I live in England and I want to see timelier access to GP, community health and mental health services. I strongly agree that we must expand training places, improve return-to-practice support, offer apprenticeships and ongoing CPD to sustainably grow GPs, nurses and mental health professionals. In my area, routine GP slots can be hard to come by, with waits of several days to a week, and referrals to mental health services can take weeks to months. Increasing training places and supporting those returning to practice would bring more experienced clinicians into NHS services sooner, and apprenticeships could attract new talent from diverse backgrounds.

We also need targeted resources to close access gaps for deprived, ethnic minority, migrant and marginalised groups. That means interpreters, culturally competent staff, and proactive outreach in estates and community hubs. For example, bilingual health workers and mobile clinics at community centres would help.

Finally, expanding appointment slots and session capacity through hiring, longer hours and optimised scheduling would reduce waits. Expanding nurse- and therapist-led clinics and better triage can free up GP time for urgent cases, while same-day and after-work slots would make services more accessible for families like mine. These changes are practical and interconnected.

As an organisation representing young people in England, we support bold steps to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services by expanding the pipeline of qualified staff. Increasing training places for GPs, nurses and mental health professionals is essential so more appointments are available when people need them. We know from our work with young people that delays in accessing care can lead to escalating problems.

Make return-to-practice support more accessible: funded schemes that help experienced clinicians re-enter the workforce after career breaks would quickly boost capacity in local clinics and mental health teams. Expand apprenticeships for nursing, mental health support roles and allied health professions to attract a broader, younger majority into healthcare and to provide paid routes into meaningful careers.

Strengthen CPD: funded continued professional development keeps teams up-to-date with new guidelines, digital triage, and early intervention approaches, improving both speed and quality of care. In our area, these changes would reduce wait times and help young people get timely support, especially in mental health.

Improving NHS111, clinical triage,, booking systems and care navigation so urgent cases are fast‑tracked would makr a real difference in my area. A streamlined flow meanss fewer calls, less duplication, and clearer next steps for patients using GP, community and mental health services. In practice, when an older neighbour needed an urgent GP appointment, the pathh from NHS111 to a booking slot was slow and fragmented. A unified triage system that immediately flags urgent cases and presents available slots across GP practices, urgent care centres and mental health crisis teams would save time andd reduce stress. A well‑staffed care navigation service could guide people to the right service first time, whether it's a same‑day GP slot, a community nurse clinic, or counselling support. Digital booking that shows real‑time availability and cross‑practice communication would prevent duplicating calls and multiple referrals. Training NHS111 operators to recognise urgent mental health needs and route them to appropriate crisis teams would also prevent delays. Overall, thrse changes would simplify patient flow and prioritise those in genuine need.

I'm not convinced that the proposed move to co-located hubs will automatically improve timely access. In practice, centralised hubs can push patients further from home, add travel barriers for the elderly, and require expensive IT systems across several organisations. In my town, a hub plan would mean longer journeys for many people and blur which team is responsible if something goes wrong. I’d rather see more GPs, nurses and social care support funded in existing practices and in community teams, with clear accountability, than shiny new buildings that may become bottlenecks.

Secondly, I agree that continuity of care for complex patients matters, but extending appointment times without increasing overall GP capacity will simply create longer waits for others and drain already stretched practices. We need stable, ongoing relationships with a small, consistent team, not a rotating cast.

Third, NHS111 and care navigation need reform, yet the current patchwork of triage and booking can cause delays and misdirection. I’ve seen calls bounce around departments and patients being booked into multiple unnecessary steps. Any plan must prioritise urgent cases, reduce duplication, and actually add front-line staff to handle the extra work.

In short, invest in people and local continuity, not costly reorganisations that risk leaving the more vulnerable waiting longer.

Fund targeted interpreters and culturally competent staff, with outreach in deprived and migrant communities to close access gaps; expand same-day GP slots and community/mental health hubs; use trusted local partners to raise awareness, guiding timely care, subject to sustainable funding.

i strongly believe thank you for inviting feedback on how to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services in Wales. Our organisation sits at the interface between hard‑pressed communities and the health system, and we see real potential in reform that recognises both the complexity of needs and the diversity of people who seek care. Any changes must be designed to reduce gaps in access for deprived, ethnic minority, migrant and marginalised groups while also easing pressure on general practice so clinicians can focus on those with the most complex needs. A nuanced balance between targeted outreach, expanded multidisciplinary care and preserved continuity of care is essential.

Targeted resources, interpreters and culturally competent staff, plus proactive outreach
- Access is routinely hindered not by lack of providers alone but by barriers to entry: language, cultural misunderstandings, transport, and fear of engaging with services. We would support dedicated, community‑facing resources that fund interpreters across primary care, community and mental health services, including after‑hours triage and same‑day allocations where needed. Receiving a GP letter or mental health appointment in one’s own language, with culturally competent staff who understand the patient’s context, should be a standard, not a luxury.
- Practical outreach is essential: multilingual appointment reminders, community health workers who share language and lived experience, and pop‑ups in faith centres, mosques, temples and community hubs in deprived areas. In Wales, where migrant communities can feel isolated, these touchpoints help people navigate the system before crises occur.
- We also need translated information about what is available, how to access help, and what to expect from appointments. Simple changes—clear phone scripts for reception staff, culturally sensitive triage questions, and consent processes that respect different norms—can reduce miscommunication and missed appointments.
- A concrete example is the regular engagement work done by community organisations with parents and carers in urban and rural pockets of Wales. When interpreters and bilingual staff are present at booking and during consultation, attendance improves and patients report greater confidence in the care they receive, which in turn improves adherence and outcomes.

Expanding multidisciplinary teams to treat routine cases and free GPs for complex care
- We support expanding multidisciplinary teams within primary care, including pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates, to manage routine or stable conditions. This would free GPs to devote more time to patients with high complexity or chronic, multi‑morbid conditions, ultimately improving safety and outcomes.
- Pharmacist oversight can substantially reduce polypharmacy risks and improve chronic disease management (blood pressure, lipid control, glycemic management) through regular med reviews, patient education and dose optimization. Physiotherapists and occupational therapists can manage musculoskeletal and functional issues in the community, reducing unnecessary GP visits.
- Paramedic and physician associate roles could extend urgent and triage capacity, including home visits for vulnerable patients, which helps avoid hospital attendance where appropriate and supports timely escalation when needed.
- A practical approach would be to pilot integrated MDT clinics within GP practices, with clearly defined governance, shared electronic records and joint care plans. Evidence from pilots elsewhere suggests better symptom control, improved patient satisfaction and fewer missed GP appointments when teams are co‑located and work to common pathways.
- It is important that these teams operate with clear referral criteria, robust supervision, and equity monitoring so that minority groups do not experience a new form of gatekeeping. We would welcome mandatory data collection on service use by ethnicity and deprivation levels to track progress toward equity goals.

Protecting continuity of care and longer appointment times for complex cases
- Continuity of care matters. For people with long‑standing conditions, mental health needs, or social determinants impacting health, a named clinician who knows the patient’s history improves safety and reduces repeated visits. We advocate for longer appointment times—especially for complex or vulnerable patients—to allow meaningful assessment, shared decision‑making and care planning.
- This could involve reserved slots for high‑needs patients, named care coordinators, and a system that ensures patients see the same clinician where possible, even when urgent care is required. Longer appointments reduce the likelihood of misdiagnosis, treatment errors and the churn of repeated contacts.
- For mental health services, continuity is even more critical. A consistent care pathway with regular check‑ins from a clinician who understands a patient’s background, culture and social pressures leads to better engagement and fewer crises.

Implementation and safeguards
- Any reform must be funded with a clear timetable and evaluation framework. We propose measurable targets: improved wait times for priority groups, increased attendance for interpreters, reduction in avoidable hospital admissions, and equity indicators by ethnicity and deprivation index.
- Workforce planning must accompany these reforms. Wales faces recruitment and retention challenges; thus, investment in training, supervision, and supportive working conditions for new MDT roles is essential to sustainable improvement.
- Data sharing and consent frameworks should be robust but practical, enabling integrated care while protecting privacy. Digital initiatives must avoid widening the gap for those with limited connectivity or digital literacy by maintaining high‑quality telephone triage and in‑person access.

In short, we are cautiously optimistic about multi‑faceted changes that bring interpreters, culturally competent staff and outreach into the core of primary and community care, expand multidisciplinary teams to manage routine conditions, and protect continuity of care for complex cases. Done thoughtfully, these steps can reduce delays, improve outcomes and ensure that no patient is left behind in our pursuit of timely, high‑quality care across GP, community health and mental health services in Wales.

I strongly support measures to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services, and I believe the changes should be practical, reliable and easy for people who work or have caring responsibilities to use. In my experience, evening and weekend clinics, along with guaranteed same‑day urgent slots, would make a real difference to everyday life and to outcomes in both physical and mental health.

First, extending access beyond traditional hours is essential. Many of us cannot take time off work for daytime GP appointments, and weekends are not always easy either if clinics are closed or only offer limited slots. A robust plan would include reliable evening clinics during weekdays and regular Saturday or Sunday sessions, with a minimum standard of late appointments and walk‑in availability for urgent cases. In practice, this would translate into guaranteed appointments for urgent non‑emergency needs on the same day, with clear triage so that those with more serious symptoms are seen promptly. When a same‑day slot exists, patients are far less likely to escalate issues or to miss vital care, and practice teams can prevent deterioration that leads to hospital visits.

Second, a streamlined urgent‑care pathway within primary care is vital. People should be able to book an urgent slot for a non‑emergency issue and be triaged quickly by a clinician who can either see them that day or organise a timely alternative, such as a home visit or rapid referral to a relevant team. In addition, a robust response for mental health is essential. A same‑day mental health triage, with quick access to an appropriate professional (be that an therapist, counsellor or a crisis MO), can prevent crises from worsening. I’ve seen friends and neighbours suffer while waiting for assessments; guaranteeing a same‑day slot would help families stabilise situations early and avoid avoidable distress.

Third, I’d like to see stronger integration between GP practices, community health teams and mental health services, backed by more flexible staffing. Clinics that operate in the evenings or weekends should have a stable workforce so patients are not surprised by cancellations or delays. Expanded community services—district nursing, physiotherapy, podiatry, and mental‑health outreach—are crucial, especially for people managing long‑term conditions. When these services can be reached promptly after a GP contact, patients receive a smoother, faster continuum of care, often reducing hospital admissions and improving quality of life.

Fourth, digital and logistical improvements would support these changes. A single, user‑friendly booking platform that prioritises urgent same‑day access, combined with reliable telemedicine options for follow‑ups where appropriate, would remove friction. Clear information about where to go for urgent care, what to expect when booking, and how long waits might be would also help people plan around work and family commitments.

From a personal standpoint, I’ve spoken with colleagues who struggle to see a GP during the working week, and I’ve witnessed the relief when a weekend clinic or a guaranteed same‑day urgent slot is available. A relative with a recent change in mental health status found it difficult to access timely support; a guaranteed same‑day slot would have made a meaningful difference to stabilising their condition. Another neighbour, managing a long‑term condition, benefited greatly when a community nurse could visit within 24 hours of a GP referral, preventing a potential hospital admission.

In summary, the most impactful changes would be: 1) reliable evening and weekend GP clinics with guaranteed same‑day urgent slots for both physical and mental health concerns; 2) a streamlined, triaged urgent‑care pathway across primary and community services; 3) expanded, well‑staffed community health teams connected to general practice; and 4) a simplified digital booking and communication system to help people navigate these options. If these components are delivered together, they will ensure timely access for working people and those with urgent non‑emergency needs, improving health outcomes and reducing unnecessary strain on hospitals.

Living in England and trying to get timely GP, community health and mental health care, I don’t think the answer is simply to push for bigger multidisciplinary teams and call that the fix for access. Expanding teams that include pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates can help in some situations, but it’s not going to magically free up GPs or get people seen quicker across the board. If anything, without careful design and funding, it risks creating more confusion about who to contact and who is responsible for your care when you’re unwell.

Why I’m wary, in practical terms:
- Continuity matters. I want to see a clinician who knows my history, especially for recurring issues or mental health concerns. If routine problems are shuffled to a rotating MDT, I could end up retelling the same story to several people, and there’s a real risk of information gaps or miscommunication. In my experience, when I’ve tried to quickly sort things like a sinus infection or a back ache, getting advice from a pharmacist helped, but for a proper diagnosis I needed a GP. If I’m sent to a team instead of booking a GP appointment, the path to a quick resolution can slow down.
- Staffing and governance aren’t easy fixes. There aren’t enough trained allied health professionals to cover every local area in a way that guarantees timely access. Even when a pharmacist or physiotherapist can handle a routine case, there has to be robust supervision, clear prescribing rules, and a reliable handover to a GP if the problem turns out to be more serious. In areas where recruitment is tough, expanding teams could simply relocate the bottleneck rather than remove it.
- Mental health remains the real sticking point. There are long waits for CAMHS and IAPT, and triaging routine mental health concerns to other professionals won’t fix the crisis in demand. My friends have waited months for non-urgent referrals; that’s not acceptable. If the aim is to improve timely access, we need more capacity in mental health separately, not just a reallocation of tasks to non-physician staff.
- The risk of fragmentation. With multiple professionals involved, you need a clear care plan and a named coordinator to avoid patients slipping through the cracks. Without strong governance, the person who attends one appointment may not be the same person overseeing the overall care plan, which can make people feel less supported, not more.

What would actually help most, in my view:
- Realistically extended GP access and dependable urgent slots. If I need to see someone today, there should be a straightforward path to a same-day appointment or a video/phone consult that feels like a real alternative, not an afterthought. Better online booking, predictable appointment times, and reliable same-day slots could shave hours or days off waits.
- Stronger digital triage and first-contact access. A booking and triage system that genuinely directs people to the right type of clinician, with a clear escalation path if symptoms worsen, would save time and reduce unnecessary visits. Video consultations can be useful for many problems, but they must be easy to access and not a barrier for those without perfect tech setups.
- Targeted investment in mental health capacity. We need more staff in IAPT and CAMHS, faster referrals, and better crisis support so people aren’t left waiting when they’re most vulnerable. This isn’t optional if people are to get timely help.
- More robust community and nurse-led services, with a clear, patient-centered route back to the GP when needed. Pharmacists and physiotherapists should handle appropriately scoped routine issues, but with explicit guidelines and a formal bridge back to primary care when a problem isn’t resolved or is turning complex.
- A single point of contact and a care coordinator for those with multiple health needs. Someone who can navigate appointments across GP, mental health, and community services would reduce duplication and improve the sense that you’re being looked after.
- Local pilots with strong evaluation. If MDTs are to be part of the solution, run careful pilots in a few areas, measure impact on wait times, patient satisfaction, and safety, and only roll out widely if there’s proven benefit.

In short, I’m not against multidisciplinary care. I’m against placing the burden on patients to navigate a more complex system while expecting the same or better timeliness. The priority should be reliable, easily accessible GP access, together with solid triage, expanded mental health capacity, and well-governed integration with community services. If MDTs are pursued, they must operate with clear roles, continuity, and a strong patient-centric design to actually deliver faster, safer care.”

I believe the key to making timely access to GP, community health and mental health services better is a bold, visible plan to grow and sustain the workforce while removing practical barriers for patients. Targeted recruitment, including international hiring, incentives and pay improvements, plus flexible working and strong wellbeing support, would help attract and keep talented clinicians who can cover evenings and weekends when people actually need appointments. In my area I’ve seen practices struggle to offer same‑week slots; with more staff and stable rotas, patients with ongoing issues would get appointments sooner and have longer, more effective consultations.

It’s also vital to protect continuity of care and extend appointment times for complex or vulnerable patients. When people see the same clinician and have proper care plans, outcomes improve and repeat visits fall. In practice, that could mean longer slots for chronic disease reviews or mental health follow‑ups, plus better social prescriber support to reduce crises.

Rural and mobility‑challenged patients need practical solutions: mobile clinics visiting villages, outreach from town centres, telehealth hubs, and travel incentives. Improving premises and parking, plus convenient digital triage and online booking, would reduce wasted trips and speed up access.

Overall, a coordinated package like this has worked in my experience and would make care fairer and quicker for more people.

i strongly believe to improve timely access, three changes would help: 1) Strengthen NHS111 with clinically led triage and streamlined booking so urgent cases are prioritised and people aren’t bounced between call handlers. In my experience, a day-long loop between NHS111 and GP reception delays care. 2) Simplify care navigation and share records so patients move through GP, community nursing and mental health without repeating information or facing multiple waiting lists. 3) Invest in co-located community hubs that integrate primary care, mental health, social care and VCSE partners, so local teams can co-ordinate care, reduce duplication, and provide faster access. Digital tools should support this: same-day slots, transparent booking status, and a dedicated care navigator. Ensure pilots include youth-friendly access and feedback loops. Barriers include staffing, data sharing, privacy, and travel in rural NI. With proper funding, these hubs could cut waiting times and improve experience. When one hub is accessible, it makes it easier to get mental health support without long delays!

From where I sit in England, expanding online booking, e-consults and remote care makes sense, but must be inclusive. Our practice rolled out online booking during the pandemic and it often cut the time to see someone. Yet a lot of older neighbours and those with limited internet still rely on phone calls or face‑to‑face slots, so we need clear non‑digital routes and reassurance that help is not more difficult to obtain. 

On mental health, I strongly support expanding community teams, early intervention, crisis response and talking therapies to shorten waits and bring parity with physical health. If someone in a family experiences rising anxiety or depression, timely access to talking therapies can be life‑changing. 

To deliver these changes, we must address staffing. Targeted recruitment, international hiring, better pay, flexible hours and genuine wellbeing support will help attract and keep clinicians. Without more GPs, nurses and therapists, digital systems and expanded teams will struggle to offer timely care. In short, combine smart digital options with real‑world accessibility and a strong, well‑supported workforce.

From my experience in England, I’m not convinced that simply expanding multidisciplinary teams or creating co‑located community hubs will reliably improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services. In practice, more hands in a patient pathway often means more handoffs, more governance, and longer waits for routine issues. I’ve seen attempts to push routine back pain to physiotherapists or to use pharmacist-led triage, only for patients to face extra steps and delays before a GP makes the final decision. Co‑located hubs promise seamless care, but the success hinges on robust IT, shared records, and clear patient routing; without that, a hub can become a maze and fragment mental health access rather than speed it up. Local funding gaps and inconsistent accountability would only magnify these problems, especially in areas with already stretched services.

If timeliness is the goal, we should prioritise expanding GP and nurse prescriber capacity, offer extended hours for routine appointments, and implement real-time digital triage that directs patients to the right clinician first time. Any hub must be locally governed with measurable targets and independent evaluation to ensure it actually improves access rather than adds complexity.

From my experience living in England and as someone in the 55-64 bracket, I think a mix of measures would help with timely access. Evening and weekend clinics and guaranteed same-day urgent slots would make a real difference for people who work full‑time or have caring responsibilities. In the past, when a routine concern or symptom turned into a non‑urgent visit, it was hard to get an appointment that fitted around work; a guaranteed same‑day urgent slot would reduce unnecessary trips to A&E and prevent delays in care. For complex or chronic conditions, preserving continuity of care is vital: longer appointment times (20–30 minutes) with a named GP who knows your history can reduce repeat visits and prevent problems from drifting.

Transport and premises problems in my rural area create real barriers: limited bus routes and crowded car parks at the health centre. I would welcome mobile clinics visiting village halls, outreach teams, and telehealth hubs in local venues, plus incentives to attract flexible staff to underserved areas. But telehealth must be accompanied by in‑person options for physical checks and for patients less comfortable with technology. Integrating mental health services in primary care and ensuring rapid access to talking therapies alongside GPs would also help.

i strongly believe timely access won't improve with generic measures; I insist on targeted resources, interpreters, culturally competent staff, and outreach to deprived, ethnic minority, migrant and marginalised communities!

From my perspective in Scotland, the most meaningful gains would come from a better mix of practical changes rather than simply extending hours. While evening and weekend GP clinics and guaranteed same-day urgent slots sound helpful, they rely on a sustainable workforce that is currently in short supply. If we can’t keep those extended hours adequately staffed, they’ll become another source of frustration for patients and burnout for staff. In practice, I’ve spent long waits with NHS 111 only to be told to call back, and by the time I could access an urgent slot, it was already full or the triage wasn’t directing me to the right service first time. There’s also a lot of wasted time bouncing between NHS 111, reception staff, and hospital services because of poor flow and duplications in booking and referral processes.

What would really help is improving the backbone: a reliable, clinically led NHS 111 with clear escalation paths, smarter care navigation that gets people to the right local service first time, and a shared, accurate urgent-care calendar across GP practices. Strengthening community mental health teams and rapid response services would also cut dependence on GP queues. If we focus on smarter triage, better digital booking, and genuinely joined-up care, waiting times drop and staff workloads become manageable without endlessly expanding hours that may not be sustainable in practice.

Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services needs a multi-pronged approach that matches how people actually move and seek care today. In rural parts and for anyone who struggles with transport, mobile clinics or regular outreach visiting towns, campuses and housing estates would help, alongside well-publicised telehealth hubs in community centres. Flexible hours, weekend slots, and incentives for GP practices to run in-community partnerships could reduce delays and parking stress. I’ve noticed parking and limited premises capacity at local clinics; a mobile unit or pop-up clinic would save students like me from missing lectures. 

On the digital side, NHS111 and booking systems sometimes feel like a maze: urgent cases get tangled in automated triage or duplicated referrals. Streamlined clinical triage, clear prioritisation for urgent needs, and a single, patient-friendly booking flow would reduce duplication and misrouting. Finally, I support investment in co-located community hubs—the kind that bring GP, mental health, social care and VCSE partners under one roof—so a young person can see a GP, talk to a counsellor, and access housing advice in one visit. If funded well, these hubs could transform local care.

I strongly support the proposed changes to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services in our area. By improving NHS111, clinical triage, smarter booking systems and care navigation, urgent cases would be prioritised and patients would experience a smoother flow rather than bouncing between different services.

From my own experience over the past year trying to arrange a same‑day GP appointment for a relative with chest symptoms, and navigating mental health referrals, the process is slow and repetitive. NHS111 can send people in circles or direct them to out‑of‑hours options, causing delays. A more capable triage system that can quickly assess severity and direct people to the right service would save time and ease anxiety.

Longer appointment times and continuity of care are essential for those with complex or chronic conditions. When my relative sees the same clinician regularly, care is coordinated, tests aren’t duplicated and we avoid repeated calls. It would help if appointment slots are protected for long‑term conditions and not siphoned off by routine checks.

Care navigation—trained staff who help book the right GP, nurse, community or mental health appointment and explain the route through the system—would cut duplication and administrative burden. A shared patient record across GP, community teams and mental health services would ensure smoother, safer, joined‑up care.

Overall, these changes would shorten waits, improve outcomes and let clinicians focus on those most in need.

Thank you for the opportunity. We welcome the proposals to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services in our area. Expanding online booking, e-consultations and remote care is a big step forward, especially for people who struggle to attend in person because of distance or disability. At the same time, there must be non-digital options and support to avoid excluding older patients or those without reliable internet. A dedicated telephone line with extended hours, plus in-person help at local hubs or clinics, would ensure no one is left behind. In our area, access would improve with evening and weekend clinics, and guaranteed same-day urgent slots for non-emergency issues, so people don’t wait days for help. For mental health, expanding community teams, strengthening early intervention, crisis response and talking therapies will help patients get timely support and achieve parity with physical health services. We’ve seen better outcomes when GP practices work with community teams and offer prompt talking therapies; this reduces escalation and keeps people supported at home.

I strongly support expanding community mental health teams, early intervention, crisis response and talking therapies to reduce waits and ensure parity with physical health. In our area, too many people experience months of waiting for talking therapies and CAMHS intake can be slow, while access to physical-health services remains comparatively prompt. Expanding multidisciplinary teams in local GP practices, with dedicated early-intervention clinicians and better linkages to social supports, would help people get help before crises escalate. A robust crisis response with 24/7 phone advice and rapid same-day assessments could prevent hospital admissions and stabilise people at home. We also need to normalise talking therapies in the community, including flexible hours and digital options to fit busy families.

Access gaps are worsened by language and cultural barriers. Targeted resources for interpreters, culturally competent staff, and proactive outreach to deprived, ethnic minority, migrant and marginalised groups would improve uptake and trust. Practical steps could include funded outreach clinics in community centres, translated information, and partnerships with local charities and faith groups to raise awareness and encourage timely help.

As someone living in rural Scotland, I welcome practical steps to improve timely access to GPs, community health and mental health services. Transport and parking deficits are real barriers. Mobile clinics visiting village halls, outreach teams stopping in towns on set days, and telehealth hubs at local libraries or community centres could massively reduce travel burdens for those of us with limited mobility. In my area, a GP can be several bus routes away; a weekly mobile clinic would be transformative, particularly for elderly residents and those with chronic conditions. Longer appointment times for complex cases are essential: continuity of care improves outcomes and reduces repeated visits, as I’ve seen when a stable clinician knows my history. We also need to invest in workforce: more training places, return-to-practice support, apprenticeships and CPD for GPs, nurses and mental health professionals. Incentives for rural postings and flexible staffing will help. A coordinated mix of on-site and remote care, with robust handovers and local data sharing, would help us access timely, holistic care without the daily trek to the city.

I strongly support changes to improve timely access by investing in co-located community hubs that bring together primary care, community health, mental health services, social care and VCSE partners. In my area the pace of GP appointments and access to mental health support can be slow, which for someone in their seventies is worrying. A single hub where you can see a GP, a nurse, a mental health worker, and get help from a social care or charity adviser on the same day would make a big difference. It would also help with continuity of care: staff know your history and can coordinate plans quickly.

Expanding multidisciplinary teams would relieve pressure on GPs. If pharmacists handle routine medicines reviews and minor side effects, and physiotherapists run early rehab and falls prevention, GPs could focus on complex care. Paramedics and physician associates could assess and treat lower-risk patients at home or in the hub, freeing clinic slots and reducing unnecessary trips. Linking these hubs with local voluntary groups ensures social needs—transport, meals, carers—are covered, so people stay independent and safer at home.

I disagree that these changes alone will fix timely access; without tackling transport, parking, and suitable premises, plus sustained funding for co-located hubs and expanded staff, rural patients won’t see real improvements.

While I recognise the aim to improve timely access, I disagree with relying mainly on the NHS111 redesign, tighter clinical triage, booking systems and care navigation as the solution - what a surprise. In my experience in Wales, these changes often add steps rather than speed things up, and they can steer people away from the right service. Last winter my partner had a high fever and a persistent cough; NHS111 sent us in circles between phone advice and online slots, with no GP appointment available for days. The result was a rushed visit to out-of-hours and more stress for a sick child. The latest tweaks would just shuffle who’s told to wait and when, not how many clinicians are on the ground. And with mental health services, the bottleneck is staffing, not triage rules; waiting lists are long because there aren’t enough staff, not because the system can’t triage properly.

What would help more is expanding training places, returning clinicians to practice, apprenticeships and CPD to grow GPs, nurses and mental health professionals long-term. That would create real capacity and a cleaner patient journey, instead of endlessly re-routing the same patients through the system.

I support investing in co-located community hubs that integrate primary, community and mental health with social care, plus mobile clinics and telehealth to reach rural areas. Increasing training and CPD will sustainably grow the workforce, improving timely access overall.

My experience in Scotland suggests the biggest gains come from protecting continuity of care and giving longer appointment times for complex, chronic and vulnerable patients. When you see the same GP who already knows your history, medicines, and risks, you get a clearer plan and fewer rounds of repeat visits trying to fix things. Longer slots would help with multiple issues in one go, reduce misunderstandings and flag problems early, which in turn cuts urgent attendances. For example, a neighbour with diabetes and anxiety found it hard to get a coherent plan because different clinicians didn’t share notes. A named clinician plus a proper care plan would have saved time and anxiety for them and the practice too. In mental health, timely access matters—short slots and waitlists can leave people feeling unheard, so faster access to talking therapies or a consistent link worker would make a real difference.

I also see value in better-integrated community teams—district nurses, physio, and social care bundled with GP hubs—to cut travel and delays and ensure people aren’t bounced between services. In the shorter term, smarter triage and same-day access for urgent issues could prevent hospital admissions and support early intervention.

In the longer term, boosting training places, return-to-practice support, apprenticeships and CPD will be essential to sustainably grow GPs, nurses and mental health professionals across Scotland, even though that takes time to come through.

I strongly agree that improving timely access to GP, nurse and therapist services is essential for our community. In my area I’ve faced a GP two weeks’ wait for a routine issue and longer waits for mental health support when a relative needed help. Expanding appointment capacity by hiring more GPs, nurses and therapists, extending session lengths where appropriate, and using smarter scheduling with triage and better digital bookings would reduce these delays.

Targeted recruitment, including international hires, attractive pay, clearer progression, flexible working and wellbeing support, is needed to grow and retain primary care staff. Flexible shifts and robust wellbeing programmes help prevent burnout and keep teams stable, which in turn improves patient care.

Also, evening and weekend clinics and guaranteed same‑day urgent slots would help working people and those with urgent non‑emergency needs. A local triage service that can quickly direct people to the right clinician, plus reliable communication about waiting times, would give older residents confidence in the system.

Overall, these changes would make access more predictable and lessen the stress of delays for many of us.

I appreciate the aim to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services, but I don’t think the changes many plans discuss will actually close the gaps we see in practice. In my experience, the big barriers aren’t just a lack of appointments on paper; they’re practical and everyday problems that hit older people, families on low incomes, and those who don’t speak English or who come from migrant backgrounds hardest.

First, targeted resources to reach deprived and ethnic minority communities are essential. I’ve seen neighbours struggle because there aren’t enough interpreters or culturally competent staff when they do manage to get through. A Polish neighbour’s mother needed help filling in forms and understanding follow‑up instructions, but the clinic simply didn’t have language support available at the time, so the appointment was effectively wasted. Outreach has to be more than posters in the language we already speak; it needs active presence in the community—regular drop‑ins at local community centres, mosques and churches, and trusted local venues where people feel comfortable. It should include trained bilingual care coordinators who can guide people through the system, help them book interpreters, and follow up on tests and referrals. Information must be in multiple languages and formats (written, spoken, and digital) so an elderly person with limited literacy isn’t left behind.

Second, we must grow and sustain the workforce, but not just by talking about training places in the long term. Yes, increasing GP numbers, nursing posts and mental health staff is vital, and I agree we need return‑to‑practice support, apprenticeships and CPD. However, these take time; in the meantime, we need practical, funded measures that keep existing staff in place and make working in underserved areas viable. That means better pay and working conditions, protected time to learn and support colleagues, and clear, fair career paths so people don’t burn out. We should also require services to have culturally competent teams who reflect the communities they serve, with accountability for reducing access gaps. Long waiting lists for mental health can’t be solved by more therapists a few years down the line; we need integrated teams, same‑day triage where possible, and culturally appropriate therapies available in community settings.

Third, transport, parking and premises deficits create real hurdles, especially for older residents and those with mobility issues. Rural and peri‑urban areas suffer most because buses are infrequent and clinics aren’t easy to reach by foot or car. I’m not persuaded by plans that assume people will always travel to the hospital or a central hub. Mobile clinics parked in housing estates on market days, outreach staff visiting care homes, telehealth hubs with on‑site help to set up devices, and local GP “satellite” rooms in convenient neighbourhoods would help enormously. Parking shortages at clinics and long walkways in aging buildings deter people who could otherwise attend; premises need to be accessible, with clear signs, good lighting, and comfortable space for carers and interpreters to stay with patients.

Telehealth has promise, but it isn’t a universal fix. It can help those who are digitally capable and already have devices and data plans, but many older residents don’t. We must pair telehealth with on‑the‑ground support: staff who can help people switch on a tablet, arrange an interpreter, and connect to a clinician in real time. A single general practice hub serving several communities, with a rotating schedule of specialist clinics (diabetes, heart health, mental health), could reduce travel while preserving personal contact.

In short, I’d support changes that prioritise targeted outreach, culturally competent and interpretable care, and practical, near‑home access options—mobile clinics, local hubs, community outreach—and that pair these with a credible, well‑funded long‑term plan to train and retain staff. Anything short of that risks widening gaps for the most vulnerable while ticking boxes on national targets. We need real, locally tailored delivery, not just promises of more staff years from now.

From my experience in England, I’m not convinced these broad changes will automatically improve timely access. Expanding multidisciplinary teams to handle routine cases sounds efficient on paper, but in practice it risks fragmenting care and confusing people about who is responsible. If pharmacists, physiotherapists or physician associates manage routine GP problems, patients may lose the continuity that comes with a regular GP, which I value for medication changes or spotting signs of something more serious. When I’ve needed quick advice, I’d rather speak to the GP who knows my history than navigate a new clinician.

Boosting community mental health teams and early intervention is essential, but it must not distract from core GP access or create longer waits elsewhere. A friend waited months for CAMHS; crisis lines are overloaded. Investment needs to reflect parity with physical health, not just rebalancing budgets.

Online booking, e-consults and remote care can help some, but they cannot be the only route. My elderly neighbour has no reliable internet, and others struggle with digital tools. We need non-digital options, adequate phone access, and clear triage pathways so nobody is left behind.

Overall, expand capacity and continuity in primary care first, with guarded rollout of digital and multidisciplinary approaches and strong safeguards for vulnerable patients.

I’m responding as a resident in England, aged in the 55-64 bracket, and I’d like to see real improvements in how quickly people can get GP, community health and mental health support. In my area, the demand is clear and growing: appointments vanish quickly, and when you finally get through, you often see a different clinician. A lot of this comes down to how we recruit, retain and support the people who deliver frontline care. I think the changes the government is considering could work well if they focus on growing the workforce and making that workforce feel valued and well-supported.

First, targeted recruitment makes sense. Rather than hoping recruitment happens by chance, we should actively focus on areas with chronic shortages and make it easier for new staff to join and settle. This could include local campaigns in colleges, universities and through community networks, plus guarantees of training opportunities and clear progression within the NHS system. Practitioners who choose to work in areas with higher need should be offered stronger induction support, reduced administrative burden in the first year, and a clear path to partnership or senior roles as they gain experience.

International recruitment can be a decisive part of solving shortages, provided it is done thoughtfully. Streamlined registration for qualified GPs and nurses, with culturally attuned onboarding, language support and mentorship in the first year, would help. In our region we’ve already seen overseas GPs join practices and stabilize appointment levels after a period of vacancies; with robust mentoring and protected time for orientation, these staff can become incredibly effective long-term contributors. Any international recruitment should come with robust safeguarding for patient safety and a clear plan to upskill clinicians in line with UK guidelines.

Incentives and pay improvements are essential. This isn’t just about attracting staff; it’s about retaining them. Financial packages that acknowledge the cost of relocation, the time needed to build patient lists, and the pressures of on-call rotas would reduce churn. Improved pay scales or targeted supplements for practices running longer hours or offering same-day appointments could help. We also need to ensure funding follows patients into the practice so that more flexible staffing models don’t jeopardise service quality.

Flexible working arrangements are crucial to keep staff rested and engaged, and they directly affect patient access. More opportunities for GP session sharing, back-to-back clinics, and weekend or extended evening hours should be remunerated fairly. Virtual or telephone triage, far from replacing in-person care, can triage non-urgent cases efficiently and free up clinicians for those with urgent needs. A sensible blend of face-to-face and digital contact could shorten waiting times without compromising care.

Wellbeing support for staff is not optional; it’s a foundation for timely patient care. Reducing administrative burden—through better IT systems, more efficient paperwork, and a dependable admin workforce—helps clinicians focus on patients. Providing structured wellbeing programmes, protected supervision time for junior staff, and access to mental health support for clinicians themselves would reduce burnout and keep teams stable long-term. In my experience, when a practice makes staff wellbeing a priority, the flow of appointments improves and patients feel the difference.

There’s also a role for expanding the broader primary care team. Increasing the use of nurse practitioners, physician associates, pharmacists, and link staff such as mental health link workers or social prescribers can relieve GPs and speed up access. If a patient’s initial issue can be handled by a nurse or allied professional, that frees up a GP to see more urgent cases promptly. Better pathways into community health services and faster referral routes into talking therapies would help too.

In practice terms, I’d like to see:
- A national recruitment fund targeted at shortages, with local targets and transparent reporting on progress.
- Streamlined, well-supported international recruitment with language and mentorship packages.
- Clear pay enhancements and relocation incentives, and funding that follows patient demand to sustain flexible staffing.
- Expansion of flexible working and extended hours, paired with fair pay for those shifts and strong digital triage to guide patients efficiently.
- A robust wellbeing strategy for staff, including reduced admin burden, access to professional supervision, and mental health support.
- Investment in the broader primary care team to handle routine tasks and give GPs more time for urgent or complex cases.

If these changes are properly funded and monitored, I’m confident we’ll see more timely access to GP appointments, quicker community health responses, and better mental health support for people in our area. It won’t be instant, but with steady investment, strong recruitment, and a real focus on staff wellbeing, we’ll build a more sustainable system that works for patients and clinicians alike.

In England, expanding online booking, e-consultations and remote care could improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services, but only if we maintain strong non-digital routes for those who can’t use these tools.. For example, last month I booked a same-day GP online and was offered slots quickly, yet urgent concerns required a phonee triage that sometimes felt sloww and left me feeling uncertain. In mental health, remote options could help people who struggle to travel, but there are still long waits for talking therapies in my area and after-hours support is limited. Crucially, digital expansion must come with real alternatives: a staffed phone line with short holds, walk-in clinics with same-day triage, and in-person appointments for those who prefer them. It would help if local hubs offered “digital access support”—free training sessions, a helpdesk, and even dataa subsidies—so older residents or those without devices aren’t left behind. Lessons from experience: ensure equity, clear choice, and robust safety nets alongsidr scalability of online services. There should also be better integration with community pharmacies and social care to ease pressure and improve coordination across teams.

From my experience in England, timely access to GP, community health and mental health services is often limited by staffing levels. The changes that would make the most difference are those that grow and retain the primary care workforce through targeted recruitment, fair pay and more flexible, sustainable working patterns.

- Targeted recruitment: expand local training placements in underserved areas and create clear pathways for local graduates to stay in their communities, with robust mentoring to help new clinicians.
- International hiring: use safe, well-supported routes for qualified GPs and nurses from abroad, with streamlined visa processes and return-of-service commitments to build confidence in local services.
- Incentives and pay: offers such as sign-on bonuses, retention payments, parity with hospital pay where appropriate, and improved pension and relocation support.
- Flexible working: more part-time and job-share posts, team-based clinics, extended hours where needed, and smart use of digital triage to avoid unnecessary visits.
- Wellbeing and admin support: protected time for supervision and mental health support; reduce burnout through workload management and better IT and clerical support.

Implement pilots in high-need areas, monitor impact on wait times and outcomes, and scale what works.

I live in Scotland and juggle a full-time job with family responsibilities, so timely access to GP, community health and mental health services isn't a luxury—it's essential. What would most improve access is simple: evening and weekend clinics and guaranteed same-day urgent slots. The current weekday-only pattern forces people to miss work or endure delays for non-urgent but pressing issues. I had a sore infection last month and couldn't get a same-day slot; the earliest appointment was three weeks away, by which time I needed antibiotics. For mental health, waiting weeks or months for talk therapies is unacceptable for someone in distress who can't switch off after a long day. A guaranteed urgent slot would prevent deterioration and reduce pressure on emergency services. Implementing this would require careful staffing—rotas, training more clinicians, and perhaps hybrid models with in-person slots for those without digital access. But the payoff would be fewer emergency calls, better morale at work, and improved health outcomes. In short, I disagree with maintaining the status quo and urge fixed evening/weekend access and guaranteed urgent slots across GP, community, and mental health services.

Access to GP and mental health services in my area can be slow, especially for those working or with carers. I think introducing evening and weekend clinics at local surgeries, plus a guaranteed same-day urgent slot, would help a lot. Two evenings a week and a Saturday morning could fit people’s schedules, with urgent non-emergency calls triaged to a same-day appointment or a clinician call-back. In my street, a neighbour waited two weeks for a GP appointment for a chest infection; an urgent same-day option might have prevented it from worsening. For mental health support, a same-day triage line or rapid-access slot with a clinician would make a real difference where waiting lists cause anxiety and sleep problems. For community health, closer collaboration between district nurses, physio, and GPs in same-day slots would reduce hospital visits.

I’m cautious about funding and staffing: longer hours demand more staff and admin, and we must guard against burnout. Any change should include clear targets, local transport options, and a mix of in-person and suitable telehealth, ensuring older residents aren’t left behind.

I don’t think simply expanding multidisciplinary teams is the best way to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services in my area. In practice, it risks creating more hand-offs, slower decision-making and a sense that no one is taking overall responsibility for my care when I’m feeling unwell.

First, continuity matters. When you’ve got a familiar GP who knows your history, you’re much more likely to get a quick, accurate assessment. In recent months I’ve watched friends and neighbours wait for a generic triage call or a nurse-led appointment before finally seeing someone who can address their symptoms. Adding pharmacists, physiotherapists or physician associates into routine care could, in many cases, mean I’m told to describe the same issue several times to different people across the same visit window. That friction alone can waste valuable time and actually lengthen the path to a proper diagnosis and treatment plan.

Second, I’m not convinced there’s enough trained staff to staff these expanded teams properly. My local practice already struggles with recruiting and retaining GPs; if funding is diverted to create larger MDTs, where does that leave the core GP service that patients depend on for urgent, complex or ambiguous problems? It’s not just about putting more hands in the room; it’s about who leads the decision and who is accountable if something goes wrong. In many cases a routine problem requires a GP’s clinical judgment and an explicit line of accountability, not a rotating cast of professionals each with a different framework.

Third, patient safety and risk management could suffer from fragmentation. A patient with multiple symptoms might be routed to a pharmacist for a medication check, a physiotherapist for musculoskeletal issues, and only later be reviewed by a clinician with overall responsibility for the case. Red flags or evolving conditions can be missed when care isn’t integrated under one lead clinician who sees the whole picture. That can be particularly worrying for older patients with comorbidities, mental health needs or social risk factors, where timing and context matter for treatment decisions.

Fourth, there’s the practical hurdle of access and scheduling. Even if MDTs are designed to speed things up, they require robust coordination, information sharing and clear referral pathways. In reality, IT systems and consent processes aren’t always aligned across different professionals, which can cause delays or duplicated tests. I’ve seen examples where a patient attends a first point of contact, gets bounced between teams, and ends up waiting days for a single, definitive plan.

What would work better, in my view, is targeted strengthening of GP capacity and better use of existing staff within a well-defined, well-governed framework. Key ideas include:
- Invest directly in GP recruitment and retention: longer appointment slots, better working conditions, and reduced admin burden so GPs can see more patients quickly and safely.
- Expand practical, time-limited access to high-quality digital triage and same-day online bookings that route patients to the most appropriate clinician without unnecessary delays, while preserving the option to see a named GP when that matters to the patient.
- Build stronger, clearer pathways for mental health when urgent access is needed, including embedded mental health practitioners within GP practices who work under a single care plan with clear accountability, rather than broad MDTs that can dilute responsibility.
- Create a small number of highly integrated, well-supported hubs in areas with the most acute access problems, but with strict governance, shared patient records and a named clinical lead to ensure continuity and safety.
- Improve out-of-hours and weekend access to urgent GP services so people don’t resort to emergency departments for non-life-threatening issues.

In short, I’m not convinced that broad MDT expansion will reliably shorten waiting times or improve care. What I want to see is stronger core GP capacity, smarter triage, reliable mental health access, and carefully piloted hubs with rigorous evaluation before rolling out more widespread changes. Any redesign should centre on patient continuity, safety and clear responsibility for outcomes.
Yes, expanding community mental health teams, early intervention, crisis response and talking therapies will cut waits and bring mental health on a par with physical health.

i strongly believe evenings/weekends and longer urgent slots sound helpful, but I worry about staff burnout and fragmented care; prioritise continuity with longer standard appointments and targeted multidisciplinary support within core hours!

Agree: protect continuity of care by offering longer appointments for complex, chronic and vulnerable patients to improve outcomes and cut repeat visits. Also invest in training: more GP/nurse mental health places, return-to-practice support, apprenticeships and CPD to sustain the workforce long term.

Access to GP, nurse and mental health services in our area can feel like a bottleneck. I’ve had to chase a GP appointment for weeks, and the nurse slot I needed was only available after a long hold. The mental health service has long waits too, and a friend on the adult liaison service waited over a month for a first talk. In the near term, increasing appointment slots and session capacity would make a real difference: hire more GPs, nurse practitioners and therapists; expand session sizes or offer extended hours and same‑day triage; use smarter scheduling and digital triage to balance urgent vs routine care; more robust staffing in call centres to cut time on the phone when people are trying to book; and maintain a mix of in-person and virtual options to fit people’s lives. In the longer term, we need to invest in training: expand training places for GPs and nurses, restore return‑to‑practice pathways, promote apprenticeships and ongoing CPD, and fund retention to avoid repeating shortages. A combined short‑term boost and long‑term workforce plan is essential.

From where I live in Scotland, I’ve learned that the real problem isn’t simply about having more services advertised on a map. It’s about getting those services to people who can’t travel far or cope with crowded city clinics. The ideas put forward—mobile clinics, outreach, telehealth hubs and incentives—sound sensible in theory, but they don’t yet add up to timely access for GP, community health and mental health care in our area.

Transport, parking and premises deficits are the stubborn blockers. Our village is miles from the nearest full-scale GP practice. The bus is infrequent, and in winter it can be unreliable or cancelled for weather. Driving everywhere isn’t always possible for older residents, and the car park at the local health centre is woefully undersized. I’ve watched neighbours circle the car park for ages, or give up and not go at all, choosing to endure symptoms at home instead of adding a long journey to their day. If a mobile clinic visits once a month, that’s useful as a reminder, but it’s not a substitute for regular, predictable access. Premises in some of the rural clinics are aged, not fully accessible, with narrow corridors and steps, narrow doorways, or bathrooms that aren’t easy for wheelchairs. Even when a telehealth option is offered, many people don’t have reliable broadband or the skills to use tablets confidently, and privacy at home isn’t always possible in a crowded house.

Telehealth hubs could help, but they can’t be a one-size-fits-all fix. A hub in a town centre won’t help the farmer who lives miles away, or the elderly neighbour who would need a long taxi ride each way. If we push people toward screens, we risk leaving behind those who are most in need: the very old, people with hearing or cognitive difficulties, and households with limited digital devices. We also know that physical examination, palpation, blood tests and other in-person checks are still essential for many conditions. In practice, telehealth often becomes a gatekeeper to care rather than a bridge to it, delaying diagnosis and treatment while people struggle to access the right technology.

Outreach and mobile clinics have their place, but they require reliable, long-term funding and consistent integration with existing GP practices. If a mobile service comes and goes, people build no trust that they’ll get timely follow-up. Continuity matters, especially for chronic conditions, mental health support and preventive care. I’d rather see a steady network of well-staffed, accessible local hubs than sporadic pop-ups that can’t offer the full range of services or referrals when someone needs them.

There is also a real need to address inequalities in access for deprived, ethnic minority, migrant and marginalised groups. Interpreters and culturally competent staff are essential, but waiting lists for interpreters are common, and bilingual staff are in short supply in rural areas. I’ve witnessed neighbours struggle to understand health information or to navigate referral pathways because interpreters aren’t available when a needed appointment is booked. Outreach should be led by trusted community organisations and delivered with real local flavour—translated materials, community health workers who share the background of the people they serve, and flexible appointment options. It isn’t enough to send a leaflet in several languages; people need consistent access, reliable interpretation, and clear pathways to care.

What I would want to see, instead of or alongside the current proposals, includes:
- Practical transport support: subsidised or free local transport to appointments, better scheduling that aligns with bus services, and free parking at local clinics or convenient community hubs with accessible parking.
- Upgraded premises: age-friendly, fully accessible clinics with enough consultation rooms, good waiting areas, step-free access, and reliable on-site facilities so people aren’t deterred from visiting.
- A blended, rebalanced service model: stable local hubs that combine GP, nursing and mental health professionals in one accessible footprint, with clear, predictable in-person slots as the default, and telehealth as a supplementary option with guaranteed digital support for those who need it.
- Sustained workforce planning: long-term recruitment and retention strategies for rural GPs, nurses, mental health workers and interpreters; incentives must be paired with real local support such as relocation packages, salary uplifts, and reduced practice administration burden, plus opportunities to train locally so people stay in the community.
- Stronger equity-focused outreach: funded interpreters available at every appointment where needed; culturally competent staff trained as standard; proactive outreach in deprived and minority communities with co-produced services, easy-to-understand information, and navigation support through trusted community organisations.
- Digital inclusion programmes: provision of devices or data subsidies, training for older residents, and simple, low-bandwidth telehealth options so people aren’t left behind by technology.

In short, the proposed changes would be a step in the right direction if they were embedded in a long-term plan that tackles the practical realities we face daily: travel time, parking, building accessibility, and the digital divide, together with deliberate, well-funded strategies to close language and cultural gaps. Until then, I remain sceptical that these measures will deliver timely access for GP, community health and mental health services to people like me who live in rural Scotland. We need dependable, local, inclusive care, not a patchwork of temporary fixes.

I think the biggest improvements would come from making NHS111 and the clinical triage process genuinely fit for purpose, and from simplifying how people book and navigate care across GP, community and mental health services. In practice this means a more joined‑up system where urgent needs are identified quickly, and then routed to the right clinician without forcing patients to repeat information or chase several different teams. 

What I’d like to see implemented:

- Strengthen NHS111 and clinical triage: NHS111 should be staffed by clinicians who can assess urgency accurately and initiate the appropriate next step on the same call. If someone presents with potential emergency or urgent issues, they should be offered a same-day GP slot or a rapid home visit when appropriate, with a clear, reliable path to escalation for mental health crises. In my experience, when I’ve phoned NHS111, the triage sometimes felt like a bottleneck rather than a bridge to care. If triage can directly book urgent slots or trigger a rapid outreach from a GP or nurse, it would save days of unnecessary waiting.

- Consistent, accessible booking systems: A single, user-friendly booking system across GP practices that prioritises urgent and same‑day slots would cut duplication and confusion. For those who prefer not to use apps, there should still be a straightforward phone option. I’d like to see triage-led bookings where staff determine the most appropriate service (GP, nurse appointment, mental health talk therapy, community physiotherapy, or social prescribing) and then secure a slot immediately. Regular reminders and real-time status updates would help people manage their health without constant follow-up calls.

- Care navigation and signposting: Dedicated care navigators should help patients plan their pathway through GP, community health, and mental health services. They could coordinate tests, referrals, and follow-ups, and ensure that a patient’s care plan is understood across teams. For older adults in particular, a navigator who checks in after an appointment to confirm what happens next can prevent falls into a second or third waiting line.

- Reduce duplication and streamline patient flow: Shared, up-to-date patient records across GP, district nursing, community therapy, and mental health teams would mean patients don’t have to repeat the same information every time they are passed between services. When I had a long-standing back issue, I found myself repeatedly re-explaining tests and results because different teams didn’t see the same notes. A unified record would also help avoid conflicting recommendations and improve safety.

- Quick access to mental health support: Access to talking therapies and urgent mental health support should be clearly integrated into the same triage pathway. For someone with anxiety spikes or a first episode of depression, a rapid appointment with a mental health professional or a crisis service should be as straightforward as seeing a GP for a physical issue. This could include rapid access lines, same-week CBT/EMDR referrals, and clearly communicated expectations about waits, with proactive follow-up.

- Flexible, extended access: Evening and weekend appointments in GP practices and community clinics would help people who work or care for others during the day. For those who struggle with digital systems, accessible in-person options at local hubs reduce the barrier to getting timely help.

- Community and out-of-hospital care integration: Strengthening district nursing, community physiotherapy, and social prescribing linked to the care navigator would relieve GP pressures and keep people well at home where possible. If someone needs a short course of physiotherapy or a home visit from a district nurse, they should not have to hunt around for the right referral; the navigator, aligned with the triage outcome, should arrange it swiftly.

- Safeguards and privacy: Any data sharing needs patient consent, with clear explanations of what information is shared and why. I’d want reassurance that this system respects privacy while still enabling faster, safer care.

From personal experience, when I had a flare-up of a chronic condition, I spent hours on phone lines trying to secure a quick appointment. If the NHS111 triage could have booked a same‑day GP slot or flagged urgent needs to a care navigator who then coordinated a stream of care across GP, community nurse, and, if needed, mental health support, I believe the outcome would have been much better and faster. In short, a more proactive, triaged first contact, plus a unified booking and navigation system, would reduce duplication, improve patient flow, and deliver timely help where people actually need it.

I’m not asking for a miracle, just a dependable, patient-centred system that recognises urgent need without delay and makes the right care accessible in the simplest possible way.
Agree. Establish co-located community hubs that bring GP, community, mental health, social care, and VCSE partners under one roof to streamline referral routes and improve timely access.

I welcome the goal of faster access to GP, community health and mental health services, but I cannot support a plan that centres on online booking and remote care at the expense of those who struggle with technology. In my village and among neighbours, internet reliability and digital confidence vary greatly, and some of us simply cannot rely on apps or online forms. Last winter a friend needed a same‑day GP appointment; online slots looked available, yet the phone lines were jammed and we ended up waiting days for anything suitable. An elderly relative found e‑consultations confusing and worrying to use, with the danger of missing important information.

Digital options can help some people, but they must sit alongside non‑digital routes: accessible telephone booking, in‑person triage, and same‑day clinics that people can reach without screens. We also need community digital‑support hubs and carers’ assistance to help those who need it most, plus clear guidance in plain language and multiple languages.

To genuinely improve timeliness, expand capacity across all channels, not just digital ones. Hire more staff for triage, extend daytime and early‑evening hours, and ensure mental health services offer quick‑access slots locally. A blended, inclusive system will shorten waits and prevent leaving older or digitally‑excluded residents behind.

I don’t think the answer is simply to recruit more staff and expand hours without fixing how our system is funded and managed. In my area, GP and mental health access remains painfully slow, and it’s not just a staffing problem. Targeted recruitment and even international hiring can help, but they aren’t quick fixes and can fail if retention, integration, language support and workload are not addressed. I’ve seen a GP vacancy linger for months, which pushes you toward urgent care and private options. Flexible working helps retain staff, yet only if there is stable funding and predictable, manageable hours rather than sporadic shifts.

What would help more immediately is expanding appointment capacity alongside smarter scheduling and better triage, including same-day slots where appropriate, so non-urgent needs aren’t parked for weeks. We also need more therapists and counsellors with local, culturally competent approaches—bookable in evenings or weekends and with clear referral pathways.

Crucially, we must invest in outreach, interpreters and navigators to close gaps for deprived, ethnic minority, migrant and marginalised communities. That means interpreters at first contact, culturally appropriate staff, and community hubs delivering GP, nurse, social care and mental health support together in one place, not scattered between several clinics. Overall, a sustained funding commitment and integrated models are essential, not just more staff.

From my vantage point in England, waits for GP, mental health and community care are still too variable. The most effective improvements would be: expand community mental health teams with early intervention and crisis response, and widen access to talking therapies so mental health care matches the urgency given to physical health. Too many people experience long waits or fragmented care before they receive help; a strong, ring-fenced mental health pathway with 24/7 crisis support and active outreach could prevent crises from escalating. 

Second, overhaul NHS111, implement robust clinical triage, smarter booking systems and care navigation to prioritise urgent cases, cut duplication and speed up patient flow. In practice, I have seen calls bounce between services, with delayed appointments; clearer triage that routes urgent concerns to rapid access slots would relieve pressure on GP practices. 

Third, build multidisciplinary teams—pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates—to handle routine cases and routine chronic care, freeing GPs to focus on complex needs. Our local practice staff already finds such roles helpful for repeat prescriptions and musculoskeletal issues, reducing unnecessary GP visits. 

These changes must be backed by adequate funding, training and integrated IT with shared records to ensure safety and continuity.

While I understand the aim to speed things up, I’m not convinced the proposed changes will reliably improve timely access for everyone. Expanding NHS111, clinical triage and digital booking risks pushing people into a system that’s not friendly to those without strong internet or digital skills—my age group included. I’ve seen neighbours struggle with repeated NHS111 call-backs and conflicting messages from different parts of the system, which ends up creating delays and confusion rather than quick access. Duplication between triage, GP reception and out-of-hours care wastes time and energy for patients who simply want to see someone promptly.

What would help more is getting the basics right: triage that truly prioritises urgent cases but with clear, fast pathways to a clinician when needed; less fragmentation and better information flow so patients don’t have to repeat their story multiple times. Expand capacity—more in-person appointment slots, flexible hours, and reliable non-digital options (phone lines and walk-in support) for those who can’t or don’t use online services. For mental health, same-day access and well-defined steps into community care are essential, not layered digital stairs that exclude some.

In short, avoid a digital-only push and invest instead in practical capacity, clearer navigation, and trustworthy non-digital supports so urgent needs are met promptly by the right service.

While I see the potential benefits of online booking, e-consultations and remote care, I strongly disagree that digital solutions alone will improve timely access. In our area many people are older, not comfortable with apps, or lack reliable broadband. I’ve seen elderly neighbours struggle to book a GP online and then miss the slot; others have had long phone queues, but at least there is a human to speak with. If we push digital-first models without adequate non-digital options, we risk widening health inequality.

What would help more: maintain more phone and in-person appointment slots, including same-day options; extend opening hours; keep walk-in clinics in community hubs; provide clear printed guidance and free, local digital support to help people book online; ensure e-consultations always offer a real clinician contact, not just a triage bot; provide aides who can assist at clinics and libraries; translate resources; ensure you can switch easily between channels.
