Longer appointments for complex and vulnerable patients to protect continuity of care, expanding teams including pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates for routine care, and more GP, nurse and therapist slots via hiring and smarter scheduling would cut waits and improve outcomes.

In my area in England, simply adding more GP, nurse and therapist slots and expanding session capacity would not, on its own, deliver timely access. The core problem is a chronic shortage of trained primary care staff and the time it takes to recruit, train and integrate new workers. Even with a few extra late clinics, I hear of long waits: my wife needed a routine appointment and it took two weeks; a friend waited months for a mental health referral; a local practice has twice advertised for GPs with limited response. Relying on international recruitment can help, but it’s slow to bear fruit and raises concerns about continuity of care, language, familiarity with local guidelines, and retention. Pay rises and flexible working are welcome but require sustained funding and career development; without a clear pipeline those staff shifts won't fill the gap fast enough. I would prefer more immediate fixes—same-day triage, expanded nurse prescribing, better use of pharmacists for minor ailments, and stronger links to community services—so patients get timely help while we build a longer-term workforce plan.

Access to timely GP, community health and mental health services has a real impact on daily life and independence. I strongly support expanding community mental health teams, early intervention, crisis response and talking therapies. With stronger teams, people can get help before problems worsen, improving parity with physical health and reducing unnecessary hospital admissions. Quick access to therapies for anxiety and depression makes a big difference.

I also welcome expanding online booking, e-consults and remote care to fit modern life. However, not everyone is comfortable with digital tools or has reliable connectivity, especially older residents. We must offer non-digital options such as telephone triage and in-person appointments and provide clear assistance to help people navigate systems.

Finally, increasing GP, nurse and therapist appointment slots via targeted recruitment and smarter scheduling is essential. In my area, mental health referrals have often waited several weeks; more same-day triage and longer afternoon sessions would ease bottlenecks and help people stay well at home.

Overall, these changes would reduce waits, support carers and deliver care closer to home.

Timely access will improve most if we protect continuity of care and lengthen appointment times for complex and vulnerable patients. In my area, our practice has begun some longer slots, but these are not universal and long-term conditions often require several visits. I’d support guaranteeing a named GP or small care-team for each patient, so one person knows my history and can coordinate tests, medications and referrals. 

For those with chronic illnesses or mental health concerns, I’d urge longer appointments—15-20 minutes minimum—so we can review medicines, symptom patterns, and social needs without rushing. A care navigator to link GP, community nurses, physio, and social care would reduce repeat visits and avoid missed signals. 

Strengthening community health teams is essential: timely district nurse input, more home visits for the less mobile, and easier pathways to talking therapies when stress or anxiety arises. Offering same-day urgent slots and flexible hours, plus transport support for older patients, would make a real difference.

I am not sure there is a one-size-fits-all fix. In my area, getting a same-day GP appointment is hit or miss. I called last month and was told there were no slots for two weeks, but the online system showed a cancellation later that day. For mental health, I know friends who have waited weeks for CAMHS referrals after being referred by a GP, and the wait is stressful. A few minor changes could help, like more same-day or after-work slots, clearer online triage that does not push people to call at 8am, and more staff to reduce delays. For community health, quicker physio and district nurse follow-ups would prevent small issues from becoming bigger problems. But I am not sure which of these would work best everywhere; maybe pilots in some areas would help identify what actually helps.

Thank you for the opportunity to respond. As an organisation working with young people across England, we regularly hear from students and early-career workers about delays in GP appointments, difficulties accessing community health services, and long waits for mental health support. I think the right changes could make a real difference, but they need to be implemented in a way that keeps care coordinated and affordable, not just faster in one part of the system.

Expand multidisciplinary teams to treat routine cases and free GPs for more complex care
- We support expanding multidisciplinary teams within GP practices and local health hubs to manage routine or low-acuity cases. If pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates can handle suitable consultations, we could relieve GP workloads and shorten waiting times for students with back pain, skin concerns, minor infections or medication reviews.
- In practice, a student with a sports-related ankle sprain or a dose review for a new contraceptive could be seen quickly by a physiotherapist or pharmacist, with GPs concentrating on chronic conditions, safeguarding, and complex investigations. This could be particularly helpful around exam periods or term-time when GP slots are harder to come by.
- However, this will require clear referral criteria, robust supervision, and good handover to keep care safe and ongoing. We need transparent performance metrics and local governance so patients don’t feel they’ve “mopped up” a problem with the wrong specialist. We’d also need to ensure this model is consistently funded across urban and rural areas to avoid postcode inequalities.

Expand community mental health teams and related supports while ensuring parity with physical health
- A broader, well-resourced network of community mental health teams, with stronger early-intervention services, crisis response, and talking therapies, has the potential to cut waits and align mental health access with physical health standards.
- From a young-person perspective, timely access to talking therapies and crisis support makes a big difference for campus life, part-time work, and retention in studies or jobs. Where waits exist or referrals feel “stuck,” people often deteriorate and end up in urgent care or A&E, which is not ideal for anyone’s wellbeing.
- But expanding mental health services must be planned with schools, universities and local services, and must avoid creating parallel systems. We need consistent staffing levels, clear pathways for escalation to urgent care when needed, and equitable access in both city and non-urban areas. We also need to guarantee data sharing with consent, so a young person’s information travels with them across services without repeating assessments.

Improve NHS 111, clinical triage, booking systems and care navigation to prioritise urgent cases and streamline patient flow
- A more capable triage process and better booking systems could reduce duplication and help patients reach the right service quickly. If NHS 111 online or call-back triage can point people directly to same-day GP slots, urgent care hubs, or mental health crisis teams, waits could fall substantially.
- Practical changes would include integrated appointment systems across primary and community services, with care navigation support (including trained navigators who understand student timetables and part-time work) to guide people to the best option first time.
- We should also guard against digital exclusion: some people may struggle with online tools, so there must be phone and in-person options, plus privacy protections and clear consent about sharing information between services.

Implementation, funding and measuring success
- Pilot approaches in diverse localities, with close monitoring of metrics such as wait times, patient satisfaction, pathways followed, and outcomes for mental health and chronic conditions. Involve young people in designing and testing these changes so the pathways fit real life.
- Ensure robust workforce planning, training, and support for new roles like pharmacists in GP settings and physician associates, with clear supervision and accountability.
- Above all, maintain continuity of care and strong GP relationships. We don’t want patients to feel they’re passed from pillar to post; the goal is better access, not more friction.

Overall, there is real potential here. If implemented with strong governance, adequate funding, and a clear emphasis on joined-up care and patient experience, the proposed changes could make timely access more achievable for GP, community health and mental health services, especially for younger people juggling study, work and personal commitments. We look forward to further details on funding, workforce planning, governance, and how patient voices will be embedded in ongoing evaluation.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment. From our experience as an organisation working with patients across urban and rural parts of England, timely access to GP, community health and mental health services remains inconsistent, and too often patient journeys involve multiple handoffs or duplicated, aimless navigation. I welcome a package of changes that puts urgent needs first, simplifies the patient pathway and makes sensible use of staff and technology. In particular, improvements to NHS111, clinical triage, booking systems and care navigation could drive meaningful, practical gains if designed with real-world constraints in mind.

NHS111, triage and booking: the current system can feel like a gatekeeper that doesn’t always know which door opens next for a given patient. I would support reforms that ensure triage is clinically led and outcome-focused, with rapid escalation for red-flag or urgent mental health presentations. Key elements would include:
- Real-time clinician triage feedback to callers, with a clear pathway to same-day urgent GP or nurse appointments when indicated, rather than defaulting to routine slots that are already booked out.
- Standardised decision support and shared patient notes to reduce repetition and miscommunication across urgent care, GP practices and community services.
- A single, user-friendly booking and triage interface that provides visible, up-to-date availability across local services, so patients can be guided to the most appropriate service first time, avoiding unnecessary hops.
- Strong care navigation roles at the local level to accompany patients through the system—helping with eligibility, transport options, and what to expect at the visit—so people don’t have to figure it out on their own.

In practice, this would mean fewer duplicated phone calls, shorter waits for urgent cases and less feeling of being bounced between services. I have heard from patients who describe calling NHS111 only to be told to call back later for a general appointment that never fits their urgent need. A clinically driven triage pathway, supported by a flexible booking system, could divert the majority of routine concerns away from urgent channels and free up clinicians to focus on those who need timely intervention.

Expanding appointment capacity in GP, nurse and therapist services: there is no quick fix, but a mix of hiring, smarter scheduling and team-based care could reduce waits while sustaining quality. I recognise the recruitment and retention challenges, particularly in primary care and mental health, but several practical steps could help:
- Increase session capacity through multi-disciplinary teams (GPs, nurse practitioners, therapists, pharmacists and social prescribers) who work together from the same care plan, freeing doctors to concentrate on complex cases.
- Expand hours and offer same-day or near-day access where clinically safe, including extended weekday slots and occasional weekend clinics, to capture urgent presentations without overwhelming weekday demand.
- Optimise scheduling with shared calendars across practices and integrated booking for physical and telehealth clinics, so a patient who needs a therapist in the town can be booked in the most efficient location without multiple referrals.
- Invest in training and retention packages to support clinicians in high-demand areas; this should be paired with reasonable workload limits and well-staffed rotas to ensure sustainable service delivery.

I would stress the need to preserve continuity of care and patient preferences. Some patients value a stable nurse or GP relationship, and any expansion should not erode this. Given the current workforce constraints, it makes sense to deploy skilled practitioners where they can have the greatest impact—e.g., nurse prescribers and cognitive behavioural therapists taking on appropriate caseloads to relieve GP pressure while maintaining quality and safety.

Transport, premises deficits and rural access: my organisation operates in mixed geographies, and transport remains a barrier for many, especially the elderly, people with disabilities and those with limited income. Parking at busy town centres is often prohibitive, and long travel times discourage timely access to non-urgent appointments. Solutions that bring care closer to people would be particularly effective:
- Mobile clinics and outreach sessions in community hubs, GP practice neighbourhood venues and parish halls to deliver routine GP checks, chronic disease reviews and mental health drop-ins closer to home.
- Telehealth hubs and digital access points in libraries or community centres, with staff to assist those less confident with technology. These should be truly inclusive—offering a mix of video and telephone options and ensuring patients can switch modes if needed.
- Incentives and infrastructure to attract clinicians to rural and deprived areas, including travel subsidies, flexible deployment and shared employment models across networks, so expertise stays local rather than vanishing to larger sites.
- Clear travel and parking information, plus thoughtful scheduling that clusters appointments for those travelling longer distances, so trips aren’t wasted by repeated queues or reschedules.

These measures would also support patients with mobility challenges who find it hard to attend multiple visits. Importantly, any mobile or telehealth approach must be backed by robust safeguarding, clinical governance and data protection. Telehealth should not be a barrier to care for those without reliable internet or digital literacy; non-digital routes must remain viable.

Implementation and evaluation: to avoid unintended drawbacks, pilots should be tightly evaluated with patient experience, wait times, and clinical outcomes tracked. Any national rollout must be matched by additional funding, capital investment in premises and equipment, and clear accountability for performance. I would also welcome patient and community watchdog involvement in design and governance so that changes serve real needs rather than theoretical efficiencies.

In summary, I support a convergent approach that prioritises urgent needs, reduces duplication, and strengthens navigation through the system, while expanding capacity and improving access for rural and mobility-impaired residents. The vision is sensible and timely, but it must be implemented with rigorous planning, adequate funding, and a commitment to inclusivity—so that everyone can access timely GP, community health and mental health care without unnecessary barriers.

I strongly support changes that would make GP, community health and mental health services timely and accessible for everyone. Targeted resources for deprived and minority communities are essential: interpreters on site or via video, bilingual reception staff, and staff trained in cultural competence so people feel understood from the first contact to follow-up. In my area, language barriers have meant families missed referrals for mental health support or struggled to navigate complex booking systems. Outreach in schools, community centres, and faith groups, with simple information in multiple languages, would help people know what support is available and how to access it quickly. Transport, parking and premises must be addressed too. Mobile clinics that visit estates and rural villages, plus outreach and telehealth hubs in libraries or youth centres, would reduce long waits and missed appointments. Incentives for practices to extend hours, hire more staff, and invest in warm, accessible premises with clear signage would make a real difference. Providing affordable transport vouchers where needed would help mobility-limited people. These measures would cut delays, improve trust, and ensure timely care for GP, community and mental health services.

Living in Scotland, I see every day how timely access to GPs, nurses and mental health support shapes the wellbeing of my family and neighbours. I’m strongly in favour of increasing capacity across primary and community care through more staff, expanded session lengths and smarter, more people-friendly scheduling. This isn’t just about shorter waits; it’s about better care, quicker reassurance and, frankly, fewer trips to A&E when things could be managed at a primary or community level.

First, we need more appointment slots by increasing staffing and expanding what each practitioner can handle. That means hiring more GPs and GP trainees, but it also means empowering nurse practitioners, allied health professionals and therapists to take on routine and triage work. In my area, a nurse practitioner-led clinic for minor infections and wound care has already relieved mountains of GP time and reduced unnecessary referrals. Expanding this model and giving therapists more slots—so talking therapies, CBT and mindfulness-based therapy aren’t stacked up for months—would make a real difference. We should also look at session length flexibility; longer slots for complex chronic conditions and mental health cases would prevent back-and-forth that drags on for weeks.

Second, smarter scheduling is essential. A robust triage system that directs people to the right professional first time can shave days or weeks off waits. That could be complemented by same-day or next-day appointments for urgent issues, with a simple online check-in to reduce front-desk queues. Digital tools should support patients in booking, rescheduling and receiving reminders, while clinicians can flag high-need patients for proactive follow-up. In practice, our practice trialed a same-day triage line last year, which cut the average waiting time for urgent issues by a couple of days and made people feel heard faster. We should expand and standardise that approach across NHS Scotland.

Third, extend access beyond core hours and into community settings. Weekend and evening clinics, as well as more drop-in slots, would help families working shifts or with school-age children. For mental health, spreading out slots and offering group programs could reach more people sooner and create peer support networks that help sustain recovery. In my community, a pilot for a weekly group for anxiety management and a carer’s drop-in has started to fill gaps where individual therapy slots were scarce. It’s not perfect yet, but it shows how expanded capacity and flexible formats can work.

Fourth, strengthen community health teams to keep people well at home and out of hospital. More district nurses, health visitors and physiotherapists would support chronic disease management, post-illness rehabilitation and home-based care, which translates into fewer unnecessary visits to GP practices and quicker access to the right support when issues arise.

Finally, let’s make this work for rural and semi-rural areas as well. The problem isn’t only about capacity; it’s about equitable access. That means targeted recruitment incentives, regional hubs, and transport Solutions to help people attend appointments. Transparent wait-time data at the practice level would also help people plan and reduce anxiety over not knowing when they’ll be seen.

From a personal standpoint, when a simple cough turned into a two-week wait for a GP appointment, I felt the friction all too clearly: a minor issue stretched into days of worry and work absences. After a local nurse-led clinic expanded its hours, I noticed how much quicker follow-ups and tests could be arranged, and how much calmer the situation felt. A family friend with anxiety was able to access a therapist much sooner because the waiting list had shortened, thanks to more slots and group programs. These aren’t cosmetic changes; they change lives day by day by reducing unnecessary stress and safeguarding people’s health.

If the system can invest in more staff, smarter scheduling and extended access, the benefits will ripple through NHS Scotland: fewer emergency visits, better chronic disease control, and more timely help for people when they need it most. I support these changes and would like to see them rolled out with clear targets, regular reporting on wait times and a strong focus on preserving access in more rural communities.

From my experience living in England, simply refining NHS111, clinical triage, booking systems and care navigation won’t deliver timely access. The real bottleneck is staffing and care capacity. If we want quicker GP, community and mental health access, the focus must be on growing and retaining the workforce.

That means targeted recruitment, international hiring, better pay and flexible working, with genuine wellbeing support to stop burnout. In my area a GP practice with 12,000 patients often has routine appointments two to three weeks out; mental health referrals take months; NHS111 often routes urgent calls to be told to ring back or to wait longer.

Introduce more staff at the front line: more practice nurses, physiotherapists, and pharmacists within primary care to handle routine issues; build local urgent care hubs that offer same-day GP slots or quick access to mental health crisis teams; ensure mental health services have rapid access slots; extend hours; ensure stable workforce.

Triaging should protect urgent cases but avoid over-filtering. NHS111 and booking systems should be used as a support, not a gatekeeper that creates extra steps; care navigation should connect patients to their local teams rather than bouncing them around.

Ultimately, without tackling staffing and integration, digital tweaks will just shuffle the queue. We need sustained investment in recruitment, retention and local multi-disciplinary teams, plus better data sharing to reduce duplication.

Timely access to GP, community and mental health services needs a coordinated, user-friendly system. I’d back strengthening NHS111 and clinical triage so urgent cases are prioritised and patients are guided quickly to the right service. A streamlined, shared booking platform across GP practices and community teams would cut duplication and long phone queues; when someone is triaged as urgent, they should see a GP or nurse same day or within 24 hours via an urgent access clinic. 

Care navigators at hubs could walk people through options, make appointments, and arrange follow-ups, so people aren’t bouncing between services. In mental health, reserved slots for urgent assessments and faster digital therapy options (phone/video CBT/peer support groups) would reduce waits. 

On capacity, more appointment slots are essential: hire more GPs, practice nurses, and therapists; extend hours—evenings and weekend slots—and optimise scheduling with protected slots for follow-ups. In my area, a local practice added two nurses and improved online booking; it cut the average wait time for a mental health triage from 3 weeks to about one week and cut missed appointments. 

Overall, investing in triage, navigation and expanded staffing, plus a unified booking system, would deliver faster, clearer pathways and fewer delays for urgent needs.

it's outrageous that agree. Streamlining NHS111, triage, booking and care navigation will prioritize urgent needs, cut duplication and ease flow. Also investing in interpreters, culturally competent staff and outreach, plus evening/weekend clinics and same-day urgent slots would help working people access timely care!

I’m responding from England and often think about how to get timely help when I need it, not just what sounds efficient on a policy briefing. I don’t dispute the value of online booking, e‑consultations and remote care in the right situations, but I strongly oppose a move that makes digital channels the default route to access. Timely GP, community health and mental health support must be available through multiple routes, with real support for people who can’t or don’t want to go online.

What worries me is the digital divide and the practical barriers it creates. In my neighbourhood, there are still households with unreliable internet or data costs high enough that using online portals feels like a luxury. My elderly neighbour struggled to navigate a new online booking system to get a same‑day GP slot and ended up waiting on long phone lines, which were often busy for hours. There are people with limited digital literacy, learning disabilities or language barriers who simply cannot rely on forms and chat functions to convey urgent needs. If policy leans too heavily on online access, these people risk being pushed further down the queue.

Mental health services are a particular concern. For someone with a severe anxiety disorder or depression, a text-based e‑consult can feel inadequate and slow to respond. I’ve seen friends who can message a clinician through an app but then wait days for a real human to pick up, whereas a phone call or in-person appointment could have resolved the issue sooner. In crisis situations, last‑minute changes to online slots or a lack of real‑time contact can be dangerous. We should not underestimate the value of a warm, human conversation in a time of distress.

That said, I recognise the potential benefits of digital tools when they complement, not replace, traditional access. Online booking can reduce clutter in reception and help people who are itinerant or have mobility issues. E‑consultations can handle straightforward requests—repeat prescriptions, minor symptoms, or follow‑ups—faster when used alongside proper triage. The problem is when a system is designed as digital‑first, rather than digital‑optional with solid offline support.

If we push ahead with digital expansion, we must build in protections for the most vulnerable:
- Maintain obvious, well-staffed non‑digital channels (phone lines with reasonable call limits, in‑person walk‑in access and drop‑in clinics) and ensure they are promoted as clearly as online options.
- Guarantee same‑day GP appointments where needed, with a real, responsive triage process that can route people to in-person care when appropriate.
- Invest in digital inclusion: offer help at the practice, run drop‑in digital clinics, and provide cheap or free data devices for those who cannot afford them; train staff to guide patients through online systems in plain language and in multiple languages.
- Ensure mental health pathways preserve immediacy: real-time crisis lines, in-person appointments when necessary, and transparent timelines for talking therapies; digital tools should support but not delay urgent care.
- Improve accessibility features in online systems (voice input, simple language options, clear appointment visibility) and guarantee those features are accessible to people with disabilities.
- Create local, community‑based access points—pharmacy hubs, community centres, or health visiting teams—that can offer face‑to‑face quick triage and liaise with GP services.
- Set clear performance metrics that specifically measure outcomes for digitally excluded groups (not just overall wait times), so policy isn’t focused on throughput at the expense of equity.

In my view, a balanced mix would deliver quicker access for many while protecting those who would otherwise fall through the cracks. Online availability can shorten waiting times for routine requests and free up face‑to‑face slots for those who need them most, but only if there is strong, visible support for people who are not online or who require non‑digital ways to access care.

Overall, the most significant change would be to embed inclusive access as a core design principle: digital tools built to speed up care, paired with robust offline options and active outreach to help every patient use the system. Without that dual approach, we risk widening health inequalities just as we try to improve waiting times.

To improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services, we strongly support a workforce-focused approach. The key changes we would back are targeted recruitment, including international hiring, supported by clear registration pathways, welcome packs and integration mentors; plus pay improvements and incentives (sign-on bonuses, relocation grants) to attract and retain staff. Flexible working patterns, including hybrid on-site and remote triage, part-time routes and job-sharing, will help bring in diverse talent and reduce strain on existing teams. We also need robust wellbeing support and manageable workloads to retain staff long term. 

In practice, a combination of extended hours, same-day slots, and multidisciplinary teams (GPs, practice nurses, mental health professionals, pharmacists, link workers) has shown to improve access. Our pilots with international nurses and GPs, coupled with relocation packages and local induction, reduced average wait times by around a third within six months in some practices. We urge government funding and a clear delivery timetable to scale these approaches, with accountability for local uptake and ongoing workforce planning.

Agree. Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services is essential for older people like me who often manage long-term conditions and caring duties. I welcome moves to strengthen NHS111 and clinical triage, streamline booking systems and care navigation so urgent cases are prioritised and patients do not double back across services. In practice, a few times I’ve called NHS111 only to be told to phone the GP again or wait days for an appointment; a single clear pathway with instant triage and a same-day slot would have avoided unnecessary anxiety and clinic visits elsewhere.

I also back expanding community mental health teams, with earlier intervention, crisis response and more talking therapies; parity with physical health waits has been far too slow. When I looked for mental health support for a relative, the waits were long and fragmented. Lastly, offering evening and weekend clinics and guaranteed same-day urgent slots would help those who still work or have caring duties, reducing missed appointments and improving outcomes.

Overall, these changes would reduce duplication, simplify patient flow and keep people healthier at home.

I disagree that these changes alone will fix timely access. We need mobile clinics, better transport and parking, flexible premises, and sustained training/return-to-practice schemes to grow GPs, nurses and mental health staff long-term.

I live in Wales and I strongly support changes that make GP, community health and mental health services more timely and easier to access. Expanding community mental health teams, investing in early intervention, stronger crisis response and more talking therapies would help people get help before issues escalate, reducing hospital admissions and improving parity with physical health services. In my area, delays can feel like a barrier to staying well and independent. 

I also want to see solutions for transport, parking and premises deficits, especially in rural parts. Mobile clinics visiting village halls or community centres, outreach teams, and telehealth hubs in libraries or local shops would cut travel time and make appointments more convenient. Incentives to attract and retain staff in rural areas—car allowances, flexible hours, supported accommodation—would tackle staffing gaps that slow access. A local teletriage and GP-remote consultation model, with same-day mental health triage, could prevent crises and speed up initial help. 

Overall, integrated, person-centred services that are easy to reach, with smarter use of mobile and digital options, would make a real difference to timely access for families like mine.

Timely access to GP, nurse, and mental health services is a pressing issue in my area. I strongly support increasing appointment slots and session capacity by hiring more GPs, practice nurses and therapists, expanding session length where needed, and introducing smarter scheduling such as extended evening clinics and proactive follow-ups to reduce wasted slots. In my experience, I recently waited two weeks to see a GP for a persistent issue, and a mental health appointment was over six weeks away; delays like these can worsen conditions and push people towards urgent or unsuitable care. Greater capacity would also help reduce unnecessary A&E visits. 

Second, ensure access for all by targeting resources to interpreters, culturally competent staff and outreach to deprived, ethnic minority, migrant and marginalised groups. Language barriers and unfamiliarity with the system have caused avoidable delays for family members; funded interpreters and community health workers can bridge gaps, build trust and improve uptake of preventive care.

Third, invest in co-located community hubs that integrate primary, community and mental health services with social care and VCSE partners for seamless local care. A hub model would enable easier referrals, better information sharing and support for social needs alongside clinical care, creating a more holistic and timely support system.

I welcome moves to widen the team around primary care in Northern Ireland to make access to GP, community health and mental health services timelier. In my experience, routine issues such as back pain take too long to see a GP. If there were multidisciplinary teams in every practice—pharmacists to review medications, physiotherapists to manage musculoskeletal problems, and trained paramedics or physician associates to do triage and simple visits—GPs could concentrate on more complex cases. This would speed up access and spare patients unnecessary trips to hospital. 

Evening and weekend clinics would help those who still work or help family members; guaranteed same-day urgent slots would ease worry when symptoms flare. I’ve seen how a same-day phone triage can prevent an ED trip, which is especially reassuring for older residents. 

Expanding online booking and e-consultations is helpful, but we must avoid leaving older or less tech‑savvy patients behind. Provide a reliable telephone triage and non-digital booking option, with staff to assist with setup if needed and alternatives like paper forms. 

Overall, these changes should reduce waiting times while keeping safety and continuity of care, and they would particularly benefit me and other older residents in our community.

Thank you for the opportunity to respond. I support expanding community mental health teams, strengthening early intervention, crisis response and talking therapies, to reduce waits and bring mental health care on a par with physical health. In our area, access to adult talking therapies can be patchy and crisis support after hours is inconsistent, which sometimes pushes people toward GP or A&E. For example, a neighbour with escalating anxiety waited weeks for CBT referral, and earlier outreach from a community team could have prevented deterioration. A more robust crisis pathway—24/7 access, mobile crisis teams, and stronger links with A&E—would help people when they need it most and ease GP workloads.

At the same time, we must protect continuity of care for those with complex or chronic needs. Longer appointment times, better care plans, and a named clinician can reduce hospital admissions and repeat visits. Any expansion must come with sufficient funding and workforce planning, plus reliable IT to share information between primary care, mental health and social care. Finally, improve access through flexible options—same-day slots, evening or weekend appointments—and ensure digital tools don’t exclude those less comfortable with technology.

Timely access is best improved by combining smarter triage with expanded capacity. In my area, NHS111 sometimes routes non-urgent calls to a GP first, which blocks slots and creates avoidable delays; tightening clinical triage and improving the booking system would prioritise urgent cases and reduce duplication. A care-navigation layer that directs patients to the most appropriate service—pharmacist consultations for minor issues, same-day nurse appointments for wound care, or rapid mental health triage—would speed help and simplify patient flow.

Second, increase GP, nurse, and therapist appointments by hiring more staff, expanding sessions (including evenings and weekends), and optimizing day-to-day scheduling. A family member recently faced a four-week wait for CBT; with more therapists and options like small group sessions, distress could be addressed sooner and hospital referrals avoided.

Third, for rural and mobility-challenged residents, address transport, parking and premises deficits with mobile clinics, outreach in village hubs, telehealth hubs in community centres, and targeted travel incentives. In our village, a monthly mobile GP visit and a telehealth drop-in would make a real difference.

Overall, a coordinated mix of smarter triage, expanded capacity, and accessible services would materially improve timely access across GP, community health and mental health services.

From where I stand in England, trying to get timely help for a cough or a sprain shouldn’t mean going through a whole chain of different professionals before someone actually makes a medical decision. I get the aim of using pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates to cover routine stuff and free GPs to focus on more complex care, but I’m worried this won’t reliably improve access in practice and could even slow things down in areas like mine where staffing is stretched. 

In my experience with the local practice, booking a same‑day slot can feel like a lottery. The phone queue is long, the online system sometimes shows nothing available for days, and when there is a “care by nurse or physio” option, it’s often booked weeks ahead. If a pharmacist or physiotherapist is the first point of contact for a routine issue, there’s a real risk of extra handoffs and more steps to navigate. Each handoff requires triage, record sharing and consent, which takes time and can frustrate someone who just needs a quick painkiller prescription or some straightforward advice.

I’m also really worried about consistency of care. Different professionals have different training and guidelines. In a mixed team, who decides when a case should be escalated to a GP? Will there be clear criteria and robust governance to avoid contradictory advice? For young people like me, continuity matters. Seeing a named clinician who understands your history builds trust, something that can be eroded if you keep seeing someone new at every touchpoint.

There are particular risks in mental health. A routine anxiety check or sleep problem can mask something more serious. Relying on non‑GP staff to triage, even with added training, may miss red flags such as escalating symptoms or risk of harm. In those moments, timely access and a direct line to a clinician who can assess risk is crucial. I don’t want to end up waiting longer because a routine issue was routed through multiple professionals first.

Yes, pharmacists, physiotherapists and paramedics can be excellent for certain conditions, and in the right circumstances they can speed things up. But the current system needs honest investment, not a rebranding of who sees you first. The problem in my area isn’t just the number of clinicians; it’s how appointments are allocated and communicated. A patient shouldn’t have to chase a dozen referrals to finally get a same‑day appointment with a GP.

If changes are to be considered, I think the focus should be on strengthening triage and access within GP practices first: more same‑day GP slots, better online triage that can route people quickly to the right clinician, and clear pathways for escalation to a GP when needed. We also need consistent, region‑wide standards for when non‑GP staff can manage routine care, with transparent referral rules and safeguards. And crucially, maintain patient choice and continuity of care; let people decide if they want to see a GP from the outset rather than a rotating cast of clinicians.

Bottom line: expanding multidisciplinary teams to handle routine issues might sound efficient, but in practice it risks delays, fragmentation and a loss of continuity for young people who rely on straightforward access and trusted relationships. We should prioritise simpler, faster access to GPs, with intelligent triage, better online systems, and robust governance to ensure safety and clarity across the system.

From living in England and using local services, I think the biggest wins would come from three linked changes: protect continuity of care and lengthen appointment times for complex, chronic and vulnerable patients; expand multidisciplinary teams to handle routine cases and free GPs to focus on the complex ones; and strengthen community mental health with early intervention, crisis response and more talking therapies to reduce waits and improve parity with physical health. 

Longer GP appointments for people with multiple conditions (for example diabetes with depression or arthritis) would help finish a review in one visit and reduce repeat bookings. Where possible, a named clinician or small care team should follow patients, with regular reviews and better access to care plans. For everyday issues, expanding teams that include pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates in urgent care or community clinics can triage and treat safely, freeing GPs for the most complex care. 

In mental health, scaled-up early intervention, faster access to talking therapies and reliable crisis support would cut waits and support families sooner. Any changes must be funded, interoperable with social care, and offer both face-to-face and digital options.

I welcome the proposals. Living in England and observing how busy clinics can be, it would help enormously to have evening and weekend clinics so people who work or care for family can get timely appointments without taking time off. A guarantee of same‑day urgent slots for non‑emergency needs would spare anxious waits and reduce unnecessary trips to A&E. I’ve seen how a minor issue can escalate if it’s left, and a quick, appropriate appointment can stop that. Expanding multidisciplinary teams—pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates—to handle routine concerns could free GPs to focus on more complex cases and long‑term management. For example, a pharmacist can advise on medicines or minor infections, a physiotherapist can help with back or knee pain, and a paramedic-led triage can direct people to the right service sooner. This approach would also benefit mental health access by enabling quicker initial check‑ins and referrals. Taken together, these changes should deliver timely, practical care for GP, community health and mental health needs across the area.

From my experience living in England and using local services, I know waits are too long. A standard GP appointment is often two weeks; mental health referrals can take 6-12 weeks; crisis lines are stretched. I understand the case for expanding community mental health teams, early intervention, crisis response and talking therapies to reduce waits and bring parity with physical health. I disagree that simply expanding these services as described will fix the problem. Without addressing recruitment and retention, funding flows, administrative bottlenecks and integration with primary care, newly created teams will exist on paper while wait lists stay long. In my town, CMHTs are staffed only at a fraction of what’s needed, so a patient referred by a GP may wait months for triage or treatment. What would help is same-day or next-day triage in GP practices; longer appointments for mental health concerns; a properly staffed crisis response with after-hours and weekend availability; better data sharing between providers; and a clear, funded plan for rapid stepped care with transparent targets. If the Government wants timely access, it must fund and implement these changes in a joined-up way, not merely announce more teams.

From my experience in England, timely access to GP, community health and mental health services remains inconsistent. To improve, we need NHS111 and clinical triage that prioritises urgent cases and routes people through a clear, joined-up pathway. This means clear red-flag criteria, clinician-led triage, and guaranteed rapid access to appropriate care, whether that is same-day GP slots, urgent mental health support, or a targeted community visit.

Booking systems should be simplified into a single, real-time interface accessible by app and phone. My own attempts to book care have involved multiple platforms and uncertain waits; a transparent, one-stop system would cut duplication and anxiety.

Care navigation should be expanded: a trained navigator who coordinates GP, community services and mental health referrals, minimising repeated questions or tests and smoothing handovers. In parallel, extending multidisciplinary teams—pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates—to treat routine conditions could free GPs for complex care, provided there is solid supervision and integration with patient records.

These changes must be funded and evaluated with clear metrics on wait times, outcomes and patient safety to avoid fragmenting care.

Boost GP and mental health access by targeted recruitment and international hires, with incentives, better pay, flexible hours and wellbeing support for staff. More staff means quicker appointments and safer, friendlier care for everyone.

I don’t believe the current emphasis on quick fixes will meaningfully improve timely access to GPs, community health or mental health services. The real barrier is the shortage of qualified staff. If we want faster, reliable access, we need a clear workforce plan: targeted recruitment, including international hiring with proper induction and integration, better pay and conditions, flexible working patterns, and robust wellbeing support so staff stay in post. In my area, practices with one experienced GP and a couple of trainees still struggle; locum turnover and fragmented care undermine continuity.

Recruiting more GPs, nurses and mental health workers and offering better pay and flexible contracts would reduce delays. Crucially, we must protect continuity of care and lengthen appointment times for complex, chronic and vulnerable patients. When the same clinician follows a patient with long-term conditions, outcomes improve and repeat visits fall. I’d push for longer standard slots (20–30 minutes for chronic cases) and stable patient panels, rather than systems that rush care or rely on short, fragmented encounters. Flexible hours, including early mornings, evenings and weekend slots, would also ease queues for working people.

Funding a deliberate workforce strategy, with retention incentives and safe staffing, is essential. Without that, digital triage or temporary fixes merely paper over the cracks.

I strongly agree that improving timely access hinges on expanding mental health capacity and making digital options accessible to all. In my area, wait times for a community mental health assessment can be long, and crisis support is often stretched. Key changes would be: (1) expand community mental health teams and embed them with GPs, offering early intervention and rapid crisis response so someone with emerging distress gets help within days rather than weeks; ensure access to talking therapies such as CBT and ACT with capacity to match physical health services; (2) boost GP access: more same day slots, longer hours and better triage so urgent cases are seen promptly; (3) modernise digital access while protecting those who cannot go online: expand online booking, e-consultations and remote care, plus non digital options such as telephone triage and in-person slots, with extra support for older or disadvantaged patients to use these tools. Personally, last year my mother needed urgent mental health support; the community team was delayed, and a local crisis line and brief CBT sessions helped avert escalation. Online booking has helped me arrange check-ins around work, but I worry some neighbours struggle without non digital options. A mixed model would reduce waits and bring mental health onto a parity with physical health outcomes.

Not sure what changes would work best. In my area of Wales, GP appointments can be hard to come by—earliest slots are often a couple of weeks away. I’ve had to use urgent care when it felt like it should have been managed by a GP. Mental health services take longer too, with unclear access points and long waits before assessments. I’d be open to easier online booking, clearer triage, and more information on after-hours options, but I’m cautious about promises that staffing will suddenly improve. A small change like better signposting to community nurses or quicker referral pathways might help some people, though I don’t know if that would solve it everywhere. Overall, any tweaks should come with honest timelines and real local detail so people aren’t left guessing.

From our position representing older residents across England, I notice that improving timely access to GP, community health and mental health services isn’t just about slotting more appointments into the diary. Real progress seems tied to wider things in our towns and villages. Many members rely on reliable local transport to reach clinics; when buses are cut or timetables shift, even same-day slots don’t help if people can’t get there. In practice, a simple phone call and a human receptionist can be the difference, especially for those who aren’t comfortable navigating online systems. So, what would help beyond the surgery? consistent community transport links, clear information in plain language about what’s available, and more outreach by nurses or social care workers to homes and care homes, reducing the need for multiple trips.

We also see gaps in mental health support in rural areas where specialists are scarce. Investment in integrated teams and community programmes, including social prescribing and crisis lines that understand older people’s circumstances, could ease bottlenecks. But any real improvement must be matched with sustained funding for social care, housing support, and cross-agency coordination so people can actually use the services when they need them.

I’m replying as someone living in England and in my late fifties. I’m strongly against proposals that rely mainly on more digital-only access or fragmented changes to GP and mental health services. In my view, the most practical and fair way to get timely access is to invest in co‑located community hubs that bring together primary care, community health, mental health services, social care and the VCSE sector. Without that, many people – especially older residents, those with limited digital skills or transport challenges, and carers – will still struggle to get timely help when they need it.

Why I’m sceptical about stand‑alone changes: digital systems can help some, but they can also exclude people who aren’t comfortable with online forms, who have poor broadband or who have cognitive or sensory difficulties. Long telephone triage queues simply push the bottleneck elsewhere. In practice, I’ve faced delays getting routine GP appointments, and I’ve watched neighbours with mental health concerns wait weeks for an initial assessment. These delays aren’t just inconvenient; they feed anxiety, trigger crises, and push people toward A&E, which is exactly where we should be avoiding extra pressure.

What would genuinely improve timely access is a hub model that is geographically and practically accessible, with real on‑site teams that can act in a coordinated way. Here’s what that would look like in my area:

- A hub in a central, well‑served location, ideally a site that houses a GP practice alongside district nurses, mental health staff, a pharmacist, physiotherapists/OTs, a social worker, and a dedicated VCSE navigator. One building, one appointment window, one care plan. That would save people from making multiple trips to different sites and repeating their story every time they see someone new.
- On‑site multi‑disciplinary teams with same‑day triage for urgent issues and regular slots for routine care, including mental health. If someone has anxiety about a mental health appointment, a same‑day initial assessment or a joint referral with a GP can prevent a deterioration in their condition.
- Strong integration with social care and VCSE partners. A single hub would offer benefits advice, housing support, and referrals to local wellbeing programmes on the spot, rather than forcing people to chase numbers and websites. For carers and older residents, this reduces the number of separate trips and phone calls they must manage.
- Flexible access throughout the week, with extendable hours and a clear plan for out‑of‑hours care. I know people who work irregular shifts or who rely on family members to get them to appointments. Evening clinics or weekend slots at the hub could make a real difference.
- Real, practical transport provisions and accessibility. The hub should be in a location with good bus links or be reachable by walking or cycling routes. For those unable to travel, there should be on‑site or nearby home visiting options from district nurses or therapists, coordinated through the hub’s care plan.
- Patient‑centred information sharing with consent. A single, secure IT system that enables clinicians across primary care, mental health, social care and VCSE partners to see a current care plan and notes would avoid repetitive explanations and conflicting advice. People would still own their data and control what is shared, but when they consent, everyone can act quickly and safely.
- Preservation of choice and local autonomy. The hub should supplement, not replace, existing GP practices. People who prefer to see their own GP should be able to do so, while the hub provides a broader access point for more complex needs. The aim is better access and better outcomes, not cost‑driven consolidation.

In practice, I’ve seen how these hubs can reduce unnecessary referrals, shorten waiting times, and improve people’s experience of care. When a patient can be seen by a nurse, a GP and a mental health worker in the same venue, with a navigator to sort out social needs, urgent issues are dealt with more quickly and more holistically. It also helps that VCSE partners bring practical support—benefits guidance, housing help, social activities—that can prevent crises from arising in the first place.

If we’re serious about improving timely access, the investment should be in these co‑located hubs with sustained funding, robust governance, integrated IT and a workforce plan that recognises the value of multidisciplinary collaboration. Digital and remote options can be used as supplements, not replacements for face‑to‑face contact where needed. My real concern is that without hub‑level integration, changes will simply shuffle problems around and leave the people who need care most behind.

Agree. More GP, nurse and therapist slots via hiring and smarter scheduling will cut waits. Co-located hubs with social care and VCSE partners will enable seamless local care, and keeping longer appointments for complex patients will improve outcomes and reduce repeat visits.

absolutely from my experience here in Wales, timely access to GP services is a frequent concern, especially for those who work or have urgent but non-emergency needs. I would welcome changes that expand accessibility: evening and weekend clinics and guaranteed same-day urgent slots so people don’t have to wait or travel far for a basic check or quick advice!

absolutely i’m in England and, from my experience in a busy local area, timely access to GP, community health and mental health services is too variable. Expanding multidisciplinary teams in primary care would help a lot. If pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates can handle routine cases—triaging, minor injuries, repeat prescriptions and simple chronic conditions—that would free GPs to focus on more complex cases. For example, a straightforward musculoskeletal flare-up could be assessed and treated by a physiotherapist or a clinical pharmacist while I still have timely access to a GP when things are more serious. Paramedics with GP partner clinics or home-visit capacity could prevent unnecessary ambulance calls or A&E trips, especially for vulnerable patients.

On mental health, stronger community teams with early intervention, crisis response and expanded talking therapies are essential. In my area, delays to talking therapies and long waits for child and adult mental health services affect families and productivity. A robust, well‑funded crisis line with same-day outreach, plus easier access to CBT, ACT or other therapies, would help people recover faster and stay connected at work and home, improving parity with physical health care.

Crucially, we need clear care pathways, integrated records and proper funding so these teams work together safely and effectively, rather than creating new silos!
More GP slots and quicker mental health help would help, but I’m not sure what actually works in practice.

I want to respond to the question about what changes would most improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services where I live. I am not convinced that the proposed mix of mobile clinics, outreach, telehealth hubs and incentives in themselves will deliver timely access for everyone, especially in rural or mobility‑restricted contexts.

Transport, parking and premises deficits create real barriers. In my area the GP practice is tucked into a small high street building with a tiny car park that charges by the hour, and the bus into town runs only a couple of times a day. People with caring responsibilities, shift workers or those with disabilities end up missing appointments or delaying care until things become urgent. Mobile clinics could help some of this, but they can become a stopgap that disappears if funding or staff shift away. They must be regular, predictable and tied to a fixed schedule and a permanent base that patients can rely on. Without that, them being on a different day each month makes matters worse rather than better. And premises matter too: if clinics are held in out-of-town hubs that require long journeys, the benefit evaporates for locals who are already struggling to squeeze a slot into their day.

Telehealth hubs and digital outreach have potential, but they are not a cure-all. In my community, many people lack reliable broadband or a usable device, and digital literacy is uneven. A video appointment is often fine for follow-ups, but for mental health and complex GP issues you need a real human connection. The idea of telehealth hubs could help if they are staffed with friendly, stable access points and offer assisted triage, but if they become the default and exclude the digitally excluded, they will entrench disadvantage. We also need to ensure privacy and data security, and to protect against over‑reliance on screens at the expense of in-person care when it is needed.

Targeted resources, interpreters and culturally competent staff are essential to closing access gaps for deprived, ethnic minority, migrant and marginalised groups. Interpreters are not a luxury; they are a necessity. But merely having interpreters on call is not enough. We need interpreters who are available at the point of contact and in common hours, plus recruitment of bilingual staff and culturally appropriate outreach workers who can build trust in communities. We should fund community health workers and link them with local groups to encourage people to seek help before problems escalate. In my area, some outreach events reach a little, but they are not sustained and families I know still feel services do not listen to them or understand daily realities like work patterns, housing stress or fear of debt.

Increasing appointment slots and capacity is crucial, but not if it is just a headline, not backed by a solid workforce plan. Waiting times for therapy can stretch to months. We hear promises of more slots through hiring and scheduling tweaks, but the underlying workforce shortages are real. General practice staffing has been under pressure for years, and mental health teams are often stretched thin. Expanding sessions without credible recruitment plans or fair pay risks repeating the same cycle of churn. We need a long‑term workforce strategy with competitive salaries, robust training pipelines and better working conditions so newly funded slots actually materialise. Also we must ensure better triage so people are directed to the right support quickly rather than waiting for long general consultations that do not fit their needs.

In short, I would push for a mixed approach that does not rely on one‑off fixes like mobile clinics alone. Invest in sustainable premises within communities, reliable transport support or subsidies, accessible parking, and predictable service locations; ensure digital access is inclusive; guarantee interpreters and culturally competent staff as part of a broader trust‑building strategy; and commit to robust workforce planning and fair recruitment to actually grow appointment capacity. Without those, delays will persist and the most vulnerable groups will continue to bear the brunt.

I strongly support investing in co-located community hubs that bring together GP, community health, mental health, social care and VCSE partners so people can access everything they need in one place, close to home. In my area in Wales, waiting times for GP appointments have grown, and trying to navigate separate services for mental health or social care often means multiple journeys and delays. A hub strategy would help by providing one door, same-day triage for urgent issues, and a shared care plan across teams.

What changes would help:
- Create accessible hubs within walking distance with integrated GP, district nursing, mental health professionals, social care and VCSE teams under one roof, with common appointment systems and shared records.
- Offer extended hours, drop-in slots and clear signposting to reduce wasted trips.
- Include on-site pharmacy, housing and welfare advice, and digital access points to support self-care.
- Ensure a multidisciplinary workforce with protected time for collaboration and a named clinician for continuity.
- Improve transport links and information about services to encourage timely help-seeking.

This model would deliver faster, more coordinated care and better experiences for families like mine.

Thank you for asking for local views. In our area, timely access to GP care, community health and mental health services would improve if we pursued a careful blend of expanding digital access alongside strong non‑digital options, and by investing in co‑located community hubs that bring primary care, mental health, social care and VCSE partners under one roof. The aim should be to make access easier, quicker and more joined‑up, without leaving anyone behind.

Digital access and remote care can be powerful. Online booking that shows same‑day slots, clear appointment types and a simple way to request triage could save people from long phone holds. E‑consultations and video or phone triage are especially useful for routine issues, follow‑ups and mental health check‑ins, which often do not require a full face‑to‑face visit. I’ve found that for some family members, online appointments and quick digital messages reduce the time to get advice and allow us to plan around work and childcare.

But there are real caveats. Not everyone can access or navigate digital systems easily: older relatives, people on modest incomes without reliable internet, or those with language barriers can be left behind if we lean too hard on online routes. In my experience, the online portal can be confusing, login issues occur, and if there’s a sudden mental health need or a safeguarding concern, a phone line and a real person are often essential. So any expansion of online booking must be paired with robust non‑digital options: a well‑staffed telephone line with short waits, the option to book in person or by walk‑in, and the ability to quickly switch to a face‑to‑face appointment when needed. Practical support could include step‑by‑step help desks in clinics, multilingual guidance, and even short digital literacy sessions run in community venues.

Non‑digital alternatives must be strong and easy to access. We should maintain enough in‑person appointments and walk‑in slots, especially for urgent or complex problems. Regularly updated phone triage should guide patients to the most appropriate level of care, not just to the next available slot. In places with poor digital infrastructure, mobile clinics or outreach sessions in community venues could keep services accessible, particularly for families who cannot travel long distances.

A longer‑term and potentially transformative approach is to invest in co‑located community hubs that integrate primary care, community and mental health services with social care and VCSE partners. A hub where a GP, district nurse, mental health worker, social worker and a voluntary sector adviser sit alongside a pharmacist and welfare rights advisor would dramatically reduce referrals and avoid multiple trips to separate sites. Proximity matters: fewer different appointments and less time wasted on coordinating care across buildings. I can imagine a centre in our town where a family could see a GP, have a mental health check, get support for housing or benefits, and be pointed towards community activities—all in one place.

However, a hub must be designed with patient choice and safety at its core. Clear information about what is offered, how to get urgent help, and how records are shared is essential. Data sharing should be governed by patient consent, with options to restrict what information is shared and with whom. We need sustainable, long‑term funding and a stable workforce, not short‑term pilots. Transport and accessibility matter too: flexible operating hours, accessible entrances, parking or good public transport links, and staff who understand the needs of diverse communities. Local leadership should involve patients in the design and ongoing evaluation of hubs, so services evolve with community needs.

From personal experience, waits for certain mental health referrals in our borough can be long, and the current system sometimes requires navigating multiple sites for different aspects of care. A properly integrated hub would simplify this and could reduce unnecessary delays. It would also provide a natural point for social care and voluntary sector services to collaborate on early‑intervention and prevention, which can cut down crises and hospital admissions later.

In summary, I think the best path is a balanced, phased plan: expand user‑friendly digital options with strong safeguards and offline supports; maintain and strengthen non‑digital routes; and invest in co‑located, well‑governed hubs that unify primary, mental health, social care and VCSE services. It should be underpinned by robust patient involvement, transparent performance metrics (waiting times, access equity, satisfaction, and outcomes), and commitments to inclusivity and lifelong digital inclusion so that no one is left behind as services modernise.

I live in Wales and I’m aware how delays for GP appointments, community health visits and mental health support can affect people, especially when you’re trying to manage a long-standing condition or support a family member. The changes that would make the biggest difference to timely access are straightforward and practical: increase appointment slots and session capacity across GPs, nurses, therapists and community teams by hiring more staff, expanding session lengths where needed, and making scheduling smarter and more flexible.

- Expand the workforce and stabilise staffing: we need more GPs and practice nurses, supported by well-paid, stable contracts so they stay in the area. Increasing locum cover where shortages occur, and bringing in qualified therapists to supplement GP practices, would instantly boost capacity. In my area, even when there is a GP on duty, the number of slots is limited and often booked weeks ahead; with more staff, there would be a real chance of offering same-day or next-day slots for urgent issues.

- Lengthen and diversify appointment types: longer appointments for complex or chronic conditions help prevent repeated visits and hospital admissions. We should also broaden session types: nurse-led chronic disease clinics, physiotherapist or occupational therapist slots, and therapist-led mental health check-ins. For families managing conditions like diabetes or arthritis, regular, longer follow-ups are far more effective than quick, back-to-back 5–10 minute slots.

- Earlier and easier access to mental health support: embed more talking therapies in GP practices and local community hubs, with clearer referral pathways and quicker access. Increasing CBT/CGT capacity, offering group therapy where appropriate, and providing online or telephone options would make help much more reachable. I know someone who waited several weeks for CBT; earlier access would have prevented deterioration in their condition.

- Smarter scheduling and triage: digital booking systems that show real-time slot availability, coupled with telephone or online triage to assess urgency, would help ensure those in need are seen promptly. Urgent same-day slots should be protected, with faster pathways for families or those with high-risk conditions. Offering some evening and weekend slots would also reduce time off work and school for appointments.

- Integrated, local hub models: bringing GP practices, nurses, pharmacists, physiotherapists and mental health staff into shared community hubs would cut travel time and streamline care. In rural or semi-rural areas of Wales, that connection is particularly valuable, reducing the need for multiple trips to different sites and helping people stay on top of their health.

- Retention and progression: alongside new hires, keeping staff in post with supportive workload management is essential. If people see a stable, capable team at their local surgery or clinic, they’re more likely to book earlier and attend, which reduces the risk of symptoms worsening and emergency care being needed.

A practical combination of more staff, expanded appointment times, and smarter scheduling would translate into tangible benefits: fewer cancellations, shorter waits, better management of chronic or mental health conditions, and less stress for patients and their families. Please keep rural Wales in clear focus, with targeted recruitment and retention support so these improvements reach every community. If funded and implemented thoughtfully, these changes could transform how quickly people in our area access essential GP, community health and mental health services.

As an organisation representing young people and communities across England, we are concerned that simply increasing the number of GP, nurse and therapist slots without guaranteeing continuity of care will not meaningfully improve timely access for those with complex, chronic or vulnerable needs. Our experience shows that the value of care is not just the number of appointments, but their quality and consistency over time. When patients with long-term conditions—such as diabetes, asthma, or mental health difficulties—see a different clinician at each visit, important details are missed, care plans aren’t followed, and confusion grows. This often results in preventable follow-up requests and repeat visits, which paradoxically worsens waiting times for those who need it most.

There are tangible, concrete changes we believe would genuinely improve access while protecting care quality:

- Preserve and strengthen continuity of care for complex cases. Where possible, patients with chronic conditions should have a named clinician or a small, stable care team who track their journey across GP, nurse, and therapist services. Longer appointments (for example, 20–30 minutes for complex cases) should be standard for this group, to enable comprehensive reviews, medication reconciliation, and proactive risk assessment. Short slots force clinicians to rush through issues, increasing the likelihood of omissions and late escalation.

- Extend appointment duration for vulnerable patients. The public health picture for young people with mental health concerns often involves layered needs—psychological support, social factors, education, and employment anxiety. Longer, more holistic sessions with the right mix of professionals (GP, nurse, mental health practitioner, care coordinator) reduce the need for multiple separate visits and improve outcomes. This approach also helps reduce the cycle of repeated appointments triggered by fragmented care.

- Invest in staffing but align it with care models that support continuity. We welcome the idea of more slots, yet the benefit is limited unless those slots are staffed by stable teams who know the patient’s history. Recruiting more GPs, practice nurses, therapists, and care coordinators should be paired with funding for longer, shared appointments and smoother handovers within integrated care teams. Flexible staffing, including joint how-to sessions for GPs and mental health professionals, could prevent the fragmentation that often drives wait times back up.

- Improve scheduling with a patient-centric triage model. Triaging should route urgent cases to the most appropriate clinician without sacrificing continuity for ongoing issues. For example, someone with newly diagnosed autoimmune conditions should not be handed off to a different clinician every time; instead, a named clinician should oversee the treatment plan even as urgent issues are addressed.

- Strengthen care pathways and data sharing. Shared electronic records accessible across GP, community health services, and mental health providers are essential. If a patient has a persistent problem, notes, care plans, and risk flags must be visible to any clinician involved in their care, reducing the need for repeat information gathering and ensuring faster, safer responses.

- Practical examples from our networks show the cost of ignoring continuity. In several areas, popular access targets have been met by simply spreading clinicians thinner or increasing new appointments with inconsistent clinicians. Young patients with anxiety or depression report that they feel “starting over” with every clinician visit, which erodes trust and makes engagement harder. Conversely, where a named clinician or stable team is in place, adherence to treatment plans improves, and patients are more likely to attend follow-ups, ultimately reducing total waiting times.

In essence, timely access must not come at the expense of continuity and meaningful contact. The most effective way to improve access for GP, community health and mental health services is to couple increased capacity with stable, longer, and more holistic encounters for those with complex needs. This approach may require upfront investment, but it will reduce repeat visits, improve outcomes, and deliver genuinely quicker, more reliable access in the long run.

I strongly support the changes proposed to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services in our area. Access to timely GP, nurse and therapist appointments in my area is still too slow, especially outside standard working hours.
