In my area, I think real progress would come from more community hubs where GP, nurse, mental health staff, and a pharmacist work side by side in one place. That would cut the number of trips and the phone queues. I've seen how school-based counsellors and local charities can offer quick support for young people, yet the waiting path to get serious help can still be slow. Also, practical barriers—reliable transport, parking, and out-of-hours access—affect whether people actually show up. Extending hours on weekends in well-connected sites and improving digital access for those with limited data would help many working parents. It’s not a silver bullet, but a more joined-up, accessible system could ease the pressure on primary care without simply pushing more demand into already stretched clinics.

I disagree with the current emphasis on reforming access without a solid plan to grow and retain staff first. In our area, long wait times aren’t just a byproduct of how appointments are booked; they’re a result of real shortages across GPs, nurses and mental health staff. Reforms risk simply shifting workload or delaying care further if the backbone—the workforce—remains stretched and burnt out.

What would actually make a difference is a workforce-led package: targeted recruitment and international hiring to plug vacancies quickly; meaningful pay improvements and clear incentives to attract clinicians to hard-to-staff areas; flexible working patterns to reduce burnout; and robust wellbeing support so staff stay and feel valued. Practical steps could include faster visa routes for clinicians, salary uplifts that reflect workload, and funding for back-office and admin support to cut non-clinical burdens. We also need a longer-term pipeline—expanding training places and retention schemes so today’s trainees become tomorrow’s experienced clinicians.

If these workforce levers are front-loaded and funded, then changes to GP, community health and mental health access will genuinely shorten waiting times rather than merely rebranding the problem.

In Scotland, timely access to GP, community health and mental health services in my area can be inconsistent, so expanding multidisciplinary teams makes a lot of sense. If pharmacists take on routine medication reviews and minor ailments, physiotherapists lead early rehab for common injuries, paramedics handle home visits and urgent triage, and physician associates support routine consultations, GPs could focus on complex care. That should cut waiting times and improve safety for everyone.

I also back investment in co-located community hubs that bring primary care, community health, mental health, social care and VCSE partners under one roof. A hub where you can see a GP, a mental health worker, a district nurse and get housing or debt advice in the same visit would minimise endless referrals and appointments, and make care feel seamless. In my experience, where such colocated models exist, people get quicker, more coordinated help and feel less overwhelmed by the system. For this to work, we need clear funding, reliable IT sharing, and strong local links with voluntary organisations to keep services flexible and accessible across the region.

To improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services, I’d prioritise growing the workforce and blending services in local hubs. First, targeted recruitment and international hiring, with clear routes for skilled clinicians to train and stay in the NHS: better pay, meaningful flexible working (split shifts, part‑time routes for experienced staff) and robust wellbeing support to tackle burnout. This should be backed by improved relocation packages, streamlined registration, and carefully designed incentives for long‑term retention, with safeguards to maintain high standards.

Second, invest in co‑located community hubs that bring primary care, district nursing, social care and VCSE partners under one roof. A well‑staffed hub can triage on the day and route to mental health teams quickly, with shared IT and single care plans to avoid repeated assessments. In my area, a pilot hub with GP, pharmacist, social prescriber and housing support reduced same‑week referrals to mental health and cut unnecessary hospital visits—but it needs more mental health staff to meet demand.

Finally, ensure long‑term funding, clear governance, and genuine service user involvement to monitor wait times and outcomes. If done right, access should be noticeably quicker and less fragmented.

There is no single silver bullet to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services in our area. What would make the biggest difference is a targeted, joined‑up approach that puts resources where gaps are widest: in deprived neighbourhoods, among ethnic minority and migrant communities, and for marginalised groups who often fall through the cracks. Based on our experience and local feedback, I’d prioritise four linked strands: targeted resources, professional interpreters, culturally competent staffing, and proactive outreach.

Targeted resources where they are most needed
- Allocate additional capacity to practices serving high-deprivation postcodes and high migrant populations. This could include extra GP slots, persistent urgent-care availability, and funded bursts of outreach where patients struggle to get timely appointments. Our area has clinics that routinely run out of same-day slots for weeks in a row; dedicated reserves would prevent avoidable delays and reduce A&E pressure.
- Invest in mobile and pop‑up services in community hubs (markets, housing associations, places of worship) to offer quick access points for checks, vaccinations and mental health triage. For families with busy work schedules or transport issues, a local, predictable access point can be transformative.
- Fund integrated care teams that can manage longer-term social determinants of health, including housing support, benefits advice and translation of essential information. Timely medical care is often hindered by non-clinical barriers; addressing these promptly improves outcomes and reduces repeat visits.

Professional interpreters and language access
- Ensure funded, on‑demand interpreters (in person, telephone or video) are available across GP, community health and mental health services. Language should never be a barrier to booking, triage or treatment, and interpretations should be provided for the languages most common in the local population.
- Translate vital information, consent forms, patient information leaflets and digital interfaces into multiple languages, with plain language versions to improve understanding and engagement.
- Train interpreters in medical terminology and confidentiality, and guarantee their availability at the moment of scheduling or at the point of contact so patients don’t face repeated requests for information or multiple reschedules.

Culturally competent staff and leadership
- Recruit and retain staff from diverse backgrounds, including frontline nurses and clinicians who reflect the communities they serve. A locally representative workforce helps build trust and improves communication.
- Provide mandatory, ongoing cultural competence training for all front-line staff, including recognition of stigma around mental health, trauma-informed care, and awareness of religious or cultural practices that shape health decisions.
- Create dedicated roles such as cultural liaison workers or patient navigators who can explain the system, help complete registrations, and accompany patients to appointments when needed.

Proactive, community-led outreach
- Partner with community organisations, faith groups, and local schools to run regular, low-stakes health information sessions, signposting, and “what to expect from NHS services” workshops. Outreach should be co-designed with communities to reflect local concerns and languages.
- Establish a community health worker programme that deploys trusted local residents to help with appointment bookings, transport arrangements, and follow-up, reducing avoidable missed appointments and improving continuity of care.
- Ensure feedback loops so communities can report barriers (e.g., long waits, confusing processes, stigma) and see how improvements are being made. Public dashboards with anonymised equity metrics would be helpful for accountability.

Measurement, governance and sustainability
- Make equity a formal performance target for GP practices and community/mental health services, with regular reporting on wait times by ethnicity, language, and deprivation index.
- Pilot targeted initiatives with clear evaluation plans and scale up those that demonstrate reductions in waiting times and improvements in patient experience.
- Guard against unintended consequences such as staffing instability or tokenistic outreach by tying incentives to sustained outcomes, staff training completion, and patient feedback.

In short, timelier access will come not just from more appointments, but from a thoughtfully funded mix of extra capacity in affected areas, robust language services, a culturally competent workforce, and genuine, ongoing engagement with the communities most affected. If these elements are bundled into a clear, funded strategy with accountability and local leadership, we will see real, equitable improvements in how quickly people can access GP, community health and mental health support.

I’m not sure what would work best. In our area the access to GPs and mental health services feels patchy. Sometimes I can get a same-day phone slot, but other times I’m on hold for ages and told to try again next week. A neighbour with a child managed to get a mental health appointment after a long wait, but another person I know had to travel across town to see a nurse rather than a GP. It seems like more predictable triage and better same-day options would help, as would clearer information on what’s urgent. I’d also like to see simpler online booking that actually shows real slots, not just what the system hopes is available. Any changes should avoid pushing people to take time off work or miss school repeatedly. I can’t say exactly what policy would fix it, but more reliable access and clearer queues would be appreciated.

We need evening and weekend GP slots and guaranteed same‑day urgent access to support working people and urgent non‑emergency needs. Also invest in mobile clinics, telehealth hubs and outreach to reach rural areas, plus streamlined NHS111 and booking systems to cut delays.

From our organisation representing older residents in England, we welcome the aim to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services, but any changes need to work for people with limited mobility and digital skills. Longer daytime opening, same-day triage and more local health hubs could help, yet we’re wary of plans that rely mainly on online booking or extended hours without enough clinicians. 

In our area, people report waiting two weeks for a GP appointment, and mental health slots can be scarce even after referral. A neighbour with arthritis struggled to get a same-day visit in a rural area, while another found it easier to get quick advice at a local pharmacy than to secure a doctor’s slot. We’d support more district nurses and mental health practitioners in local clinics, plus better integration with social care so hospital discharges don’t stall on follow-up needs. Transport support and simpler triage lines would help older people who cannot use smartphones. Any changes should be funded, locally led, and preserve patient choice rather than simply shifting bottlenecks to elsewhere.

Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services could be improved by two linked changes in my area. First, protect continuity of care and lengthen appointment times for complex, chronic, and vulnerable patients. I’ve seen how a hurried 10-minute slot leaves both me and my clinician chasing issues across several visits, and how a named clinician with a stable care team makes it easier to spot patterns and adjust treatment. For mental health, longer initial assessments and regular follow-ups with the same clinician would reduce drop‑offs and unnecessary crises. 

Second, address staffing through targeted recruitment and retention. This means expanding GP training places, using international recruitment where appropriate, offering pay progression, flexible hours and wellbeing support to avoid burnout. In my town, wait times spike when staff leave for better conditions elsewhere; stabilising the workforce would deliver steadier access and better care. 

Practical steps include keeping digital triage to manage demand while safeguarding timely slots for ongoing care, and expanding roles for nurses, pharmacists and social prescribers to support primary care teams. If these approaches are funded and coordinated, timely access should improve while care quality remains safe and person-centred.

I understand the aim of speeding up access, but simply adding more GP, nurse and therapist slots won’t fix the underlying problrms in my area.. The real bottleneck is staffing and organisation. Our local practice struggles to recruit full‑time GPs, so we rely on locums who can’t guarantee continuity of care. Even when extra slots open up, they’re quickly filled and I’m back to waitin weeks for a follow‑up which isn’t acceptable for older patients with multiple long‑standing issues. Expanding sessions woul take years and a lot more money, and budgets are strained; without stable workforce planning we’ll just chase numbers, not outcomes. Mental health teams are stretched too, so extra slots won’t help if therapists are shuffled elsewhere or left with backlogs from previous referrals. As for NHS111 and care navigation, prioritising urgent cases on paper makes sense, but the reality on the ground is different. Phone triage can be confusing, and for many of us with limited digital literacy, online booking and apps are a barrier. I’ve had NHS111 push me toward a call-back or self-care path when my symptoms needed prompt assessment, which then meant a late in‑person visit and more anxiety. Any change must include robust staffing, longer and connecte appointments, and simple, locally trusted ways to book that don’t leave older people behind. It’s not just about more slots; it’s about sustainablr systems that actually keep people out of crisis.

Access to GP, community health and mental health services must prioritise continuity of care, not just speed. In my experience living with chronic arthritis and intermittent anxiety, 10-minute GP slots rarely capture the full picture. I’ve seen different clinicians at successive visits, forcing me to repeat decades of history, re-tell side effects, and re-negotiate a management plan. This leads to delays, duplicated tests, and, ultimately, more visits.

What would help most is protecting continuity while improving timeliness. Specifically:
- longer appointments for those with complex or long-term conditions (20–30 minutes) so meds, pain management, and function can be reviewed properly.
- a named GP who oversees my care across primary and community teams and mental health services.
- a shared, up-to-date care plan accessible to GPs, district nurses and therapists, updated as my situation changes.
- integrated records and coordinated case management so each service sees the same information.
- stable staffing or rostered clinicians so I can depend on seeing the same person.
- timely mental health follow-ups with a consistent clinician, rather than repeated hand-offs.

This approach would reduce repeat visits and crises, and keep people out of hospital.

I think timely access would improve where transport, premises and outreach are aligned with the needs of marginalised groups. In Scotland, gaps for deprived and ethnic minority communities stem from language barriers, trust and limited awareness of what’s available as well as distance. I would welcome: funded interpreters and multilingual staff in GP and mental health services; cultural-competence training for front‑office staff; and outreach workers who visit community hubs—churches, mosques, schools—to help people book appointments and navigate care. 

Transport and premises matter too. Better bus routes and affordable parking near clinics would cut delays, and mobile clinics that visit villages weekly would help those with limited mobility. Many centres are old or not fully accessible; we need step-free entrances and private spaces for mental health care. For rural access, telehealth hubs in local libraries or community centres, with staff to assist clients, could extend reach while retaining personal contact. I’d also like to see incentives to recruit and retain staff in underserved areas, plus protected time for outreach and partnership with local groups. A winter health bus in my village would have saved people missed appointments last year.

I live in England and am in my seventies. I’ve seen access to GP, community health and mental health services become more difficult to secure, especially for routine care and urgent needs. The proposal of evening or weekend clinics and guaranteed same-day urgent slots sounds sensible on the surface, but I’m not convinced it will deliver consistently without creating new problems. In my experience, late clinics put extra pressure on already stretched staff and can erode the continuity of care that many older patients rely on when managing chronic conditions. If you shift appointments to evenings and weekends, you risk fewer longer-term relationships with a regular GP who knows you and your history. Transport becomes a real hurdle in the evenings for those who depend on bus services or family help, and safety gets harder at night in many towns.

What would help more is robust same-day urgent triage with a dedicated team, better home visits, and clearer pathways for mental health that don’t depend on another shift pattern for doctors. We need extended hours that still preserve continuity, plus more community-based support, listed transport assistance, and digital literacy help for those who can use online booking. In short, improve scheduling without sacrificing the trusted, ongoing care many of us value.

From where I live in Scotland, I don’t think simply expanding multidisciplinary teams will reliably improve timely access. Yes, teams including pharmacists, physios, paramedics and physician associates can handle routine cases, but without robust governance, training, and common information systems, patients end up shuffled between clinicians and lose the continuity we rely on. In practice, my local practice has tried nurse-led triage to speed bookings, which helps some days but leaves older, vulnerable patients unsure who their long-term clinician is. 

What would help more is fixing the backbone first: aggressive, targeted recruitment and retention—international hires, better pay, flexible and shift patterns, and genuine wellbeing support—so vacancies don’t spill into weeks and force unnecessary locums. I’ve seen relatives wait months for mental health referrals; quick triage is useful, but only with sustainable investment and clearly defined pathways.

Beyond that, I’d value ring-fenced same-day slots, extended hours, and deeper digital triage with a guaranteed in-person option when needed, plus co-located mental health teams tied into primary care with stable staffing. If we build predictable, well-supported teams and real continuity of care, timely access will improve more reliably than reconfiguring services without addressing core staffing and governance.

In my view, the single most effective way to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services is to combine stronger primary care capacity with smart, team-based working, while also making sure we grow and support the people delivering those services over the long term. It’s not one fix, but a bundle that works together.

First, expand multidisciplinary teams to handle routine and follow-up cases. In practice, that could mean more pharmacist-led clinics for medication reviews, minor ailments and long-term condition management, which would free GPs to deal with complex or higher-risk patients. I’ve seen practical benefits when a pharmacist can sort out a medication issue or identify adverse drug interactions during a quick clinic, rather than a patient waiting weeks for GP input. Physiotherapists in early access clinics for back and joint pain would also reduce backlogs in GP lists and cut waiting times for people who need hands-on musculoskeletal care. Paramedics and physician associates could be deployed for home visits and stable chronic disease checks, especially for older residents who struggle to come into a surgery. The key is clear triage and well-defined roles so patients get the right clinician first time, without compromising safety or continuity of care.

Second, invest in access and flexibility so people can actually get seen promptly. That means more same-day slots, extended hours, and urgent-care streaming to appropriate teams. Teletriage can be a start, but it must be backed by real capability in local teams to see people quickly, including home visits where appropriate. We also need robust, interoperable IT and shared records so a pharmacist, a GP and a mental health practitioner can see up-to-date information and coordinate a plan, rather than duplicating tests or asking the patient to repeat the same history.

Third, strengthen mental health input at community level. We need well-resourced community mental health teams, with access to crisis points and early intervention services. Training more workers in high-demand areas and giving GP practices a clear handover process to mental health specialists would stop people slipping through gaps while waiting for slots. Where possible, peer support and digital self-help tools should be offered as a first step, but there must also be timely pathways into face-to-face or video-based care when needed.

Even as we push for these service changes, we must grow the workforce sustainably. This requires a parallel track of investment in training places, return-to-practice schemes, apprenticeships and ongoing CPD for GPs, nurses and mental health professionals. In my area, there are staff who have scaled back or left for reasons of burnout or lack of progression. If we don’t address long-term workforce rotation, supervision, and sustainable career pathways, new capacity will simply be built on a shaky base. Expanding training places and reintegrating experienced professionals who’ve stepped away would help; this could be supported by formal return-to-practice programmes, mentoring, and protected time for CPD.

A practical balance could be: a funded plan to pilot expanded multidisciplinary teams in several practices, with clear performance metrics (wait times, patient satisfaction, safety indicators, and readmission rates). If pilots show reduced GP pressures and quicker access for routine care, the model should be scalable, with funding that reflects local population needs. It is also essential to involve patients and carers directly in designing access routes, because what works on paper may not translate to lived experience, especially for older residents who rely on predictable, steady routines.

Realistically, the changes should be phased. In the short term, I’d prioritise: more immediate multi-disciplinary slots for simple, common needs; targeted return-to-practice and CPD incentives for clinicians; and stronger community mental health pathways. In the medium term, broaden the team-based model and invest in training pipelines. In the long term, ensure sustainable funding and governance so that new capacity isn’t just a quick fix but a reliable part of our NHS system.

Ultimately, patients want to know they can get a timely appointment with someone who knows their history and can act promptly if it’s routine, while complex cases get the attention they deserve. A coordinated, team-based approach backed by ongoing training and well-managed workforce growth feels like the most realistic and fair way to deliver that in everyday life.

Yes, I think this is one of the most important steps to make health care feel reliable again. As someone who works part‑time and studies, evening and weekend GP clinics would make timely access manageable, not just a weekday luxury. When I’ve needed quick advice about a sore throat or a stressed mental‑health moment, waiting days feels too long, and urgent slots should be guaranteed the same day rather than being a rarity. Expanding access across GP, community health and mental health teams, with rapid referrals and clear triage, would prevent problems from spiraling.

To deliver this, I support targeted recruitment and international hiring to fill shortages, plus incentives, pay improvements and flexible working patterns that include wellbeing support. If staff feel valued and less burned out, they’ll stay longer, and access times will drop. Local practices could trial Saturday or late‑night clinics or virtual slots for urgent concerns, easing weekday pressure and supporting students around exams and shifts.

Sustainable funding and transparent targets are essential so improvements last. With more available slots and better workforce planning, people in our area will get help when they need it—faster and safer.

From our perspective as an organisation in England, the most effective changes to improve timely access are not generic increases in appointment slots alone, but targeted, equity‑driven actions. We need to allocate resources specifically to reduce gaps for deprived and ethnic minority, migrant and marginalised groups: funded interpreters on site or quickly accessible tele-interpretation; staff trained in culturally competent care; and active outreach in communities via mobile clinics, multilingual information, and partnerships with schools, mosques, churches and community centres. In practice this means easier, multilingual appointment systems, extended hours, and local access hubs so people aren’t deterred by transport or work constraints. 

We also need to grow the workforce for the long term: more training places for GPs, nurses and mental health professionals; robust return‑to‑practice support; apprenticeships; and protected CPD. Expand community mental health teams, with early intervention, crisis rapid response and talking therapies, to achieve parity with physical health. Without these targeted, sustainable changes, waits will persist even as general capacity rises. We must see concrete local plans with measurable access improvements.

In my area in England, timely access to GP, community health and mental health services often feels like a patchwork. I’m 18-24 and juggling studies and part‑time work, so when I do need care I want something that’s quick, straightforward and trustworthy. I also worry about people who don’t have the same digital access or language skills as me, and I think the biggest gains would come from targeted, practical changes built around real community needs.

First, we need to target resources to close gaps for deprived, ethnic minority, migrant and marginalised groups. That means ensuring interpreters and multilingual staff are readily available at every touchpoint and that appointment systems can be accessed in multiple languages without long waits. It’s not enough to have a translation on the website; when someone phones or walks in, they should be able to get an interpreter without being bounced around. I’ve seen cases where someone who speaks limited English had to wait days for an interpreter to be arranged or was asked to bring a relative to translate, which adds stigma and privacy concerns. Outreach works too: pop‑up clinics in community centres, faith venues, and schools in areas with historically low uptake, plus targeted information in languages other than English about how to book, what services exist, and how triage works. Regular, visible engagement with trusted local organisations—food banks, community groups, migrant support services—can rebuild trust that health services have sometimes lost.

Second, there should be more staff who understand local realities and are representative of the communities they serve. That means culturally competent training for all clinicians and reception staff, and deliberate recruitment from diverse backgrounds. A practice I know started to recruit bilingual health workers and trained reception teams to recognise non‑clinical cues that someone might need support navigating the system. It made a real difference in how comfortable people felt making an appointment. We need similar momentum across mental health services, where stigma and misunderstanding can delay help. For example, simple changes like staff who know how to explain cognitive‑behavioural therapy options in plain language, or who can route people toward culturally appropriate community supports, can shorten the time to initial contact and reduce drop‑out later on.

Third, digital innovations can dramatically improve timely access, but only if we keep non‑digital options robust. I book most routines online because it’s quick and I can see slots and what services exist, including e‑consultations that let you describe your issue before a live appointment. That’s great for non‑urgent needs and saves clinic time. But not everyone has reliable broadband, a private device, or the confidence to use a new app. My grandmother, who lives nearby, still finds phone triage—her main route to ask for help—much easier than navigating an online form. So, we should expand online booking and video‑consultations while guaranteeing alternatives: a strengthened telephone triage service with interpreters, same‑day walk‑in slots at local hubs, and in‑person clinics in community centres. Digital inclusion must be funded: subsidised data or devices for families in need, free public Wi‑Fi in clinics, and “digital champions” in communities who can help people sign up and use the tools.

A practical mix would be: same‑day or rapid triage slots for GP and mental health referrals; extended weekday hours and some weekend clinics to fit student and part‑time work schedules; and a streamlined pathway from GP to mental health teams with clear expectations about timelines and what happens next. In mental health, I’d like to see a stronger “step‑care” approach so people aren’t kept waiting for what they don’t need, while those who need urgent help have rapid access to a professional—whether in person or via a secure video link.

Fourth, better use of local data and accountability. Services should publish regular, easy‑to‑read dashboards showing access by language, ethnicity, disability, and deprivation measures, and set annual targets for improving timeliness. A culture of continuous improvement means staff can learn from gaps: if a locality notices long waits for interpreters on Monday mornings, they can adjust staffing in advance rather than reacting after the problem has built up.

Finally, practical parking brakes on these ideas: secure funding for workforce development and interpreters; robust, privacy‑protecting technology that’s easy to use; and clear information about how to access services, what to expect from triage, and how to switch between digital and non‑digital channels without losing momentum.

Overall, I think the biggest improvements come from a combination of targeted outreach and staff development to close access gaps, together with flexible digital options backed by inclusive, non‑digital routes. When people can get timely, culturally competent care through the channel they’re most comfortable with, everyone benefits—from the person needing a quick GP appointment to someone requiring mental health support who might otherwise drop out of the care pathway.

I want to see timelier access to GP services, community health support and mental health care across Wales, including rural areas, without compromising quality or people’s trust in the system. My view sits between different approaches: I can see real value in co‑located community hubs that bring GP appointments, district nursing, mental health workers, social care and local VCSE partners under one roof or in a tightly connected network. In practice that could mean a single site or a well‑coordinated cluster where a young person can see a GP, talk to a mental health professional, and get help arranging support in education or housing, all with a clear, same‑day intake if needed. But I also worry about centralising too much in one place. If hubs become distant from where people live or if transport is a barrier, the convenience could be lost rather than gained. Any model needs strong local governance, straightforward data sharing between services (with robust privacy protections), and flexible access points so people can choose telehealth, in‑person or hybrid options according to what’s practical for them and their families.

From my own experience and what I’ve heard from peers, there are real benefits to more integrated pathways. When a young person can be referred from primary care straight into a multi‑disciplinary team that includes mental health, substance misuse support, school/college liaison and social services, the chance of a crisis or a chronic issue spiralling reduces. But co‑located hubs will only work if they are properly funded, staffed and designed with young people in mind—accessible evenings, clear signposting, and spaces that feel welcoming to someone who might not be used to dealing with mental health services. It also has to avoid long waits for appointments simply because a hub is “efficient.” The idea should be to shorten the path from concern to care while preserving flexibility and choice.

Another strong strand is expanding community mental health teams, increasing early intervention and enhancing crisis response and talking therapies. I’ve seen more of my peers struggle with delays in CAMHS or with over‑strained school counsellors when they need timely help. If teams that can respond quickly—especially in a crisis—are expanded, it could prevent more serious episodes later on. Early intervention makes sense; it can keep people engaged with education and work and reduce the overall burden on acute services. That said, expansion must be matched with quality training, cultural competence, and capacity to tailor approaches to different communities, including Welsh‑medium services and rural families who may face transportation challenges.

And yes, increasing GP, nurse and therapist appointment slots is essential, but it must be implemented thoughtfully. Extra slots are only valuable if they are reliable and predictable. I’ve waited too long for appointments and heard of friends missing study or work because of awkward scheduling. Hiring more clinicians is part of the answer, but we also need smarter scheduling—same‑day triage for urgent concerns, protected slots for students during term times, and targeted appointment blocks for repeat mental health check‑ins. Telehealth options can help, but we must avoid widening the gap for those without fast internet or private space at home. A blended model—face‑to‑face when you need it, with secure online booking and quick triage—would suit many young adults who juggle education, work, and family responsibilities.

In all of this, transport and geography matter. Rural communities in Wales can’t rely on a single hub in a city; there needs to be a network of accessible services within reasonable travel times, plus smart referral pathways to specialist care when required. Community involvement matters too—VCSE partners, schools, universities and youth organisations can help with outreach, information sharing and peer support. I’d like to see genuine patient and public involvement in planning, piloting and evaluating these changes, with clear metrics on wait times, experience, and health outcomes.

Overall, I’m cautiously optimistic. The right combination of co‑located hubs, expanded mental health teams, and expanded clinical capacity could dramatically improve timely access and parity between physical and mental health care. But it has to be designed with young people in mind, with explicit commitments to local flexibility, rural access, data protection, and consistent funding. If the reforms are rushed or too centralised, they risk becoming another layer of bureaucracy that doesn’t land where it’s needed. A phased, co‑designed approach that tests new models in different regions, learns quickly from what works, and scales proven approaches would be the most credible way forward.

it's outrageous that i disagree that the quickest route to timely access lies in extending GP hours or speeding up digital bookings alone. In our area, what consistently reduces wait times is strengthening mental health capacity in the community. Expanding community mental health teams, investing in early intervention, robust crisis response, and more accessible talking therapies would deliver real parity with physical health.

For example, in our city a young person waited nine weeks for a CBT course; someone in crisis waited days for a response from the out-of-hours line, and families struggle with the gatekeeping between primary care and specialist services. When community teams are co-located with GP practices, referrals are faster, co-ordination improves, and people feel supported before crises escalate. We need more funding for early intervention projects in schools and colleges, and 24/7 crisis support with clear referral pathways to speaking therapies.

In short, cosmetic changes to appointment systems won't close the gap. The most effective changes are expanding mental health capacity at the community level so that physical and mental health are treated with equal urgency!

Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services matters, especially for someone like me with long-standing conditions. The changes that would help most are protecting continuity of care and lengthening appointment times for complex, chronic and vulnerable patients. When I see the same GP, we can keep track of my meds, adjust plans quickly and spot problems before they escalate, which reduces repeat visits. Lately I’ve waited too long for annual reviews because 10– or 15‑minute slots aren’t enough to cover all tests and medications. I’d welcome a system that guarantees named GP continuity and, where possible, longer appointments—20–30 minutes for complex cases; 40–60 minutes for annual reviews. 

Equally important is better integration with community health and mental health teams. Having a nurse or psychologist attached to the practice, with joint care plans and access to social prescribing, would help manage anxiety, mobility problems, and sleep issues at home. A clear triage pathway that offers same‑day slots for urgent concerns, while routing non‑urgent matters to a convenient appointment, would free clinicians to focus on those who need it most. For frail or housebound patients, consider home visits or reliable remote check‑ins to prevent hospital trips.

Investing in the workforce and in gentle, person‑centred care will reduce repeat visits and improve outcomes.

Living in Wales, I recognise how delays in GP, community health and mental health services add stress. I strongly support actions to improve NHS111, clinical triage, booking systems and care navigation so urgent cases are prioritised and patient flow is simplified. In my experience, calling NHS111 can be slow and data sometimes isn’t shared with my GP, causing duplication and wasted trips.

I’d like a 24/7 clinical triage team that can assess urgency and give a clear booking route—either a same-day GP or nurse appointment, a timely mental health assessment, or a community nurse visit. A single integrated booking system across GP practices, community services and mental health teams would let me see available slots in one place and reduce multiple forms. Strong care navigation could guide carers and relatives so we don’t repeat information or chase different services.

Specific steps: add NHS111 frontline with qualified clinicians; implement shared records to speed referral and avoid duplication; publish local wait-time targets; expand community hubs to support access without long travel.

Living in England, I’d welcome a real boost to GP, nurse and therapist appointment capacity. More available slots and expanded sessions would cut waits for everyday care, catch issues early, and help with mental health triage before problems worsen. Shorter waits also reduce strain on urgent care and improve satisfaction when you just need timely advice or a check-up.

But I’m wary of boosting numbers without protecting continuity of care. For people with complex or chronic needs, keeping the same clinician and having longer appointments makes a big difference to outcomes. In my experience, when I can’t consistently see my usual GP or speak with the same therapist, I end up repeating history, juggling medications and needing extra visits that could have been avoided with a fuller initial session.

What would help most:
- hire more GPs, practice nurses and talking therapists, and expand the length and depth of sessions where needed
- optimise scheduling so urgent same‑day slots are available while longer slots are reserved for complex cases, with a named clinician where possible
- introduce care coordinators and multi‑disciplinary teams that hand over smoothly between primary and community services
- offer extended hours (evenings/weekends) and secure digital triage to direct people to the right service without delay
- monitor wait times and patient experience to ensure faster access does not come at the expense of continuity

In practice, a local surgery trialling a mix of extra GP slots with longer chronic-care appointments showed reduced overall waiting times, but only when continuity was preserved; that balance is what I’d like to see rolled out nationally.

From where I’m living in England, the biggest wins would come from sorting NHS111 and the booking system so urgent cases get priority, cut duplication and speed up patient flow. NHS111 triage should push urgent problems straight to a clinician who can offer a same-day slot or clear escalation, with a simple digital check that feeds into a live queue rather than a maze of phone calls. Sharing data across GP, community and mental health teams would prevent patients from repeating the same information several times and help avoid delays.

Protecting continuity of care matters too. For those of us with chronic conditions or complex needs, longer appointment times and a named clinician or care navigator would reduce missed signals and repeated visits. A policy of longer initial assessments (20-30 minutes) for complex cases, plus a reliable follow-up plan, would make a real difference.

On staffing, we need targeted recruitment, international hires where appropriate, better pay, flexible hours and wellbeing support to grow and retain primary care staff. In our area, shortages show up as long phone queues, scarce same-day slots and slow mental health referrals. A coordinated package—triage reform, longer appointments for complex cases, and robust recruitment—would improve timely access, provided there’s clear accountability and steady funding.

I understand how crucial timely access is for GP care, community health, and mental health support, especially when needs are urgent. In my area there are real delays: GP appointments can be booked several weeks ahead, nursing follow-ups for chronic conditions are sometimes scarce, and referrals to talking therapies for mental health can take a long time. I would welcome changes that increase appointment slots and session capacity, but only if they’re backed by sustainable staffing and funding.

What would help: first, more clinicians—GPs, practice nurses, and therapists—with targeted roles to cover evenings and weekends and with a plan to retain staff rather than relying on temporary locums. Second, expand how services are delivered: longer appointments for complex cases; more nurse-led clinics for ongoing conditions; group sessions where appropriate; and dedicated slots for mental health referrals and low‑intensity therapies. Third, smarter scheduling: same‑day urgent access where possible; protected slots for routine follow‑ups; trained reception teams to triage effectively; and a robust digital booking system with reminders, plus options for video or phone reviews when suitable. Fourth, stronger community links: outreach visits for frail or home‑bound patients and better coordination with pharmacies and social care to prevent bottlenecks.

Overall I support expanding capacity, but it must come with clear workforce planning, funding and ongoing monitoring to protect quality and ensure fair access for all.

Mobile clinics, outreach and telehealth hubs could ease transport, parking and premises deficits in rural areas, but funding should also target interpreters and culturally competent staff to close gaps for deprived and minority communities.

Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services in our area is constrained by persistent workforce pressures. The changes most likely to improve access are a coordinated package centred on growing and retaining staff, with careful implementation. First, targeted recruitment: expand GP training posts and allied health pathways, with outreach through medical schools and career changers, plus clear progression routes into primary care leadership roles. Second, international hiring as part of a managed programme: robust induction, language and clinical governance support, mentoring, and equitable integration into teams to ensure patient safety while expanding capacity quickly.

Third, pay and incentives: a sustained uplift to base pay, location-based supplements for rural or underserviced areas, and relocation or sign-on grants where justified, linked to visible career development and retention commitments. Fourth, flexible working and wellbeing: offer part-time or job-sharing GP roles, flexible clinic hours, protected time for admin and professional development, and proactive wellbeing support (supervision, mental health days, workload management) to reduce burnout and staff turnover.

Fifth, structural and technological changes: invest in multidisciplinary teams within community hubs, digital triage and appointment systems to prioritise urgent cases, and co-located mental health professionals to shorten referral times. Finally, ensure strong governance, ongoing monitoring of patient outcomes and patient experience, and a local workforce plan that balances international recruitment with growing domestic talent so access improvements are sustainable.

I strongly support changes that put funding behind co-located community hubs integrating primary, community and mental health services with social care and VCSE partners for seamless local care. In our area, people often experience delays and frustration because different services sit in separate buildings and run on separate contact routes. A single, well-managed hub would cut out a lot of that back-and-forth and get people the help they need much more quickly.

How this would improve timely access
- A hub provides a single point of contact for GP, nursing, mental health and social care needs, with rapid triage so those with urgent concerns can be seen the same day where possible.
- Integrated teams can coordinate care plans in real time, so a patient who needs a GP, a mental health review and social support doesn’t have to tell their story twice or wait for multiple referrals.
- Long waits for mental health support would be reduced by colocating mental health specialists with primary care, allowing early intervention and quicker escalation when necessary.
- Flexible hours and same-day slots would be more feasible in a hub setting, especially if staffing is planned across disciplines rather than siloed into separate services.
- Local hubs located near bus routes and in accessible buildings would cut travel time and stress, especially for families with children or older residents who often struggle to navigate multiple offices.

Why this approach works, with practical examples
- When services share space and systems, care plans can be updated and shared instantly with consent, so a nurse or social worker can check in with you during the same visit or call you back with the next steps in hours rather than days.
- A dedicated care navigator within the hub could guide patients through appointments, referrals and social support options, which would be especially valuable for those with complex or ongoing needs.
- Co-located hubs encourage a stronger workforce model: multidisciplinary training, cross-referrals, and mutual support reduce burnout and improve consistency of care. This matters for communities that have historically faced barriers to accessing timely services.
- VCSE partners bring local insight and trusted relationships—they can run group sessions, peer support, and practical help (like housing or debt advice) right alongside clinical teams, helping to address determinants of health before crises occur.

Personal experience that informs this view
A relative recently needed both primary care and mental health support within a tight timeframe. The process involved multiple calls, several different offices, and a long wait for a referral to a specialist. If there had been a co-located hub nearby, with a unified triage team and a plan shared across GP, mental health and social care, the pathway would have felt seamless. Not only would it have saved time, it would have reduced anxiety and helped us feel supported by a consistent team who knew our situation. For families facing similar situations, a hub model would make the difference between timely help and a missed window for early intervention.

What should be prioritised in implementation
- Establish pilot hubs in a few diverse neighbourhoods, with ring-fenced funding to recruit multidisciplinary staff and fund shared IT systems.
- Ensure the hub design includes environmental accessibility, language support, and clear public information so people know where to go and what they can expect.
- Create governance that brings NHS teams together with local authorities and VCSEs to maintain a patient-centered approach and accountability for timely access metrics.
- Track outcomes not just in numbers of appointments but in user experience, continuity of care, and reduced escalation to crisis services.

In short, investing in co-located community hubs that integrate primary, community and mental health services with social care and VCSE partners is the change most likely to improve timely access. It aligns local resources around the patient, reduces wasted time and repeated navigation, and builds a more resilient, preventive system for our communities. I urge policymakers to prioritise this approach and to design pilots carefully with genuine local involvement so the benefits can be rolled out widely and equitably.

absolutely it's hard to say what changes would dramatically improve timely access across GP, community health and mental health in my area. I do notice GP appointments can be hard to get quickly; often you end up waiting a couple of weeks for a routine slot, and triage by phone can mean the next step drags on. A relative waited months for counselling, and another local nurse visit was postponed after hospital discharge. Some practices are trialling online booking or weekend clinics, which helps a bit, but it's not universal. I think any measures that genuinely shorten waits without cutting care quality could help, such as more staffing, flexible urgent slots, or regional hubs, though I'm not convinced which would be best everywhere!

Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services in my area remains uneven, particularly for people who work long hours and for those facing language or cultural barriers. I think any improvements should address both who we reach and when services are open. 

First, target resources to reduce gaps for deprived, ethnic minority, migrant and marginalised groups. This means more interpreters on-site or via video, multilingual booking and information channels, and staff training that covers local cultural contexts. In practice, a Polish-speaking neighbour delayed a GP visit because there was no translator and phone booking felt opaque. Working with trusted local groups, faith centres and community hubs could help people understand what’s available and how to access urgent help without fear of stigma or costs. 

Second, expand access hours and guarantee same-day urgent slots. Evening and weekend clinics would suit many shift workers and students, and a clear pathway for urgent non‑emergency needs could prevent deterioration. From experience, after-hours triage can misdirect people, and delays around mental health concerns can worsen quickly without a timely appointment. Co-locating mental health clinicians with GP practices and a reliable urgent slot system would be especially valuable. 

Any rollout needs proper funding and ongoing monitoring of waiting times, language access, and patient satisfaction to ensure improvements reach those who need them most.

Timely access depends on people getting the right care first time. I support expanding multidisciplinary teams to handle routine cases so GPs can focus on complex care. In my area, pharmacists already help with minor ailments; if they’re embedded in care teams and linked to quick access to physiotherapists and physician associates, patients with back pain or minor injuries could be treated faster without waiting weeks for a GP appointment. I’ve seen how physiotherapy and gait advice can avert unnecessary GP visits. 

We also need to target resources, interpreters, and culturally competent staff to reach deprived and migrant communities. Language barriers and cultural differences can delay help; dedicated interpreters and outreach workers could improve appointment uptake and adherence. 

Finally, NHS111 and triage must be improved: better booking systems and care navigation to prioritise urgent cases, reduce duplication, and smooth patient flow. A streamlined phone/online triage that redirects to appropriate professionals would cut delays and avoid multiple calls. Mental health services also need quicker assessment and clearer referral pathways to talking therapies so people aren’t left waiting.

To improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services, the most effective changes are to grow the workforce sustainably through training, return-to-practice support, and new apprenticeship routes, backed by robust CPD funding. Increasing training places across Scotland—particularly in rural and underserved areas—will reduce bottlenecks in GP practices and community hubs and help get patients seen sooner. Expanding funded return-to-practice programmes and retraining for clinicians who have paused their careers will keep skills current and encourage retention.

From conversations with local teams, shortages in key roles often drive delays. Apprenticeships for healthcare assistants, nursing associates and mental health support staff can deliver frontline care earlier while providing clear progression. Providing protected CPD time and easy access to up-to-date digital learning will help staff meet evolving guidelines without burning out. Strengthening multi-disciplinary community teams and improving appointment triage and scheduling can ensure patients are directed to the right service quickly, whether that’s a GP, a district nurse or a mental health professional.

In short, a long-term, well-funded pipeline that combines training, return-to-practice support, apprenticeships and CPD is the most reliable way to improve timely access now and sustain it for the future.

Access to GP, community health and mental health services must be built on a sustainable, well-supported workforce and better outreach to those who currently slip through the cracks. In the short term, I’d push for targeted fixes that can be felt quickly: ring-fenced funding for additional interpreters and culturally competent staff in practices and community hubs; proactive outreach to deprived and ethnic minority, migrant and marginalised communities; clearer, community-based pathways linking GP practices with mental health teams, social care and voluntary sector services. 

In the medium to long term, a strategic expansion of the workforce is essential. Increase training places for GPs, nurses and mental health professionals, with strong return‑to‑practice support, apprenticeships and CPD to grow the workforce sustainably. Align this with integrated care models so new clinicians are embedded in local teams rather than isolated in clinics. 

Crucially, protect continuity of care and lengthen appointment times for complex, chronic and vulnerable patients. Longer slots can reduce repeat visits, improve outcomes and ease pressure on urgent access. Support stable clinician teams and predictable rosters, plus flexible, extended hours where demand exists. 

Operationally, invest in practical fixes: co-located services and patient navigators in communities; better digital triage with rapid human follow-up; and targeted outreach through schools, community centres and faith groups to raise awareness of available help. In my area, wait times and language barriers remain the main obstacles; these measures would address both.”

As an organisation delivering health and wellbeing services across Scotland, we welcome and strongly support the proposed changes to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services. Extending access through evening and weekend clinics would be a practical step for working people and families who struggle to attend during standard hours. Guaranteed same-day urgent slots would help prevent deterioration of non‑emergency conditions and reduce avoidable A&E attendance. In our experience, when people can’t get timely GP or nurse appointments, they delay care or escalate to crisis services; flexible hours would relieve that pressure. 

Expanding community mental health teams, with a focus on early intervention, crisis response and evidence-based talking therapies, would close the gap between mental and physical health care and cut waiting times. We’ve seen better outcomes when families can access a trained CAMHS or adult community mental health clinician more quickly, rather than enduring long waits. 

Investing in co-located community hubs that bring together primary care, community and mental health services with social care and VCSE partners would deliver seamless local care. In practice this would mean one-stop assessment and care plans, simpler referrals, and closer collaboration with housing, poverty support and voluntary groups. We urge funding and workforce planning to enable place-based hubs across Scotland.

I represent a youth-focused organisation in Wales, and we strongly welcome proposals to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services. Modernising NHS111, expanding clinical triage, smarter booking systems and better care navigation will prioritise urgent cases, reduce duplication and simplify patient flow. In practice, a trained clinician triage at NHS111 would direct someone to the right service first time, with clear same-day slots for urgent care and rapid access to mental health support where needed. In our area, people often endure repeated phone calls and multiple forms before a GP appointment appears, or are bounced between GP and mental health services. A digital booking platform and integrated triage would cut that red tape. We also want to see investment in co-located community hubs that combine primary care, community health and mental health teams with social care and VCSE partners. For young people, hubs near campuses and town centres would make it easier to access counselling, GP appointments and practical support in one visit, reducing travel and stigma. These changes would lessen pressure on A&E and create a smoother, more local care pathway.

I support increasing GP, nurse and therapist slots through hiring and expanded sessions with optimised scheduling, plus expanding community mental health teams, early intervention, crisis response and talking therapies to cut waits and improve parity with physical health.

In our area in Northern Ireland, the issue of timely GP, community health and mental health care feels more about how services are organised and how easily an older person can access them, rather than a single policy fix. Waiting times and travel gaps hit people who rely on regular contact with health professionals, especially in rural parts where the nearest GP or nurse might be several villages away. I know several neighbours who struggle to book a routine GP appointment within a week or so, and for anyone needing mental health support the wait can stretch for months. It is not just a question of money but of putting in place practical steps that work for older folk who may not be able to travel far or navigate complex systems easily.

From personal experience there are a few changes that would make a real difference, even if they are not glamorous reforms:
- GP access on the ground. It would help if practices could offer more same day or next day slots, with some early morning or late evening hours for those who work or struggle with transport. A reliable nurse or clinician triage system so that someone with a minor but persistent issue can be seen promptly would also relieve pressure on GPs. In winter, manageable urgent care taken closer to home is a real comfort for older people who cannot drive far.
- More support in the community. Increasing district nursing capacity, physiotherapy and occupational therapy visits in the home would cut down on hospital visits and keep people healthier at home longer. A simple, single point of contact for a care plan would stop people feeling they are bounced between services. In practice, when a neighbour needed rehabilitation after a fall, a quicker arrival of a community team would have eased anxiety and speeded recovery.
- Mental health access that is genuinely timely. Waiting months for talking therapies is unacceptable for many, including those of us whose mental health needs shift with age and illness. More counsellors and psychologists, plus better outreach to rural villages, would be a big step forward. It would help if there were clear routes for crisis support that provide a rapid response, not days of waiting for a call back. Some areas have mobile mental health teams visiting villages; expanding that model could make a real difference here too.
- Integration and a clear route through the system. I would value a care co ordinator or a small team that could bring GP, community health and mental health together for a person who has several needs. A simple, trusted contact who coordinates appointments could save time and prevent frustration.
- Practical support around transport and information. If you cannot drive or access a computer easily, getting to appointments becomes a real barrier. A reliable patient transport option for older people, and a straightforward phone line or in person help to book and reschedule, would reduce missed appointments. It is also important to keep non digital options alive; not everyone can or wants to use online booking.
- Information about expectations and timelines. People want to know roughly how long waits might be for various services and what can be done in the meantime. Public reporting of waiting times and simple guidance on what to do if a condition worsens would help families plan and feel safer.

If these changes were pursued as a package, with attention to rural circumstances and the needs of older residents, I think we would see more timely access across GP, community health and mental health services. It is about practical access points, not just money, and about keeping people well at home for as long as possible. I am hopeful that a patient, joined up approach can be achieved here with sensible investment and a clear front door to services.

Agree. To improve timely access, we must protect continuity of care and lengthen appointment times for complex, chronic and vulnerable patients. When someone has multiple conditions, a named GP or a small, stable care team who knows their history reduces the need to repeat symptoms and questions and helps spot warning signs early. Longer slots—ideally 20-30 minutes for complex cases—are essential; rushed 10-minute slots often miss concerns and drive repeat visits later.

In practice this means longer booked slots for chronic disease reviews, mental health check-ins and after-hospital follow-ups, with proactive care planning and written care plans that are reviewed regularly. It also means co-locating or closely linking community health nurses, physiotherapists and therapists with GP practices so people can access physio, counselling or district nursing in one place, saving time and trips.

Same-day triage should be available, but where possible patients should be seen by their own team to preserve continuity. Invest in flexible digital scheduling and brief remote check-ins to support, not replace, face-to-face care. This approach should reduce avoidable hospital visits and crises, and lead to better outcomes for patients with complex needs.

In our part of Scotland, timely access to GP services, community health and mental health support matters more than ever as we age. I would welcome a framework that expands online booking, e-consultations and remote care, but also guarantees robust non-digital options so no one is left behind. My experience and conversations with neighbours show that when digital options are well designed and supported, they can make a real difference to waiting times and to staying well at home.

What would help most
- More online booking and e-consultations, with clear triage. My own GP practice has got better at letting you book slots online and send a quick message about symptoms. A recent mild chest infection was dealt with in a day or two: I filled in a short form, had a nurse call-back the same afternoon, and the prescription was ready to collect the next morning. For many people, this saves days of waiting and unnecessary travel. We should extend this to all routine GP appointments and to urgent same-day triage so people with worrying symptoms are prioritised quickly.
- Flexible remote care, with face-to-face as the default when needed. Video or phone appointments are particularly helpful for routine reviews, mental health check-ins or medication reviews. In winter, being able to speak to a nurse or counsellor without a long journey is a blessing. At the same time, there must be a clear path back to in-person care when physical examination or a social contact is important. A mixed model keeps care timely while preserving personal contact.
- Strong support for remote monitoring and community-based digital services. For chronic conditions, home blood pressure monitors and glucose meters that feed results to my clinician can prevent crises and cut down on unnecessary visits. Remote rehab classes for back pain or heart health, run from local hubs, would keep people moving and reduce hospital referrals. If possible, extend digital group sessions for carers and bereavement support so people have timely, ongoing access to help.

Non-digital options to ensure inclusion
- Keep robust telephone access and in-person booking. Not everyone has a smartphone or reliable broadband, and some people prefer human contact. A dedicated, well-staffed telephone line with reasonable waiting times is essential, as is a straightforward option to book in person at the practice with a real person available to help.
- Local digital support and outreach. Simple, friendly help at community venues—libraries, community centres, or village halls—where staff or trained volunteers assist people to use online booking or complete an e-consult form. In some communities, weekly digital help sessions run by volunteers have made a big difference.
- Clear guidance and staff training on digital literacy. Frontline teams should have training to explain online options, manage expectations about response times, and assist those who struggle with technology. Practitioners should also be trained to identify when a patient needs a non-digital route and to switch seamlessly.

Equity and resilience
- Invest in connectivity where it’s weakest. Rural areas still face gaps in broadband and mobile signal; improving this is essential for remote care to be reliable.
- Ensure choice, speed and safety. Any expansion of online and remote care must be backed by strong privacy protections and simple, patient-friendly explanations of how data are used and stored.
- Monitor impact and adjust. Local pilots comparing waiting times, travel burden and patient satisfaction between digital and non-digital pathways will help us learn what works best in real communities.

Overall, I support expanding digital access to GP, community health and mental health services, provided we keep human contact at the heart of care and put strong options in place for those who cannot or prefer not to use digital channels. When done right, this can shorten waiting times, reduce unnecessary travel and help people stay healthier and supported in their own homes.”

Expand online booking, e-consultations and remote care, but maintain non‑digital options and staff for in‑person access to avoid excluding older or disadvantaged patients. Introduce evening/weekend clinics and guaranteed same‑day urgent slots alongside more GP, nurse and therapist appointment slots.

it's outrageous that i strongly support changes that invest in co‑located community hubs and expand mental health services, because this would cut waits and make care feel seamless. In my area GP slots are often hard to get, and I end up navigating several different buildings for different services. A local hub that brings GP, community health, mental health teams, social care and VCSE partners under one roof would save time and avoid repeating my story to multiple people. It would also host link workers and quick triage so I could get a same‑day plan, with onward referrals if needed.

Equally important is expanding community mental health teams, early intervention, crisis response and talking therapies. If these were more available locally, people wouldn’t wait weeks for a referral, and crises could be de-escalated before they require urgent care. In pilots elsewhere, patients report faster access and better parity with physical health services. As a student, I want trusted local care that’s easy to reach, flexible and stigma‑free!

I strongly agree that the changes proposed could bring much swifter access to GP, community health and mental health services here in Wales. A co‑located hub where primary care, nurses, mental health professionals, social care and voluntary groups work side by side would mean people can get same‑day help, simple investigations, and follow‑ups without endless travelling between buildings. In my experience a single, friendly hub would also help us older residents stay connected and informed, with clearer opening hours and better sign‑posting for urgent needs.

Expanding multidisciplinary teams—pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates—would let many routine concerns be sorted quickly and safely, freeing GPs to concentrate on more complex cases. I’ve waited too long for routine checks and would welcome seeing a pharmacist or a physiotherapist handle minor medical questions or mobility reviews while a GP handles the more tricky matters.

And better NHS111 triage, booking systems and care navigation would reduce duplication and organise flows so urgent cases are seen sooner. A straightforward, reliable booking process and better guidance on next steps would make life easier for someone like me who has mobility limits and relies on timely support.

Improving NHS111 and clinical triage, plus streamlined booking and care navigation, would help prioritise urgent cases, cut duplication and simplify patient flow. However, it must be backed by adequate staffing, clear deadlines, and robust IT to avoid new bottlenecks.

it's outrageous that timely access to GP, community health and mental health services needs a mix of tweaks rather than one big fix. As a student in Scotland, I’ve found GP slots can be two weeks away and uni mental health waiting lists are 4–6 weeks, which makes it hard to get help when I’m stressed about exams. It might help to have more same-day or next-day GP slots, plus a clearer online booking system that shows availability across small local hubs. Extending hours in evenings could also fit study schedules. For mental health, quicker access to talking therapies via campus or local hubs—even drop-in evenings or weekend slots—would help reduce delays. More community health staff, like district nurses and pharmacists with later hours, could take some burden off GPs. I’m not sure which single change would work everywhere; different areas have different bottlenecks, but better triage, digital check-ins, and more integrated care across services seem worth trying!

I strongly support changes that would speed up timely access to GP, community health and mental health services by expanding multidisciplinary teams. Bringing in pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates to handle routine cases would free GPs to focus on more complex care and patients would get seen sooner. In practice, this makes a lot of sense for people like me who often deal with non‑urgent but annoying health issues that currently end up waiting weeks for a GP appointment.

In my area, the pressure on GP appointments is obvious. A simple sinus infection, a pulled muscle, or a routine medications review can take weeks to arrange with a GP. I’ve recently benefited when the local chemist ran a walk‑in pharmacy clinic for minor ailments. The pharmacist diagnosed my issue quickly, gave sensible advice, checked my medicines for interactions, and recommended a safe over‑the‑counter course. It saved me queuing at the practice and gave me peace of mind the same day. If such pharmacist‑led clinics work well for minor problems, they can be expanded to cover more routine care and free up GP time for people with complex or chronic conditions.

Physiotherapists involved earlier in the patient journey can be a real game changer for musculoskeletal issues. In a neighbouring practice, there are now physio‑led triage sessions where patients with back pain or knee problems are assessed and given targeted exercise plans or manual therapy. The vast majority go home with practical steps and a plan, and only a minority need a GP follow‑up. This not only speeds up recovery for patients, but it also reduces the number of GP visits for something that can be managed well with education, exercise and guidance. I’d encourage more co‑location of physiotherapy services within GP hubs so patients can be seen quickly in a single place.

Paramedics taking on a broader urgent‑care role could transform how we access care after hours or at weekends. When something feels urgent but isn’t life‑threatening, a trained paramedic practitioner could assess at home or in the clinic, manage straightforward issues, and refer to physio or pharmacy where appropriate. This would ease the load on urgent care services and hospital A&E, and it would be especially welcome for older residents who may struggle with travel to a clinic during working hours.

Physician associates have a valuable part to play in handling routine reviews, minor infections, skin conditions, and medication management. At my local practice, a PA supports the GP with walk‑in slots and routine follow‑ups. This arrangement has noticeably shortened waiting times for patients and helped the GP devote more time to complex cases and vulnerable patients. It would be important to ensure consistent training and clear scope of practice so patients always know who to see for what, and that prescribing safety and documentation standards are maintained.

Mental health access often lags behind physical health access, so integrating mental health practitioners into GP clinics would be a strong step forward. Quick access to talking therapies, low‑intensity CBT, and social prescribing within the same building would help people manage stress, anxiety and mild depressive symptoms before they escalate. In our area there are pilots where mental health nurses and coordinators sit within GP teams, enabling faster triage and signposting to community supports. That kind of seamless access makes a real difference to people’s wellbeing and can prevent crises that would otherwise require more intensive treatment.

To make this work well, the reforms must be backed by good governance, clear scopes of practice, robust training, and strong data sharing so records stay coherent across professionals. Funding should support long‑term workforce planning, with incentives for practices to adopt integrated MDT models and to provide flexible, same‑day slots or extended hours where possible. Digital triage and online booking should be embedded, with safety nets to ensure patients with complex needs aren’t bounced between services.

Overall, expanding multidisciplinary teams is a practical, patient‑centred way to improve timely access. It aligns with the realities of daily life for many people in England and could deliver meaningful, lasting improvements in both physical and mental health outcomes.

I live in England and I’m writing as an individual who cares deeply about how we access healthcare now and in the years ahead. I believe the changes proposed would make a real difference to timely access to GP services, community health and mental health support, especially for older people and for those in deprived or ethnically diverse communities who often face additional barriers. In my experience, when you can get a same‑day or next‑day GP appointment, and when you can speak with staff who understand your language and culture, it makes all the difference to managing long‑term conditions and preventing crises.

First, targeted resources, interpreters and culturally competent staff are essential. In our town there are many families who speak languages other than English at home. It’s not enough to publish leaflets in a couple of languages; clinics need funded interpreter services across GP surgeries, hospitals and mental health settings, and staff should receive ongoing training in cultural humility and effective communication. I’ve seen how even small miscommunications can delay treatment or lead to people not following through with care plans. Practical steps could include funding for on‑site interpreters, translation of appointment reminders and instructions into the languages spoken locally, and support from patient advocates who can help people understand options and navigate the system.
