Outreach to deprived communities—through mobile clinics, local community centres, schools and faith groups—would help reduce gaps in access, particularly for migrants and marginalised groups who may be wary of health services or unfamiliar with how to access them.

Second, expanding community mental health teams and ensuring early intervention, crisis response and talking therapies are readily available would close the gap between mental and physical health care. I’ve witnessed the relief when a family member could access a community mental health nurse who visits at home and coordinates with the GP, rather than waiting weeks for a referral. Expanded community teams, with more crisis resolution support and timely talking therapies (including CBT and other evidence‑based approaches), would shorten waits and improve outcomes. It’s crucial that mental health care is offered in community settings as promptly as physical health care would be, so people don’t deteriorate while waiting for a service they urgently need. A better crisis response pathway—24/7 if possible—paired with better information and navigation support, would help people stay safe and connected, reducing emergency admissions.

Third, we must grow the workforce sustainably. Increasing training places, providing return‑to‑practice support, expanding apprenticeships and strengthening continuing professional development are essential for GPs, nurses and mental health professionals to meet growing demand. In our area, high patient lists and staff shortages lead to longer waits and fatigue among clinicians. Clear commitments to expand medical and nursing training places, provide practical re‑entry routes for those who have taken career breaks, and fund CPD across primary and mental health care would pay dividends in the medium and long term. Local partnerships between health boards, universities and employers could offer flexible training options that align with older workers’ needs and encourage people to stay in the workforce. I would also welcome investment in allied roles—practice nurses, social workers, and mental health workers—so teams can function at full capacity and offer timely, coordinated care.

In summary, the most impactful changes would be a combination of funded interpreters and culturally competent staff, proactive outreach to underserved communities, expanded and readily accessible community mental health services with strong crisis support, and a sustainable drive to train and retain a skilled workforce. If these elements come together, we would see faster GP access, better prevention and management of long‑term conditions, and mental health care that truly keeps pace with physical health care. Thank you for considering these ideas.

Expand multidisciplinary teams including pharmacists, physios, paramedics and physician associates to handle routine care, but also invest in interpreters and culturally competent staff to reach deprived communities; ensure outreach alongside digital access to reduce gaps in GP and mental health services.

I welcome the proposals to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services. Expanding multidisciplinary teams within GP practices and local clinics would enable routine problems to be managed swiftly, freeing GPs to concentrate on complex care. For example, pharmacists could handle minor ailment consultations and repeat prescriptions, a physiotherapist could triage and treat common musculoskeletal problems, paramedics could carry out home visits for low-risk cases, and physician associates could staff urgent‑care clinics. In our organisation’s experience, a local pilot where a physiotherapist joined morning clinics cut waiting times for back-pain appointments and allowed GPs to review escalating cases sooner.

We also need to address transport, parking and premises deficits. Mobile clinics visiting village halls or rural hubs, outreach teams targeting care‑homes and deprived wards, telehealth hubs in community venues, and incentives for practices to extend hours or co‑locate services would noticeably improve access for rural and mobility‑impaired residents. A simple, funded timetable of mobile clinics and a network of telehealth links would reduce the need for long journeys and help people get timely mental health support as well. Overall this approach would keep patients well and out of A&E.

I don’t believe simply expanding online booking, e-consultations and remote care will reliably improve timely access, especially for older or less well-off residents. In my experience, online systems can be slow, confusing and prone to outages, and many people I know lack reliable internet or feel uneasy using apps. A few months ago I tried to book a same-day GP appointment online; the system froze and I ended up on hold for twenty minutes when I phoned, which defeated the purpose of quicker access. A neighbour in their eighties needed to visit the surgery in person to secure a slot, and any delay risks his health.

For mental health and community services, remote options can help some with distance or mobility, but they are not a substitute when you need urgent reassurance or a proper assessment. A walk-in or same-day in-person slot, plus effective telephone triage, would make a real difference. We also need clear wait-time information and more staff to create genuine same-day availability.

Please maintain and strengthen non-digital channels alongside digital ones, and provide real support for those who struggle with technology. That balanced approach would improve timely access for everyone.

As a youth-focused community organisation representing young people in England, we welcome proposals to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services. We see two changes as essential, but they must be implemented with safeguards and clear funding.

First, expand multidisciplinary teams: extend roles of pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates to manage routine, non-complex cases and triage. This would free GPs to focus on complex cases and reduce wait times. In our experience, young people with musculoskeletal injuries or contraception queries often face delays; pharmacist-led clinics or physio triage could resolve many issues within a week, with proper supervision and referral pathways back to GPs when needed.

Second, invest in co-located community hubs: bring primary care, community health, mental health, social care and VCSE partners under one roof with extended hours and digital access. This would help seamless referrals and easier access for students and part-time workers. However, hubs must guarantee data sharing, safeguarding, service continuity, and flexible appointment slots, including evenings and online options.

Overall, these steps could improve timely access while keeping care patient-centred and locally accountable.

absolutely thank you for the chance to share my views. In rural parts of Northern Ireland, timely access to GP, community health and mental health services can feel like a postcode lottery. When I or my neighbours need help, we don’t want promises—we want practical, reliable ways to get seen quickly, close to home. I’d like to see a package of changes that makes use of mobile solutions, staff development and smarter training so we can all have confidence in the system again.

Transport, parking and premises deficits create big barriers. A practical start would be to deploy regular mobile clinics that visit village halls, community centres and care homes on set days. These mobile teams could offer essential GP consultations, blood pressure checks, chronic disease reviews, simple diagnostics and nurse-led clinics for chronic conditions. Easy booking through a local pharmacy app or text service, with clear satellite locations and wheelchair-accessible venues, would mean fewer trips to the town centre. Outreach teams could target the most vulnerable—older residents, people with mobility issues, and those who are housebound—checking in with home visits or pop-up sessions near residents’ doors.

In tandem, establish telehealth hubs in local community spaces—libraries, community centres, or GP surgeries—where people can access devices and support from trained staff. A modest investment in devices, 4G/5G connectivity, and staff time to help patients set up video calls would dramatically cut waiting times. For those needing face-to-face care, flexible premises with improved parking and access would help; free or discounted parking for patients using weekday clinics could remove a recurrent hurdle.

A broader shift to interoperability would enable triage and booking to flow smoothly between mobile, community and traditional GP settings. Digital triage could route urgent cases to same-day slots while non-urgent issues are directed to the most appropriate service. The objective is to shorten waiting times while reducing unnecessary travel and bottlenecks at fixed sites.

On the workforce side, recruiting and keeping primary care staff is essential if these improvements are to last. Targeted recruitment campaigns—looking beyond local pools—should include international hiring where needed, with streamlined registration, visa support and settlement packages for clinicians who move to rural NI posts. Incentives should include pay progression tied to rural placements, relocation grants, and protected out-of-hours support. Flexible working arrangements, job-sharing and more predictable rosters would help clinicians balance patient care with wellbeing, which in turn reduces burnout and improves patient safety.

Wellbeing support for staff must be embedded. Access to confidential occupational health services, peer-support networks, and dedicated hours for professional development will help retain the staff we rely on. I’ve seen colleagues leave because the strain becomes too much, and we’re left with gaps when we most need continuity of care.

Investing in training and staff development is the long-term answer. Increasing training places for GPs, GPs in specialty training, nurses and mental health professionals will grow the workforce we need. Return-to-practice schemes—paired with practical, funded retraining—could bring back experienced clinicians who paused their careers. Apprenticeships for support roles and expanded CPD opportunities for all primary care staff would create a sustainable pipeline and provide clear progression paths. In my own circle, people who returned to care through apprenticeship routes or CPD upgrades have become reliable anchors for local services.

To make this work, we need cross-border cooperation with universities and health trusts to align training with rural needs, and a robust funding framework that ensures these measures are financed in the long term, not as short-term pilots. Real-time data on access times, waitlists and patient satisfaction should guide ongoing adjustments and help us demonstrate both safety and value.

In short, I’d like to see a combined package: mobile and outreach services to bring care closer to people; telehealth hubs to remove geography as a barrier; targeted recruitment with meaningful incentives and flexible working to attract and retain staff; and stronger training, return-to-practice and CPD pathways to grow a resilient workforce for GP, nursing and mental health services in the years ahead. If these elements are funded and coordinated, timely access to essential care in rural Northern Ireland can become the norm rather than the exception.

To improve timely access, expand teams with pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates handling routine cases, offer evening/weekend slots and guaranteed same-day urgent appointments, and tackle transport and premises deficits with mobile clinics and telehealth options, especially in rural areas.

i really think i represent an organisation working across our region to improve access to GP, community health and mental health services, and I strongly support the proposed changes. To grow and retain primary care staff, we need targeted recruitment and international hiring supported by clear incentives, pay improvements and genuinely flexible working patterns, underpinned by robust wellbeing support. In our area, recruitment campaigns that attract skilled clinicians from abroad and flexible shift models, plus wellbeing programmes, have helped reduce vacancies and improve continuity of care.

Expanding online booking, e-consultations and remote care is essential, but we must not leave vulnerable groups behind. I advocate for a strong digital pathway alongside non-digital alternatives—telephone lines, walk-in hubs and in-person triage—so older patients and those with limited digital access can still receive timely help. In practice, we’ve seen benefits from online slots and remote check-ins, with local community sites offering assisted digital support where needed.

Finally, widening multidisciplinary teams—pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates—can handle routine cases, freeing GPs to focus on complex care and urgent mental health needs. Pilot schemes in our region have shown faster response times and improved patient experience, underscoring the value of integrated teams in delivering timely care.

i strongly believe i support preserving continuity of care with longer appointments for complex and vulnerable patients, expanding multidisciplinary teams (pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics, physician associates) for routine cases, and offering evenings, weekends, and guaranteed same-day urgent slots to improve timely access to GP, community and mental health services!

Develop mobile clinics and telehealth hubs, with outreach to rural areas, plus flexible transport assistance and parking fixes; alongside increasing GP, nurse and therapist slots, better scheduling, and staff recruitment to reduce waits.

absolutely as an organisation representing residents in Northern Ireland, we fully support proposals to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services. The changes that would help most are evening and weekend clinics and guaranteed same-day urgent slots. Many older people still in work, or who care for spouses, simply cannot attend day clinics; later hours and weekend availability would make a real difference, reduce missed appointments and prevent problems from escalating. In our area, where public transport is limited after 6pm, a late clinic in a local health centre has proven popular and has cut referrals to A&E. Guaranteeing same-day urgent slots for non-emergency issues would also ease pressure on daytime services and provide reassurance. For mental health, rapid access to an urgent same-day slot can prevent crises and hospital admission, which is especially important for older adults who may be isolated. We also urge strengthened community teams, with better triage so people are directed to the right service promptly. With proper funding and workforce planning, these changes are achievable and would benefit many in Northern Ireland!

I live in England and I see it varies in my area. Sometimes I can book a GP appointment within a week, but other times the earliest slot is two weeks away. I recently heard of a neighbour waiting two months for a mental health assessment, which seems far too long. Community health and district nurses are good when they visit, but their clinics often run only in the mornings and weekdays, which is hard for people who work or have carers’ duties. Transport, waiting times and call-handling also get in the way; I’ve had to wait on the phone for ages to get through to book.

What might help? More same-day or next-day urgent slots, better online or phone triage that actually leads to timely follow-up, extended evening opening, and more local drop-in points for checkups. Improving integration between GP, community teams and mental health so a plan can follow a patient through quickly would help. But I’m not sure what would work best everywhere; needs local tailoring.

From an organisational perspective in Scotland, I believe reforms focused solely on speed,, such as more online booking or shorter slot times, wil not deliver timely access to GP, community health or mental health services. The thread tying care together is continuity: longer appointments for complex, chronic and vulnerable patients are essential to achieve better outcomes and reduce repeat visits. In my experience across several practices, brief check-ins often miss emerging problems and drive patients back for the same issue within weeks. Expanding digital access can help, but it must not exclude anyone. We need non-digital options with adequate support for those with limited digital literacy or connectivity—telephone triage, in-person booking, and local access points with staff available to assist. Crucially, the reform package must addrrss workforce capacity. Without targeted recruitment, international hires where appropriatr, meaningful pay improvements, flexible patterns and robust wellbeing support, primary care will struggle to cope with demand. Longer-term workforce planning, training pipelines, and incentives to retain clinicians are essential to drliver sustained improvements in access and safety. In short, timely access will follow from protecting continuity, offering a balanced mix of digital and non-digita routes, and investing in the people who provide care.

I think the most effective change to improve timely access would be to grow the primary care and mental health workforce through more training places, robust return-to-practice support, and clear apprenticeships, supported by high-quality CPD. In my area, GP and mental health slots are booked weeks in advance, and a local clinic recently had to pause new registrations because staff shortages left them unable to cope with demand. Expanding GP training places across medical schools and GP specialty training would help, alongside funded return-to-practice schemes for GPs, nurses and therapists to re-enter practice with up-to-date skills. Creating structured apprenticeships for nursing associates and mental health support workers would provide clear career paths and faster recruitment. We also need protected CPD time and funded refresher courses so existing staff can keep up with new guidelines without burnout. Better collaboration between training providers, NHS trusts and GP practices, plus flexible training options (evenings, weekends) would help people train while they work. Taken together, these steps would deliver steadier access to GP, community and mental health services over the longer term.

ACCESS TO GP, COMMUNITY HEALTH AND MENTAL HEALTH SERVICES REMAINS TOO SLOW IN OUR AREA. GP APPOINTMENTS ARE OFTEN WEEKS AWAY; NHS111 SOMETIMES MISROUTES URGENT CONCERNS, CREATING DUPLICATION AND DELAYS; TALKING THERAPIES AND CAMHS WAIT MONTHS. THE CHANGES NEEDED ARE SYSTEMIC, NOT COSMETIC. FIRST, GROW THE WORKFORCE: TARGETED RECRUITMENT, INCLUDING INTERNATIONAL HIRING, WITH ROBUST ONBOARDING, BETTER PAY, FLEXIBLE HOURS AND STRONG WELLBEING SUPPORT TO RETAIN STAFF. WITHOUT DURABLE STAFFING, OTHER FIXES WON’T LAND. SECOND, FIX TRIAGE AND BOOKING: A WELL-RESOURCED NHS111 WITH CLINICAL TRIAGE, PRIORITISING URGENT CASES AND A CLEAR CARE-NAVIGATION PATH TO THE RIGHT SERVICE; REAL-TIME CAPACITY DATA TO REDUCE BOUNCING BETWEEN SERVICES. THIRD, EXPAND MENTAL HEALTH CAPACITY: MORE COMMUNITY TEAMS, EARLY INTERVENTION AND CRISIS SUPPORT, WITH FASTER ACCESS TO TALKING THERAPIES SO PARITY WITH PHYSICAL HEALTH IS ACHIEVED. MY EXPERIENCE BACKS THIS: I WAITED THREE WEEKS FOR A GP APPOINTMENT; CAMHS WAITS HAVE BEEN SIX MONTHS FOR RELATIVES. IF WE WANT TIMELY ACCESS, WE NEED SUSTAINED STAFFING GROWTH, SMARTER TRIAGE, AND STRONGER MENTAL HEALTH PROVISION, NOT JUST QUICK DIGITAL TWEAKS.

Access to timely GP, community health and mental health services is crucial for me and many neighbours in later life. When a health issue arises, waiting for days or chasing multiple numbers can make a small problem become a bigger one. I would like to see changes centred on making NHS111 and clinical triage smarter, simplifying booking, and using dedicated care navigators to steer people to the right place first time, with urgent needs prioritised. First, NHS111 and clinical triage should be strengthened so urgent cases are directed quickly to the right service. In my experience, a lot of time is spent on initial triage questions that don’t always clarify how urgent the situation is, or end up with referrals to services that have little immediate capacity. I would support guaranteed prompt callbacks and a clear escalation pathway for potential emergencies, with a guarantee of a GP or urgent care appointment within 24 hours when someone’s symptoms threaten their safety or daily function. The triage should have clear, age-sensitive standards and an option for a home visit if mobility or transport is a barrier. Second, booking systems must be simplified and joined up across GP practices, community clinics, and mental health services. A single local hub that can book on the day for urgent needs, while offering routine slots in a predictable pattern, would save time and reduce duplication. For example, I have spent days chasing a referral and then repeating the same information to different teams. A central booking systrm with shared, real-time availability and the ability to book multiple services in one call would greatly reduce that duplication. Reminders and clear instructions should br standard, with options to book by phone for those who do not use online systems. Third, care navigatio should be a core part of the NHS offer. A trained care navigator could assess needs over the phone or in person, explain options, and arrange coordinated care across GP, community nursing, physiotherapy, podiatry, and mental health. When I needed support after a fall, a navigator could have lined up a same-day GP assessment, a home visit from a district nurse, and a referral to physiotherapy—all without me having to repeat stories to each service. Care navigators should also helpp families and carers, with consent, so that relatives can assist in arranging appointments and following up on care plans. Mental health services need particular attention. Waits for talking therapies and crisis support can be long, especially for older people who may be reluctant to seek help remotely. Local teams should offer same-day crisis access, with options for home visits or in-person sessions as appropriate. Integrating mental health records with physical health data (with consent) would speed up care planning and reduce the need to re-tell personal history at every appointment. Accessibility and dignity must be central. Not everyone is comfortable with online booking, and many older people may have sensory or mobility challenges. Any system must retain telephone and in-person booking, with simple, large-print information and help for carers to book on behalf of someone who cannot manage it themselves. I understand staffing and capacity are constraints, but better triage, streamlined booking and care navigation should reduce duplication and unnecessary journeys to hospital. If put in place, these changes would help ensure urgent cases are prioritised, routine issues are managed efficiently, and people receive the rightt support at thr right time—without endless chasing or avoidable delays. In short: a smarter NHS111, a single, user-friendly booking hub, and trained care navigators who can coordinate across GP, community, and mrntall health services would make a meaningful difference in timely access in our area.

I’m concerned that simply expanding online booking, e‑consultations and remote care will widen gaps rather than speed up timely access. In Scotland, many patients, especially older folk, those with limited broadband, and people in rural areas, struggle with digital systems. A neighbour with poor mobile reception can’t book a same‑day slot online, and my grandmother still finds phone lines hard to navigate and not transparent about what’s available.

What would help most is a strong mix of non‑digital routes: guaranteed same‑day GP appointments and a reliable telephone booking line with short hold times; more walk‑in or drop‑in clinics; mobile or outreach clinics in remote communities; and extended hours including evenings and weekends. Clear triage should ensure urgent cases are seen quickly. 

Digital options should be optional, with robust support: help desks, access in libraries or community hubs, devices loaned where needed, plain‑English guidance, and interpreter and accessibility features. Importantly, e‑consults must not replace in‑person assessments when that’s what patients need, especially for mental health.

A hybrid approach, backed by additional staffing in GP and mental health teams, would reduce delays without leaving vulnerable residents behind.

I strongly support the proposed changes to grow our GP, nurse and mental health workforce through more training places, return‑to‑practice support, apprenticeships and ongoing CPD, and to protect continuity of care with longer appointment times for complex and vulnerable patients. In my area, GP slots are increasingly hard to come by and waiting times can stretch to several weeks, which means chronic conditions aren’t managed promptly. A longer appointment for people with multiple needs would stop the pattrrn of repeat visits and repeated handovers between different clinicians. Return‑to‑practice schemes have already helped colleagues who paused their careers to come back with confidence, bringing essential local knowledge and easing workload pressure. More apprenticeships and funded CPD would also attract reliably trained staff into community services, aligning skills with new digital tools and evolving best practice. Personally, I’v seen how continuity matters: my elderly neighbour with COPD benefited far more when he could see the same clinician who knew his history rather than starting from scratch each visit. A friend waiting for a community mrntal health assessment faced long delays; timely, stable access would reduce crisis episodes and hospital use. If these changes are implemented together, they should improve timely access, support better long‑term outcomrs and genuinely ease pressure across GP, community health and mental health services.

In my part of rural England, timely access to GP, community health and mental health services is patchy and sometimes disheartening, especially for those of us who rely on cars or public transport that only runs sporadically. I’d welcome a package of changes that recognises the practical realities of mobility and distance, while still keeping high standards of care. The core idea is to bring services closer to people where they are, and to make it easier to access them when they matter most, without adding extra trips and stress.

First, mobile clinics and outreach should be a staple, not a last resort. A well‑organised schedule of weekly or biweekly mobile GP and nurse clinics could visit village halls, community centres or even farms in outlying hamlets. These mobile teams could offer blood tests, vaccinations, chronic disease reviews and minor ailments, with a simple referral pathway to the main practice if anything serious is detected. In practice, this would save neighbours from travelling long distances for a routine check, while freeing space at busy town‑centre surgeries for urgent needs. I’ve seen how a monthly nurse‑led outreach visit in a nearby village has made it much easier for pensioners to stay on top of their conditions without the long trip into town.

Second, dedicated outreach for mental health and community health work is essential. Small, local teams could provide home visits or short, community‑based talking therapies, with quick access to crisis support when needed. For people who don’t use smartphones healthily or feel uneasy in clinical settings, a familiar community centre or library can become a safe space with trained staff available to help with appointments, digital check‑ins and ongoing support. I recall a neighbour who felt overwhelmed by the process of booking a mental health appointment far away; a local, trusted counsellor visiting a village venue would have removed that barrier and reduced delays.

Third, telehealth hubs should be embedded in rural infrastructure. Setting up modest, well‑staffed telehealth suites in libraries, village halls or GP practice buildings with privacy screens and assistive help could dramatically cut waiting times. Patients could have video or telephone consultations with GPs, specialists and mental health clinicians, and then be directed to mobile clinics or outreach for any necessary in‑person care. It’s vital these hubs are supported by real hands‑on help: staff who can log patients into the system, check accessibility needs, and ensure digital poverty doesn’t become a barrier.

Transport and parking are not afterthoughts; they’re enablers. Transport subsidies or vouchers for medical appointments, better co‑ordination of hospital and GP transport, and reliable community minibuses would stop people missing appointments because of a car breakdown or a late bus. Parking at younger or more remote surgeries should be free or low‑cost, with clear signage and enough spaces for disabled patients. Where parking is tight, a simple on‑site queuing system and a nearby drop‑off point can make visits less stressful. These measures would be especially valuable for older adults and carers who shoulder a large part of the burden when access is difficult.

Incentives are needed to attract and retain staff in rural areas. Flexible contracts, relocation allowances, and guaranteed protected time for clinical leadership and professional development would help recruit GPs, nurses and mental health workers to the most underserved communities. A stable workforce matters just as much as new facilities; it means patients can expect consistent care rather than revolving doors of temporary cover.

Premises matter too. Where there are gaps in capacity, modular clinics or partnerships with local schools, churches or community spaces can provide interim consult rooms with proper privacy and disability access. Over time, a small number of well‑designed satellite clinics could be staffed with a core team who know the local community’s needs.

Finally, any plan must be evaluated with patient experience at its heart. Local patient groups should help shape pilot schedules, measure outcomes (wait times, travel burden, no‑show rates, satisfaction), and adapt services as needed. Data sharing across primary care, community health and mental health must be seamless but secure, so a patient’s care plan is coherent rather than fragmented.

Taken together, these changes would make access feel practical, timely and respectful of people’s lives. For families and older residents in particular, a future where a nurse can visit your village, where a telehealth hub can bridge a gap, and where there’s real incentive to work in rural services, would be a meaningful improvement. I’m encouraged by the potential for a coordinated, locally designed approach to make timely care a reality rather than a hopeful aim.

Living in England as a young person, I want quicker, easier access to GP, community health and mental health services. Too many friends and even me have faced waits for talking therapies or crisis support, especially outside working hours. If we expand community mental health teams with a strong emphasis on early intervention and crisis response, people would get help before issues escalate and mental health parity with physical health would feel real.

Key changes I’d like: more predictable same-day or next-day appointments, better signposting, and a clear crisis pathway with rapid intake, home visits when needed, and immediate phone or video checks. Expanding talking therapies in local hubs would cut long waits and help students who can’t travel far to access support.

Additionally, growing multidisciplinary teams—pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates—would free GPs to focus on complex cases. For example, a pharmacist-led review for anxiety meds, a physio-led back-pain pathway, and a paramedic-led urgent home visit could catch problems earlier and reduce university or work absences.

Overall, more funded staff, extended hours, and improved digital triage would make timely care a normal, reliable option rather than an exception.
Yes, expanding online booking, e‑consultations and remote care would speed access, provided non‑digital options and extra support remain for older or less tech‑savvy patients.

Support expanding online booking and e-consultations, but ensure non-digital alternatives and staff support are available so older or disadvantaged patients aren’t left behind, and local clinics retain walk-in options.

I support targeted recruitment, international hiring, better pay, incentives, flexible work, and wellbeing to grow primary care staff in NI, but funding stability and training must accompany to safeguard local services.

From my experience living in England, timely access isn’t just about the next appointment; it’s a web of connected services that can feel like they’re pulled in different directions. I’ve tried to book a same-day GP call-back in the town where I live and ended up waiting on the phone for ages, with the earliest in-week slot two weeks away. Online booking can be helpful, but it’s not reliable for everyone, especially older or less tech-literate neighbours who still rely on a quick phone call. For mental health, a friend waited several weeks for talking therapy, and our local crisis lines feel stretched after hours. Community health feels uneven too: district nurses and home visits can be late or cancelled, and the local pharmacy often becomes a bottleneck when prescriptions take days to process. Transport matters as well; some rural routes and weekend services are patchy, meaning people miss appointments just because they can’t get there on time. Changes that reflect local patterns, plus more staff and flexible hours, would matter more than a single blueprint, but they must involve patients in designing them.

I’m responding as an individual living in England, and I strongly support changes that would make GP, nurse and therapist appointments easier to secure and less time-consuming. In my area, waits for a routine GP appointment can stretch to one or two weeks, and getting timely access to mental health support often feels threadbare. I believe the most effective improvements would combine expanding capacity with smarter use of digital tools, while always keeping non‑digital routes available for those who need them.

What I’d like to see most:

- More appointment slots and longer sessions where needed
  - Hire additional GPs, nurse practitioners and therapists, and bring in robust multidisciplinary teams so that a patient can see the most appropriate clinician without being bounced between services.
  - Expand session lengths for complex or mental health care to prevent rushed consultations and the need for repeat visits the same week.
  - Introduce more flexible hours, including early mornings, evenings and some Saturday slots, so people who work or have caring responsibilities can access care without taking time off.
  - Use smart rostering and data-led demand forecasting to ensure peak times have enough capacity, and to reduce the awful burst of queuesFirst thing Monday mornings.

- Expanded online booking and digital care, with strong non‑digital options still in place
  - A user-friendly online booking system that clearly shows same‑day and next‑week slots, with simple e‑consults to share symptoms or concerns and receive a clinical response within 24–48 hours.
  - Video or phone consultations should be normal options for suitable problems, freeing up in‑person slots for people who need physical examination or who prefer face‑to‑face care.
  - For more routine issues, a triage path that allows a clinician to triage remotely and then offer an appropriate next step (e.g., self-care advice, a short video check‑in, or a booked appointment) would save time for everyone.

- Non‑digital access and support so no one is left behind
  - A strong and well publicised telephone line with trained staff who can triage urgent needs and book slots is essential, especially for older patients or those with limited digital skills.
  - Maintained access to in-person booking windows, walk‑in clinics, and home visits for people with mobility challenges or those living in rural areas.
  - Local authority and practice liaison to help patients who struggle with digital tools – for example, community digital champions in libraries or GP hubs who can help people set up online accounts, learn how to use e‑consults, and book appointments.

Why these changes are important to me

- My family has benefited from online booking and quick triage in the past year, but the gains shouldn’t come at the expense of those who can’t or won’t manage digital tools. A system that offers both digital and non‑digital routes is more resilient and fair.
- More capacity means not only shorter waits but better continuity of care. If a patient can see a clinician who understands their medical history and concerns, the appointment is more likely to be effective and resolve issues sooner, reducing downstream demand.
- Mental health access is a particular concern. Delays there can have serious consequences. Investing in more therapists, shorter waiting lists and integrated care—working alongside schools and employers to support early identification and treatment—would have a real, tangible impact on people’s well‑being.

Practical examples from local experience

- A local practice recently introduced an online booking portal, which noticeably cut the friction for people who can plan ahead. However, there are still weeks-long gaps for mental health slots, and the phone line remains congested for urgent concerns. Scaling up both the number of clinicians and the sharing of appointment capacity across disciplines would help translate digital gains into real, timely access.
- There have also been occasions when a same‑day or next‑day appointment would have prevented a minor issue from escalating. Flexible hours and more in-person slots would make a big difference here.

Safeguards and implementation

- Any expansion must come with clear staff recruitment and retention plans, appropriate funding, and robust governance to protect patient safety and data privacy.
- Regular reporting on wait times, appointment mix (in-person vs digital), and patient satisfaction will help identify gaps quickly and keep the system responsive.

Overall, the changes I’m supporting would make timely access to GP, community health and mental health services more reliable and equitable, without sacrificing the personal, human element of care. I’m confident that with proper investment and thoughtful design, patients in England will see meaningful improvements in how quickly and effectively they can get the help they need.

Expanded community mental health teams, early intervention, crisis response, and talking therapies are essential to reduce waits and parity with physical health. Pair this with evening/weekend GP clinics and guaranteed same-day urgent slots to help working residents.

Living in England and studying, I notice timely access to GP and mental health services can be patchy. I'm not sure this answer fits the main question exactly, but some tangential thoughts that might help people like me.

When I tried to book a GP appointment for a cough, the earliest slot was two weeks away and the phone line was busy for ages. A friend waiting for talking therapy started with a months-long wait. On campus, the wellbeing service is helpful but stretched.

A few ideas beyond the usual policy tweaks: bring GP and mental health help closer to student housing with mobile clinics in evenings or weekends; create stronger links between university counsellors and NHS services so referrals are smoother; expand digital options—secure messaging and quick video triage to point people to the right service; and ensure affordable transport to appointments for those without cars.

If there’s room for quick wins, I’d back campus outreach, after-hours video triage, and better NHS-university coordination. These changes could improve timeliness without needing a huge rebuild of services.

I am glad to see a focus on making timely access to GP, community health and mental health services easier. For someone like me, living in a rural area and relying on help to stay independent, these changes could make a real difference to daily life and peace of mind. I strongly support improvements to NHS111 and the way triage and booking work, to prioritise urgent cases, cut duplication and simplify patient flow.

Firstly, the way people access help needs to be clearer and faster. NHS111 should be able to triage with clinical input and offer same-day or next-day GP appointments when there is genuine urgency, while guiding less urgent cases to the most appropriate service quickly. A streamlined booking system across NHS111, GP practices and urgent care would save people from repeating their story multiple times and from being bounced between services. In practice, this could look like a single, easy-to-use online portal that shows available slots across GP practices, urgent care hubs, and community clinics, with simple options to book by phone if online access is difficult. Real-time triage notes should be shared securely with the clinician who takes the appointment, so patients do not have to repeat information or wait while an incorrect pathway is pursued. Small improvements, such as immediate confirmation and text reminders, can prevent missed appointments and wasted journeys.

Reducing duplication is important. People in my village often describe having to repeat the same symptoms to several staff or being told to “call back later” when the problem feels urgent. A unified patient record, with consent to share essential information between GP, community nursing, and mental health services, would prevent miscommunication and delay. A simple care-navigation role could act as the consistent guide for patients, especially the elderly or those with multiple conditions, helping them move smoothly from primary care to physio or social support when needed.

Transport, parking and premises are particular barriers in rural areas. Mobility problems, limited bus routes and long drives make timely access hard. I support mobile clinics visiting village halls or community centres on a rotating timetable, so people can access GP and basic health checks without long journeys. Outreach teams could assess needs at home for those who cannot travel, with referral pathways to community nursing or physiotherapy. Telehealth hubs in local libraries or community venues could offer video consultations for those who struggle with travel, paired with a simple loan-a-device scheme or in-workshops to help people learn to use the technology. Where possible, incentives for clinicians to work in rural areas, extended appointment hours and safer, easier parking at clinics would also help.

Telehealth has a clear role, but must be plain to use. For older patients, interfaces should be straightforward, with large text, simple language and options for telephone calls where video is difficult. Home monitoring devices—blood pressure, glucose, heart rate—could feed into a shared record so practitioners can spot issues early and act quickly. Training and support for patients and carers to navigate these tools would reduce anxiety and improve outcomes.

On mental health, I welcome expansion of community mental health teams, early intervention and crisis response. It remains essential that mental health parity with physical health is not just a slogan but reflected in service design and funding. Waiting times for talking therapies and crisis support can be too long, especially for people with complex needs or those in rural settings. A stronger “one front door” approach—where primary care, crisis services, and community mental health teams coordinate from the outset—would reduce delays. Quick access to crisis lines, same-day triage, and home-based or community-based crisis response would prevent crises from escalating. I have heard from neighbours about the stress of waiting weeks for an appointment; quicker access to evidence-based talking therapies, including early trauma-informed approaches, would help many stay well and avoid hospital admissions.

In my experience, a handful of well-placed changes could make a big difference: a single, user-friendly booking and triage system; shared records that protect data but cut repetition; mobile and telehealth options for rural and mobility-impaired patients; and a fully resourced and integrated mental health pathway that offers early help, crisis response and solid talking therapies on par with physical health services. I urge policymakers to fund and pilot local co-design with patients and carers, monitor outcomes, and roll out what works fastest.

Thank you for listening to older residents like me. With these improvements, we can stay healthy, connected and independent for longer, without unnecessary trips or stress when we or our loved ones need care.
I agree: protect continuity of care and extend appointment times for complex and vulnerable patients, improving outcomes and reducing repeat visits across GP, community and mental health services.

From our organisation representing older residents in England, I find myself drifting to the practical realities that slow access more than the policy rhetoric around GP and mental health services. While boosting hours or pushing online booking can help some, many of our members face day-to-day barriers that aren’t always addressed in mental health strategy briefs. The most immediate improvements would come from tackling transport and digital exclusion: more local outreach clinics in community hubs, mobile GP visits to rural villages, and a pool of volunteer drivers to get people to appointments without long waits for buses. In our town, an elderly neighbour can’t book online and the phone line is busy for days; she relies on a relative to ring for her, which isn’t feasible for everyone living alone.

Alongside that, better integration between surgeries, pharmacies and social care could shave hours off waiting. Things like same-day pharmacy pickups after a short GP call, clearer triage, and reserved slots for those with mobility limits would make a real difference. And in winter, when transport is worse and clinic spaces feel crowded, these practical fixes matter even more. Thank you for listening to the lived experiences of older residents in shaping any changes.

Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services will hinge on three linked moves: expanding frontline capacity, embedding interpreters and culturally competent care, and strengthening community delivery. In our area, delays hit disadvantaged and ethnic minority residents hardest, especially where language barriers and stigma deter people from seeking help. 

First, recruit and retain more primary care staff. This means targeted international recruitment, sensible incentives, flexible working patterns (evenings and refined part-time options), and robust wellbeing support to prevent burnout. Our experience shows clinics with multilingual staff and culturally aware reception teams see higher attendance and better engagement. 

Second, make interpreters and cultural competence routine. Guarantee interpreter services across GP appointments and mental health triage; provide ongoing cultural competence training; run outreach clinics in community centres and places of worship to reduce travel and mistrust.

Third, expand community health teams and early intervention in mental health. Prioritise proactive home visits for high-need groups, integrated links to social care, and rapid crisis response with accessible talking therapies to narrow waits and improve parity with physical health.

This requires stable, long-term funding and workforce planning, not short-lived pilots. With sustained investment and strong local collaboration, we can cut waits and ensure timely, appropriate care for all communities who currently fall through the cracks.

Timely access will improve most if we combine capacity expansion with smarter triage and care navigation. On capacity, NHS Scotland should recruit and retain enough GPs, practice nurses and therapists, and extend session lengths for mental health where needed. Increasing slot capacity through longer or more frequent appointments, plus options for group education and digital consultations, can free up urgent slots. In my area, routine GP waits of 2-3 weeks and therapy waits of many weeks push people to A&E or drop out. 

On triage and booking, we should strengthen NHS111 and clinical triage with rapid access to urgent care pathways, and give patients a straightforward, real-time booking system. Shared care plans and a single front door between GP, community teams and mental health services would reduce duplication and confusion. A nurse-led urgent triage line that can book same-day GP, nurse or mental health slots would be especially valuable, as would better digital appointment visibility. 

Phased rollout: pilot expanded GP/nurse/therapist capacity in high-need practices over 12 months; simultaneously test integrated triage and care-navigation tools with clear success metrics around wait times and equity.

From my experience in Wales, expanding online booking and e-consultations alone won't deliver timely access for everyone. My grandmother in a rural village has patchy broadband and struggles with online forms, while the local phone line often has long waits. When my own family member needed a same-day appointment for a response to anxiety, slots wer booked online but the phone line couldn'tt connect in time, and we saw a delay in getting a clinician. Relying mainly on digital channels risks excluding older patients, those with low digital literacy, and people on modest data allowances. To really improve timeliness, we need more same-day GP slots, extended hours, and better in-person triage, plus more community health and mental health staff who can sre patients quickly. Crucially maintain non-digital options phone triage with predictable callbacks, walk-in clinics, and flexible referrals. A blended approach funded with workforce and transport support will reduce delays far more effectively than digital expansion alone.

From our organisation’s experience working with communities across England, improving timely access to GP, community health and mental health services requires targeted resources and culturally competent outreach. Targeted resources, interpreters and staff who understand diverse cultures are essential to close access gaps for deprived, ethnic minority, migrant and marginalised groups. In practice, multi‑agency outreach in community hubs, plus dedicated bilingual liaison workers, has helped reduce barriers and improve uptake of primary care and mental health support. Expanding community mental health teams, bolstering early intervention, crisis response and talking therapies would directly cut waits and move parity with physical health closer. We’ve seen early intervention reduce escalations when families and schools are supported early, and rapid crisis response can avert hospital admissions when accessible 24/7. More flexible, evidence‑based talking therapies should be available with culturally sensitive delivery options, including group and digital formats.

At the same time, simply expanding GP, nurse and therapist appointment slots must be done with sustainable staffing, sensible scheduling and adequate funding. Longer appointment times for complex cases, realistic recruitment and retention plans, and integration with social care, housing and translation services are essential to ensure new slots translate into real access rather than longer queues.

If implemented with a strong equity focus and robust delivery plans, these changes could deliver timely, fair access for all communities.

Living in a small town in England, I find that the question of quicker access to GP, community health and mental health services sits beside broader issues we face as pensioners. What helps me most isn't only faster appointment slots but practical support that keeps us well at home. Reliable transport is a constant hurdle: some days the bus is late, or the timetable seems built around commuters rather than older people who need mid-morning visits. Digital booking, while efficient for some, leaves many of us behind, and a simple phone line with patience and clear language would make a real difference.

What also matters is integrated care that respects long-standing relationships with local GPs, and good co-ordination between social care, community teams and voluntary groups. My village centre runs weekly check-ins for loneliness, which can flag issues before they become crises, but secondary mental health support often takes too long. If councils invested in better social care, more carers and clearer information, it would ease pressure on clinics and perhaps improve timeliness in the long run.

I strongly support changes that make GP, community health and mental health services more timely, especially for working people like me. Evening and weekend clinics, plus guaranteed same‑day urgent slots, would be a real improvement. It means fewer people needing a day off work or waiting days for an appointment, and it would reduce the pressure on urgent care when someone has a worrying symptom that isn’t a full emergency. 

I also back expanding multidisciplinary teams within practices and community hubs. If pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates can handle routine issues, it frees GPs to focus on complex care and high‑risk patients. For example, a back‑pain flare or a minor infection could be managed quickly by a nearby physio or pharmacist with a same‑day check, supported by digital triage, so I don’t have to wait weeks. 

In my experience, timely access to mental health support is often delayed by GP bottlenecks; integrated teams and rapid triage would help people get the right help sooner and prevent deterioration. Overall, these changes would deliver safer, more convenient care and reduce avoidable crises in our area.

absolutely i welcome the proposal to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services. From my perspective as someone in their early sixties who works full time, the current pattern of appointments often clashes with work and family commitments. Too many times I’ve had to wait days or even weeks for a routine GP slot, or chase urgent care only to find the next available option is not until much later in the week. That delay is not just inconvenient; it can let conditions worsen and add avoidable stress for patients and carers.

Extending hours and guaranteeing same‑day urgent slots would make a real difference for working people and for urgent non‑emergency needs. Evening clinics on two or three weekdays, plus a weekend session, would give options when daytime appointments are hard to fit in. A guaranteed same‑day urgent slot, with a reachable in‑person or video appointment for escalating concerns, would stop people from letting symptoms drift or from turning to A&E as a last resort. In practice, I’ve seen shrewdly run after‑hours clinics in nearby practices reduce queues and waiting times for those who cannot take time off work. Widespread adoption of this model, with appropriate staffing, would bring tangible relief across communities.

Alongside extended hours, it’s essential that mental health and community care keep pace. Quick access to talk therapies, counsellors, or community‑based mental health support within primary care reduces the risk of crises and hospital admissions later. A same‑day slot for urgent mental health concerns should be part of the standard arrangement, with the ability to route to the most appropriate professional quickly.

To deliver these improvements, we must grow and retain the primary care workforce. I support targeted recruitment, including international hiring, incentives, and pay improvements, coupled with flexible working and wellbeing support. Practices across the country are already strained by GP and nurse shortages; relying on late‑care evening sessions only works if there is enough staff to staff them safely. Providing attractive entry points and career pathways—for example better remuneration bands for extended hours, international recruitment with robust integration and support, and fast‑track training for nurses, physician associates and GP registrars—will help build a stable workforce.

Flexible working is not just a perk; it’s a necessity for retention. Predictable rotas, safe staffing levels, access to clinical supervision, and protected time for wellbeing activities will reduce burnout and improve patient care. In my local area, a practice that introduced flexible hours and staff wellbeing days reported better morale and fewer cancellations, which translated into more reliable access for patients. Complementary measures, such as multidisciplinary teams with nurse prescribers, pharmacists, and mental health professionals embedded in primary care, would free up GPs to focus on those cases that truly require doctor-level care while maintaining timely access for everyone.

Of course, these changes must be delivered with strong governance and a focus on equity. Rural or remote communities can face different barriers, so we should tailor rollout to local needs and guarantee digital access where in‑person care isn’t immediately possible. Transportation, appointment triage, and clear communication about what constitutes urgent need will be important to get right.

If these steps are taken seriously and funded accordingly, we can expect shorter waits, earlier intervention, and a calmer experience for patients and staff alike. I strongly urge policymakers to back extended evening and weekend access, guaranteed urgent slots, and a robust, well‑supported primary care workforce to deliver timely care where it’s needed most!

Access to timely mental health carr remains patchy in our area, and delays push people toward GP or hospital crises. I would like to see a broader expansion of community mental health teams, strongrr early intervention, faster crisis response, and more talking therapies to bring mental health on a par with physical health. In practice, referrals for talking therapies often takee many months, and neighbours I know wait weeks for a first appointment with a counsellor after a GP referral, with some deteriorating in the meantime. A 24/7 crisis line and mobile crisis teams that can visit people at home would prevent avoidable hospital admissions, especially for older residents wit mobility challenges. Early intervention – proactive check-ins, home visits, and coordination with social care – could help people stay independent longer. Funding and staffing must match ambition; regional disparities must be addressed. We also need clear referral pathways and transparent waiting-time data, plus flexible options between in-person and remote support to accommodate transport and comfort levels. If delivered with proper oversight and funding, these changes coul reduce waits and improve parity with physical health.

From where I live in Scotland and as someone in the 65+ age group, timely access to GP, nurse and mental health services would greatly improve if we extend appointment slots and expand capacity. My top changes are: increase staffing—more GPs, nurse practitioners and therapists—and broaden session length where needed; optimise scheduling to provide same-day or next-day slots for urgent needs, and introduce regular protected slots for vulnerable patients. When our practice added two extra nurse clinics and reworked triage, waiting times fell and my neighbours could get flu jabs, blood tests and small health concerns resolved sooner. Second, invest in co-located community hubs that bring primary care, community health, mental health, social care and local VCSE partners under one roof. In nearby areas this has reduced hospital visits by enabling quick referrals after discharge and providing a one-stop checklist of support, from mental health check-ins to home-care assistance. A local hub would save trips, reduce confusion, and help carers and older residents plan care better. Also, ensure friendly digital booking with staff support so those less comfortable with tech aren’t left behind.

i really think as a resident of England aged 65+, I know older neighbours who delay GP and mental health care because of waiting times and travel difficulties. I support changes that grow and sustain primary and community services through people and training.

First, targeted recruitment and better pay with flexible working and wellbeing support. Practices turning to international doctors or nurses, with relocation assistance and clear career development, would help fill long-standing gaps. Flexible hours, part-time GP roles and strong staff wellbeing would keep skilled clinicians long enough to reduce delays.

Second, more training places and return-to-practice schemes. Increasing GP and nursing training slots, plus apprenticeships and CPD, would build a steady pipeline of qualified staff, so patients aren’t kept waiting for care years later.

Third, targeted outreach and culturally competent staff. Providing interpreters and locally trusted community health workers, plus outreach in deprived and ethnic minority communities, would close access gaps. In my area, such steps have improved attendance at clinics when people feel understood and welcomed.

If these measures are put in place, I’m confident timely access to GP, community health and mental health services will improve for many of us, especially the most vulnerable!

I live in England and, from personal and family experience in our area, timely access to GP, community health and mental health services remains inconsistent. I strongly support investing in co-located community hubs that integrate primary care, community teams, mental-health services, social care and VCSE partners. If done well, these hubs could make it much easier for people to get the right help quickly, with fewer handoffs and less time wasted on navigating multiple organisations.

What I’d want to see:
- Real co-location and one-stop access points: A neighbourhood hub that houses a GP practice, district nursing, a mental-health team, a community matron, social care coordinators and local VCSE organisations (charities, carers groups, faith-based societies) under one roof or linked floor space. This would reduce multiple trips to different sites and enable patients to be seen by the right professional in a single visit when possible.
- Unified access and care navigation: A single point of contact, with care navigators, who can triage requests and book slots across services. An integrated appointment system and shared care plan would stop patients from repeating their story to every service and would speed up assessments and follow-ups.
- Multidisciplinary teams and shared records: Regular joint meetings of GPs, nurses, mental-health workers, social workers and community volunteers to discuss complex cases. A secure, consent-based shared record would allow clinicians to see medical history, social needs and current support plans, so care is coordinated and notduplicated.
- Timely, flexible access: Same-day triage slots for urgent GP issues, timely mental-health screenings and early-intervention programmes. Offer extended hours, including early mornings or early evenings, and some Saturday slots to reduce work-day barriers.
- Integrated care pathways for mental health: Clear, rapid access routes into talking therapies, crisis support and community-based peer networks, with crisis response available within hubs or via a fast referral link to on-call teams. The idea of a “mental-health hub” where people can be seen promptly, with social care input if needed, would stabilise crises and prevent unnecessary A&E visits.
- Strong social-care and housing links: Co-located social care staff who understand housing, benefits and carer needs, so that people aren’t bounced between agencies. Joint care planning with timely social-support packages can prevent deterioration and avoid hospital admissions.
- Local commissioning and governance: Long-term funding for hub infrastructure, with local stakeholders (including patient representatives and VCSE partners) involved in decision-making. Clear performance metrics on waiting times, continuity of care, and patient experience.
- Workforce and training: Investment in a stable, multi-disciplinary workforce to staff hubs, with robust recruitment, retention packages and cross-training so staff can work flexibly across primary, community and mental-health roles.
- Digital access with a human touch: Online triage and virtual consultations where appropriate, but with robust in-person options for those who need them. Ensure accessible technology for older residents and those with limited digital skills, and maintain language and disability accommodations.
- Safeguarding and privacy: Strong governance around data sharing, with explicit and easily understandable consent processes to build trust while enabling seamless care.
- Local tailoring and equity: While the hub model has wide benefits, it must be tailored to different community needs—rural areas may need different transport solutions or telehealth enhancements, while urban hubs must consider place-based partnerships with local organisations and schools.

From personal experience, when a family member faced a mental-health crisis and a chronic health need, a co-located hub would have reduced the back-and-forth between services. If a single point of access existed, with a shared plan and a care navigator who could co-ordinate GP, district nursing and mental-health support, the journey from first concerns to stable treatment would be smoother and faster. A well-run hub also supports carers and helps prevent avoidable hospital visits by catching issues early and addressing social determinants in parallel with medical care.

In short, the most impactful change would be investing in genuinely integrated, physically co-located hubs with shared records, joint care planning and a strong emphasis on timely access, extended hours and community involvement. This approach would improve continuity, reduce delays and create a more humane, efficient local health system that better supports people in their communities.
As an organisation, we notice wider concerns around funding cycles and digital records integration. While not a direct answer, improving data sharing and oversight could help services plan capacity.

To improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services, I would prioritise protecting continuity of care and lengthening appointment times for those with complex, chronic or vulnerable needs. A named GP for these patients and longer slots can help manage multiple conditions in one visit, reduce conflicting advice, and cut avoidable follow-ups. In my own experience, seeing the same doctor over many years allows us to coordinate medicines and tests more reliably; when every visit is a new clinician, things slip and waits lengthen.

I also think we need better integration across services. A shared care plan between primary care, community nurses and mental health teams would prevent duplication and delays. For mental health, quicker access is essential, but should be paired with ongoing support rather than periodic crisis care. Where possible, protect some slots for urgent but non-life-threatening issues to avoid the week-long waits.

Any changes must be realistic in staffing and funding; otherwise longer appointments just push people elsewhere. If funded and implemented consistently, these steps could improve outcomes and reduce repeat visits.

From a community perspective in Wales, I disagree with policy directions that aim to improve timely access mainly by pushing more appointments or digital-only approaches without safeguarding continuity of care. For people with long-term or complex needs, rushed slots and changing clinicians often lead to missed signals and repeated visits, ending up costing more time and anxiety in the long run. We need to protect a named GP or clinician for ongoing conditions, and lengthen appointment times to 20-30 minutes when multiple conditions or mental health concerns are involved. In my area, a patient with diabetes and depression had two short GP visits last year that failed to coordinate care with the nurse and the mental health team; it took months before proper management was in place. Longer appointments would catch issues earlier and reduce hospital use.

I welcome longer-term workforce strategies—more training places, return-to-practice support, apprenticeships and CPD—but they must be funded and scheduled across Wales to create sustainable, supported roles in every locality, not just bigger cities. Also ensure local Welsh language and cultural needs are met, and that training pipelines align with real service delivery, not just numbers.

I live in rural Scotland and juggle work, family and the weekly round of appointments, so timely access to GP, community health and mental health services matters well beyond a single question. What would help feels bigger than one policy tweak: it’s about how the whole system links up when you’re balancing school runs, shifts and a quiet moment of distress. I get frustrated when a neighbour waits weeks for a routine GP check, and mental health pathways can feel like separate tracks with their own calendars. I’ve tried video triage, which cut some waiting time, but when the connection dropped during a moment of anxiety it reminded me that digital-only solutions can leave people without a private space or reliable broadband. Pharmacy teams and physio-led clinics provide practical help, yet Saturday transport to outreach sessions is patchy, which can disadvantage carers. The real bottlenecks seem to be workforce stability, fluctuating funding, and the gaps between primary care and social care. Any improvements will need to account for rural geography, digital equity, and ensuring staff can deliver consistent, ongoing support rather than quick fixes.

Simply speeding up appointments won't address the root problems. What would help most is protecting continuity of care and lengthening appointment times for complex, chronic and vulnerable patients. Short slots fragment histories, miss subtle changes, and push people into repeat visits. In my area, a relative with diabetes and cardiovascular risk saw new clinicians every few months; crucial context was lost, leading to a late hospital admission. A system that guarantees longer, regular slots with the same GP or care team would cut this and reduce duplication.

NHS111, triage and booking must prioritise urgent need without turning routine problems into a maze of calls and transfers. Better care navigators and integrated booking that preserves patient context would streamline flows rather than clog them with repetitive triage steps.

Finally, we need to expand community mental health teams, early intervention, crisis response and talking therapies to reduce waits and achieve parity with physical health. My experience shows mental health support often arrives too late; we need 24/7 crisis options and quicker access to evidence-based talking therapies, not just digital tools.

Yes—by strengthening NHS111 and clinical triage, modernising booking systems and care navigation to prioritise urgent cases, we can cut duplication and streamline access to GP, community and mental health services.

We disagree that short-term fixes alone will improve timely access. In rural areas transport, parking and premises block care. Expand mobile clinics, outreach, telehealth hubs and monetary incentives; plus sustainable growth by boosting GP/nurse mental health training and return-to-practice schemes now.

Access to timely GP, community health and mental health services will improve most if we invest in co-located community hubs that integrate primary care with community health teams, social care and VCSE partners. In our area, a pilot hub near the library has enabled same-day triage, joint care plans for people with long-term conditions and quicker referrals to mental health services, cutting unnecessary visits and reducing carer burden. I would like to see more hubs replicated with shared records, extended hours and a clear single point of contact.

At the same time, digital access has a role: expand online booking and e-consultations so people can book slots or get advice without waiting. But we must provide non-digital alternatives and support for those who are digitally excluded, including older patients, carers and low-income households. That means adequate phone lines, in-person slots and digital coaching.

For the workforce, increasing training places, return-to-practice support, apprenticeships and CPD is essential to sustainably grow GPs, nurses and mental health professionals in the long term. Our organisation has funded a CPD group for practice nurses, but shortages persist; stable career pathways and manageable workloads are critical.

In summary: accelerate co-located hubs with integrated teams, enable flexible digital access with non-digital options, and invest in workforce development to secure timely care now and in the future.

Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services is a priority for me and many neighbours. To improve, I think we need more appointment slots across GP, nurse and therapist services by hiring more staff, expanding session capacity, and using optimised scheduling, including same-day slots and protected slots for vulnerable patients. My experience this winter showed that even for routine checks, waiting two to three weeks is not uncommon, which risks deteriorating health. For mental health, shorter waits would prevent crises.

Additionally, targeted resources to reduce gaps for deprived, ethnic minority, migrant and marginalised groups are essential. Interpreters, culturally competent staff, and outreach through trusted community groups can help people book and feel safe to attend. Mobile clinics in estates and clearer information in multiple languages would help.

However, we must consider sustainability: recruitment, retention, fair pay, flexible working conditions, and wellbeing support are needed to grow and retain staff, otherwise expansion will struggle. Digital access should be complemented by assisted face-to-face options for those less comfortable online. With proper funding and governance, these changes could make a real difference.

Yes—by hiring more GPs, nurses and therapists, expanding slots and improving scheduling, plus dedicated interpreters and culturally competent staff, we can cut waiting times and reach deprived and minority communities more effectively.

I strongly agree that timely access to GP, community health and mental health services will improve when we tackle transport and premises gaps alongside better targeted outreach. In rural and mobility‑limited areas, mobile clinics visiting village halls on set days, improved parking and accessible premises, plus clear signage, would bring urgent GP and mental health support closer to people. I’ve seen a telehealth hub set up at our local library network that helped a neighbour book urgent follow‑ups without a long trip, which showed how much easier access can be with sensible hubs. Incentives for practices to offer extended hours, same‑day slots and outreach clinics would cut waiting times and support continuity of care. For deprived and migrant communities, funded interpreters and culturally competent staff, plus outreach through trusted local groups, are essential to close access gaps and build trust. Online booking and e‑consultations should be expanded, but non‑digital routes must remain: phone triage, paper forms and help to get online for those who need it. Combined, these measures would mean faster help and fewer people slipping through the cracks in my area.

To improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services, I’d like to see targeted investment in four areas. First, more interpreters and multilingual staff across primary care, with guaranteed in-person as well as telephone interpretation, so families who don’t speak English well can book and be understood without delay. In our area, when a Bengali-speaking receptionist was funded at one practice, wait times dropped and appointment bookings became easier.

Second, culturally competent recruitment and training for front-desk and clinicians. Regular training on cultural norms, stigma, and how mental health symptoms present in different communities would help reduce miscommunication and build trust.

Third, proactive outreach to deprived and migrant communities—community health workers visiting mosques, temples, markets and community centres, providing appointment signposting, vaccination info and mental health leaflets in multiple languages.

Fourth, longer and more flexible access options, including same-day GP triage slots, extended hours, and better online booking with language preferences. For mental health, faster referral pathways for IAPT/CAMHS and integrated care in schools and youth services would make a real difference.

These changes would reduce barriers and translate into faster, fairer care for all.

Thank you for inviting views on how to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services. From where I sit in England, with years of experience navigating NHS services for myself and friends, I believe the changes outlined could make a real difference if they are well targeted and well implemented.

First, addressing gaps for deprived and ethnic minority communities is essential. Too many people struggle with language barriers or feel their cultural needs aren’t understood. Bringing in more interpreters and ensuring staff are culturally competent makes care more approachable and safer. In my town, appointments are sometimes booked through bilingual families or friends, which isn’t ideal and can lead to missed follow-ups. I’d like to see dedicated resources for interpreters across GP surgeries and community clinics, plus outreach workers who visit community centres, mosques, temples and churches to explain services in plain language and invite people to seek help early, before crises develop. Collecting data on who is waiting longest and where language or cultural barriers are strongest would help target these resources more fairly.

Second, transport, parking and premises must be tackled, especially in rural or mobility‑challenged areas. I’ve heard of patients delaying or missing appointments because buses run infrequently, parking is limited, or the premises are not easy to access for those with mobility issues.
