A practical approach would be mobile clinics that visit villages on a regular schedule, complemented by outreach teams that can triage patients in their own communities. Telehealth hubs in local libraries or community centres could give people a familiar, low-cost way to have consultations without a long journey. It would help to provide incentives for practices to open at more flexible hours and to co‑locate services (for example, mental health workers in GP or community clinics) so people can get several needs met in one journey.

Third, I believe there should be visible, supported pathways to care that reduce waiting times across GP, community health and mental health. Expanding community mental health teams, with a strong emphasis on early intervention, crisis response and accessible talking therapies, would help many who still see physical health as the default and mental health as something separate. In our area, waiting times for talking therapies can be years, which is unacceptable when early help can prevent more serious disclouding later. We need staff who can offer timely assessments, short‑term therapies in community settings, and clear stepping‑stone routes so people aren’t bounced around between services. Parity with physical health should be the norm, not the exception, with urgent mental health care available in evenings and weekends for those in crisis.

Specific examples that would help include:
- More interpreters available across GP practices, with ongoing training in cultural competence for clinicians and reception staff.
- Regular mobile GP clinics and nurse-led outreach in remote or high‑need communities, with flexible appointment windows.
- Telehealth hubs run in partnership with local libraries or community centres, with staff to assist patients in booking and using video or telephone appointments.
- Incentives for practices to extend premises accessibility and to employ community health workers who understand local needs and can navigate social determinants of health alongside medical care.
- Expansion of community mental health teams, early‑intervention services, crisis response and accessible talking therapies, with a clear, joined‑up referral pathway to avoid delays.

I’ve seen how even small improvements—like a confident interpreter present at a first appointment, or a nurse from the community helping families understand a treatment plan—can make a big difference to whether someone engages with care promptly. If these changes are funded with reliable, long‑term investment and coordinated across NHS, social care and local authorities, I believe access will become much fairer and timelier for people who have traditionally slipped through the cracks.

Please consider local pilot schemes with robust evaluation so we can learn what works best in different settings and replicate successes. In the end, timely access is about making care available where people live, in language they understand, and in formats that suit their lives. That would be a meaningful step toward keeping our communities healthier and less anxious about seeking help when it is genuinely needed.

From our experience working across communities in Northern Ireland, timely access to GP, community health and mental health services will not improve meaningfully without addressing the workforce shortage. Targeted recruitment, accelerated international hiring, better pay, flexible working and genuine wellbeing support are essential to grow and retain primary care staff. We have seen practices struggle to fill posts; international recruitment helps but is hampered by registration delays and language support challenges. An accompanying national package of incentives and clear career paths would speed up fills, reduce reliance on locums and stabilise service delivery. 

We also need to protect continuity of care and offer longer appointment times for complex, chronic and vulnerable patients. Short slots drive repeat visits and poorer outcomes. Digital options have a role, but expanding online booking and e-consults must be matched with non-digital routes and support to avoid excluding older or poorer groups. 

Finally, create integrated teams and co-located services so that referrals are smoother and follow-up is timely. In short: invest in the workforce, protect continuity, and ensure digital access doesn’t come at the expense of those who need face-to-face care.

I don’t think the proposed tweaks on their own will deliver timely access where I live. In rural and outer-town parts of England, transport, parking and old premises are the real blockers. Buses run infrequently, trains aren’t reliable, and parking at GP practices can be limited or charged. Mobile clinics and outreach are a good idea, but only if they’re regular, predictable and properly staffed—not a faint hope you’ll catch a pop‑up clinic once in a season. I’d favour a fixed schedule: weekly mobile units in communities with clear notices and accessible premises, plus dedicated spaces for privacy. Telehealth hubs could help, but only where there’s reliable broadband and local support to help people join calls, not just a link text. 

Evening and weekend clinics would help working people, but we must fund and staff them fully; otherwise it just shifts demand elsewhere or burns out staff. For urgent non‑emergency needs, guaranteed same‑day urgent slots are essential, not a promise that drifts into the next day. NHS111, triage and booking systems also need to be smarter: a simple, real‑time view of capacity, better care navigation, and fewer hand-offs to prevent duplication and delays. 

In short, the concept is right, but implementation and funding must be far more robust to work.

Access to GP, community health and mental health services in our area would improve most if we address the staffing shortfall head on and invest in people. The bottleneck isn’t just about more appointment slots; it’s about a workforce that is stretched, burnt out and sometimes aging in parts of town. What would make a real difference is a coordinated package to grow and sustain primary care teams—starting now.

First, targeted recruitment to grow the pipeline of clinicians and support staff. I’d like to see stronger collaboration with local universities and medical/nursing schools to create clear routes into primary care. Quick wins could include expanded practice placements for students, fast‑track return‑to‑practice schemes for clinicians who’ve paused for family or health reasons, and dedicated regional recruitment squads that attend job fairs, advertise in community hubs and run local open days. I’ve heard from colleagues that having a visible local pathway makes people consider staying or returning rather than moving to another region. Partnerships with apprenticeships for healthcare assistants and health coaches would also broaden the team so patients get the right support at the right time.

Second, expand international hiring in a responsible, well‑managed way. We still have a real gap in primary care capacity and in mental health teams, and bringing in skilled clinicians from abroad can help plug that gap quickly. That would require streamlined visa routes for essential workers, practical relocation support, and a robust induction that includes NHS systems, language and cultural training, and a strong buddy/mentoring network. It’s important this is about complementary capacity, not replacement, and that new staff are supported to deliver high‑quality care from day one. In neighbouring towns, international colleagues have brought valuable experience and helped teams offer more flexible slots and continuity of care; with proper governance, this approach can work here too without compromising patient safety or staff wellbeing.

Third, pay and incentives must reflect the workload and the public service value of primary care. Up‑to‑date pay scales, sign‑on bonuses for hard‑to‑fill posts, retention payments, and improved pension and holiday terms would make a real difference. I’ve heard from a few frontline staff who’ve considered leaving because the financial and workload pressures are hard to balance with family life. A meaningful uplift would help attract new staff and keep those already here, which in turn reduces wait times for patients.

Alongside recruitment and pay, flexible working and wellbeing support are essential. GPs and their teams should be able to offer more flexible hours, job sharing, and safe, supported part‑time arrangements so experienced clinicians can remain in practice while meeting family or caring responsibilities. Extending opening hours into evenings and weekends, with robust triage that directs people to same‑day slots when appropriate, would substantially cut waiting times. Reducing admin burden through better IT, efficient electronic health records, and more practice‑based admin support would also free clinicians to see patients rather than chase forms.

Protecting staff wellbeing is not a luxury; it’s a necessity for timely care. Regular clinical supervision, confidential counselling, and formal wellbeing networks should be built into every practice. Protected admin time, reasonable workloads, and dedicated time for team debriefs after difficult cases would help reduce burnout and keep teams cohesive. The mental health pathway should be simpler to navigate for both patients and staff, with faster internal referrals and clearer case management.

To turn these ideas into reality, I’d like to see pilots in the most stretched areas with clear targets and transparent reporting. Track wait times, patient experience, and staff retention month by month and publish results so communities can see the impact. Involve patients and frontline staff in the design and evaluation of new services so they meet real local needs.

From my own experience, delays in routine GP access and in mental health referrals have been unsettling. When a same‑day slot is available, it makes a big difference to people’s confidence in the system and prevents problems from escalating. If we can recruit more people, support those who join with strong development and wellbeing packages, and offer flexible, patient‑centred care, I am confident waiting times will fall and the quality of care will rise across GP, community and mental health services.

To improve timely access, expand online booking and e‑consultations, but keep non‑digital options with support for older or disadvantaged patients; also offer evening/weekend clinics and guaranteed same‑day urgent slots to help working people with urgent needs.

I welcome the way this consultation focuses on making GP, community health and mental health services more timely and responsive. In our rural area, delays aren’t just inconvenient—they affect people’s health and independence, especially for those of us who are mobility‑limited or lack reliable transport. I’d like to see a package of practical, well‑funded steps that combine easier access with strong support for the staff who deliver these services.

Transport, parking and premises deficits are a big barrier. A reliable schedule of mobile GP clinics visiting our village, town hall or community centre on set days would cut journeys for many of us who can’t drive or must rely on infrequent bus services. It would be even better if these mobile services could carry basic diagnostics (blood pressure, glucose, wound checks) and coordinate with a patient’s regular record so we don’t have to repeat information each time. Clear, accessible parking near the premises, with dedicated spaces for disabled drivers and lifts or step‑free access, would make a real difference. Where ageing premises can’t immediately be refurbished, temporary but fit‑for‑purpose spaces in local schools, libraries or church halls with decent heating, clean toilets and privacy screens would help—alongside clear signage and a simple booking line.

Outreach and telehealth hubs should be part of a blended model, not a stopgap. I’ve seen how a telehealth hub in our community centre—staffed a couple of mornings a week with a nurse to help navigate devices—has lowered barriers for older residents to access nurse appointments, mental health check‑ins and follow‑ups after hospital discharge. For those who can’t travel, a video link or a telephone triage service that can schedule same‑day or next‑day GP slots and arrange home visits where appropriate would be invaluable. Partnerships with local libraries and community groups could provide safe, quiet spaces with simple digital coaching for people who are new to technology. Crucially, these hubs must be well‑funded, with robust cyber security and user‑friendly platforms that protect patient information while keeping processes simple for older users.

Timely access to mental health care needs deliberate design as part of primary care, not a separate but distant service. A local system where a mental health professional sits in a community hub a couple of days a week, with quick referral links from GPs and practice nurses, would help people who don’t want to travel far to seek support. Where possible, proactive outreach to carers and families—via medication reviews, sleep management, and stress reduction strategies—could prevent crises and reduce unnecessary A&E attendances.

To grow and retain the primary care workforce, I would support targeted recruitment and retention measures. Rural and mobility‑limited areas often lose staff to urban centres or warmer locations with easier commutes. A mix of targeted recruitment, international hiring where clinically appropriate, and sponsored return‑to‑practice pathways would help fill vacancies more quickly. Practical incentives matter: enhanced rural hardship allowances, relocation assistance, and clearer pay progression for those taking on longer or more flexible hours. Flexible working arrangements—job sharing, weekend posts, and longer annualised hours with protected time for training and wellbeing—would make these roles more sustainable, particularly for those of us who have spouses who still rely on us. 

Wellbeing support for staff must be explicit and funded. Access to confidential peer networks, supervision, and protected time for mental health and burnout prevention isn’t optional; it’s essential to maintain safe, compassionate care in small teams. A stable workforce is the backbone of timely access, and that means long‑term funding with sensible workforce planning, not short‑lived pilots.

I’ve witnessed the difference when a service becomes reliable and reachable. Last winter, when snow and road closures blocked longer journeys, a planned mobile clinic and telehealth option would have meant diabetic reviews or blood pressure checks didn’t get deferred for weeks. My neighbour’s mother, who has limited mobility, benefited from quick mental health support through a local hub’s video link—a sort of “no‑fright, no‑ride” gateway to care that kept her stable at home. If such approaches are scaled up with clear governance, we could see fewer late presentations, fewer hospital admissions, and better overall wellbeing for people in rural communities.

If this package is to work on the ground, it needs clear delivery milestones, transparent funding streams, and strong local engagement. I would like to see:
- A national framework for mobile clinics and telehealth hubs with guaranteed annual funding and defined service standards.
- Ring‑fenced capital and running costs for accessible premises, with rapid temporary spaces where refurbishment is slow.
- A workforce strategy that combines targeted recruitment with flexible working, competitive pay, and serious wellbeing supports, including international recruitment where appropriate and well‑managed return‑to‑practice routes.
- Strong data sharing protocols that protect patient privacy while enabling seamless care across GP, community health and mental health services, with patient and carer involvement in designing pathways.
- Evaluations of pilots against patient experience, wait times, health outcomes and staff wellbeing, with scaled expansion only after demonstrated benefit and value for money.

In short, timely access will come from a blended, well‑funded approach that puts patients in the centre, supports staff to stay in the job, and uses local solutions to meet local needs. I hope the government will back these commitments with long‑term funding and practical implementation plans, so people like me can rely on high‑quality care when we need it most.

To improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services, I wouldd prioritise two changes. First, extend GP hours with consistent evening and weekend clinics. This would help working people and those with caregiving duties who struggle to attend during the day. Second, guarantee a same-day urgent slot for non-emergency issues, with robust triage by phone or online so you can be seen quickly when symptom flare. In practice, these plans should be locally piloted with protected staffing and clear booking rules to avoid delays or unintended bias. In my area I’ve faced delays when trying to book a GP appointment; last year my partner needed urgent mental health support after work and we waited several days to see someone, which was far from ideal. An integrated approach, with community health workers and mental health staff co-located with GP practices, would speed up referrals and reduce repeated journeys. Digital booking tools and reliable triage are essential to make this work. Any expansion must be adequately funded and subject to rigorous monitoring to prevent widening inequalities, especially in more rural part of Scotland and among people with limited internet access.

I think boosting training places, return-to-practice programmes, apprenticeships and ongoing CPD could help, but I worry about funding and local staffing capacity matching demand. Long-term investment to grow GPs, nurses and mental health workers should improve timely access, alongside better triage and digital services.
I DON'T THINK SIMPLY EXPANDING GP SLOTS OR CO-LOCATED HUBS WILL FIX DELAYS; IN MY AREA WAITS PERSIST, AND WE ALSO NEED LONG-TERM FUNDING, BETTER WORKFORCE RETENTION, AND FLEXIBLE, OFF-PEAK ACCESS.

I strongly support changes to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services in Wales. Targeted resources are essential to close gaps for deprived, ethnic minority, migrant and marginalised groups. Providing interpreters and culturally competent staff in local practices, community hubs and outreach services would help people understand their options and attend appointments. In my village, language barriers have deterred people from seeking help, so outreach in Welsh and community languages would make a real difference.

Evening and weekend clinics and guaranteed same-day urgent slots would help working people, carers and those with urgent non-emergency needs juggle their commitments. I have seen how a Saturday slot at the local centre reduces travel and wait times for older residents with transport challenges.

Expanding multidisciplinary teams—pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates—can manage routine issues quickly, freeing GPs to concentrate on complex cases. For example, a pharmacist-led medicine review and a physio-led early rehab for back pain or joint problems would shorten waiting times and improve safety.

Overall, these steps would make timely care more predictable and fair for everyone in our community.

i really think in our area in England, timely access to GP services or mental health care often hinges on the system around the appointment, not just the clinician you see. I work full‑time and have school‑age children, so securing a same‑day slot can feel near impossible; phone queues stretch long and online booking can fail during busy mornings. When my family has needed mental health support, waiting lists have been lengthy and the next steps weren’t always clear. We’ve occasionally found relief through local pharmacies for quick advice or used urgent care as a bridge, but that isn’t a sustainable solution for ongoing issues.

What might help? I’d support investment in integrated, multi‑disciplinary community hubs where a single appointment can involve a GP, nurse, counsellor and social care link, with clearer pathways between NHS 111, urgent care and specialist mental health teams. Expanding same‑day triage slots and extending opening hours could ease pressure, provided staff workloads are managed. It’s also important to keep non‑digital routes open—phone lines and in‑person access—so people without reliable internet aren’t left behind. Any changes should preserve flexibility for working people and carers while reducing avoidable delays and fragmentation in care!

From my experience in Northern Ireland, timely access to GP, community health and mental health services remains inconsistent. There are gaps around interpreter services for minority and marginalised groups, and outreach to deprived communities is patchy, which means people delay seeking help. To improve access, I would prioritise targeted resources: fund on-demand interpreters and culturally competent staff, with stable funding for community health workers who can visit housing estates, care homes and quiet streets to raise awareness and help with bookings. Mobile clinics or community hubs in areas with poor transport links could provide GP and mental health drop-ins outside usual hours. Improve NHS111 and care navigation: modernise booking systems, ensure triage prioritises urgent cases, and reduce duplication—so a patient with chest pain gets a prompt appointment rather than a repeat call. In parallel, expand multidisciplinary teams (pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics, physician associates) to handle routine follow-ups, but with clear protocols, supervision and strong care coordination so GPs can focus on complex cases and maintain continuity. Any expansion must be funded and well integrated with existing practices to avoid fragmentation.

In our area of Scotland, I notice that the main issue isn't only the number of GPs but when you can actually speak to someone. Last month I tried to book a same-day appointment; I was on hold for 25 minutes, and the earliest slot was two weeks away. My wife’s recent mental health referral ended up with three separate calls and two different online forms, each with its own delays. A friend with an elderly parent found the weekend nurse clinics were cancelled because staff were pulled to hospital wards. The impact is that we end up managing conditions at home longer than is ideal, which can worsen health and increase hospital visits later.

I see some potential fixes, like more flexible hours, better on-the-day triage, and longer community-led mental health drop-ins; and some clinics are piloting simple online booking. But in rural parts, digital access and broadband remain inconsistent, so online-only approaches can leave people behind. Any improvement probably needs a mix: in-person, phone, and digital options, with local hubs to reduce travel and weather-related cancellations.

i really think i live in rural England and I don't think the suggested changes alone will improve timely access. Transport gaps, scarce parking, and the cramped conditions at the village practice mean many people miss or delay appointments. Mobile clinics parked in village halls, outreach teams, and local telehealth hubs could bring GP, community, and mental health support closer to home. Evening and weekend clinics, plus guaranteed same-day urgent slots, would help working people and urgent non-emergency needs. Yet these will only work if we solve staffing shortages; targeted recruitment, international hiring, better pay, flexible hours, and wellbeing support are essential to grow and retain clinicians. In my area, when a single GP leaves, queues swell and same-day slots disappear for weeks. We also need clear funding, robust transport links for patients, and safe premises with proper parking. Please back pilot schemes that combine mobile access, outreach, telehealth, and strong workforce incentives, with local evaluation to show real improvements!

In my area in England, timely access to GP, community health and mental health services would be most improved by three linked changes: expanding and strengthening community mental health teams; protecting continuity of care with longer, more thorough appointments for complex needs; and targeted work to close access gaps for deprived and minority communities through better interpreters, culturally competent staff and active outreach.

First, expanding community mental health teams and boosting early intervention and crisis response would make a real difference. When someone is in the early stages of mental health difficulty, or when a crisis hits, rapid, coordinated support stops problems from escalating. In practice this means more community-based teams with psychiatrists, psychologists, social workers and peer support workers who can see people quickly, offer same-day or next-day assessments, and stay connected as needs evolve. I’ve seen friends and colleagues struggle to access timely talking therapies because waiting lists are long or the support is only available after a crisis. If there were stronger local CMHTs, with flexible outreach, home visits when necessary and closer links to GP practices, people would recover faster and avoid hospital admissions. Access to evidence-based talking therapies such as CBT or family therapy should be scaled up, with parity to physical health services in funding and policy priorities, so people aren’t treated as “mental health” as a second-class concern.

Second, protecting continuity of care and allowing longer appointment times for those with complex, chronic or vulnerable conditions would reduce repeated visits and poor outcomes. For patients with multimorbidity or learning disabilities, the current time-limits mean important nuances—medication changes, side effects, social needs—get missed. When a single clinician or a consistent team follows a patient over time, care plans can be tailored, medications reviewed safely, and warning signs caught early. In my experience, longer appointments or a guaranteed longer slot for complex cases would also ease the administrative bottlenecks—fewer repeat calls, less time wasted on handovers, and better adherence to care plans. This approach would pay off by reducing emergency visits and hospital stays, and by giving people the reassurance that someone responsible is overseeing their health journey.

Third, we must actively reduce access gaps for deprived, ethnic minority, migrant and marginalised groups. This requires targeted resources, interpreters, culturally competent staff, and proactive outreach. I’ve seen how language barriers and limited information in non-English languages can deter people from seeking help or following through with referrals. In communities with high migrant populations, even when clinics exist, people can miss appointments because interpreters aren’t readily available or staff aren’t trained to understand different cultural perspectives on illness and treatment. Practical steps include funding dedicated interpreter services for primary care and mental health settings, training for clinicians on cultural humility and trauma-informed care, and deploying outreach workers who partner with local community groups, faith groups, schools and workplaces to raise awareness about available services. Dropping in with pop-up clinics in community hubs, offering appointments outside standard hours, and providing multilingual digital resources would also help. By actively reaching out and listening to communities, we can design services that people trust and feel comfortable using.

Taken together, these changes would level the playing field between mental and physical health services and deliver faster, more person-centred care. With stronger CMHTs, longer and more flexible appointments for complex cases, and a committed focus on removing language and cultural barriers, people would get the right support when they need it, reducing crises and improving outcomes for families and communities across our area.

In short: invest in robust community mental health teams, protect continuity with longer appointments for those who need them most, and actively reach out to and resource deprived and minority communities with interpreters and culturally competent care. If funded and implemented, this combination would make timely access a standard rather than a hope, easing pressure on GPs and hospitals while helping people live healthier, more secure lives.

Our organisation recognises the urgency of improving access to GP, community health and mental health services, but the change that would most improve outcomes is to protect continuity of care and lengthen appointment times for those with complex, chronic or vulnerable needs. Short slots aimed at speeding access often miss important details, leading to more follow-ups, repeated tests and, ultimately, avoidable hospital visits. I’ve seen cases where a patient with diabetes, chronic pain and anxiety could not be given a full med review and psychosocial check in a single 10-minute appointment; the lack of continuity meant crucial symptoms were overlooked until crises developed.

Practical changes to prioritise would include: 1) guaranteeing longer standard appointments for patients with multiple long-term conditions or mental health needs; 2) ensuring a named GP or stable care team for continuity across GP, community health and mental health services; 3) expanding roles for practice nurses, therapists and care coordinators to share the load while preserving a consistent clinician; 4) stronger integration across primary, community and social care with shared care plans; 5) patient-tailored triage that directs urgent needs to appropriate specialists without breaking continuity with the same clinician where possible. 

If speed is prioritised over stable relationships, patients will bear the cost through worse outcomes and higher long-term demand. Investment should be in time and team-based continuity, not merely shorter waiting times.

Agree Obviously.... Investing in mobile clinics, outreach, and telehealth hubs will tackle transport and premises gaps; ensure interpreters and culturally competent staff reach deprived communities; expand online booking while maintaining non-digital options for the elderly.

Co-located hubs that bundle GP, community and mental health services with social care and VCSE partners sound efficient in theory, but in Northern Ireland they risk creating new bureaucratic hurdles and uneven access. Our budgets are already stretched, and pushing resources into multi‑agency hubs can slow decision‑making and leave rural areas behind where getting to a hub isn’t practical. A hub might improve coordination, but without strong governance, clear funding lines and stable staffing it could simply delay urgent care or shift demand around rather than solve it. For working people, weekend or evening clinics are welcome in principle, but guaranteed same‑day urgent slots only work if there is reliable, predictable staffing. Right now we struggle with shortages in mental health and primary care, so the added complexity could worsen waits rather than shorten them.

A more immediate fix would be to bolster existing GP practices: fund more clinicians, protect time for same‑day mental health appointments within primary care, and implement robust digital triage to direct people quickly to the right service. Also invest in community link workers and flexible out‑of‑hours arrangements within current networks to prevent rural patients from being left out. In short, we need stronger staffing and clearer governance, not just bigger, multi‑agency hubs.

I'm not convinced expanding multidisciplinary teams will improve timely access; older patients value continuity with their GP, and delegating routine care could fragment decisions and delay urgent issues.

Agree. To improve timely access, the most impactful changes would be to protect continuity of care and lengthen appointment times for those with complex, chronic or vulnerable conditions, so we get proper reviews first time. For example, with my partner’s diabetes and arthritis, a standard 10-minute slot often meant we rushed through symptoms and forgot to address medication interactions. We need longer (20-30 minutes) slots or a named clinician who follows the patient over time. This reduces repeat visits and hospital-like crises. 

Also, ensure same clinician or small care team for ongoing conditions, with a proactive care plan and a dedicated care coordinator to catch issues early. Improve access through triage with clinical staff who know the history, plus same-day slots for urgent concerns. Strengthen links with community services (nurse-led clinics, physiotherapy, social support) and make mental health pathways easier to navigate with quick referrals and timely talking therapies. Digital reminders and secure messaging should complement, not replace, face-to-face care. Overall, these steps would smooth journeys, cut unnecessary visits, and improve outcomes in GP, community, and mental health services.

AS A REPRESENTATIVE OF A LOCAL COMMUNITY ORGANISATION IN ENGLAND, I MUST SAY I STRONGLY DISAGREE THAT THE QUICKEST FIX FOR TIMELY ACCESS IS SIMPLY TO RECRUIT MORE TRAINEES OR HIRE STAFF FROM ABROAD WITHOUT SAFEGUARDING HOW CARE IS DELIVERED DAY-TO-DAY. THE REAL BOTTLENECK IS CONTINUITY AND THE LENGTH OF CONSULTATIONS FOR PATIENTS WITH COMPLEX, CHRONIC OR VULNERABLE NEEDS. IN OUR AREA, A PATIENT WITH DIABETES, HYPERTENSION AND ANXIETY OFTEN SEES A DIFFERENT GP AT EACH VISIT, AND THAT FRAGMENTED CARE LEADS TO DUPLICATED TESTS, MISSED SIGNALS AND AVOIDABLE HOSPITAL VISITS. LONGER, REGULAR APPOINTMENTS WITH A NAMED CLINICIAN WOULD IMPROVE OUTCOMES AND REDUCE REPEAT VISITS IN THE LONG RUN. TRAINING AND RETURN-TO-PRACTICE SCHEMES ARE WELCOME, BUT THEY MUST BE PAIRED WITH SUSTAINABLE WORKLOADS, FLEXIBLE WORKING AND WELLBEING SUPPORT SO NEW STAFF STAY.

WHAT WOULD HELP MOST: LONGER CONSULTATIONS FOR COMPLEX CASES (RATHER THAN SQUEEZING EVERYONE INTO 10-MINUTE SLOTS), PROTECTED PATIENT LISTS WITH THE SAME CLINICIAN, INTEGRATED TEAMS INCLUDING MENTAL HEALTH WORKERS, AND STABLE ROSTERS THAT ENABLE GENUINE CONTINUITY. TARGETED RECRUITMENT, INTERNATIONAL HIRES AND CPD CAN HELP, BUT ONLY IF FUNDED ALONGSIDE EXPLICIT COMMITMENTS TO PRESERVE CONTINUITY AND STAFF WELLBEING.

From my perspective as an older resident in England, I’m worried that changes focused on NHS111, clinical triage and rapid booking may actually harm those of us with chronic or complex needs. In practice, NHS111 can send people to urgent care without a full history, and triage can misjudge what counts as urgent. The result can be delays for people who need careful assessment, not a quick phone call. Booking systems that require endless online steps or queuing across multiple services often waste trips to the wrong place and leave older folk exhausted chasing appointments.

I do think care navigation has a place, but it must not replace continuity. Lengthier appointments for complex patients are essential; otherwise we end up with repeat visits, more tests and more hospital referrals. Expanding multidisciplinary teams could help with routine tasks, yet without a clear named clinician coordinating everything, it risks fragmentation and a loss of personal knowledge about my situation. Pharmacists, physiotherapists and physician associates can help, but only if there is a steady chain of accountability and proper information sharing with my GP.

What would help most is systems that improve urgent triage while preserving continuity: a GP-led care plan for chronic cases, longer appointment times, and a single point of contact who coordinates across NHS111, community and mental health services.

Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services would be best improved by investing in co‑located community hubs that bring together primary care, community health, mental health teams, social care and VCSE partners. When services are co‑located or seamlessly linked, people can get triaged on the day, with faster follow‑ups and a holistic care plan, instead of bouncing between different offices and referral letters. In my area, where a hub approach has been piloted, patients can see a GP, chat with a nurse, and access social support in a single visit or via a linked appointment, which noticeably reduces waiting times and confusion. Expanding this with integrated back‑office systems and shared electronic records would prevent duplications and speed up part of the process for everyone.

Equally important is targeting resources for interpreters, culturally competent staff and outreach to deprived, ethnic minority, migrant and marginalised groups. On‑site interpreters, translated reminders, and proactive outreach by community workers to signpost and help book slots would make a real difference for people who currently delay care. Extending hours and offering flexible booking would also help those juggling work and caring responsibilities. Overall, a joined‑up, inclusive hub model with strong community partnerships is what will shift urgent access from a backlog to timely care.

I, as an older resident, support improving NHS111, clinical triage, and streamlined booking and care navigation to prioritise urgent cases, reduce duplication, and speed up access to GPs, community, and mental health services.

From my experience in England, timely access to GP, nurse and mental health services remains variable. The most impactful change would be to increase appointment slots and session capacity by hiring more GPs, practice nurses and therapists, and by expanding session lengths where appropriate to cover complex needs. Improving scheduling with more same-day triage, extended hours, and predictable slots (including some weekend availability) would cut the weekly scramble to fit in an urgent issue. I’ve waited weeks for a GP appointment even after contacting a practice for a same-day slot, and mental health referrals often take months; more integrated booking systems and efficient use of digital consultations when clinically appropriate could help. We should also consider group sessions for common conditions to widen access without sacrificing quality. 
However, there are still gaps for deprived and marginalised groups. We should target resources for interpreters and language-concordant clinicians, plus outreach through community groups to raise awareness of services. Training staff in culturally competent care, translating information into key languages, and offering mobile or community-based clinics in high-need neighbourhoods would reduce barriers. A dedicated outreach program in my area (with local schools, mosques and community centres) helped families navigate the system last year. Overall, I support a combined capacity and equity approach with measurable targets on wait times and language access.

As someone living in England and mindful of the pressures on our local NHS, I’m wary that simply adding evening and weekend GP clinics plus guaranteed same‑day urgent slots will automatically improve timely access. My concern is that without the right staffing, proper triage, and a focus on continuity of care, these changes could simply move the bottleneck rather than fix it.

First, staffing is the real constraint. Our surgeries already struggle to recruit and keep GPs, nurses and the necessary support staff. Extending hours would require more clinicians and back‑office teams, not just a tweak to the timetable. If new posts are funded but not filled, patients end up with the same delays, just at odd times. It’s reasonable to want more access, but it won’t materialise out of thin air; it needs a serious programme to recruit, retain and train practitioners who can stay in post for the long term.

Second, continuity of care matters, especially for older people like me. An urgent or late‑hour slot may mean seeing a different clinician each time, with a patchwork of notes and care plans. My own experience and what I’ve heard from neighbours is that ongoing GP relationships help prevent miscommunications and duplication of tests. When you juggle urgent slots with multiple clinicians, you risk losing the thread of someone’s medical history, which can compromise safety and treatment quality.

Third, access isn’t purely about the clock. Evening and weekend travel can be difficult or unsafe for those with mobility problems, those who rely on carers, or people without reliable transport. Dark evenings, parking issues, and the cost of getting to a clinic after work may exclude the very people who need help most. It’s not only about availability; it’s about being able to use that access safely and conveniently.

There’s also a risk that bolstering evening/weekend slots will siphon capacity away from daytime services. If the system tries to push more urgent slots into off‑peak times, routine care for chronic conditions, follow‑ups, and preventive work may suffer. We already see backlogs in routine checks, vaccinations, and management of long‑term illnesses; widening hours without expanding the workforce could simply shuffle problems to a different time of day.

Mental health requires particular caution. Urgent slots are not a substitute for a well‑funded, well‑staffed mental health system with crisis teams, community support and timely therapy. For people in distress or with severe anxiety and depression, you need coherence across services and dependable access to a trusted clinician, not just a late appointment with someone new who doesn’t know their history.

What would work better, in my view, is a targeted, well‑resourced approach:
- Ensure a robust, adequately paid workforce: more GPs, nurse practitioners, practice nurses, and allied health professionals, with clear career paths to attract and retain staff. Any extended hours plan must be paired with real recruitment and retention effort.
- Invest in continuity by creating reliable teams in hubs or “care where you live” models, so a patient can see familiar clinicians even for urgent slots.
- Use smart triage and targeted online/phone access to identify truly urgent cases, with clear pathways to in‑person assessment when needed, rather than blanket same‑day access for all.
- Maintain daytime access but balance it with safe, accessible after‑hours options, including transport support where needed and safe, well‑supervised clinics in well‑lit, well‑staffed sites.
- Strengthen mental health integration: rapid access to crisis support, same‑day/community teams, and guaranteed pathways to therapy and advise when needed, rather than relying on GP clinics alone.
- Focus on patient‑centred delivery: easy booking, reliable appointment times, and consistency, so people aren’t left waiting in limbo or repeating histories.

In short, I want improvements that actually expand and sustain access, not a shift of the same problems to evenings and weekends. Any policy should be evaluated against real capacity to hire, train, and retain staff; the value of continuity of care; safety and practicality for older, less mobile residents; and the ability to integrate with mental health and community services. A well‑designed combination of targeted extended hours, robust triage, and stronger workforce investment would be more likely to improve timely access than simply widening clinic hours.

In my area, timely access to GP services, community health and mental health care is a real lived issue for working people like me. I’ve seen routine GP appointments slidr into weeks, and when something urgent comes up the system dorsn’t always offer a same‑day slot reliably. Mental health referrals can be slow too, and that delay can turn minor concerns into bigger worries. I want to see a system that is capable now, while also building the workforce we’ll need in the long term. To tackle this, I’d prioritise three linked strands: 1) Build the size and skills of the workforce for the long term - Increase training places for GPs, nurses andd mental health professionals, and expand return‑to‑practice support for those who’ve stepped back. It’s not just about training new people; it’s about making sure people can come back into care with up‑to‑date skills and confidence. Apprenticeships and enhanced CPDD woul help create a more flexible career path that keeps talent in the system. - I’ve heard from colleagues and seen in practice how workload and burnout limit what clinicians can offer. A more sustainable piprline—well-supported trainees, robust supervision, and clear pathways back into practice—would translate into more timely appointments for patients without compromising safety. 2) Expand access windows and urgent care capacity - Routine appointments have to be more predictable, and urgent access should be guaranteed. Evening and weekend clinics, plus guaranteed same‑day urgent slots, would make it far easier for people who work standard hours to get seen without taking a day off. - A practicall step would be dedicated urgent‑care slots within GP hubs or local community clinics, with a simple triage process that directs truly urgent issues to same‑day care and routes less‑urgent matters to the next available appointment. This would reduce the bottleneck that currently pushes people to A&E for non‑emergency needs. 3) Do more to make access fair and easy, including digita and non‑digital options - Expanding online booking and e‑consultations can speed things up, reduce missed calls, and make it easier to find a slot. But I know that not everyone is comfortable with digital tools, and some people—older patients, those with limited data, or people without home internet—fac real barriers. - We need non‑digital option that work as well as digital ones: robust telephone triage, clear telephone lines with shorter wait times, and in‑person appointment booking at local hubs. It would help to have ‘digital champions’ or staff in community spaces (libraries, community centres) who can help patients book and use onlin systems. Equally important is to maintain walk‑in or same‑day nurse‑led clinics for those who can’t wait or don’t have online access. - A practical example from my area: when I tried to book for a routine check, the online system showed limited slots for weeks, while the phone line often resulted in long holds. An integrated approach—clear online booking with guaranteed next‑day urgent slots and a responsive phone option—would cover both the digitally savvy and the digitally excluded. Beyond these, better integration between GP, community health and mental health teamm would help people move seamlessly through care pathways. Co‑located services and shared care plans mean you don’t hav to repeat you story every time you switch from primary care to mental health support. Clear referral criteria and rapid access to talking therapies would also cut waiting times and prevent deterioration. In short, we need a credible, cross‑system plan that expands the workforcr, widens access windows, and preserves accessible routes for people who aren’t online. If these changes are implemented togehteer—with durable funding and measurable targets for wait times and same‑day slots—I think timely access to GP, community health and mental health services in my area would feel markedly more reliable and less stressful for patients and their families.

Access to GP appointments, community health and mental health services in my area remains uneven. The changes that would have the biggest impact, in my view, are: 1) a stronger NHS111 and clinical triage process that reliably flags urgent cases and directs people to the right next step, not into long general queues; 2) a unified, user-friendly booking system across GP, community teams and mental health services so people don’t have to recount their story or juggle multiple phone numbers; 3) trained care navigators who can explain local pathways, book appointments, coordinate home visits or community nursing, and follow up after urgent care; 4) steps to reduce duplication—shared records (with consent) and more consistent referral criteria so tests and forms aren’t repeated; 5) transparent timelines and escalation points so patients know what to expect.

Recently, NHS111 helped arrange a same-day GP visit for chest symptoms, which was reassuring, but I then experienced a slow, opaque handover to mental health services. A neighbour's family also found the mental health referral routes unclear and duplicated in effort. With proper investment and clear governance, these changes could improve timely access while protecting patient choice and safety.

From a resident perspective in England, transport, parking and premises constraints can create delays just when people need help most. The proposals I back would prioritise mobile clinics visiting rural villages and mobility-limited households on a regular schedule, extended GP hours at local hubs, and better parking and disabled-access at surgeries. Mobile clinics paired with outreach workers and phlebotomy teams would mean routine checks without long trips, and telehealth hubs in community venues (libraries, clinics) would offer quick video or phone access while preserving privacy.

For mental health, expanding community mental health teams, early intervention, crisis response and talking therapies is essential to get people the right help sooner and close the gap with physical health services. Additional investment in CMHTs, crisis teams and stepped-care pathways would cut waits and prevent crises. In my area, a small expansion of a CMHT and peer-support line noticeably reduced hospital referrals.

Finally, co-located community hubs merging primary care, community services, mental health, social care and VCSE partners would create seamless local care. A pilot hub in our town has already shown quicker GP triage, better social support coordination, and fewer journeys for families. More funding and shared data would help these hubs scale nationwide.

I don’t believe we’ll fix timely access by tinkering with appointment systems or expanding a few roles alone. The real blockages are staffing shortfalls and poorly integrated services. The changes that would help most are long‑term and concrete: targeted recruitment, including international hires, with fast‑track processes, meaningful pay improvements and retention incentives, plus flexible working and robust wellbeing support so experienced staff stay in post. In my area, practices are stretched to breaking point; patients wait weeks for routine GP contacts and longer for mental health support. When staff feel valued and can balance work with home life, vacancies begin to fill and access improves.

Investing in co‑located community hubs that bring primary care, community health, mental health, social care and VCSE partners under one roof or on a linked digital platform could make care genuinely seamless. A hub in another town reduced repeated referrals and cut the number of trips required by letting people see a GP, a counsellor and a social prescriber in one visit. I’ve seen a relative needing both GP advice and mental health support, and care was far smoother when services were coordinated rather than shuffled between separate buildings. These workforce and hub changes, properly funded and sustained, will actually improve timely access in the long run.

Agree. To improve timely access, the two most effective changes are: 1) targeted recruitment and retention of primary care staff, including international hiring, enhanced pay, attractive flexible working patterns, and dedicated wellbeing support. When a local practice expanded recruitment and offered more flexible hours, turnover fell and patients could get appointments within the same week instead of waiting many days. 2) investment in co-located community hubs that combine primary care, community health, mental health services, social care and VCSE partners. A nearby hub now houses a GP, district nurse, a mental health link worker and a voluntary sector information service in one building, with shared records and same-day triage for urgent cases; patients report smoother care journeys and fewer separate visits. Additional steps that would help: stable multi-year funding for workforce and digital infrastructure, plus robust digital triage and simpler referral pathways to reduce admin delays. Emphasising wellbeing and career development will keep staff here, which is crucial for timely access across GP, community and mental health services.

Transport gaps, limited parkin and premises deficits in rural Wales mean timely access to GP, community and mental health services is uneven. We propose a mix of mobile clinics and outreach teams visiting villages, community halls and schools, plus telehealth hubs in local centres with on-site staff to help people with digital access. Incentives to recruit and retain staff in rural posts—flexible contracts,, relocation support, housing assistance—will be essential to sustain improved access. We also see value in improving NHS111, clinical triage, and booking systems to prioritise urgent cases, reduce duplication and streamline patient flow, provided there are clear care pathways and solid data sharing between GP, communit and mental health services. In practice, this could mean shared triage notes, simple booking interfaces, and a team approac to care navigation that respects carers and older residents who struggle with digital tools. In our area, winter transport issue and limited parking have delayed follow-up for chronic conditions; a pilot mobile clinic or village hub would help, with evaluation to ensure equity and value for money.

Disagree—the plan overlooks rural and mobility-limited patients. Invest in mobile clinics, outreach, telehealth hubs and incentives; expand mental health teams, plus evening/weekend urgent slots to cut waits.

Support targeted recruitment and international hiring with fair pay, flexible working and wellbeing support to grow and retain primary care staff; but ensure rigorous training, proper induction and sustained funding to truly improve timely GP, community and mental health access.

I welcome and wholeheartedly support the changes proposed to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services. Expanding multidisciplinary teams – including pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates – will let routine issues be treated by the most appropriate professional, freeing GPs to focus on complex cases and those with multiple conditions. In my area, a physiotherapist-led back‑pain clinic within the practice has meant fewer GP appointments for straightforward musculoskeletal issues and quicker, more targeted care. I also strongly support evening and weekend clinics and guaranteed same‑day urgent slots. Many neighbours work long hours or have caring responsibilities, so access outside standard hours would stop minor problems from escalating into urgent ones. A trial of extended hours by our local practice was well used and noticeably reduced wait times. Finally, increasing training places, return-to-practice support, apprenticeships and CPD is essential to sustain a capable workforce. As a 65+ resident, I value continuity of care, and more training pathways will attract and retain GPs, nurses and mental health professionals locally, reducing travel and delays for patients like me and my family.

No, quick tweaks won’t fix access. We need long-term investment: more training places, return‑to‑practice support and CPD; expand multidisciplinary teams with pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates; fund co‑located hubs linking primary, community, mental health and social care for seamless local care.

Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services is too variable in our area, and that inequality hurts older residents who rely on steady care. I support a long‑term, workforce‑led approach to change, with sensible caveats about funding and local planning. Specific changes that would help include: 

- Increase training places for GPs and nurses: more medical school places and GP registrar posts linked to local practices so clinicians settle in and stay locally. 
- Expand return-to-practice support: funded schemes, flexible hours, refresher courses and mentoring to bring clinicians back after career breaks, reducing gaps when staff retire or move. 
- Grow apprenticeships and CPD: local routes for training nurses, therapists and mental health workers; attract career changers and ensure ongoing professional development so teams stay capable of handling demand. 
- Strengthen community multidisciplinary teams: better collaboration between GPs, district nurses, pharmacists and talking‑therapies to triage quickly and manage conditions in the community, cutting unnecessary hospital visits. 
- Ensure concrete, measurable delivery: protected CPD time, clearer recruitment incentives in hard‑to‑fill areas, and transparent waiting‑time data so progress is visible.

In practice, I’ve seen GP appointments delayed by weeks and mental health referrals stretch into months, which is unacceptable for those of us in later life who need continuity of care now.

Access to GP, community health and mental health services in our area could be improved through a careful mix of targeted resources and real-world delivery changes. Language barriers and cultural misunderstandings repeatedly slow care: in one practice an interpreter wasn’t available for a family with limited English, so important details were lost and appointments ran late. Providing interpreters or on-demand translation services, plus robust cultural competency training for front-line staff and more community health workers drawn from local migrant and marginalised groups, would help reduce gaps in access. On transport and premises, many people experience delays due to parking difficulties, limited bus routes or working hours that clash with clinic times. Pilot mobile clinics at community hubs, supermarkets or housing estates in the evenings and on weekends, plus small telehealth hubs in libraries or community centres, could cut unnecessary travel and waiting. Incentives for practices to extend hours, offer same-week mental health slots, and collaborate with local voluntary groups would also support timely access. I’d like to see targeted pilots in the most deprived areas with clear, ongoing feedback from residents to measure real improvements and keep services responsive to need.

Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services would improve most if we adopt a blended model that respects both digital and non-digital routes. Expanding online booking, e-consults and remote triage can reduce waiting times and help people with straightforward needs, but there must be safe, non‑digital equivalents and support for those who are digitally excluded. In my street, an elderly neighbour struggles with apps, yet a phone call remains essential.

Crucially, we must protect continuity of care and give longer appointments for complex, chronic or vulnerable patients. A longer slot with the same clinician for, say, diabetes or depression management would reduce repeated visits and improve outcomes, even if a digital option exists.

Finally, expand multidisciplinary teams to handle routine cases and free GPs for complex care. Pharmacists, physiotherapists and nurse prescribers can handle medication reviews and musculoskeletal advice, while mental health staff embedded in practices can offer brief interventions early. I’ve seen a practice where a pharmacist-led review reduced emergency helplines, and it worked well. The risks are ensuring privacy, robust training, and maintaining in-person access when needed.

Overall, a carefully funded mix would help, but must not leave parts of the community behind.

From my experience living and working in England, timely access matters, but not if it comes at the expense of continuity of care. Short-notice GP slots and urgent same-day access are useful, yet they often fragment treatment for people with complex, chronic conditions and mental health needs. I’ve seen my own family twice be assigned to different GPs within weeks, forcing us to repeat histories and risk missing subtle changes in symptoms. That repeated hand-off means more visits, not fewer, and slower progress.

I’m skeptical about a policy push toward large co-located hubs unless they come with strict governance: clear leadership, shared records, and a named clinician accountable for each patient’s plan. Without that, hubs risk duplication and gaps in care.

Evening and weekend clinics could help working people, but only if they preserve continuity—patients should be offered slots with their usual clinician or a protected team. Urgent same-day slots should exist, but they must be integrated with ongoing care plans.

Preferred changes: longer appointments for complex cases; protected time with a named GP; robust IT sharing; and co-located hubs governed by accountable teams with patient input.

I strongly support creating co-located hubs that join GP, community and mental health with social care and VCSE partners, and expanding training, return-to-practice and CPD to sustainably grow the workforce; this will improve timely access locally.

In my area, timely access to GP, nurse and therapist appointments can be inconsistent, so I strongly support changes to increase appointment capacity and flexibility. This means hiring more GPs, nurses and therapists, expanding session lengths for complex cases, and smarter scheduling to fill gaps—including more same-day slots and extended hours in evenings and weekends. In my practice, even a small increase in clinicians would cut waits, reduce urgent phone calls and help people manage chronic conditions before they worsen. A recent experience for me was needing a GP for a persistent issue; the earliest slot was about a week away. If there were more slots and better triage, I could have had guidance sooner and avoided unnecessary uncertainty.

For mental health and therapy, expanding therapist slots and allowing longer appointment blocks for complex cases would improve outcomes and reduce repeat visits. I have seen friends struggle to access timely counselling, and longer, regular sessions would make a real difference.

I also back expanding online booking, e-consultations and remote care, but with robust non-digital options and support to avoid excluding older or disadvantaged patients—phone triage, in-person sign-ups, and help booking through carers or community groups. Protecting continuity of care with longer appointment times with the same clinician for chronic or vulnerable patients would further improve outcomes and reduce repeated contacts. Overall, these changes would shorten waits and keep people healthier and less stressed.

From where I sit in England, I want better access, but I fear the proposed push to online booking and remote care will lock out many older and less tech‑savvy patients. In my local practice the online slots often show none available, and the phone lines are flooded for hours. I’ve had to travel to the surgery to book a routine blood test because I couldn’t get through by phone. Not everyone has reliable internet or the digital skills to use e-consults, and some carers are not always available to help. So please keep non‑digital routes: a clearly staffed telephone line, in‑person booking at reception, and staffed helpdesks to assist with online forms, plus home visits for those who cannot travel.

Evening and weekend clinics would help, but only if there are enough GPs and nurses to run them without compromising daytime care. In practice, when Saturday clinics ran, doctors felt stretched and senior staff pulled away from chronic care management. Urgent same‑day slots sound good, but they must be true urgent slots with proper triage and longer appointment times, not rushed slots that trade off continuity. Mental health care, in particular, suffers when digital triage replaces real clinician contact; timely, in-person or video contact with a familiar clinician is essential.

Crucially, people with complex, chronic or vulnerable needs benefit from continuity and longer consultations. A fixed GP who knows my history saves time and reduces repeat visits. Please fund a blended system that protects continuity, expands access without excluding anyone, and gives longer appointments when needed.

Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services is a real challenge where I live in Scotland. I’d support expanding community mental health teams, including early intervention and crisis response, with more talking therapies available locally. If someone can get a counsellor or supported self-help early, it stops problems from growing and reduces pressure on urgent services. Strengthening NHS111, clinical triage and care navigation with a clearer booking path would prioritise urgent cases, reduce duplication and help young people like me move through the system more quickly.

At the same time, for people with long‑term, complex needs, continuity of care is essential. Longer appointment times and a named clinician who can follow a patient across services would likely improve outcomes and cut repeat visits. In practice, I’ve seen friends face scattered referrals and changing GPs which makes building trust hard. Investments in digital booking, stable care teams and local crisis lines could work together to deliver both speedy access and steady, person‑centred care.

i really think timely access to GP, community health and mental health services is essential for maintaining health and preventing crises. In my area, evening and weekend slots are scarce, and urgent non‑emergency issues can escalate while I wait for a same‑day appointment. A practical change would be extended-hours clinics in GP practices for at least two weeknights and a Saturday morning in every practice. Guaranteeing same‑day urgent slots—either via telephone triage with a definite slot or an on‑call clinician—would help working people who cannot take time off. Better integration of mental health into primary care is also needed, with immediate access to a counsellor or psychologist when a crisis is identified, to prevent deterioration. My own experience: I’ve rearranged work to access early or late appointments, and a relative waited two weeks for a mental health referral before things worsened. I welcome pilots to test these approaches, provided funding covers extra staff, robust triage, and transport considerations, and that patient choice remains respected. If rolled out thoughtfully, these changes could cut avoidable crises and ease pressure on urgent care!

Access to timely GP, community health and mental health services would improve most if funding targeted at the gaps in our area: interpreters and culturally competent staff, plus active outreach to deprived, ethnic minority, migrant and marginalised groups. For example, multilingual helplines and community health workers visiting local markets and mosques or churches help people who otherwise miss appointments. I’ve seen families miss GP rounds because language barriers and lack of trusted staff kept them from booking.

Evening and weekend clinics, with guaranteed same-day urgent slots, would make a real difference for working people and those with urgent non-emergency needs. I work shifts and often have to take a day off, or wait weeks for a non-urgent slot; weekend clinics would fit around families and carers.

Finally, increasing appointment slots across GPs, nurses and therapists through targeted hiring, expanded sessions and smarter scheduling would cut waits. In practice, more staff and longer slots for mental health therapy would reduce drop-offs and improve continuity of care. Of course, this needs proper funding, robust data to prevent disparities, and accessible booking options (online and phone) for those with limited digital access.

From my experience in Scotland, timely access to GP and mental health services in my area varies; last year I waited three weeks for a routine GP appointment, and a neighbour struggled for months to access local mental health support. This shows how fragile current capacity is. In the short term, targeted recruitment, international hiring, incentives and better pay are needed to attract and retain staff. Flexible working and stronger wellbeing support would reduce burnout and keep teams stable, letting practices offer more slots.

For working people, I would welcome evening and weekend clinics and guaranteed same-day urgent slots; a straightforward triage system could direct patients to the right clinician and protect capacity for urgent cases. An urgent non-emergency slot in every practice would prevent avoidable crises.

Longer term, increasing training places, return-to-practice support, apprenticeships and CPD will sustainably grow GPs, nurses and mental health professionals. Better use of multidisciplinary teams, including pharmacists and allied health professionals, can share workload and shorten waits while maintaining quality.

Overall, a balanced package that combines recruitment, flexible hours and long-term training is essential to make access timelier and more reliable.

I understand the aim to speed up access by expanding online booking, e‑consultations and remote care. However, I strongly disagree that digital expansion alone will deliver timely, fair access. In practice it often harms those who are already at a disadvantage. My neighbour, aged 72 and not confident with tech, can’t reliably use online systems; my own attempts to book a same-day appointment for my child last month were hampered by slots vanishing within minutes online and a constantly busy phone line. Waiting days for routine care forces parents to consider A&E, which is unfair and inefficient. 

Transport and premises are real blockers too. In our rural area, limited parking and long distances make in-person visits daunting, even for those who can use digital tools. I’ve seen mobile clinics and outreach work when funded, but they’re inconsistent. A plan should add mobile clinics rotating through villages, telehealth hubs in libraries or community centres with staff to assist, extended hours and weekend clinics, and transport support—subsidised travel, flexible parking, and better access to well-equipped premises. 

A balanced mix—digital options plus robust non-digital routes and local outreach—would actually improve timeliness and equity.

Agree. The changes that would most improve timely access are those that protect continuity of care and lengthen appointment times for complex, chronic and vulnerable patients. In my area, people with long-standing conditions often see different clinicians at each visit, which leads to fragmented care and unnecessary repeat trips. Allocating longer slots—20 to 30 minutes for routine reviews and medication changes—would give GPs and practice nurses time to assess symptoms, review medications, and adjust plans without delaying care. Continuity matters: seeing the same GP or small care team builds knowledge, reduces errors, and lowers hospital admissions from missed signals. 

For mental health and community services, longer initial assessments and integrated teams (GP, nurse, psychologist, social worker) in a single appointment would cut waiting times and prevent crises. When a complex patient has a coordinated plan, rather than separate, staggered contacts, outcomes improve and follow-ups become fewer. Flexible access, including a few extended hours or reserved slots for high-need patients, would also help. 

In short, protecting continuity and investing in longer, well-coordinated appointments would improve outcomes, reduce repeat visits, and deliver timely care for aging residents dealing with chronic and mental health needs.

Agree. Improving NHS111 and clinical triage, along with streamlined booking and care navigation, would prioritise urgent cases and reduce duplication, making it easier to access GP, community health and mental health services promptly and with clear patient flow.

I understand the aim to cut waiting times, but I strongly disagree with plans that push online booking and remote care as the main fix without solid, non-digital access for those who need it most. In my area, many elderly residents struggle with apps and phone systems, and interpreters are not reliably available when bookings are made online - what a surprise. We need targeted resources—trained interpreters, culturally competent staff, and active outreach into deprived and migrant communities to help people know what services exist and how to use them. For example, a Bangladeshi pensioner neighbour of mine missed a GP appointment because the system is online-only and the phone line is hard to get through after work hours. Community workers visiting local centres to explain services and help with on-the-spot triage would make a real difference. We also need more capacity: extra frontline staff, longer opening hours, and mobile clinics in estates, plus guaranteed non-digital booking via phone, in person, or at community venues. Mental health services particularly need same-day slots and culturally appropriate counsellors. Remote options have their place, but without these safeguards the elderly and disadvantaged will be left behind. A balanced approach is essential, not a digital-only fix.

Agree. In England, timely access to GP, community and mental health services remains hampered by workforce gaps and geographic barriers. The proposal to expand training places, return‑to‑practice support, apprenticeships and CPD is essential for sustainable growth of GPs, nurses and mental health professionals. A steady pipeline of locally trained staff reduces reliance on agency hires and helps communities develop a sense of continuity in care.

From our experience, targeted recruitment and flexible working are critical. We’ve run a mobile GP outreach van and a community telehealth hub in rural areas, which cut waiting times and improved access for families and carers. This should be scaled and complemented by transport improvements, better parking and flexible premises usage so clinics can operate in convenient locations.

International recruitment, enhanced pay, wellbeing support and clear career progression are also important levers to attract and retain staff, especially in rural or deprived areas. If implemented together, these measures will shorten delays, improve early intervention in mental health and reduce avoidable hospital visits, benefiting patients and staff alike.

From our organisation representing older residents in England, we welcome the push to expand online booking, e-consults and remote care as a route to timelier access to GP, community health and mental health services. Digital options can cut waiting times and streamline triage when implemented well. However, many of our members remain digitally excluded due to age, cost, or limited local connectivity. For instance, in our area roughly a third of residents over 75 do not have reliable internet at home, and some live in places with weak mobile signals or poor broadband. Online portals can be harder to navigate for those with limited IT literacy or sensory impairments, and we have heard of urgent issues being inadvertently delayed when staff expect patients to use digital channels first. Therefore, any expansion must be paired with strong non‑digital alternatives and support.

We propose: extended telephone triage and same‑day telephone or in‑person appointments; in‑clinic drop‑in slots for those who cannot use online services; community hubs with trained staff to provide digital assistance; and funding for devices and affordable data plans for low‑income households. Crucially, collect data on wait times by modality to ensure equity and maintain multiple pathways to access.

Living in England and dealing with the realities of everyday healthcare, I think the changes that would most improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services are twofold: firstly, a robust expansion of community mental health teams, early intervention pathways, crisis response, and talking therapies to close the gap with physical health services; and secondly, a pragmatic, well-staffed approach to growing and keeping the primary care workforce so these services can actually be delivered without burning people out. I’m cautiously optimistic, but I’m also wary of simply piling on more services without solving the underlying capacity and workforce problems we consistently see on the ground.

On the first front, expanding community mental health teams and early intervention makes obvious sense. In my area there are times when a referral to a talking therapy service is received, but the wait to start treatment feels interminable, sometimes weeks or months. Early intervention services that can identify anxiety and depression before they become entrenched could really change people’s trajectories, especially for younger adults who might otherwise slide into crisis. I’ve seen instances where crisis response teams could have made a difference if they could operate with more immediate response windows and clearer pathways back to ongoing care, rather than re-triaging individuals who end up in A&E because there was no urgent, workable alternative. If these teams are properly integrated with GPs and schools, workplaces, and community services, we could address symptoms earlier and reduce the long-term burden on both people and the system. In practice, that means more flexible talking therapies (including digital options where appropriate), stronger liaison with primary care, and robust 24/7 crisis support so people aren’t left waiting alone when things feel urgent.

That said, the best-designed plan can choke on its own ambition if the workforce isn’t there to deliver it. My concern is that even with more teams and better referral routes, if GPs, nurses, therapists and support staff are stretched thin, the promised improvements won’t land at the patient’s doorstep. We need a targeted, coherent strategy to recruit and retain staff who can actually work in teams that match patient demand. That includes targeted recruitment within the UK and, where appropriate, international hiring, supported by realistic visa routes and induction that makes new clinicians productive quickly while safeguarding quality and patient safety. It also means meaningful pay progression, better incentives to work in underserved areas, and more flexible working patterns that acknowledge family life and mental health among clinicians themselves. Flexible scheduling, part-time routes into practice, and protected time for professional development could help reduce burnout and improve retention.

In my experience, improving access also hinges on practical supports around the workforce. For example, funded wellbeing programmes for frontline staff, supervision and peer support, and clear career pathways within primary care and community services. The goal isn’t just to hire more people but to keep them healthy and motivated so they stay in the job long enough to build trust with patients.
