Flexible working and improved staffing mixes—like more first-contact physiotherapists or nurse practitioners in GP settings—could alleviate some GP bottlenecks and free GPs to focus on complex cases. A reliable IT backbone, shared care plans, and timely access to patient data across community and primary care are essential so that teams can coordinate without duplication or information gaps.

I’d also want any major expansion to come with strong local accountability and patient involvement. Patients and communities should help shape what “timely access” means in practice: what counts as urgent, what constitutes reasonable waiting times, and how to triage in ways that aren’t purely demand-led. Rural and underserved urban areas must not be left behind by a one-size-fits-all model, and we should track equity of access as a core metric.

Overall, I’m open to a more ambitious mental-health and community-care agenda, provided it’s matched with a credible workforce plan, sensible funding, and robust implementation that puts patient experience and clinician wellbeing at the center. If we can pair expanded services with real improvements in recruitment, retention and flexible working, we could see genuinely faster access and better parity with physical health care. But I’m wary of promises without the people and systems to back them up.

Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services would improve most if we invest in co‑located community hubs that integrate primary care, mental health, social care and VCSE partners. Putting these services under one roof makes referrals smoother, care more holistic and people less likely to fall through the cracks.

In my area there’s been a small hub trial where a GP, a nurse, a mental health worker and a social prescriber share the same building and calendar. On the day I visited for anxiety, I was able to see a GP and talk to a mental health practitioner in the same place, with a clear plan and fast follow‑up. I’ve waited weeks for mental health appointments after ringing my GP; a co‑located model would route you to the right person quickly and prevent gaps in care.

What’s needed next: dedicated funding for hubs in every neighbourhood, integrated IT so records move with you, extended hours and same‑day triage, and strong links with local charities and community groups. Also ensure patient voices shape local leadership. This approach would ease pressure on urgent services and keep people healthier at home.

To improve timely access, protect continuity of care with longer appointments for complex cases and expand multidisciplinary teams (pharmacists, physios, paramedics, physician associates) to handle routine visits, freeing GPs for high-need patients.

As an organisation responding from England, I disagree with relying on generic capacity increases alone to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services. The proposals will only work if they are backed by targeted resources for deprived, ethnic minority, migrant and marginalised groups: funded interpreters, bilingual staff, culturally competent training, and active outreach with trusted community organisations to close real access gaps. Evening and weekend clinics and guaranteed same-day urgent slots are essential improvements, but they must be delivered with real capacity and protection for those slots, not as a token gesture.

In practice, without dedicated funding for outreach and staffing, these measures will be underutilised. For example, in our area interpreters and multilingual professionals significantly boost attendance and trust, whereas language barriers alone cause delays and miscommunication in urgent cases. Likewise, working people struggle to attend daytime appointments; without workable after-hours provision and reliable urgent slots, health needs deteriorate.

If these changes are pursued, they must include ring-fenced money for interpreters, targeted outreach, and culturally competent recruitment, plus explicit equity targets and monitoring to ensure the most vulnerable actually benefit, not just consultation-chasing headlines.

In our area, timely access to GP, community health and mental health services is variable, and I think there’s a real opportunity to improve it by combining digital solutions with solid non-digital options. I’m broadly in favour of expanding online booking, e-consultations and remote care, but only if we also invest in keeping traditional channels and practical support for people who can’t or don’t want to go digital.

Online booking and e-consults can cut down wasted time and speed things up for lots of people. I’ve used online booking to secure same-day slots for routine matters and it’s often quicker than waiting on a phone queue. When a simple follow-up or a query about a prescription comes up, an e-consult can be a convenient way to get a quick response without a trip to the surgery. For mental health, remote options can help people who find it hard to travel or who need flexible timing around work or childcare. And digital triage can help direct people to the most appropriate service, freeing up clinicians to focus on those who need urgent or face-to-face assessment.

But there are real caveats. My mother, who is in her late sixties and not at all confident with digital tools, struggles with online portals and gets anxious about entering medical information online. If we rely too heavily on digital channels, we risk leaving people behind, especially older residents, those with limited broadband or data, and people with low digital literacy. I’ve also encountered situations where an e-consult felt too generic and didn’t capture the nuance of a symptom or the concerns a patient has. In those moments, speaking to a person on the phone or turning up in person is still the best option.

To make any expansion work, we need a robust mix of channels, not a one-size-fits-all approach. Key changes I’d like to see include:
- A guaranteed mix of access options: online booking and e-consults, plus clearly advertised telephone triage, same-day walk-in access and in-person appointments where appropriate. If a same-day slot isn’t available online, there must be a swift alternative by phone or in person.
- Strong non-digital support: reception staff with time to guide people through booking options, and “assisted digital” sessions where trained volunteers or staff help patients set up online accounts, understand how to submit an e-consult, or navigate digital symptom checkers.
- Community anchors for digital access: funding for public Wi‑Fi in libraries, community centers, and GP practices, plus devices on loan for those who can’t afford them. This would help people complete online bookings, access digital mental health tools, and participate in remote appointments.
- Inclusive design for mental health services: ensure remote options complement, not replace, in-person care, with clear signals for when a face‑to‑face visit is necessary. Expand community and primary care mental health teams so people can be seen quickly, with options for after-work or weekend appointments where possible.
- Staff training and workflow redesign: clinicians and reception staff should be equipped to triage digital requests effectively, with protocols to escalate quickly if a patient’s needs aren’t adequately addressed online. Internally, we need reliable back-up systems so online channels don’t fail because of a tech glitch.
- Transparent performance indicators: measure wait times by channel, not just overall averages, and publish how quickly patients receive appropriate care across GP, community health and mental health services. Use patient feedback to adjust channels and processes.
- Safety and privacy assurances: reassure patients that data shared online is protected and that sensitive information is treated with the same care as in person, with options to discuss more sensitive issues by phone or in person if preferred.

In short, the goal should be timely access for everyone, via multiple routes tailored to individual needs. Digital options should reduce friction for those who can use them while not becoming a barrier for those who can’t. If these changes are implemented with proper funding, training and ongoing evaluation, we can improve access for most people and avoid widening health inequalities.

I live in Scotland and work full‑time, so timely access to GP, community health and mental health services must fit around working hours. I strongly support bringing in evening and weekend clinics and guaranteeing same‑day urgent slots. This would reduce missed work, urgent care visits and the risk of conditions worsening when people can’t access care quickly.

A future model should include co‑located community hubs that integrate primary care, community health, mental health and social care with VCSE partners, so local care is seamless and coordinated. In my area, having to travel between GP, a mental‑health service and social support can waste time and add stress. If there were a hub open late on two weeknights and Saturday mornings, with a named care coordinator and guaranteed same‑day urgent access, I could get a symptom check, a mental‑health check‑in, and, if needed, social support all in one place. This would improve continuity and reduce repeat appointments. I’ve seen similar hubs work well in other parts of Scotland, delivering shorter waits and more collaborative care. Please invest in rolling out this model with strong VCSE partnerships to address both medical and social needs in communities.

From our organisation’s perspective in England, timely access to GP, community health and mental health services is not being solved by tinkering around the edges. We strongly disagree with the view that minor tweaks will close the gaps. The most effective changes require expanding community mental health teams, robust early intervention, improved crisis response and widening access to talking therapies, all supported by ring-fenced funding and clear national benchmarks to achieve parity with physical health. In addition, we need to scale multidisciplinary teams—pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates—to manage routine cases so GPs can prioritise complex care. 

What this would look like in practice is integrated hubs where a patient can access GP, mental health clinician, physio and pharmacist in one visit; 24/7 crisis lines with rapid in-person or remote response; and streamlined referral pathways with interoperable data sharing to cut duplication and delays. In our area, CAMHS waiting times remain lengthy and many talking-therapy slots are scarce; out-of-hours support is inconsistent. Without these systemic changes, current access will not meaningfully improve and health inequalities will persist.

Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services is crucial for young adults in Wales, especially students juggling study and work. I strongly agree that changes proposed will help. First, we need to grow the workforce in primary care: targeted recruitment, including international hiring, supported by pay improvements, relocation assistance, flexible working and wellbeing support. This could mean more GPs, nurse practitioners and reception/administrative staff, with flexible rosters and longer-term career progression, so practices aren't burning out staff. In my area I have seen appointments cancelled or moved because someone was off sick; more stable staffing would reduce that. Second, expand community mental health teams and early intervention services. More staff in MDTs, robust crisis response and expanded talking therapies would close the gap with physical health services and prevent crises. Waiting times for CAMHS in Wales can be too long; expanded teams would help. Third, increase appointment slots and capacity by hiring more clinicians and expanding sessions, plus smarter scheduling. Evening and weekend slots, online triage and efficient booking systems would help students like me fit care around lectures and part-time jobs. Overall, these measures would deliver faster, fairer care and keep people healthier and less anxious about accessing help.

Improving timely access will hinge on strengthening NHS111 and clinical triage, modernising booking systems, and better care navigation to prioritise urgent cases and reduce duplication. For NHS111, I would support a more capable clinical triage that can fast-track genuine urgent GP, community health, and mental health needs to same‑day slots or rapid assessment teams, with a clear hand‑over to the right service. In practice, it would mean fewer bounced calls and quicker, actionable directions rather than vague advice to recontact later. 

A single, connected booking system across GP practices, community clinics, and mental health services would be transformative. Real‑time visibility of appointments, online booking, and the ability to transfer information between services would prevent duplicating assessments and repeated history-taking. 

Care navigation roles in surgeries and hubs could guide people to the most appropriate service first time, whether that is a same‑day GP appointment, a mental health crisis line with quick intake, or a fast‑track to community nursing. 

In my experience, when routing is clearer and slots are available promptly, urgent needs are met sooner, and the pressure on urgent care flows improves. I’d welcome targeted investment to implement these connected, triaged pathways.

As a local health organisation, we warmly welcome the focus on improving timely access to GP, community health and mental health services. In our experience, people often endure long waits for talking therapies, limited same-day GP availability, and delayed support after crises. The overarching aim must be to bring mental health on an equal footing with physical health, so that people get the right help at the right time, close to home.

First, expanding community mental health teams and strengthening early intervention, crisis response and talking therapies is essential. When someone in our community begins to struggle with anxiety, depression or emerging psychosis, rapid access to assessment and stepped care can prevent escalation and hospital admission. We would support doubling down on home-based and community-based teams so people can be seen quickly in their own environment. That also means guaranteeing timely access to evidence-based talking therapies—cognitive behavioural therapy, dedicated anxiety and OCD pathways, and talking therapies for mood disorders—with capacity to offer brief, targeted interventions or longer-term plans as needed. A robust crisis response that can reach people within hours, 24/7, and includes liaison with A&E and primary care, would reduce avoidable crises and hospital use. Importantly, integrating these teams with GP practices and local community services can create a seamless care pathway and improve outcomes.

Second, to grow and retain the primary care workforce we need focused recruitment and staff wellbeing at the core. Targeted recruitment, including international hiring where appropriate, needs to be supported by streamlined registration, welcome incentives and clear career development. Practical steps include improving pay and benefits, offering flexible working arrangements, and providing strong wellbeing and supervision packages to tackle burnout. In our area, vacancies in GP and nurse roles have a direct impact on patient access and wait times; reducing turnover and creating sustainable rosters would translate into more consistent appointment availability. We have seen practices that introduced longer-term rotas, protected time for professional development, and more supportive supervision report better morale and a gradual increase in patient access. A strategic package that makes general practice a desirable, well-supported career would pay dividends in better access and continuity of care.

Third, increasing appointment slots and session capacity across GPs, nurses and therapists is fundamental. This requires not only hiring more clinicians but also expanding session capacity and using smarter scheduling. Concrete steps include hiring additional GPs and nurse practitioners, expanding therapy slots (including group sessions for chronic conditions and early intervention), and extending hours to early mornings, evenings and some weekends to suit patients who cannot attend during traditional hours. Optimising booking systems—triage by telephone or online, same-day triage for urgent cases, and dynamic scheduling that can shift slots between primary care, mental health, and community services—can markedly cut waiting times. Where clinics have introduced one-stop triage, increased same-day access and a mix of short and longer follow-ups, people report shorter waits and more consistent continuity of care.

Finally, these changes must be implemented with a clear focus on equity. Access should improve across urban and rural areas, with targeted outreach to underserved communities and easy access to digital and face-to-face options. We urge robust data monitoring so that wait times, referral-to-treatment intervals and crisis admissions are tracked and used to adjust commissioning and service design.

In short, expanding community mental health teams and early intervention, growing and sustaining the primary care workforce, and expanding capacity through smarter scheduling are mutually reinforcing steps. Taken together, they would shorten waits, improve outcomes, and help people feel supported by a system that treats mental and physical health with equal importance. We stand ready to support the planning and delivery of these changes, and to work with NHS England, CCGs and local authorities to secure the necessary funding and governance to deliver durable, patient-centred improvements.

Better co-ordination between GP, community and mental health teams would help, but I’m unsure which changes would actually improve timely access in practice; more clarity on funding and local capacity is needed before committing to specific measures.

From my vantage in England, improving timely access means directing resources where gaps are widest and making services easier to reach for the most marginalised. I strongly support targeted outreach to deprived and ethnic minority communities, with interpreters and culturally competent staff in GP practices and in mental health services. In our area, having interpreters on site or by phone, plus translated appointment letters and community-engagement workers, would remove many barriers. Mobile clinics in council estates and more flexible hours would also help those who cannot take time off work.

Online booking and e-consults are valuable, but must be accompanied by non-digital options and support for the elderly. A simple telephone line, or a local walk-in slot, can prevent delays when technology fails. NHS111 and triage should prioritise urgent cases, streamline bookings, and provide clear care navigators so people aren’t shuffled between services.

My own experience last winter showed how a care navigator helped us access urgent mental health support quickly, avoiding a long wait. If these changes are implemented, GP, community health and mental health services will be timelier and more fair for everyone.

Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services in Scotland remains uneven, with longer waits in many communities. To improve access, two linked approaches are needed. First, strengthen the workforce: targeted recruitment, including sensible use of international hiring where appropriate, enhanced pay and career progression, flexible working patterns (such as split or four‑day weeks) and robust wellbeing and supervision support. This would help grow and retain primary care staff and reduce vacancy‑driven delays. In our experience, practices that invest in morale, mentorship and sustainable staffing plans see more consistent appointment availability and better patient retention, rather than relying on short‑term fixes alone. It must be part of a credible, funded workforce strategy with clear return on investment for high‑quality care.

Second, invest in co‑located community hubs that integrate primary care, community health, mental health and social care with VCSE partners. Shared records, same‑day GP triage, joint assessments and streamlined referrals can cut waiting times and remove needless handoffs, which benefits older patients and carers. In our area, pilots that co‑locate services and extend access hours have reduced unnecessary referrals and improved patient experience. Governance, funding and IT integration will be crucial; the model should be locally tailored, sustainable beyond pilots, and evaluated for patient outcomes and equity of access.

Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services is something that affects me and my friends, not just on paper. In my area, the biggest gains would come from making the first contact smoother and then guiding people to the right service quickly. That means a stronger NHS111, smarter clinical triage, better booking systems, and real care navigation that reduces duplication and confusion in patient flow.

First, NHS111 and clinical triage need to be rock solid. When you’re worried about a health issue, you want a reliable triage process that can judge urgency without sending you on a wild goose chase. I’m in a situation where I’ve had to call NHS111 and then wait for a GP slot that’s not available that day. A really robust triage system would flag urgent cases immediately and offer the best next step—whether that’s a same-day GP slot, a clinician-led video check, or a fast referral to urgent care. Digital triage tools that assess symptoms and risk, with a quick escalation path, would help a lot. It would also spare people the stress of guessing what to do next when a situation could worsen over a weekend or after hours.

Second, the booking and appointment system needs to be unified and clearer. A single, real-time booking interface across local GP practices, with transparent same-day slots, would save hours of phone-hopping and repetition. Ideally, there would be clear options for in-person, video, or phone consultations, with automatic reminders and the ability to swap channels if someone feels more comfortable emailing or texting than speaking on the phone. For mental health in particular, a direct route from triage to the right talking therapies should exist, so the waiting list isn’t the first thing people encounter. In my experience, I’ve seen people give up after navigating multiple portals or calling several times to check if there’s any appointment left; a unified system would cut that duplication dramatically.

Third, care navigation and better patient flow would make a real difference. Trained care navigators could map a person’s needs across GP, community health services, pharmacy, and mental health teams, then steer them toward the most appropriate and fastest route. They’d also help consolidate information from different visits so patients don’t have to repeat the same history to every new clinician. In practice, this could mean a navigator coordinating a plan that includes GP review, a community nurse visit, and a mental health follow-up, with one shared care plan visible to all providers (with patient consent). Right now, I hear about people repeating symptoms and tests because records don’t show what was already tried or what happened in a prior appointment; better data sharing would cut out those duplicates and speed things up.

For mental health specifically, I think urgent triage and easier access to talking therapies are essential. Waiting times for therapy can be a real barrier and chat-based or digital options could help fill gaps while people wait for in-person slots. Quick access to crisis lines and warm transfers to local mental health teams would also make a big difference for those in distress.

Implementation will require investment in training and in data sharing that respects privacy. If the NHS can fund cross-provider triage capacity, unify the booking landscape, and empower care navigators to coordinate care across settings, we’d see fewer missed slots, less duplication, and a smoother path to the right help when people need it most. In short, a stronger first contact point, smarter booking, and better navigation would make timely access much more achievable for young people like me and for our families.

Prioritise longer, continuity-focused slots for complex, chronic patients while expanding multidisciplinary teams for routine care; simultaneously boost overall capacity with better scheduling and hires to reduce waits, but guard against fragmenting care for vulnerable patients.

I disagree; boosting training places, return-to-practice support, apprenticeships and CPD, plus more multidisciplinary teams, can help—but only with long-term funding, retentionn and smarter local commissioning to actually speed up GP, community and mental health care.

To improve timely access in my area, we need a practical mix of options. Evening and weekend clinics plus guaranteed same-day urgent slots would help working people like me and others who can’t take time off, and would ease pressure on A&E for non-emergency issues. I’ve felt the squeeze when a mental health slot wasn’t available quickly enough and I had to wait, which only worsened stress. 

I’m also supportive of expanding online booking and e-consultations to speed things up, but we must avoid leaving behind older or digitally disadvantaged residents. Non‑digital routes—telephone triage, in-person walk-in slots, and community outreach—need to be retained and well publicised so no one is excluded.

Crucially, for complex and chronic conditions, continuity of care matters. Longer appointment times (60 minutes where needed) and a named clinician following through with reviews would reduce repeated visits and improve outcomes. These changes should be rolled out with adequate staffing and funding, and monitored on wait times and patient experience to ensure they actually help where they’re most needed.

I don’t think simply expanding online booking and e-consultations will deliver timely GP, community health and mental health care across my area. For many of us, digital access isn’t universal: elderly relatives, low‑income households, and those without reliable internet can be left waiting longer or stuck in phone queues. In my neighbourhood, it’s common to try online booking only to face long hold times or slots that disappear before you can finish a request. When urgent mental health issues arise, I worry about delays if triage pushes people into online forms rather than quick human contact.

We also need continuity and adequate appointment length for complex needs. Short slots with shifting clinicians undermine trust and proper management of chronic conditions. I’d push for longer, guaranteed slots for those cases, and insist on continuity with the same GP when possible.

Finally, while online tools are useful, we need embedded evening and weekend clinics and guaranteed same‑day urgent slots to help working people and urgent non‑emergency needs. A mixed model with strong non‑digital access, longer appointments and stable GP assignments will deliver real improvement, rather than a digital‑only push that excludes people like my family.

I welcome the proposal to improve timely access to GP, community and mental health services. In our area, long waits and multiple calls can leave people anxious. To help, targeted recruitment and international hiring could fill GP vacancies more quickly, backed by incentives, better pay, flexible working patterns and a focus on staff wellbeing. When teams feel supported and able to balance shifts, patients benefit from steadier access, including more evening and weekend slots.

NHS111 and clinical triage must be sharper. A streamlined booking system that directs urgent cases straight to the right clinician would cut duplication and reduce wasted time. Care navigation should guide people through the system—booking, transfer to mental health services, or community nurses—without repeating information.

Investing in co-located community hubs that bring primary care, district nursing, mental health, social care and VCSE partners under one roof would be transformative. In my town, a hub would help my neighbour with dementia and explain care options more clearly. Please fund pilot hubs and scale up successful models.

Living in England, I notice that timely access to GP and mental health services often depends on small, local factors rather than grand promises. For my family, getting a same‑day GP appointment can mean calling before opening and still watching slots vanish within minutes. Online booking sometimes shows a slot that isn’t really available, while video slots can exist but then we’re stuck waiting days for tests or advice. Travel to a health hub when the nearest practice is full adds another layer of difficulty, especially if mental health support is in a different town or only accessible by a long bus ride.

Staff shortages in nursing or admin teams push back routine checks and make urgent triage harder. It’s not glamorous, but better admin, clearer appointment updates, and more predictable callbacks would stop small problems from spiraling. I’d welcome more integrated care hubs where GP, physio, and counsellor work from the same site with streamlined records, and the option of flexible hours to fit working families.

Ultimately, there isn’t a one‑size‑fits‑all fix. Local staffing, clearer scheduling, and reliable access routes feel like practical steps that could make timely care more affordable in daily life.

Living in Englandd and navigating health services as a young adult, I see how timely access to GPs, community health and mental health support can shape everyday life, from exam stress to managing anxiety or a worsening mood. In my experience, GP slots can feel squeezed, with some weeks where you’re redirected to urgent care or told to ring back later. When mental health support is involved, the waits for talking therapies or early intervention can be longer than for physical health issues, and that gap isn’t just inconvenient – it can let problems fester. I’ve heard friends describe long waits for CAMHS referrals during which symptoms worsen, and I’ve seen peers miss study deadlines because they avoid seeking help until a crisis point. These aren’t isolated anecdotes; they reflect a system that still treats mental health with slower urgency thann physical health, even though the need for timely, early support is clear. I think the most meaningful improvement would come from expanding community mental health teams, investing in early intervention and crisis response, and making talking therapies more accessible and responsive. If community mental health teams grew in size and geographic reach, with dedicated staff for young adults and better links to universities and student services, people would get help before problems escalate. Closer collaboration wit GPs, schools, and campus wellbeing services could create smootherr referral pathways and reduce duplication of assessments. An urgent, 24/7 crisis response option—whether through mobile teams or a rapid-access line—would help prevent crises from spiraling and lessen the burden on A&E. Talking therapies need to be more available, not just in a central clinic but in community settings or campus hubs, with flexible hours to fit student timetables. It isn’t enough to offer a few evening slots here and there; there should be predictable access during term-time, with options for in-person, online and blended approaches. A stepped-care model that guarantees faster access for higher-need cases and effective, evidence-based therapies such as CBT or other appropriate modalities is essential to achieve parity with physical health services in both tone and timeliness. I’m cautiously optimistic about co-located community hubs that integrate primary care, community and mental health services social care and VCSE partners. The concept of a one-stop site—ideally near publicc transport, with accessible hours and clear navigation—could dramatically reduce the “where do I start?” burden. In practice,, hubs could offer same-day triage, rapid referrals to appropriate teams, and social support in one place, which would be especially helpful for students facing housing instability or financial stress alongside mental health concerns. That said, these hubs must be designed with robust governance, stable funding, and strong data-sharing protocols that protect privacy while enabling timely referrals. The risk is that, without sustained investment, such hubs become fashionabl pilots that fizzle out before embedded practice takes root. Practical steps I’d like to see include: - A robust expansion plan for community mental health teams, including flexible staffing to cover evenings and weekends and strong links to schools and universities. - Clear targets for early intervention, with rapid-access slots and fast-track referrals from GPs and campus wellbeing services. - Reliable 24/7 crisis suppor with mobile response options and closer liaison with hospitals and community teams. - Expanded access to talking therapies with capacity to handle peak times (for example during exam periods) and multiple delivery modrs. - Investment in co-located hubs that are genuinely multi-disciplinary, well-funded, and governed by a unified care pathway, with input from patients and local VCSE groups to ensure services meet local needs. - Safeguards for digital exclusion and language / accessibility barriers, so improved access doesn’t leave parts of the community behind. - Transparent, public performance metrics on wait times,, wait-to-see rates, and patien satisfaction so people can gauge progress. From a student and young-adult perspective, the underlying aim should be parity with physical health in both seriousness and speed. If policy makers cann deliver on workforce expansion, streamlined pathways, and well-structured,, community-based hubs, those changes would translate into quicker help for people like me and my friends when we need it most. The challenge is ensuring those improvements are not just promises but are delivered with continuity and accountability over time. Overall, there’s real potential here, but the success will hinge on sustained investment, coherent local implementation and genuinely joined-up care that makes it easier—not harder—to get timely support when it’s needed most.

As someone living in England and in my mid-forties, I strongly support changes that improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services. The most effective steps would be to offer evening and weekend clinics and to guarantee same-day urgent slots for non-emergency needs. In my experience, getting a same-day appointment during standard hours is often impossible, which means symptoms linger and stress rises. Evening and weekend clinics in a local hub—close to where people work or live—would make it easier for busy staff and parents to get seen without taking multiple days off Obviously.... A guaranteed same-day urgent slot would prevent non-urgent concerns from turning into escalations, and would be particularly helpful for mental health triage, where a quick assessment and access to support can make a real difference. Better digital booking and clear signposting across GP, community nursing and mental health services would further reduce delays and improve continuity of care.

Expanding community mental health teams and talking therapies, with early intervention and crisis response, alongside more GP, nurse and therapist slots, plus evening/weekend clinics and guaranteed same-day urgent slots, would cut waits and improve parity for working people, subject to sustainable funding.

absolutely improvements to NHS111, smart clinical triage, and better booking and care-navigation could prioritise urgent cases, reduce duplication, and simplify patient flow—yet must be backed by adequate capacity and safeguards to avoid disadvantaging non-urgent or digitally marginalised patients!

For my area, allocate targeted resources for interpreters and culturally competent staff, while expanding multidisciplinary teams (pharmacists, physios, paramedics, PAs) to handle routine care, and bolster training and return-to-practice schemes to grow GPs and mental health staff long term.

I welcome practical steps to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services. The changes that will help most in the long term are growing the workforce and sustaining it: increasing training places for GPs, nurses and mental health professionals, strong return‑to‑practice support, and expanded apprenticeships and CPD. Without building capacity, temporary fixes will simply shift bottlenecks around. In the shorter term, offering evening and weekend clinics and guaranteeing same‑day urgent slots would make access workable for people who work full‑time or have caregiving responsibilities. I’ve sometimes needed a weekday GP appointment and found the only realistic options were late in the day or not available for weeks. A predictable same‑day urgent slot would reduce needless worry.

Thirdly, expanding multidisciplinary teams—pharmacists to handle repeat prescriptions and common concerns, physiotherapists for back and joint issues, paramedics and physician associates in GP hubs—would free GPs for complex cases and improve throughput. In my area a pilot where a physio supported triage led to faster advice for a friend, showing what is possible. Please fund and roll out these models with clear referral routes and quality standards.

I want to see changes that genuinely make it easier to get timely GP, community health and mental health support here in England, and I think there are three practical levers that would make a real difference. First, protect continuity of care and lengthen appointment times for complex, chronic and vulnerable patients. When someone has several long‑running issues—diabetes plus anxiety, for example—speaking with the same clinician and having a longer, unhurried slot leads to a safer plan, better medication decisions and fewer repeat visits. I’d like to see a model where complexity determines the appointment length and where the clinician, care navigator and any care plans stay aligned across reviews. That consistency would reduce confusion and late‑stage crises, and it would save time and distress for patients and their families alike.

Second, expand multidisciplinary teams to take routine workloads off GPs and keep complex care with clinicians who specialise in different areas. In my experience, co‑ordinated teams that include pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates can handle many of the routine checks and minor conditions efficiently. A pharmacist embedded in the practice can review medicines for people taking several drugs, identify interactions, and set up adherence supports; a physiotherapist can manage early musculoskeletal problems, which often curbs unnecessary GP visits; paramedics can support home visits for urgent but non‑life‑threatening needs; physician associates can handle many standard consultations, providing GPs with more space to focus on complex cases. Mental health professionals within primary care—nurses, therapists or counsellors who work alongside GPs—also shorten waiting times by offering early intervention, triage and timely referrals. In a local clinic I know, a pharmacist review reduced medication errors and a physiotherapist clinic cut the time to a first appointment for back and joint issues from weeks to days. It felt like a win for both patients and the clinic.

Third, grow the future workforce through more training places, return‑to‑practice support, apprenticeships and CPD. The NHS faces real staffing pressures, and without expanding the pipeline we’ll struggle to sustain improvements in access. Increasing GP and nurse training places, plus structured return‑to‑practice schemes with mentoring, would help fill vacancies and reduce burnout over time. Apprenticeship routes for allied roles and targeted CPD investment would keep skills current and allow teams to push down routine care to trained non‑GP clinicians, freeing GPs to concentrate on the most complex cases. In the medium term, this approach builds stable teams that patients can rely on, reduces the bottlenecks caused by staff turnover, and supports better long‑term outcomes.

To make these changes work, I’d also advocate for visible, measurable milestones and local accountability: minimum appointment lengths for complex cases; clear roles within multidisciplinary teams with defined care pathways; and regular reporting on wait times, same‑day access slots and patient satisfaction. If funded and implemented well, these reforms could shorten waiting times, improve safety and preserve continuity of care for people who need it most.

Overall, strengthening continuity of care, embedding diverse professional teams in primary and community settings, and growing the workforce are practical, sustainable steps that would significantly improve timely access for GP, community health and mental health services in my area.

While I understand the push to speed up access, I’m concerned that simply expanding online booking, e-consults, and remote care will leave behind vulnerable patients. Timely access requires both digital and non-digital routes. In practice, my family has benefited from online bookings for routine issues, but when symptoms escalate or when a relative is elderly and unconfident with tech, online systems fail. NHS111 triage is improved on paper but can still be slow; I’ve faced duplicated forms and having to repeat information across GP and mental health services, which wastes time and increases risk.

What would help: robust NHS111 with clear telephone triage plus escalation to urgent GP slots; same-day triage for mental health; unified booking systems that prioritise urgent cases and reduce duplication; care navigators who help guide patients through ENT, mental health and community services; permanent non-digital options: telephone lines, in-person bookings at reception, and community hubs with staff to assist. Also ensure data sharing between services so you don’t repeat history.

In short: keep online options, but fund non-digital access and strong triage to prioritise truly urgent cases and smooth patient flow.

Living with chronic conditions and the realities of aging, I’m keen to see improvements that make timely access realistic while not sacrificing continuity of care. In practice, I’ve found that the benefit of a regular GP who already knows my history is too often undermined by very short appointment slots. For complex or vulnerable patients like many in my age group, longer, more considered consultations – perhaps 20 to 30 minutes for with-me-for-life-type care – would help clinicians pick up underlying issues, adjust plans without having to re‑book repeatedly, and reduce avoidable hospital visits. If we can protect continuity, we’ll see fewer repeat appointments for the same problem and better treatment plans that make a real difference in outcomes.

That said, I recognise the longer term reality that the workforce needs to grow if we’re to deliver this consistently. A sustainable supply of GPs, nurses and mental health professionals is essential. In the short term, I’d welcome more structured return‑to‑practice support, apprenticeships and ongoing CPD that enable capable staff to move into areas with high demand. We don’t just want more people; we want people who stay and build relationships with communities. From my perspective, increasing training places must go hand in hand with robust retention incentives, reasonable workloads, and decent facilities to prevent burnout. A practical step would be to pilot longer appointment blocks in areas with known shortages and carefully monitor whether longer slots reduce follow‑ups and late referrals before expanding district‑wide.

Transport, parking and premises deficits are a real barrier, especially for rural and mobility‑limited residents. In our town, the distance to a GP or mental health clinic means many cannot attend without careful planning or a car‑ride service. Parking is a continual stress when appointments run late. To address this, I’d support a mix of mobile clinics that visit villages on a regular schedule and a network of telehealth hubs hosted in community venues like libraries or village halls where privacy can be safeguarded. Such hubs could offer phased triage, enabling a nurse or GP to assess remotely and then direct patients to the most appropriate next step. Incentives could attract clinicians to rural posts—things like relocation subsidies, flexible hours, and additional financial support for practice managers who coordinate multi‑site services.

From my own experience, I’ve seen the value of outreach and proactive care. A nurse‑led outreach clinic in a nearby village reduced unnecessary trips for several chronic conditions by offering blood pressure, glucose checks and medication reviews on a monthly basis. If we roll this out more widely, combining it with integrated digital records and simple consent processes for remote consultations, we could shorten waiting times while preserving the continuity of care that so many of us rely on. For mental health, quicker access matters as much as quality. A stepped‑care approach with timely phone or video check‑ins, same‑day triage where possible, and strong links with community services would help avoid crisis episodes and reduce the strain on primary care.

Overall, I’d back a measured programme that prioritises protected continuity and longer first consultations for complex cases, paired with a parallel long‑term strategy to grow the workforce and make services accessible outside traditional clinics. The key is balance: we must keep clinicians supported and patients nearby, whether that’s through better premises, mobile or hub‑based services, or smarter use of telehealth. If these elements are coordinated, with patient voices informing design and regular outcome reviews, timely access can improve without compromising the quality and empathy that older patients value.

it's outrageous that agree. Expanding online booking, e-consults and remote care can make GP, community and mental health services more timely, while non-digital options are kept open so no one is left behind. In my area, same-day GP slots are tight; online triage could direct non-urgent cases to a quick video or phone check, freeing in-person slots for those with urgent needs or complex care. I use online booking for routine matters and it saves time, but my elderly neighbour struggles with apps; clinics should offer simple phone booking, drop-in digital help desks, and clear printed guides. For mental health, rapid access pathways—coaching, talking therapies, or crisis lines—should be available both remotely and face-to-face, with same-day triage so crises are addressed fast. For community health, more home visits and community clinics in local hubs would reduce travel and delays.

On the workforce side, recruitment must grow: targeted roles, international hiring, better pay, flexible hours and wellbeing support. Our practice recently recruited international nurses and extended hours; waits dropped and patient feedback improved. Continued investment with robust induction is essential to sustain this progress!

Living in England and aged over 65, I’ve seen how timely access to GP, community health and mental health services can swing from reasonable to frustratingly slow, often depending on where you live and what time you ring or visit. I’m not against expanding recruitment and offering flexible working, pay improvements, and wellbeing support to grow and retain primary care staff. But I also think we must fix the systems that bottleneck patient flow. In my experience, it’s as much about smoother booking, better triage, and clearer navigation as it is about more doctors and nurses.

What would help most, in my view, falls into three intertwined strands:

1) Strengthen the workforce with practical, patient‑facing improvements
- Targeted recruitment and international hiring: I would support bringing in GPs, practice nurses and district nurses where shortages are acute, with robust induction and mentorship to ensure confidence in local guidelines and cultures.
- Better pay and flexible working: If staff feel valued and can balance family life with work, turnover would fall and teams would be more stable—benefiting patients who rely on continuity.
- Wellbeing and safe staffing: Regular supervision, appropriate breaks, and manageable rosters reduce burnout. When clinicians feel cared for, they deliver better care and stay longer in the job.
- Practical deployment: Fund and empower primary care networks to use floating staff, urgent care slots, and extended hours in a predictable way so patients know where to go for same-day problems.

2) Fix the booking, triage and navigation so urgent needs aren’t delayed
- NHS111 and clinical triage: NHS111 should efficiently identify genuinely urgent cases and route them straight to urgent care, same-day GP clinics, or community teams when appropriate. This requires more clinical triage staff and clearer escalation protocols, so a caller with a chest pain or a severe mental health crisis isn’t bounced around.
- Consistent booking systems: A unified, simple booking platform across GP practices and community services would reduce duplication and confusion. For older patients who are not comfortable with online systems, telephone booking must remain straightforward, with informed, human assistance readily available.
- Care navigation and reception training: Frontline reception and call handlers often serve as the gatekeepers. If they have better training to understand a patient’s symptoms, they can triage quickly and direct people to the right service, avoiding multiple referrals or repeated calls.
- Integrated patient records: A shared record across GP, district nursing, community physiotherapy and mental health services would prevent requests for the same information multiple times and reduce delays when someone moves between services.

3) Expand community and mental health capacity with clear pathways
- Community services: Increase capacity in district nursing, community physiotherapy and rapid access to allied health professionals so people can stay home safely rather than wait for hospital-based care. Timely home visits and reliable discharge planning would help prevent readmissions.
- Mental health: More timely access to community mental health teams, crisis support and timely stepping-stone care after a crisis is essential. Shorter waits for talking therapies and stronger crisis response would make a real difference for people who are vulnerable.
- Local evidence and accountability: Local clinicians should be able to show monthly data on wait times and access, with transparent reporting and a clear plan to close gaps in underserved areas.

Concrete examples from my experience underscore the need for system changes (as if that will ever happen). A few months ago, my neighbour needed a same-day GP appointment for a chest infection, but the earliest slot offered was a fortnight away. In the meantime, NHS111 directed him to self-care, which wasn’t safe, and when he finally got a nurse’s assessment, the care plan was fragmented between primary care and the community team. A simple, well‑structured triage pathway and a unified booking system could have redirected him sooner to the right clinician, with fewer steps and less anxiety.

I also know several people who have struggled with mental health access. Waiting times for talking therapies have varied, and I’ve heard of people feeling bounced between NHS111, GPs and the community team without a clear, timely plan. Strengthening urgent pathways and ensuring rapid access to the right mental health professionals, with a clear handoff between crisis and community support, would relieve a lot of distress and prevent needless GP visits.

In short, I’d prioritise three practical changes: building a stable, well-supported workforce; overhauling booking and triage so urgent needs are identified and routed quickly; and expanding community and mental health capacity with clear, navigable pathways. All of this needs funded, long-term planning and local accountability so improvements are visible to patients who rely on them every day, including those of us who are older and more cautious about navigating a confusing system.

I think the changes that would most improve timely access are to increase appointment slots across GP, nurse and therapist services by expanding staffing and optimising scheduling. This means recruiting more GPs and practice nurses, extending weekday hours and adding weekend clinics, and giving nurse practitioners a clearer role in managing routine care and same‑day triage. For mental health, expanding therapy capacity with more qualified therapists, longer appointment blocks, and options for group or digital CBT can help reduce waits.

A streamlined triage system—phone or video—so patients are directed to the right clinician the same day would free up scarce GP slots for those with urgent needs. Investing in training and retention to prevent turnover is essential for continuity of care. In my local area, I’ve experienced a two‑week wait for a GP appointment and several weeks for counselling; even modest capacity gains—2–3 extra GPs, one more mental health therapist, and extended hours—would make a noticeable difference. An online booking system showing real‑time capacity would also help people plan around work and family commitments.

Access to timely GP, community health and mental health services is something I’ve become increasingly frustrated by, especially as someone who still works full time and tries to fit care in around a busy week. When you work late, pick kids up from school, or if you’re dealing with an urgent but non‑emergency issue, the system often feels geared to daytime hours and it shows. I’ve seen neighbours have to take time off work to attend a daytime appointment that could have waited or ended up with a late evening or weekend slot being the only realistic option. That rhythm isn’t sustainable for people who contribute to the economy and care for families; it pushes people into A&E or lets issues fester, which later become bigger problems for the NHS to sort out.

To address this, the changes I’d prioritise are simple and practical: establishing regular evening and weekend GP clinics and guaranteeing same‑day urgent slots across GP, community health and mental health services.

First, evening and weekend clinics. Practices should offer predictable extended hours, for example two to three evenings per week (until 7.30pm or 8pm) and Saturday mornings. The aim isn’t to remove daytime slots but to widen them so working people can access care without taking multiple days off. These sessions should be staffed by a mix of GPs, nurse practitioners and qualified health staff, with continuity where possible so patients see someone they know. It would also help if these extended hours were promoted as a normal, routine option, not a last‑ditch service. In my area I’ve seen gaps where late‑afternoon slots vanish after a couple of weeks when a few clinicians are on leave, which defeats the purpose. A solid, recurring pattern would give people confidence to plan ahead and seek help before problems escalate.

Second, guaranteed same‑day urgent slots. Urgent doesn’t always mean life‑threatening, but it does mean a clinician should see you that day or within 24 hours. We need a system with triage that reliably flags urgent non‑emergency needs and funnels them into a same‑day appointment, whether that’s with a GP, a nurse, or a mental health professional. This would also require robust online booking and a responsive telephone advice service, so people without easy internet access aren’t left behind. I’ve personally experienced situations where a same‑day urgent slot would have prevented a longer delay or unnecessary worry, especially for chest infections, severe back pain, or sudden mood or anxiety spikes that could spiral if ignored.

Mental health deserves equal urgency. It’s hard to justify why someone facing a mental health crisis or escalating symptoms should wait days for help when physical health services can offer same‑day slots. A clear rule that urgent mental health concerns are allocated a same‑day appointment, with rapid access to a crisis team if needed, would make a real difference. I’ve heard from friends and colleagues that delays in talk‑therapy or counselling appointments can leave people feeling isolated and pushed toward more acute services; shortening that gap would improve people’s wellbeing and reduce avoidable admission rates.

Of course there are practical caveats. extending hours requires funding, staff and careful workforce planning to avoid burnout and ensure safety. It will be important to guard against simply shifting demand without expanding capacity. Any plan should include recruitment incentives, flexible staffing models, and protected time for clinicians to maintain high standards of care. It’s also essential to preserve equity: maintain a strong front‑line phone service, offer interpreters, and ensure access for those who rely on public transport or who don’t use online booking.

Finally, these changes must be measured. Set targets for accessible slots, track how quickly urgent cases are seen, monitor patient satisfaction, and publish results so communities know whether the system is delivering. Local area plans should be transparent about what is offered and when, with the ability to adjust based on demand.

In short, extending GP hours into evenings and weekends and guaranteeing same‑day urgent slots for urgent non‑emergency care would make a tangible difference for working people and for those with urgent mental health needs. If implemented with proper funding, staffing, and a focus on equity and safety, these changes could reduce avoidable hospital visits and keep people healthier—while giving patients a practical, reliable path to care when they need it most.

Living in England and navigating services in my 60s, I see real potential in expanding community mental health teams, early intervention, crisis response and talking therapies to reduce waits and improve parity with physical health. I would support these changes, provided they are properly funded, staffed and integrated with GP services.

In practice, more locally based teams that can respond quickly, with options for home visits during crises, would help families like ours. A faster, transparent triage process so someone can access talking therapies within weeks rather than months is essential. Early intervention for anxiety and mood disorders could prevent deterioration and hospital admissions.

I also back protecting continuity of care by allowing longer appointments for complex, chronic and vulnerable patients, and by ensuring they can see the same clinician where possible. In my area, rushed slots and repeating the same history at every visit undermine care and drive unnecessary A&E use. An integrated digital record between GPs and mental health teams would reduce duplication and delays.

Overall, I support the move in principle, but only with sufficient funding, clear workforce planning and a firm commitment to continuity of care and patient-centered scheduling.

From my experience living in England, simply increasing GP, nurse and therapist appointment slots or promising evening and weekend clinics is not a reliable fix. Recruiting and retaining qualified staff is slow and uncertain; without enough doctors, nurses and therapists to fill the extra slots, waits will just shift rather than shorten. I’ve waited several weeks for a routine GP call, and I know neighbours who have waited longer for mental health support; expanding slots on paper doesn’t guarantee quality care in practice.

Guaranteed same‑day urgent slots sound appealing, but they can crowd out ongoing care and place extra pressure on triage teams and after‑hours services that older people already rely on. Evening sessions may improve access for some, but many of us have mobility issues or carers to consider, and traveling after dark is not easy.

What would help more in my area is steady investment in workforce planning: more training posts for GPs, nurses and therapists; longer appointment times with continuity of care; and smarter scheduling tied to patient need rather than raw slot numbers. Also, stronger community mental health teams and better coordination with local clinics would reduce unnecessary visits and improve timely support.

i strongly believe timely access to GP, community health and mental health services is something that directly affects my day-to-day life and the people around me. I’m pleased to see this being prioritised because for many young people, school, part-time jobs, and family commitments mean we can’t always slot in long waiting times or multiple visits. The changes I’d like to see focus on two clear aims: making services easier to reach for everyone, and making the care people receive more effective when they do get in front of a clinician.

First, we need more targeted resources to close access gaps for deprived, ethnic minority, migrant and marginalised groups. In my area there are pockets where people struggle with language, transport, or simply knowing where to go for help. For someone who doesn’t speak English well, booking appointments can feel overwhelming, and interpreters aren’t always available when you need them. I’ve seen a friend who relies on a family member to translate in a GP chat, which is not ideal for privacy or accuracy. I’d like to see more interpreters on site, not just telephone services, and more staff who speak the community languages here. Training existing staff in cultural competence and hiring multilingual clinicians would help people feel understood and reduce miscommunication that delays care.

To reach people who are not yet engaged with services, outreach must be more proactive. Mobile clinics and pop‑up sessions in community hubs, colleges, and faith centres can help people who won’t or can’t travel to a clinic. Outreach workers who reflect the local communities can build trust, explain what help is available, and assist with booking. Multilingual outreach materials—online and in paper form—could explain red flags, how to access same‑day slots, and what mental health support looks like. In practice, if a local clinic ran a weekly drop‑in with a clinician who speaks multiple languages and a translator on hand, more people would come forward early instead of waiting until a crisis.

Second, continuity of care and longer appointment times are essential, especially for complex, chronic, and vulnerable patients. I’ve noticed that when people see different GPs at each visit, important details get repeated, or important history is missed. For those with long-term conditions or mental health concerns, a longer first appointment—even 30 minutes instead of 10–15—can save time later by allowing a proper assessment, a clear plan, and follow‑ups arranged. Keeping a stable team means patients know who to contact, can build trust, and are less likely to “fall through the cracks.” For mental health, initial assessments and ongoing therapy can require significant time to build rapport, review medications, and adjust care. Longer slots in the right settings would likely reduce repeated referrals or crisis interventions.

Concrete steps that would make a real difference include:
- Increase interpreters and cultural‑competence training across GP practices and mental health teams, with on‑site interpreting rather than sole reliance on third‑party services.
- Fund community outreach and mobile clinics in deprived areas and in places young people frequent (universities, colleges, youth centres), with visible multilingual staff.
- Provide more same‑day or rapidly triaged slots, and allow patients to choose longer appointment times when they need them, not just when they demand it.
- Protect continuity of care by improving GP rostering so patients can see the same clinician or team where possible, and ensure longer appointment times for chronic or complex cases.
- Expand flexible access options (evenings and weekends) and improve digital booking tools to easily reserve longer slots and to flag when language or interpretation support is needed.
- Integrate services more closely so a patient’s GP, community health worker, and mental health professional share information securely and coordinate care to avoid duplicated tests and mixed messages.

Personally, I’ve seen how a timely, well‑coordinated approach can change outcomes. When a friend had ongoing mental health concerns and language barriers, a local outreach nurse who spoke their language helped navigate referrals, and a temporary language‑friendly group session was set up in a community centre. The improvement in engagement and follow‑through was immediate, and it reduced repeated crises in the weeks that followed. If similar approaches were available across the board, I’m confident we’d see fewer avoidable visits, better management of conditions, and students staying in work or study rather than taking time off for constant appointments or waiting for referrals.

In short, targeted resources for interpreters and culturally competent staff, plus stronger emphasis on continuity of care and longer appointment times, would make timely access not just a promise but a lived reality for many young people and their families. I’m sure that with sensible funding and committed local leadership, these changes could transform health outcomes for our generation and reduce the burden on the system in the long run!

I cannot see these changes as the most effective way to improve timely access in our area. The emphasis on mobile clinics, outreach and telehealth hubs sounds modern, but in practice it risks creating more patches than solutions. In rural and mobility‑limited areas, unreliable transport, scarce parking, and variable premises conditions mean patients miss appointments when sites change or close unexpectedly. A parent driving to a temporary clinic often faces nowhere to park or long walks from a distant lot; the delays can be acute for mental health crises or urgent GP concerns. Telehealth relies on broadband that isn’t universal here; it can substitute for minor issues, but it cannot replace hands‑on assessment or timely urgent care. Expanding multidisciplinary teams is helpful in theory, but without stable GP access and clear care pathways, patients get bounced between professionals and still wait weeks for simple, follow‑up appointments.

My priority would be keeping high‑quality, locally anchored GP practices with extended hours, better patient transport options, and properly funded premises with safe, convenient parking, plus integrated digital records that support continuity. Only then should we scale other innovations. I want a system that prioritises reliability and consistency over stop‑gap fixes that shift the burden to patients and staff alike.

Expanding online booking, e-consultations and remote care should be part of the solution to make GP, community health and mental health services more timely. But to avoid excluding often digitally inexperienced or older residents, these must be paired with robust non-digital options and support to navigate them. 

In my area in England, online booking works well for routine appointments and quick mental health check-ins, yet my neighbour in their mid-60s often cannot login and waits on a busy phone line. A non-digital route with screened phone triage and staff who can book on behalf would prevent delays. Additionally, access is still hampered by transport issues: in rural pockets, buses are infrequent and parking at surgeries is limited. 

Practical steps include: regular mobile clinics visiting village halls or community centres; outreach teams that can visit homebound patients; telehealth hubs in libraries or GP hubs with privacy screens and trained assistants; incentives to attract GPs and mental health professionals to rural postings; extended hours and better parking and accessible entrances at premises. 

I support a blended approach that expands digital access while investing in human support and local outreach so no one is left behind.

Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services is a real concern in our area, especially for anyone who works standard office hours. The idea of evening and weekend clinics and guaranteed same-day urgent slots sounds attractive in theory, but I’m not convinced this package will deliver reliable, safe care for everyone, and I worry it could create new problems or push costs onto already stretched services.

Evening and weekend clinics
- Staffing and sustainability: Extending hours requires more clinicians and support staff. In my experience, when practices tried a single late clinic or a Saturday session, the slots were frequently hard to fill, or staff burnout rose quickly because the extra hours weren’t matched with long‑term funding or a stable pipeline of doctors and nurses. Without a strong, ongoing funding commitment, these hours can become a cost without a clear benefit.
- Demand vs. capacity: There’s a real risk that demand will outstrip supply during extended hours. If people start turning up in lower numbers, clinics may cancel or reduce hours, which just adds to confusion and uncertainty for patients.
- Continuity of care: For complex or ongoing issues, patients value seeing the same clinician who knows their history. Evening slots risk fragmenting care if patients see different people every time, which can slow down correct diagnoses and appropriate management.
- Real-world impact on working people: I work full-time and can book a daytime appointment, but many in my circle struggle to take time off without risking pay or job security. A few extra evening slots won’t help if there isn’t certainty about consistent availability, if travel and parking add to the burden, or if a late appointment still ends up with a long wait in reception.

Guaranteed same-day urgent slots
- Triaging pressure: A promise of same-day urgent access sounds good, but it relies on a robust triage system and real capacity. If urgent slots are overbooked or delayed, it pushes people into A&E or into overburdened urgent care hubs, which undermines the purpose of primary care.
- Quality and safety: In urgent situations, there’s a risk of rushing assessments or substituting GP oversight with a temporary clinician, which can compromise continuity, record accuracy, and safety for patients with complex needs or polypharmacy.
- Systemic constraints: There are also real budget and workforce constraints. Without a clear plan to expand the total number of qualified staff and to fund longer-term operations, these “same-day” promises can become a revolving door of unsustainable expectations.

Expanding multidisciplinary teams (pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics, physician associates)
- Role clarity and safety: Multidisciplinary teams can help with straightforward, routine cases, but if roles aren’t clearly defined and tightly integrated with GP leadership, patients risk receiving care that doesn’t fully address their conditions. For example, a back-to-work musculoskeletal issue or chronic pain often requires a GP to interpret history, medications, and red flags in context.
- Coordination and records: To work well, MDTs need seamless information sharing, standardised referral pathways, and strong governance. If a patient sees a pharmacist or physiotherapist first, there must be rapid, reliable back‑referral to a GP for anything that’s complex or if medications need adjustment. Without this, information can be siloed, leading to gaps or duplication of tests.
- Mental health considerations: For mental health, turning to non-medical clinicians for routine issues may help some people, but crisis, safety planning, and complex comorbidities require a trained clinician who can assess risk and coordinate with social care, housing, and employment supports. Fragmented pathways risk people slipping through the cracks when someone can only address one aspect of their needs.
- Patient acceptability: Some patients value a familiar GP approach, or a GP-led plan that can be scaled up if symptoms worsen. If care becomes more diffuse across several team members, patients may feel less confident and disengaged from their own care plans.

What I’d prefer, and what might actually work better
- Targeted pilots with strong evaluation: If these changes are pursued, run careful pilots in small areas with clear metrics on wait times, patient satisfaction, safety, and clinician burnout. Learn and adjust before scaling up.
- Long-term workforce and funding commitment: Any extended hours or MDT expansion needs a realistic plan to recruit and retain staff, provide ongoing training, and give guaranteed funding for salaries, cover, and admin support.
- Clear patient pathways and governance: For every MDT, there must be well-defined roles, escalation routes to GPs, and robust information-sharing. Patients should not have to navigate a maze of different providers to get the same result.
- Digital and triage improvements alongside, not instead of, in-person access: Better online booking, transparent wait times, and effective telephone or video triage should accompany any extended hours. These tools can reduce unnecessary visits and help people get timely care when it’s truly needed.
- Mental health integrated care: Strengthen community mental health services and crisis lines so people get rapid access to appropriate support, with a clear route to GP or specialist care when risk or complexity requires it.

In summary, while the proposed changes aim to improve access, I fear they’re optimistic about capacity and underestimate the risks of fragmentation, burnout, and unsustainable costs. A more cautious, evidence-based approach—focused on staffing, governance, and integrated care—would likely deliver tangible improvements without compromising safety or continuity of care.

We should also expand access with extended hours: evening and weekend clinics and guaranteed same-day urgent slots for working people with urgent non-emergency needs. Any changes must be funded, staffed with safe ratios, and backed by clear governance on triage, data sharing with patient consent, and equity of access. We should run pilots with independent evaluation and meaningful patient involvement before scaling up.

Our organisation strongly supports the proposed changes to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services in our area.
