Thank you for the opportunity to respond. We are a youth-focused community organisation operating in England, and we regularly hear from young people about the practical impact of delays in primary care and mental health services. The core aim should be to get people seen quickly when they need help, while building a sustainable workforce that can support longer-term health needs. I think a multi-layered approach is needed, with clear delivery plans and strong implementation oversight to prevent temporary fixes from slipping back into longer waits.

What would improve timely access now
- Increase GP, nurse and therapist appointment slots by expanding workforce capacity and making scheduling more efficient. In practice this means more GPs, practice nurses, nurse prescribers and therapists, plus flexible staffing models across practices. Local clinics could run extended hours and same-day triage slots, with clear pathways to quicker mental health screening for those presenting with anxiety, depression or stress-related symptoms. We’ve seen cases where a same-day triage nurse quickly identifies urgent needs and redirects patients to the most appropriate clinician, reducing the back-and-forth and missed school or work days.
- Optimise scheduling and use digital tools cautiously but effectively. Online booking should be reliable, with visible wait-time indicators and patient-self-rostering options where appropriate. Telehealth can help, but it must be complemented by in-person slots for assessments where contact matters, and by proactive outreach to patients who miss appointments.
- Expand team-based primary care models. Multidisciplinary teams in communities, with better integration between GP practices, pharmacists and mental health practitioners, can share follow-up work and reduce bottlenecks. For example, nurse-led chronic condition clinics that handle routine follow-ups while GPs focus on complex cases can free slots for urgent care.
- Build clearer flow from primary to community mental health services. A more direct connection between GP/nurse triage and early intervention teams would cut delays. Practitioners in schools and colleges should have streamlined referral routes to community teams so young people don’t bounce between services.

Expanding community mental health teams, early intervention and crisis response
- Expand early intervention and crisis response capacity. Young people’s needs often intensify quickly; having rapid access to talking therapies, family involvement options and crisis response teams near schools or youth hubs would prevent deteriorations. We should see more locally based crisis support that operates beyond standard office hours and can mobilise quickly when risk is present.
- Improve parity with physical health services. Mental health care often trails behind physical health in terms of funding, staffing and timely access. Equitable staffing investments, with dedicated teams for youth, should be part of routine NHS planning. More accessible talking therapies (CBT, ACT, and digital CBT where appropriate) paired with available social support would help close this gap.
- Strengthen links with education and youth services. Schools, colleges and community organisations are often the first to notice distress. Better co-operation with these settings and joint care plans would shorten waiting times and keep people engaged with support that suits their daily lives.
- Ensure quality and safety in crisis pathways. Quick access is essential, but so is appropriate safety planning and continuity of care. Clear protocols, supervision for frontline staff and easy-to-understand information for patients and families are crucial.

Longer-term workforce development
- Increase training places and return‑to‑practice support. To sustainably grow GPs, nurses and mental health professionals, we need more training places in medical schools, nursing programs and psychology/therapy training. Return-to-practice packages with supervised placements would help people re-enter the workforce after a break, reducing long-term gaps.
- Expand apprenticeships and career pathways. Apprenticeships that blend practical service delivery with study can attract a broader range of people into health roles, including those who may not follow traditional university routes. This should be coupled with robust mentoring, supervision and clear progression routes.
- Invest in continuing professional development (CPD). Ongoing, funded CPD is essential to keep skills up-to-date and to support staff who take on new roles, such as extended-scope practice or mental health first aid. This also helps with staff retention and morale, which in turn improves patient access.

Important cautions and ways to implement
- Funding and workforce planning must be long-term and predictable. Short-term injections of capacity can collapse if staffing isn’t sustained. Plans should include recruitment pipelines, retention packages and local flexibility to respond to demographic shifts.
- Co-design with young people. We should involve patients and service users in designing appointment models, booking interfaces and crisis pathways. Real-world feedback from the community will improve both access and the relevance of care.
- Data and transparency. Clear targets, regular reporting on wait times and service activity will help build trust and enable responsive adjustments. Local collaborations between NHS providers, local authorities and the voluntary sector can share best practices.
- Equality considerations. Access should be equitable across urban and rural areas, and services must be accessible to people with disabilities, those who speak languages other than English, and those with different working hours or caring responsibilities.

In summary, timely access will come from growing the workforce in a planned, well-supported way, redesigning pathways to shorten wait times, and investing in the long-term pipeline from training to CPD. We support the vision of expanding capacity and strengthening early intervention and crisis services, provided there is robust implementation, stable funding, and genuine involvement of young people in shaping the services that affect them. Only with sustained commitment and practical delivery plans can we deliver the parity and reliability that young people deserve.

To improve timely access, the most effective change would be to increase the number of appointment slots across GP, nurse and mental health services by hiring more clinicians and expanding session capacity. In my area, GP times are scarce—getting a same-day or even next-day slot is rare, and a 2-week wait is common for routine issues. Increased staffing, including additional GPs and practice nurses, would help shorten those waits and enable longer appointment times for complex symptoms. For mental health, IAPT and local counselling services have long waits (several weeks). Hiring more therapists and enabling longer or more frequent slots would allow earlier intervention and reduce crisis referrals. I’ve had colleagues who waited two months for therapy intake, which worsened anxiety and work stress.

Additionally, optimised scheduling would make a big difference: more flexible hours (evenings and Saturdays), clearer triage to direct people to the right service, and better digital booking with real-time availability. Expanding group education sessions on chronic conditions could also free up individual slots. These changes would make care more proactive and keep people well, rather than waiting until problems escalate.

i strongly believe thank you for the opportunity to feed in. In our area of England, getting timely access to GP appointments, community health services and mental health support can feel like a daily challenge for families and working people. I’m not against the idea of bigger, longer-term workforce planning, but I want to see changes that are practical now and sustainable over the next decade. Increasing training places across the board would help ease bottlenecks in the medium to long term. More GP trainees and more nurses and allied health professionals entering community teams could gradually reduce wait times in places like ours where demand is high and appointments fill quickly. In practice, that means investing in more practice-based tutors, protected time for supervision, and partnerships between colleges, trusts and smaller practices to spread training more evenly across urban and rural areas.

Support for return-to-practice is the other piece that could unlock more capacity sooner. We’ve seen people take a break for family or caring responsibilities, then struggle to re-enter as patient demand grows. Flexible routes—bridging modules, mentored placements, and funded clinical placements that fit around work and family life—would help bring experienced professionals back into GP, community nursing and mental health teams. It’s important that indemnity, regulatory requirements and digital competency updates are addressed as part of these packages so returning clinicians don’t face unnecessary delays or financial barriers.

Apprenticeships and CPD also deserve strong emphasis. Apprenticeships can widen access to roles like nursing associates, physician associates and mental health support workers, creating clear on-ramps into primary care teams. If we can link apprenticeships to strong progression paths—toward qualified nursing or clinical roles—these schemes should help improve retention by giving staff tangible long-term goals. Our local teams are already piloting some of these approaches, and when people see a tangible career route and receive dedicated training, morale and stability improve—at least in the short term.

Meanwhile, CPD must be meaningful and protected. Clinicians often cite a lack of time and funding for training as a barrier, so protected time for learning, funded courses and practical skill refreshers (such as motivational interviewing for mental health, digital triage, and safe prescribing for pharmacists in primary care) should be standard, not optional. In our practice, a CPD day focused on urgent care triage helped staff reduce unnecessary face-to-face appointments and improved patient flow on busy mornings. If CPD is to work at scale, it needs to be consistent across regions; I’d also like to see more standardised digital competencies so teams can share best practices and learn from one another.

Of course, all this must be accompanied by smarter workforce deployment. We need to maximise the role of pharmacists, physiotherapists and care coordinators within GP and community teams to relieve doctors and nurses of non-clinical tasks. Digital improvements—streamlined booking, virtual quick triage, and integrated care records—could help ensure that appointments go to the right professional first time and that urgent cases aren’t waiting behind routine checks.

This is a long-term plan, and its success will hinge on funding, governance, and the ability to attract and retain people in every part of the country, not just in the places with the strongest recruitment. I would like to see clear national targets for reducing waiting times linked to local delivery plans, with transparent reporting on progress and disparities between urban and rural areas or more and less deprived communities. If these changes are combined—more training places, genuine return-to-practice routes, robust apprenticeships, meaningful CPD, and smart workforce deployment—then timely access to GP, community health and mental health services can improve in a way that’s fair and sustainable for patients, clinicians and taxpayers alike. I’m cautiously hopeful that this approach can work, provided it is funded, well managed, and grounded in real, on-the-ground needs rather than purely policy aims.

Thank you for asking. From where I’m standing, timely access to GP, community health and mental health services in England is uneven, and that uncertainty makes planning life—from studies to work—tough. I’d really welcome changes that knit primary care and mental health more tightly together, while making sure young people aren’t left waiting months for something that should be available within days. My views come from seeing friends struggle to book GP visits, and from hearing peers describe long waits for CAMHS or university counselling that doesn’t always fit their schedules around lectures and part-time work. On the flip side, I’ve also seen the value of truly integrated local services where a single point of contact can steer you to GP, nurse, mental health support and social care in one place. So my thinking is twofold: expand core mental health capacity with early intervention and crisis response, and back that up with physically co-located hubs that bring services together for seamless local care.

What changes would help most

- Expand community mental health teams and early intervention, with strong crisis response and talking therapies: It’s essential to grow multidisciplinary teams that can offer timely assessment, evidence-based therapies and rapid escalation if someone is in crisis. Early intervention in psychosis, youth-focused counselling, and brief, scalable talking therapies (CBT, DBT-informed approaches, sleep and stress management) need to be available without long waits. In practice, that means more mental health nurses, social workers, therapists and peer-support workers embedded in every locality, with clear referral pathways from GPs and schools. Reducing the lag between initial contact and a first session would materially improve how young people feel about accessing help and reduce crises that stem from delays.

- Strengthen crisis response so help is available when it’s needed most: A 24/7 crisis line, mobile crisis teams that can reach a young person quickly, and safe, welcoming spaces for urgent support would prevent avoidable hospital admissions. In my experience, timely crisis support can be the difference between someone staying in a dangerous loop and getting stable enough to start longer-term therapy. That requires reliable funding, clear operating hours, and protocols that enable rapid escalation to inpatient care only when appropriate.

- Normalise parity with physical health: Services for mental health should be as straightforward to access as a GP appointment for back pain or a physical issue. That means same-day or next-day urgent slots, predictable waiting times, and transparent communication about delays. I’d like to see publicly reported waiting-time dashboards by locality for GP, CAMHS, community nursing and talking therapies, so young people know what to expect and can plan accordingly.

- Invest in co-located community hubs with social care and VCSE partners: The most transformative change would be building local hubs where primary care, mental health services, social care, and voluntary, community and social enterprise partners are physically under one roof or linked by a shared IT and appointment system. A hub could house a GP practice, a mental health nurse, a counsellor, a social care worker, and a VCSE advisor offering employment, housing or welfare guidance. For me, this would remove the stress of juggling multiple referrals and failing to hear back from different teams. A practical example would be a campus or high-street hub where students, young families, and small employer staff can walk in for a same-day triage, then be fast-tracked to the right service in one place.

- Create streamlined, patient-centred referral and care-planning systems: Shared electronic records with consent-based access, agreed referral criteria, and joint care plans would save people from repeating their story to every new clinician. That would also support safer out-of-hours care and better data on what works locally. It’s important this technology respects privacy, with clear opt-ins for young people and robust governance.

- Build the workforce and sustainable funding model: We need stable, long-term funding for these hubs and for the expanded mental health teams, not short-term pilots that end when budgets tighten. This includes training pipelines (students in health and social care, apprenticeships in mental health support roles), better pay and career development so staff stay in community settings. In my experience, staff turnover and long vacancies directly translate into longer waits for patients.

- Ensure real partnership with young people and local communities: Co-design with students, youth workers and VCSE organisations so services reflect actual needs—hours that fit study schedules, online booking options, multilingual staff, and culturally competent resources. I’ve seen peer-led groups and community mentors make a big difference when they are genuinely involved in planning and delivery.

Practical steps for local areas

- Map and publish current wait times across GP, CAMHS, community nursing and talking therapies; set time-bound targets for reductions in each pathway.
- Pilot co-located hubs in diverse neighbourhoods, with clear governance, shared appointment systems, and joint care plans for families and young people.
- Introduce 24/7 crisis pathways with mobile teams and crisis-lite clinics attached to hubs.
- Allocate ring-fenced funds for early intervention services and for ongoing maintenance of hubs, with annual public reporting on outcomes and equal access metrics.
- Strengthen school and college partnerships to identify needs early and link students to appropriate services through streamlined referrals.

If these changes are done thoughtfully, they can reduce waiting times, improve parity with physical health, and give young people a clearer, less intimidating route to care. For me, the aim is a local system where turning to “someone to help” doesn’t require navigating a maze of separate services. A well-connected hub that brings GP, mental health support, social care and community organisations together would be a real step forward in delivering timely, compassionate care that fits with our lives.

Overall, I’d support a bold push towards expanded mental health capacity and integrated, co-located local hubs, provided the plans are co-designed with young people, properly funded and backed by transparent performance data. These changes have the potential to make access genuinely timely and to close the gap between mental and physical health care in our communities.

Our organisation welcomes measures to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services in England. A more holistic approach is needed to genuinely reduce waits and improve outcomes.

I strongly agree that timely access to GP, community health and mental health services will improve if we invest in co-located community hubs that bring primary care, community teams, mental health services, social care and VCSE partners together in one place. In my town, a pilot hub where a GP, a mental health nurse, a social worker and a link worker from a local charity operate alongside district nursing has helped reduce referrals and shorten waiting times. People can get same-day triage, quicker access to counselling or a mental health check, and support that doesn’t require navigating multiple phone lines.

To grow and retain staff, targeted recruitment, international hiring, incentives, pay improvements, flexible working and wellbeing support are essential. A nearby practice has introduced flexible shifts and wellbeing budgets, which has improved morale and coverage during peak demand. Scaling this approach across more sites would help everyone access care sooner and reduce burnout.

Expanding multidisciplinary teams is also key: pharmacists to review medicines and manage minor issues, physiotherapists for MSK care, paramedics for home visits, and physician associates to handle routine reviews. This would free GPs to focus on complex cases and speed up access for urgent concerns. It should be backed by good IT links and clear care pathways to protect patient privacy and continuity of care.

Access to GP, community and mental health services in my area can feel piecemeal, with long phone queues and referrals that get stuck in different teams. I would support investment in co-located community hubs that integrate primary care, mental health, social care and VCSE partners. In theory it would make it easier to see the right person quickly, with a single point of entry and better information sharing across services. In practice, it would only work if there is stable, long‑term funding, clear governance, and real 24/7 accessibility. I’ve seen friends miss appointments after phone triage pushes them onto hold for ages, and a migrant friend frustrated by lack of interpreters in the intake process; colocated hubs must include interpreters, culturally competent staff, and outreach to deprived and ethnic minority communities to avoid new barriers.

Additionally, there should be flexible access: extended hours, walk-in slots, and mobile/community outreach for those who can’t travel. I’d like to see success measured by reduced waiting times, better suicide and crisis response, and genuine involvement of young people in design.

In my area, timely access to GP, community health and mental health services would improve most if we combined flexible access with stronger capacity and a broader skill mix in primary care. For someone who works full‑time, the current pattern of available slots often feels restrictive and unresponsive to urgent but non‑emergency needs. I would welcome a two‑track approach: improve off‑peak access while expanding the workforce and the ways care can be delivered.

First, establish regular evening and weekend clinics with guaranteed same‑day urgent slots. Being able to book after work or at the weekend would make a real difference for working people and parents who cannot take long lunch breaks or unpaid leave. The system should start with a robust triage process by phone or online and reserve a fixed number of urgent same‑day slots daily. If someone has a fever, a severe throat infection, or a sudden flare‑up of a chronic condition, they should be able to see a clinician the same day rather than waiting weeks. To prevent wasted slots, triage should direct patients to the most appropriate path—an in‑person GP visit, a nurse‑led clinic, or a pharmacist for minor ailments—and offer teleconsultations where appropriate.

Second, increase appointment capacity by expanding staffing and optimising scheduling. We need more GPs and nurses, but also smarter use of time. Longer, meaningful appointments for complex or multi‑condition patients would reduce repeated follow‑ups and improve outcomes. A shift toward more nurse and therapist appointments, with protected time for care coordination, would free GPs to focus on what only they can do. Local clinics should be funded to recruit and retain staff, with clear pathways for ongoing training and career development. A coordinated scheduling system that distributes demand more evenly across the day—avoiding long waits for routine care while keeping space for urgent needs—could shave significant time off waits.

Third, broaden multidisciplinary teams to treat routine cases and free GPs for more complex care. Pharmacists can handle minor ailments, review medications, and manage some repeat prescriptions; physiotherapists can run quick turnaround musculoskeletal clinics for back and joint pain; paramedics and physician associates could conduct home visits or initial triage in the practice setting. In mental health, more in‑practice therapists and case managers, alongside stepped‑care options and group sessions, would expand reach without overloading psychiatrists. Digital tools—online CBT, guided self‑help and remote monitoring—should be offered as a complement, while ensuring they remain accessible to people with limited internet access or language needs.

Fourth, we must safeguard timely mental health access specifically. I’ve seen waits for talking therapies grow, and families tell me about delays in CAMHS that feel unacceptable. A stepped‑care model, with rapid triage, brief interventions within a week, and swift escalation to higher‑intensity therapy when needed, could transform the experience. Any digital delivery should be inclusive—offering translation services, phone options, and face‑to‑face alternatives for those who need them. Local workshops or group therapies can also reach more people without sacrificing quality.

Finally, the changes must be designed with equity in mind. We should maintain non‑digital booking routes and ensure interpreters are available. Ongoing local consultation with patients, front‑line staff and community groups will help tailor services to real need and avoid widening gaps for the digitally excluded or those living in more isolated areas. If these programmes are piloted with clear targets for wait times, patient satisfaction, and clinical outcomes, I think they can move timely access from a postcode lottery to a dependable part of NHS care that supports working people, carers and families dealing with non‑emergency health concerns.

While I welcome the aim of reducing waits, I disagree that the main answer is simply to expand community mental health teams, push early intervention and more talking therapies as standalone solutions. In practice, timely access will not improve unless GP capacity is addressed first: in my area, people wait weeks for a standard GP appointment, and mental health referrals can stall because primary care contracts are stretched. Crisis response is similarly stretched; there have been occasions when someone in acute distress waited hours for a response, leaving them in distress. Expanding teams without adequate funding for recruitment, supervision and 24/7 availability risks creating more bureaucracy and longer overall waits. I believe targeted resources matter most: interpreters and culturally competent staff, outreach to deprived and minority communities, and consistent access in local hubs. For those who do not speak English or distrust the system, interpreters and culturally sensitive care are not optional add ons but essential. Also invest in GP capacity with extended hours, simpler booking, and mobile clinics in hard to reach areas.

Long-term gains depend on expanding training, return-to-practice schemes, apprenticeships and CPD to sustainably grow GPs, nurses and mental-health staff. In the near term, pair these with improved triage, extended GP hours and local multi-disciplinary hubs to reduce delays now.

I understand the aim of targeting resources, interpreters, culturally competent staff and outreach to reduce access gaps for deprived, ethnic minority, migrant and marginalised groups. However, I disagree that this on its own will deliver timely access to GP, community health and mental health services in our area. The core bottlenecks are not solely language or cultural barriers but insufficient overall capacity and inflexible appointment systems. In Scotland, many practices report GP and nurse shortages, with routine slots two weeks away and urgent same-day needs often left unaddressed. Even when interpreters are available, they are not guaranteed for every call or face delays at triage, which can push urgent issues out of the window for weeks. Outreach programmes are valuable but too variable and do not reach everyone who needs them, especially older residents who struggle with online booking or complex referral pathways.

What would help most is a system-wide uplift: more frontline clinicians (GPs, nurses, mental health professionals) and better retention, extended and flexible hours, and greater use of nurse-led and pharmacist-led triage to free GPs for more complex cases. Interpreters and culturally competent staff should be funded as core, on-demand services with guaranteed availability, but only as part of a universal improvement in access—through longer opening hours, simpler appointment processes, and sustained funding for community link workers who can navigate people through the system and reduce avoidable delays. This combined approach would address the root causes, not just the symptoms of disparity.

From a Welsh perspective, timely access to GP, nurse and mental health services matters for me and people I know. I support increasing appointment slots by hiring more GPs, nurses and talking therapists, expanding sessions and using smarter scheduling so a slot is available when it is really needed. In practice, waiting times in my area mean people delay care, and minor issues become bigger problems. A family member recently needed a mental health assessment; the wait exceeded a month, while routine physical health care moved more quickly. Extending hours into evenings and weekends would help those who work standard hours, and introducing flexible digital triage can cut wasted trips, as long as people still get real human contact when needed.

But I’m cautious about only boosting GP capacity without strengthening community mental health teams and early intervention. We need better crisis response, more accessible talking therapies, and parity with physical health in terms of funding and workforce planning. Investment must be predictable and targeted for rural and Welsh-speaking communities, with transport support where relevant. Overall, I welcome actions to expand capacity, provided they are accompanied by robust mental health services and clear delivery timelines.

Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services will improve most if we focus on growing and keeping the staff who deliver them. In my area, delays stem from vacancies and burnout, so I’d prioritise targeted recruitment campaigns in local colleges and universities, plus outreach to commuter towns, with clear progression routes to retain people. International hiring should be embraced with streamlined visa routes, recognition of professional qualifications, and solid cultural induction, supported by mentors to shorten adaptation time. Incentives such as student loan repayments or relocation grants, and pay improvements that reflect workload and out-of-hours commitments, would make these roles more attractive.

Flexibility matters: more part-time and job-share options, extended daytime and Saturday clinics, and a robust locum pool to cover holidays without draining daily capacity. Robust wellbeing support is essential—protected supervision, access to mental health resources for staff, manageable workloads, and peer support. Investments in training posts and digital triage with nurse practitioners can free up GPs to see urgent cases sooner. With coordinated funding and leadership, these changes could lift access within months rather than years.

Improving timely access to GP, community health and mental health services in our area would be greatly helped by expanding multidisciplinary teams. Having pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates handle routine issues such as minor infections, back pain, medication reviews and triage would free GPs to concentrate on complex cases. In practice, our local practice already sees faster waits for routine queries when a pharmacist is available in the morning to review medicines and advise on minor ailments. This model should be rolled out widely with proper governance, training and clear pathways to escalate when needed. Secondly, offering evening and weekend clinics as well as guaranteed same-day urgent slots would make a real difference for working people and those with urgent non-emergency needs. Thirdly, we need to grow and retain primary care staff through targeted recruitment, international hiring, better pay, flexible working and wellbeing support. That combination would help stabilise teams, improve continuity of care and reduce burnout, which in turn improves access.

In my area, I’ve seen the frictio points in GP, community health and mental health services first-hand, especially when trying to fit care around a busy work week. I’d like to see two or three local pilots that mix extended hours, more urgent slots and digital triage, with clear targetss on average wait times and patient satisfaction. Importantly, any expansion must include staff wellbeing: sustainabl rostering, protected time for training, reasonable workloads, and opportunities for staff feedback. Without that, gains could be short-lived as burnout rises and turnover increases. Finally, ensure equity in access. Provisions must considerr people with transport constraints, those who rely on public services, language barriers and digital exclusion. The most effective improvements will be those that arr offered in multiple formats (in-person, video,, telephone) and at venuess within reasonable reach of different communities. Overall, a thoughtful mix of expanding capacity and expanding access windows—with rigorous monitoring and staff support—would likely deliver the most tangible improvements for my area. It wouldn’t be a silver bullet, but it would address the real bottlenecks I’ve seen: queues for routine GP care, difficulty fitting appointments around work, and htee lengthy waits for mental health support. I’d support a staged rollout with clear milestones and feedback loops to ensure the plan works for patients and for the hardworking teams delivering it.

We strongly support the proposals to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services in our area. I STRONGLY AGREE THAT THE PROPOSED CHANGES WOULD IMPROVE TIMELY ACCESS TO GP, COMMUNITY HEALTH AND MENTAL HEALTH SERVICES. i strongly believe to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services, I would support expanding multidisciplinary teams in primary care. Access to timely GP, community and mental health care is uneven in our area, especially for those with full-time jobs. A practical path forward would combine extended access hours with smarter triage and booking.

First, extend GP and community health hours: offer at least two weeknights until 8pm and a weekend clinic in every locality, with guaranteed same‑day urgent slots for non‑emergency needs. This would help parents, shift workers and those with urgent symptoms who can’t attend in standard hours. Staffing must be funded and rota‑friendly to avoid burnout.

Second, overhaul NHS111 and care navigation: invest in robust clinical triage (more clinician input, safer algorithms) and direct booking into urgent slots across GP, urgent care and community teams. Simplify patient flow to reduce duplication—one coherent care pathway with a navigator who can book, follow up and transfer records (while respecting data privacy). Ensure non‑digital access channels remain strong and transparent.

My organisation has heard from residents who wait days for GP access, or get bounced between NHS111 and local services, delaying help for mental health crises. A combined approach—expanded access hours plus streamlined triage and navigation—would improve avoidable delays, while keeping safety and equity at the forefront.

i strongly believe from my perspective in Scotland, the idea of co-located community hubs that bring together GP practices, community health teams, mental health services, social care and local VCSE partners sounds promising for timely access. In practice, when I have tried to get mental health support, bottlenecks and multiple referrals often mean days or weeks before someone picks up. A hub with an integrated appointment system and a single point of contact could reduce those delays and provide wraparound support for needs like housing or benefits through VCSE partners. However, I worry about how it would work on the ground. The success depends on clear governance and funding to prevent staff burnout and ensure real joint working rather than handoff after handoff. It also needs flexible hours and accessible transport, particularly in more rural pockets of Scotland. Data sharing must be transparent, with consent and strong privacy safeguards; staff need joint training to avoid confusion about who leads a case. Overall, I would support piloting a few co-located hubs with robust evaluation, focusing on patient experience, wait times, and the ability to signpost quickly to social care and mental health supports. If designed inclusively, this could improve local care without eroding patient choice!

I strongly support the changes proposed to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services. Expanding community mental health teams and investing in early intervention, crisis response and talking therapies will reduce waits and bring mental health care closer to parity with physical health. This means more integrated teams with same-week access to assessment, quicker referral pathways from GP, and robust crisis services that can respond within hours rather than days. I’ve seen local families struggle when mental health symptoms escalate because timely support isn’t available, risking unnecessary escalation and hospital admissions. 

On primary care staffing, there is a real need to grow and stabilise the workforce. If practices can recruit and stay with staff, patients would access slots sooner, benefit from safer phone or video triage, and enjoy more consistent after-hours provision. I’d also welcome extended and easier access to mental health crisis lines and direct pathways to talking therapies to shorten waits and improve outcomes.

absolutely from where I sit in Scotland, the biggest win would be more appointments and longer slots, especially for mental health. I’ve waited a couple of weeks for a GP appointment and found access to specialist mental health support sometimes slower than I’d like, which pushes people toward out‑of‑hours services or self‑management that isn’t always safe.

That means hiring more GPs, nurses and therapists, expanding session lengths, and offering flexible hours so people who work can get seen. But simply adding slots won’t help if booking remains opaque. I back improvements to NHS111 and the clinical triage and booking systems: urgent cases flagged and fast‑tracked, clearer pathways to see a clinician, and a less fragmented patient flow with fewer duplicate requests. A slick digital booking system with real‑time availability, text reminders and navigator support would help older or less tech‑savvy patients.

Investing in co‑located community hubs that bring primary care, community teams, mental health and social care together is attractive, but must be carefully planned to avoid longer travel for rural residents and to protect privacy. Shared records and collaborative staff, plus robust funding and evaluation, would be essential. Overall, I support a measured, piloted approach with safeguards!

In my area, the change that would most improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services is not a single tweak but a package that protects continuity of care for people with complex or chronic needs and, at the same time, ensures appointment times are long enough to cover what actually needs doing. When you manage long-term conditions or vulnerability, a named clinician and a stable team makes the care plan coherent and safer. Without that, you end up repeating histories, chasing referrals, and health outcomes can worsen because small issues aren’t picked up early enough. I’ve seen this firsthand with relatives and in my own experience: a rotation of different GPs means medication reviews get hurried, notes don’t always align, and we’re back on the phone asking for the same information again a few weeks later. That creates avoidable delays and more visits further down the line, which isn’t efficient for anyone, especially people with complex needs who are most at risk of deterioration.

Longer appointment times are essential for complex cases. I’d suggest a minimum of 15–20 minutes for standard complex or chronic care reviews, with 25–30 minutes for initial assessments in mental health or when social factors (like housing, work, or carer duties) are involved. In practice, that would mean that a routine check becomes a genuine, clinically useful visit rather than a quick box-tick. It also allows time to discuss side effects of medicines, review care plans, and arrange the right multidisciplinary input without having to chase multiple follow-ups. In mental health, longer slots could accommodate risk assessment, safety planning, and signposting to appropriate support at the first point of contact; a rushed 10-minute slot simply isn’t enough to build trust or stability for someone in crisis or mounting anxiety.

Timely access needs reliable triage and same-day options, but with safeguards so people aren’t parked in a queue for hours. A robust booking system that prioritises urgent needs, plus the option for same-day slots in practices with enough staffing, would help. Importantly, triage should be conducted by trained staff who understand when a patient needs a quick in-person appointment, a video consult, or a referral to a community service. For those who need in-person care, the capacity should be there, not just a policy promise.

A more integrated, multidisciplinary approach would also improve access and outcomes. In my area, I’ve benefited when a practice has a nurse prescriber, a pharmacist who can review medications, and a physiotherapist or mental health professional embedded in the team. This reduces inappropriate GP referrals, speeds up appropriate management, and frees GP time for those with the most complex needs. For example, a musculoskeletal issue could be managed by a physio rather than waiting for a GP slot, while a medication review could be led by a pharmacist. The result is faster recovery and fewer repeat visits.

Mental health services benefit particularly from easier pathways into talking therapies and crisis support. Embedding mental health clinicians in primary care, expanding social prescribing, and ensuring quick access to IAPT or equivalent services would prevent escalation and support earlier recovery. Of course, digital access can help with convenience, but we must avoid leaving people behind who lack online access or digital literacy; maintaining a telephone and in-person option is essential.

Practically, I’d advocate for a staged rollout: pilot extended appointment times and named-carer continuity in a few practices first, with clear metrics (waiting times, patient outcomes, hospital admissions, and patient satisfaction). If the pilots show reduced repeats and better condition control, scale up with appropriate funding, workforce planning, and ongoing patient feedback. It’s also important to involve patients and carers in designing these changes so they hit the issues that matter most in real life—transport, carer burden, and working hours.

In short, timely access would improve most where care is continuous, collaborative, and properly resourced. Longer, consistent, team-based appointments for those with chronic and complex needs, paired with smart triage and strong mental health and community health integration, would likely yield quicker, safer care and fewer repeat visits in the long run.

i really think access to GP, community health and mental health services needs a workforce plan that grows and retains staff while keeping care accessible for all. I fully support the proposed changes to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services. In my area many slots are 10 minutes, which forcrs rushed consultations and then more follow-ups. Longer slots would prevent small issues from turning into bigger problems and would cut overall drlays Third, invest in integrated community hubs where GP, district nursing, physioo and mental health teams share a single care plan. Keeping the patient in one loop, rather than being shunted between services, speeds up genuinely needed help and avoids repeating questions. Finally, digital triage should speed access without eroding continuity. Urgent flags must stil reach the patient’s named clinician when appropriate. I’m writing as someone living in England who sees how uneven access to GP, community health and mental health services can be, especially in deprived areas and for people from ethnic minority or migrant backgrounds. I disagree with ideas that simply “make access easier” in a generic sense without targeting the underlying gaps. What would actually make a real difference is urgent, well-funded action aimed specifically at those communities that currently fall through the cracks: consistent interpreters, culturally competent staff, and proactive outreach.

Language and interpretation are fundamental. In practice, I’ve seen appointments booked online or over the phone where there’s no interpreter available, or where interpreters aren’t guaranteed for a family’s preferred language. This isn’t just inconvenient; it leads to miscommunication, missed symptoms, and sometimes wrong treatment plans. It’s common for multilingual patients to be offered a rough, ad-hoc translation by a family member, which raises safeguarding and confidentiality concerns. We need guaranteed access to professional interpreters across primary care, mental health, and even urgent or triage calls, with booking systems that actively flag language needs and allocate interpreter time as a standard part of every appointment. If a practice truly cannot provide that, it should flag and re-route to services that can. Digital patient information and triage tools also need to be multilingual and tested with real users from those communities, not just translated brochures that sit unused.

Culturally competent staff aren’t a luxury; they’re a necessity for accurate assessment and trust. This means not only language skills but training in cultural norms around health beliefs, stigma, gender preferences, and family dynamics. In our area, some clinics feel distant or unable to respond to concerns about mental health in ways that respect cultural sensibilities, which pushes people away from seeking help until crises hit. I’ve heard of situations where a clinician assumed a presentation was “stress” rather than recognizing specific cultural expressions of distress, delaying support. We should actively recruit and retain staff from a range of backgrounds, with mandatory, ongoing training in cultural competence and anti-discrimination, and allow flexible appointment options (for example, female-only clinics if requested, or gender-appropriate staff for sensitive issues). It’s also vital to ensure interpreters and bilingual staff are available not just in GP practices but across community health teams and mental health services.

Outreach to deprived and marginalised groups must be a core component, not an afterthought. Mobile clinics, pop-up bases in community centres, and longer opening hours in areas with high deprivation would help. But outreach must be genuine, driven by community voices rather than just “awareness campaigns” that do not translate into easier access. I’d like to see paid community health workers or “link workers” from within communities who know local language nuances, can help navigate services, and can accompany people to appointments where appropriate. Partnerships with faith groups, local charities, and schools can normalise help-seeking and ensure information is realistic about what services can provide and how to access them quickly.

Targeted resource allocation is essential. Generic funding on a national level often ends up whittled down by administrative overheads or distributed according to population, not need. We need dedicated funding that follows measured inequities: more GPs and nurse hours in high-need neighbourhoods, long-term investments in translation and interpretation services, and sustained support for mental health services in areas with long waiting times and high deprivation. This includes revising payment and staffing models so practices aren’t pressured to rely on temporary staff who lack familiarity with the local community. And there must be transparency: publish equity metrics showing how access and outcomes improve for specific groups, with consequences if targets aren’t met.

From a personal perspective, improvements that fail to address language, cultural relevance and proactive outreach feel incomplete. For families who are newer here or who speak languages other than English at home, a five-minute telephone triage that offers no interpreter or a clinician who doesn’t understand their background isn’t “timely access” it’s a barrier that pushes people toward urgent, sometimes crisis-driven care instead of proactive, preventive support.

So, while I welcome the aim of improving access, I believe the changes most likely to work are:
- guaranteed, funded interpretation in all primary and mental health contacts; multilingual digital and written information; and interpreter-friendly triage processes.
- deliberate recruitment of culturally competent staff and ongoing compulsory training; flexible service models that respect cultural and gender needs.
- proactive, community-led outreach with visible presence in the places people trust and already attend, backed by stable funding and long-term commitments.
- robust equity data collection and public accountability so progress (or lack of it) is clear and consequences follow underperformance in reducing access gaps.

Without these targeted mechanisms, policies risk being well-meaning but ineffective, leaving the most marginalised groups without timely care when they need it most. I want to see real, measurable moves to close the gaps, not just general promises of easier access.

A good starting point would be a named clinician for ongoing care, with 30–45 minute slots for those with long-term or multiple conditions. This would reduce mixed messages and ensure better continuity. For my own experience, quick 10-minute GP slots and rushed referrals left me repeating the same concerns over months until something escalated.

Use practical triage (phone/video) to direct people to the right professional (physiotherapist, pharmacist, mental health worker) without clogging GP slots. If we just pile in more short appointments, waits will shift rather than shrink, especially for the most vulnerable. What matters is continuity plus time, not more of the same.

i strongly believe thank you for inviting a response. Our organisation represents many older residents across England, and we want to see better timely access to GP, community NHS services and mental health care. We recognise that digital tools can speed things up, but we remain concerned that a shift that prioritises online booking, e‑consultations and remote care above all else will leave a significant slice of the population behind. In particular, I think of the many neighbours and clients who rely on a simple telephone call or a face‑to‑face appointment, and who still struggle when the only obvious route is a screen or an app.

What would help most, in our view, is a careful, two‑track approach that expands digital access while preserving easy non‑digital routes. Here are the changes we think would work best in practice:

- Keep and strengthen non‑digital access alongside digital expansion
  - Maintain robust telephone triage and same‑day call‑back slots, with clear indication of how quickly someone will be seen.
  - Guarantee same‑day in‑person appointments where clinical need is urgent, and ensure home visits are available for those who cannot travel easily.
  - Build more local walk‑in clinics or pop‑up clinics in community spaces so people don’t have to navigate a complicated system just to get a consultation.

- Make online booking and e‑consultations genuinely useful for those who use them, but easy to bypass for those who can’t
  - Invest in a user‑friendly online booking system with a simple, well‑advertised option to book by phone at every stage, plus a reliable auto‑attendant that doesn’t drop into a black hole when demand peaks.
  - Ensure e‑consultations are properly triaged by a real clinician with timely responses, and that there is always a real option to speak to a clinician the same day if symptoms worsen.
  - Provide non‑digital alternatives alongside digital ones in every service description, so people know what their best route is without confusion.

- Prioritise digital inclusion and practical support
  - Fund local schemes to help older people and those with low digital literacy to get online safely, including ‘digital buddy’ schemes, group learning sessions at libraries or GP surgeries, and clear printed guides.
  - Guarantee access to affordable internet and devices for those who need them, or offer loan devices through community groups and GP practices.
  - Train reception and practice staff to recognise digital exclusion and offer immediate assistance, including arranging a phone appointment or a home visit when appropriate.

- Make mental health access reliable and appropriate
  - Remote mental health care can be helpful for follow‑ups and low‑risk cases, but initial assessments and crisis support should always be available in person or by a clear, rapid telephone route.
  - Ensure crisis lines are easy to reach with sensible triage that does not require navigating an online portal first, especially for older patients who may be anxious and unfamiliar with digital tools.
  - Integrate mental health services with community support, so people have a trusted point of contact, whether via a GP, a nurse, or a community worker.

- Keep care coordinated and accountable
  - Improve information sharing between GP practices, community services and social care so that a patient’s needs aren’t lost in the system when transitioning from one service to another.
  - Set measurable targets for decreases in waiting times that apply to all routes (digital and non‑digital). Track access by age, disability and deprivation to avoid blind spots.
  - Pilot digital initiatives in a few diverse areas first, with independent evaluation and a firm commitment to keep or expand non‑digital routes if results show inequities.

Personal experience from our network backs this approach. In our area, when online booking goes down or the app is slow, many older residents default to ringing the practice first thing in the morning and get stuck in long queues, sometimes for days. A neighbour in his eighties recently missed a same‑day appointment because he can’t use a smartphone and has trouble with the on‑screen forms; his wife spends hours guiding him through the process, which isn’t fair and it puts his health at risk. Remote consultations are convenient for follow‑ups, but there are cases—such as new neurological symptoms, eye issues, or severe anxiety—where waiting for a video link or giving a history over chat simply isn’t workable. For mental health, a quick, warm phone call with a clinician who can assess risk and arrange timely in‑person support makes all the difference, not only the convenience of a video screen.

We will support the digitisation where it genuinely improves access and quality, but only if every individual can still obtain an appointment quickly by telephone or in person, and if non‑digital options aren’t treated as second best. Please require explicit assurances that no one is left behind during this transition. A staged roll‑out with strong inclusion measures, funded digital‑inclusion programmes, and clear, simple pathways for those who cannot or will not use online services is essential if this is to work for all older people, all communities and all  beyond.

We look forward to working with you on a balanced plan that truly improves timely access for GP, community health and mental health services without leaving the most vulnerable behind!

- Multidisciplinary teams in local hubs: A GP and practice nurses, a district nurse or allied health professional, a mental health practitioner, a social worker, and a link worker from a VCSE partner all co-located or closely connected with shared spaces and digital records. - Integrated funding and governance: A pooled or jointly funded budget across health, social care and VCSE partners, with shared performance targets and patient-reported outcome measures. Clear governance and patient involvement would be essential so people feel they have a say in what the hub delivers and how it runs.
- Shared information and consent: A common care record or interoperable IT systems, with patient consent processes that are straightforward and respect privacy. Information sharing should be timely and secure, enabling clinicians to see a full picture of someone’s needs and avoid repetitive assessments.
- Access and inclusivity: Flexible hours, easy access by public transport or on foot, step-free access, hearing and translation services, and digital inclusion measures for those who struggle with online booking. In rural areas, mobile hubs or outreach clinics could travel to communities that are hard to reach.
- Navigation and signposting: A dedicated care navigator or care coordinator who helps patients move between services, coordinates appointments, and connects people with social prescribing, housing advice, or occupational health as needed.
- Focus on outcomes and learning: Local pilots with explicit evaluation, so we can see reductions in unnecessary A&E attendances, shorter waiting times for mental health referrals, and improvements in patient experience. Results would feed back into how hubs are developed elsewhere.

I’ve seen elements of this in practice already in a small town centre where a GP practice sits with district nursing and a local charity that runs social activities and welfare support. There are drop-in sessions, same-day urgent care slots and quick connections to a mental health practitioner who knows the local community. For someone with a chronic condition, it’s much easier to get a care plan that covers physical health, mental wellbeing, and social needs in one place. The downside is that these hubs are not universal. Too often they’re a patchy feature rather than a systemic shift, and access can still depend on whether you can travel to the hub, whether there’s a slot available, or whether you’re comfortable with digital booking.

There are real caveats we must address to make this scalable and fair. Co-location alone won’t remove wait times or staff shortages; it requires sufficient workforce planning and sustainable funding. IT systems must be interoperable, not a patchwork of separate databases. We also need to preserve patient choice—people should still be able to access services in their usual GP practice or local clinic if that’s their preference. And we must guard against creating a two-tier system where only certain areas get fully integrated hubs while others lag behind.

If done thoughtfully, with strong governance, meaningful patient involvement, and robust, long-term funding, the hub model could transform how quickly people get the right support. It should be part of a broader strategy that also addresses workforce resilience, digital inclusion, and the social determinants of health. My key asks would be: ensure joint funding with clear accountability; deliver interoperable systems with straightforward consent; build in flexible access for all communities; and measure impact not just on wait times, but on patient experience and long-term outcomes.

Overall, I’m cautiously optimistic about co-located community hubs as a mechanism to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services. The potential is there to create more seamless, person-centred care—provided it’s backed by sustainable funding, strong governance, and a genuine commitment to equity across all local areas.

i strongly believe agree: hire more GPs, nurses and therapists, expand appointment slots and session capacity, and optimise scheduling to cut waiting times and improve timely access to GP, community and mental health services!

Support expanding community mental health teams, early intervention, crisis response and talking therapies to cut waits and improve parity with physical health; but ensure long-term funding, staffing, and that co-located hubs truly are accessible, with clear data sharing and strong VCSE involvement from the start.

From our experience delivering primary, community and mental health services across diverse settings in England, timely access is built on transport, digital connectivity and well‑designed care pathways, not on clinic hours alone. In rural and mobility‑limited areas, parking and premises deficits still deter people from seeking help, so we welcome a mix of solutions.

First, mobile clinics and targeted outreach: regular GP and nurse visits to village halls, market towns and care homes, coordinated with social care support, scheduled in advance and publicised locally.

Second, telehealth hubs: staffed digital booths in libraries or community centres with loan devices and assistance, plus home‑based video options for stable cases, linked to the patient’s usual GP for continuity.

Third, care navigation and triage: invest in NHS111 and clinical triage that prioritises urgent cases, reduces duplication and guides patients to the right local team, with smooth handoffs to primary, community and mental health services.

Fourth, co‑located hubs: fund one‑stop, co‑located primary, community and mental health services with social care and VCSE partners; ensure accessible premises and parking, with care plans co‑designed with local people.

Sustainability and data sharing must underpin any approach, with clear evaluation and local flexibility to respond to changing needs.

Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services in our area remains inconsistent. I support a model that builds co-located community hubs, integrating primary care, district nursing, community mental health and social care with VCSE partners. In practice, a hub could coordinate appointments, housing and welfare advice alongside clinical care, reducing trips and duplication. My experience shows how a lack of integrated pathways leads to repeated calls, long waits and scattergun referrals.

To make this work, the NHS111 and triage process must be improved to prioritise urgent cases, with clear pathways into local services. The current booking systems can be frustrating and opaque, causing delays and misrouting. A single care-navigation function could guide patients through the options, flag urgent needs, and prevent duplication of services.

Finally, increase capacity: expand GP, nurse and therapist slots by hiring staff, extending session lengths where needed, and optimising scheduling to match patient demand. I’ve seen private-sector neighbours absorb demand by adding afternoon clinics; similarly, funded expansion in the NHS could cut waits, keep people out of A&E, and build resilience in the community long term.

I strongly welcome and support the proposed changes to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services in our area. From my own experience living in a rural part of England, I can see how transport, parking and the limits of current premises create real barriers to timely care, especially for older neighbours and those with limited mobility. If we can address these practical hurdles, people will be more likely to seek help when it’s needed, not when it’s convenient for the clinic’s timetable.

Transport, parking and premises deficits are the first things that jump out. Buses don’t run often, pavements are potholed, and the main surgery car park is full long before the first appointment. A neighbour with limited mobility spends over an hour getting to and from a 10‑minute GP slot, and they’re not alone in that. To alleviate this, I’d like to see a network of mobile clinics that visit village halls, community centres and rural lay-bys on a rotating schedule. A GP or nurse van offering routine checks, blood tests, vaccines and minor ailments in the local community would save travel time and make it far easier for people to keep up with care. And when it’s not practical to get in-person care, the mobile service could coordinate with out-of-hours or telehealth for follow‑ups, reducing the need to travel again.

Outreach and better premises access would also help. Regular outreach sessions at libraries, churches and care homes could perform simple checks (blood pressure, diabetes risk assessments, mental health triage) and then quickly refer people to the most appropriate local service. If some practices could share extended premises hours or rotate weekend and evening clinics among several nearby sites, the squeeze on parking and waiting rooms would ease. This kind of shared approach could keep services closer to communities that would otherwise struggle to reach them.

Telehealth hubs offer another practical step. In our town, a small telehealth hub in the library, staffed by someone who can help people log in and navigate the system, could unlock access for many who currently feel left behind by digital rules. Video consultations with GPs or mental health professionals, plus remote triage, can be particularly valuable for mobility‑limited residents or those living far from the main surgeries. It’s important that telehealth complements, not replaces, in-person care—certain conditions demand a face‑to‑face approach—but it could handle routine follow‑ups, urgent non‑emergency checks and mental health check‑ins more efficiently, freeing up clinics for those who truly need in‑person care.

Incentives to support rural access are essential. Providing travel time allowances or extra funding to cover on‑call costs can encourage clinicians to deliver flexible, local services without burning out. Support for outreach days, weekend clinics and after‑hours sessions would help practices meet the needs of people who work shifts or have family responsibilities. When clinicians feel their work is recognised and supported, they’re more likely to offer extended hours in rural settings.

Evening and weekend clinics with guaranteed same‑day urgent slots would be a game‑changer for many working people and those with urgent non‑emergency needs. A robust triage system by phone or online could identify truly urgent cases and reserve same‑day urgent appointments, while still providing standard daytime slots for routine care. In my experience, a guaranteed urgent slot could prevent unnecessary deterioration in someone with anxiety or a new mental‑health concern and reduce the pressure on A&E departments.

Taken together, this mixed model—mobile access, targeted outreach, localized telehealth hubs and sensible incentives—would bring services closer to residents, reduce travel and parking problems, and deliver timely care when it’s most needed. It would also build trust in the system if people felt a service could come to them or be reached quickly for urgent concerns, without sacrificing the quality of in‑person care. I hope these changes are given the proper funding and logistical support to realise a more accessible, patient‑centred NHS in our area.

Access to timely GP, community health and mental health services is a particular challenge in many parts of England, especially where transport is limited, parking is tight, and premises feel cramped or outdated. Our organisation supports a targeted mix of solutions that can deliver quicker, more predictable access while also strengthening the overall care system locally. In practice, this means scaling mobile and outreach options now, while investing in longer‑term, co‑located hubs that bring primary care, mental health, social care and the VCSE together in one accessible place.

Immediate improvements that would make a real difference include:
- Expanding mobile clinics and outreach teams that can visit villages and towns on predictable rosters, including evenings and weekends to reach working people. Mobile GP and nurse prescribers, supported by mental health outreach workers, can handle routine reviews, chronic disease checks and early signs of deteriorating mental health, reducing the need for travel to larger towns. Where possible, these mobile services should be integrated with pharmacy drop‑offs, on‑site blood pressure and blood sugar monitoring, and same‑day access to basic diagnostics.
- Establishing telehealth hubs embedded in community spaces such as libraries, community centres or GP practice hubs. These would offer high‑quality video consultations with clinicians, accompanied by on‑the‑spot digital support for those less confident with technology. In addition to video, a strong telephone triage system and remote monitoring for chronic conditions would help many patients receive timely advice without a long journey.
- Improving transport and parking to reduce avoidable delays. We need a coordinated, patient‑centred transport offer, including subsidy schemes, volunteer driver networks and better timetabling with local bus services, so people can reach their appointments reliably. Parking should be expanded or repurposed at existing hubs to remove a common bottleneck that discourages patients from attending.
- Upgrading premises where needed. Many smaller sites operate in spaces that are not truly accessible or adaptable for the range of services now expected. We support flexible, modular refurbishments or new, purpose‑built spaces that can accommodate same‑day GP slots, multidisciplinary clinics, and quiet rooms for mental health consultations. Accessibility must be a non‑negotiable baseline.

Alongside these immediate steps, a more joined‑up, longer‑term model is essential. Co‑located community hubs that integrate primary care, community and mental health services with social care and VCSE partners offer the strongest path to seamless local care. In practice this would mean:
- Building and funding multi‑disciplinary hubs where GPs, district nurses, mental health professionals, social workers, and VCSEstaff work alongside housing, benefits advisers and community pharmacists, all inside one accessible site. Shared intake and care navigation would enable people to move smoothly between services without repeating stories or waiting for separate appointments.
- Embedding social care and community services in the same hub, with well‑defined care pathways and care coordinators. This reduces fragmentation, helps people with complex needs to access housing support, benefits advice and home‑care services promptly, and prevents unnecessary crises that lead to hospital admissions.
- Ensuring a strong role for VCSE partners in co‑design and delivery. Local voluntary and community groups often know the barriers that patients face and can help with outreach, health literacy, and social‑prescribing links. Co‑location makes it easier for patients to access social and mental health supports at the same time as primary care.
- Creating digital and information governance that supports safer data sharing while protecting patient privacy. A patient‑facing portal, with consent‑based data sharing across the hub, would help patients see a single, up‑to‑date care plan and reduce the need to repeat information.

To realise these changes, we need stable, long‑term funding and a workforce plan that recognises the realities of rural and mobility‑limited areas. Financial incentives to recruit and retain clinicians in underserved locations, live‑in or relocation support, protected time for outreach work, and practical arrangements for flexible staffing will be essential. Simultaneously, a phased rollout with local pilots should be evaluated against clear metrics: time to appointment from referral, no‑show rates, patient satisfaction, hospital admission rates for ambulatory care sensitive conditions, and the degree of care coordination achieved across the hub network.

From our experience of working with rural and mobility‑impaired communities, the blend of mobile, digital and co‑located hub approaches offers the most tangible gains in timely access. A patient who can walk into a nearby hub for a same‑day GP slot, a mental health check, and social‑care advice, with transport arranged or provided, will experience far less friction than the current model where separate appointments are scattered across distant locations. If designed with local involvement and adequate resources, these changes could deliver quicker access, better quality of care, and fewer avoidable crises.

We urge policy makers to fund a national framework that supports both immediate mobile and telehealth enhancements and the strategic development of integrated, co‑located community hubs. This should be accompanied by local consultation, robust evaluation, and a commitment to improving transport, parking and premises—so that the benefits reach the patients who need them most.

Timely access to GP, community and mental health services remains inconsistent across England. I support policy to expand community mental health teams, strengthen early intervention and crisis response, and widen access to talking therapies because these can reduce long waits and promote parity with physical health. However, these ambitions require a credible workforce plan and sustained funding, with clear integration into general practice and schools, social care and third-sector partners. 

In practice, we need: expanded teams across adults, children and older adults, with ring-fenced funding for early psychosis and perinatal mental health; crisis resolution and home treatment teams that can respond quickly, plus 24/7 crisis lines; guaranteed same-day urgent slots and extended hours through GP practices and community hubs; sensible use of digital tools and remote consultations, while ensuring those without digital access are not left behind. 

Personal experience reinforces this: a relative waited several weeks for CBT; a local urgent appointment system with after-hours slots would have avoided escalation. Extended evening/weekend clinics would help working people. Implementation must include transparent milestones and robust workforce planning to balance quality, safety and capacity.

From a resident in rural Scotland, I disagree that the proposed changes will reliably improve timely access. Transport remains a daily barrier: buses are infrequent, car parking at clinics is limited, and many households rely on cars that can’t always be spared for medical trips. Mobile clinics and outreach teams could bring care closer to home, but they must be predictable, adequately funded and integrated with local pharmacies and schools. I’ve seen a mobile unit visit a village hall for two hours every fortnight; people queued, but follow‑ups were scheduled weeks later, so urgent issues still waited. Telehealth hubs in community centres or libraries are promising, provided there is decent broadband, privacy, and available interpreters. 

Staffing is equally critical: we need more GP, nurse and therapist slots, achieved through targeted recruitment, incentives to work in rural posts, expanded session capacity and smarter scheduling. We also need interpreters and culturally competent staff embedded in practices serving deprived and ethnic minority communities; language barriers are a real cause of missed appointments and delayed care. Outreach to migrant groups, training for staff, and reliable interpretation services must be funded long‑term. 

In short, a sustained mix of mobile and telehealth options, plus expanded staffing and better scheduling, is essential; otherwise transport and cultural barriers will keep delaying timely access.

I welcome the focus on making GP, community health and mental health services more timely, especially in rural Scotland. Transport and parking bottlenecks, plus small premises, currently slow people from getting the care they need. In my village, the lone clinic has a tiny car park and winter drives can be treacherous, which means delays for appointments and follow‑ups.

Proposals that would make a real difference: mobile clinics visiting village halls or community centres on regular days to bring GP checks, nurse visits and mental health drop‑ins closer to home; targeted outreach by district nurses and mental health teams to care homes and parish centres to catch people who can’t travel; telehealth hubs set up in libraries or community venues with private rooms and strong broadband for quick triage and follow‑ups without long journeys; incentives for GPs, practice nurses and therapists to work in rural areas, including relocation grants, workload support and protected time for home visits.

Also, practical changes like longer, extended-hours slots, easy online booking, and better premises with ample parking would remove real barriers. If these steps are coordinated and funded, timely access in my area would improve markedly and relieve a lot of stress for patients and carers alike.

I appreciate the aim to improve access, but I’m concerned these proposals won’t reliably translate into faster, safer care in our area. Expanding community mental health teams and early intervention sounds sensible, but without enough staff and proper funding it risks creating more points of contact rather than quicker help. In practice, referrals still queue for months, and people wait weeks for assessments before any treatment begins. Crisis response must be tightly integrated with GP services and backed by clear escalation routes; otherwise folks end up in out-of-hours services that feel distant and confusing.

Online booking and e-consultations offer benefits, but they aren’t a universal fix. Many older residents in my street struggle with smartphones or broadband, and some households share devices. If we push to digital-only access, we’ll exclude a sizeable slice of the community. Non-digital options must be maintained and well advertised, including frontline phone triage and drop-in slots.

Expanding multidisciplinary teams could relieve GP pressures, but only if there are robust care pathways and shared medical records; otherwise patients risk fragmented care and inconsistent follow-up. My priority is sensible investment in GP staffing, same-day access where possible, and a digital plan that includes real non-digital routes so no one is left behind.

Support investing in co-located community hubs that integrate primary, community and mental health with social care and VCSE partners; alongside expanding training and return-to-practice, ensuring sustainable funding and robust data sharing to avoid siloed services.
Disagree with focusing solely on online booking; expand digital options but ensure robust non-digital routes and support for elderly and disadvantaged patients to avoid exclusion.

As an organisation working with communities across England, we strongly support changes that protect continuity of care and lengthen appointment times for complex, chronic and vulnerable patients to improve outcomes and reduce repeat visits. When patients see the same clinician over time, treatment plans stay coherent, warnings are spotted earlier, and errors fall away. In our area, service users with long‑term conditions say they value a named GP who understands their history and can make informed decisions without repeating every detail at each visit.

We propose longer initial and follow‑up slots for complex cases (ideally 15–20 minutes, with flexibility to extend) and protected continuity where a patient’s named clinician remains their primary point of contact. This reduces urgent calls and the need for multiple appointments.
