Online tools help fit appointments around work and family, and can speed up routine follow‑ups. For my 82‑year‑old neighbour, phone triage or a home visit is essential. Digital coaching and access points at community venues would help prevent exclusion!

I support targeted resources—interpreters, culturally competent staff, outreach—to reach deprived and minority communities in my area; but we also need longer, appointment times for complex patients to protect continuity of care and reduce repeat visits.

Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services in my area would be improved by focusing on continuity of care and longer appointment times for those with complex needs, alongside stronger integrated teams. I’d prioritise: 1) guaranteeing a named GP or a small, stable care team for people with chronic conditions so care plans are followed consistently; 2) lengthening standard consultations for complex or vulnerable patients to cover medical review, mental health checks, and social support without forcing repeat visits; 3) robust urgent access pathways, including same-day GP slots and clear, rapid triage for mental health crises, with quick connections to psychology or community teams; 4) truly integrated primary care with co-located nursing, social prescribing and district nurses, all sharing care plans and records to reduce duplication; 5) improved digital triage and secure messaging to direct patients to the right clinician quickly while protecting continuity. In my experience, when a patient sees the same clinician for multidisciplinary reviews, outcomes improve and repeat visits fall. Adequate staffing and stable teams are essential to making this work, especially in areas under pressure in Northern Ireland.

absolutely support investing in co-located community hubs that bring GP, mental health, social care and VCSE partners together for smoother local care, and improve triage and booking to prioritise urgent cases—while ensuring non-digital options stay available for older or disadvantaged residents!

As an organisation representing residents and local health partners in England, we welcome the Government’s focus on improving timely access to GP, community health and mental health services. The pressure on primary care and community teams is real, and we believe the most durable solution is to grow the workforce in a sustainable way. In our experience, the bottlenecks are often about capacity and continuity of care, not just demand, so any set of changes should target long‑term staffing while also improving patient pathways. Our position is to support a package that expands training, supports those returning to practice, and creates clear, supported career progression through apprenticeships and continuous professional development (CPD). Real-world delivery will require stable funding, regional planning, and better integration across services.

What changes would most improve timely access?

1) Increase training places and broaden the pipeline into primary care and mental health
- Expand GP training places and early exposure to community settings so more trainees complete rotations in general practice, community nursing, and mental health teams. In areas with GP shortages, more flexible training schemes that encourage trained doctors to stay locally would reduce departures for “better”–pay or location elsewhere.
- Scale up nursing, allied health professional (AHP) and psychiatrist trainee places in district health networks, with protected placement time in GP practices and community teams. This helps build teams that can triage and manage problems earlier, rather than relying on a single GP to see every patient.
- Create regional training hubs that partner hospitals, NHS trusts and local authorities to provide realistic pathways from student to clinician in primary and community care, with a clear route to job completion in the same area. This is not only about numbers; it’s about ensuring new staff are equipped with practical skills for the settings they’ll work in.

2) Strengthen return-to-practice support for clinicians
- A streamlined return-to-practice offer for GPs, nurses and mental health professionals who have paused their careers. This would include modular refresher courses, supervised placements, and funded indemnity bridging, so people can re‑enter practice quickly and safely.
- Simplified re‑registration processes where appropriate, with accelerated access to retained expertise. Flexible roles, such as portfolio careers or part-time locum-to-permanent pathways, would help people rejoin without losing momentum in their lives.
- Targeted incentives for earlier‑career staff to stay in high‑demand areas after return, including clinical mentoring and peer support networks to rebuild confidence and competence.

3) Expand apprenticeships and CPD to grow career ladders and raise quality
- Extend apprenticeships that start with health care assistants and nursing associates, offering a clear route to qualified roles and senior responsibility within GP and community teams. Apprenticeship pathways should culminate in recognized qualifications that support independent patient care, including mental health support.
- Increase available CPD funded by the system for all front‑line personnel—GP reception staff, nurses, mental health workers and pharmacists—so that teams can stay up to date with guidelines, digital tools and best practice in triage, early intervention and safeguarding.
- Ensure CPD is accessible locally, including protected time for learning during shifts, and provide online, bite-sized options for those juggling busy schedules.

4) Strengthen long-term workforce planning and locality delivery
- Develop workforce plans that are data‑driven, identifying gaps at practice, cluster and regional levels, and tying training numbers to real local demand forecasts. This helps avoid overreliance on ad‑hoc recruitment campaigns that don’t fill long‑term gaps.
- Invest in “grow your own” schemes in schools and colleges near NHS sites, with early exposure to healthcare careers and clear progression routes into GP, nursing and mental health roles. Local placements help retain staff in the areas where they are most needed.
- Create integrated care hubs where GP practices, community nurses, mental health teams and social care work side by side. Co‑location and shared digital records reduce handoffs, speed up triage and shorten waiting times for initial assessments.

5) Improve access and triage at the front door
- Expand same‑day access with ring‑fenced slots for urgent cases, backed by trained triage staff who can direct patients to the most appropriate service quickly—be that a GP, a nurse‑led clinic, a mental health professional, or a social care partner.
- Invest in digital triage and virtual consultations where appropriate, while ensuring staff have the training and support to use these tools safely and effectively. Digital options should reduce friction and administrative burden, not replace human care where it is needed.
- Enhance post‑assessment follow‑ups and continuity of care so patients aren’t repeatedly re‑triaged. A dedicated care navigator in each practice or cluster could smooth transitions between services and reduce avoidable delays.

6) Funding, governance and measurement
- Deliver multi‑year funding with clear milestones and accountability for improving wait times, access to same‑day appointments and patient satisfaction. Stable funding supports workforce development, retention, and long‑term planning.
- Establish simple, transparent metrics for timely access across GP, community and mental health services, with public reporting so communities can track progress and hold providers to account.

In summary, improving timely access requires expanding and sustaining the workforce through more training places, robust return‑to‑practice routes, and clearly mapped apprenticeship and CPD opportunities, all underpinned by thoughtful, local workforce planning and better integrated services. If Government commits to a long‑term, place-based plan that delivers these elements, we will see more timely access, better patient experiences and, ultimately, better health outcomes for people across England.

We are ready to engage with local partners to develop pilots, share evidence from best practice, and help implement these changes in a way that fits the needs of our communities.

Expanding online booking, e-consults and remote care should be central, but not exclusive. In my area, online booking is straightforward and I used an e-consult last month to request a prescription renewal; the triage chat was answered quickly and the nurse followed up the same day. It saved me a trip and helped me fit care around work. Yet I know not everyone is comfortable with digital tools or has reliable broadband, especially older relatives. So it’s essential to preserve phone bookings, in-person triage and walk-in slots, and to offer simple guides and a local navigator to help people use the digital options.

Transport, parking and premises deficits are a real barrier, particularly in rural Scotland. Mobile clinics visiting villages weekly, outreach clinics in community halls and telehealth hubs in libraries or community centres could bring services closer to people’s doors. Incentives to recruit and retain rural GPs and mental health staff, plus clear, local information about how to book and access these services, would help reduce delays, ease pressure on busy town practices and support carers and mobility-challenged residents. A blended, patient-centred approach would improve timely access and reduce stress for families across our communities.

I strongly support changes to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services. In my area, getting to appointments can be a real hurdle because of limited public transport, scarce parking and clinic locations that feel hard to reach. Mobile clinics and outreach teams that visit villages and town centres would bring services closer to people, especially those without cars. Telehealth hubs with drop-in times could cut travel and wait times; incentives for practices to run regular telehealth sessions and extended hours would also help. Expanding capacity by recruiting more GPs, nurses and therapists and optimizing scheduling—for example, extended morning and afternoon slots, better triage and more group sessions—would reduce backlogs. Providing evening and weekend clinics would support working people and parents. Guaranteeing same-day urgent slots or rapid triage in mental health services could prevent crises. In my experience, when clinics run weekend slots or offer same-day urgent slots, urgent concerns are addressed sooner and overall demand on emergency services falls. These combined measures would greatly improve timely access.

Yes—prioritise urgent cases through improved NHS111 and triage, streamline bookings, cut duplication; also expand mobile clinics, telehealth hubs and outreach to overcome transport and rural access problems.

Living in Scotland and responding as an individual, I’m convinced that the biggest gains in timely access to GP, community health and mental health services would come from targeted, locally tailored action rather than blanket promises. In my view, the gaps we see are not just about waiting times; they’re about language barriers, cultural misunderstandings and outreach that never quite reaches the people who need it most. If we really want quicker, fairer access, we should invest in targeted resources, interpreters, culturally competent staff and active outreach to deprived, ethnic minority, migrant and marginalised communities.

Targeted resources for the places and people most affected
- Ring-fenced funding for GP practices and community health teams serving the most deprived SIMD deciles. That money should fund not just more appointments, but flexible delivery models: extended evening and weekend clinics, same-day urgent slots, and nurse-led triage to reduce GP bottlenecks. In practice, this would mean residents in high-deprivation wards aren’t competing with the same-day slot system as wealthier areas and can actually get care when symptoms start.
- Local health and social care partnerships should pilot dedicated outreach teams that can operate in community hubs, schools, mosques, churches and cultural centres. The aim isn’t to replace clinics but to lower the barrier to entry—easy access points where people already are, with staff who understand local contexts.

Interpreters and language access as standard
- Interpreters must be available on site across GP practices, hospital departments and mental health services, with real-time telephone or video interpreting as a default, not an exception. Patient information sheets, consent forms and after-visit summaries should be translated into the languages most spoken in the area.
- Recruit and retain bilingual staff who reflect local communities. It’s not enough to rely on family members to translate; that can breach confidentiality and misrepresent medical history. In my area, when language barriers arise, appointment quality drops and important details get lost.

Culturally competent staff and trauma-informed care
- Put mandatory, ongoing training in cultural competence and trauma-informed care at the heart of the workforce. Front-line receptionists, nurses, and GPs should be equipped to recognise how stigma, gender norms, and cultural health beliefs shape help-seeking. A more diverse workforce across GP practices and mental health services would also improve trust and retention.
- Establish cultural liaison roles within practices who can guide patients through the system, explain treatment options in an understandable way, and flag potential barriers early.

Active outreach and navigation
- Employ community health navigators or peer champions from local communities to help people understand how to access services, book appointments, and follow through with care plans. These navigators can also help families manage care for relatives who may struggle with appointments or complex health information.
- Coordinate with voluntary organisations to run regular drop-ins at community venues where people can get quick health checks, mental health signposting and information about available support, with interpreters available on-site.

Data transparency and governance
- Collect and publish data on access by language, ethnicity, and deprivation, and use it to steer resources where they’re most needed. It’s frustrating when services trumpet improvements without showing who actually benefits. Transparent dashboards would keep pockets of need visible and accountable.
- Use data to avoid cookie-cutter solutions. Different communities have different barriers; what helps one group may not help another. Local pilots should be designed with community input and with clear exit criteria if they don’t deliver timely access improvements.

Mental health services—same-day access and continuity
- Mental health pathways must include same-day or next-day access where risk is present, with clear, supported pathways into talking therapies, local CAMHS, and crisis support. In practice, I’ve seen delays where urgent mental health needs were not immediately acknowledged due to language or cultural factors; that gap can be dangerous.
- Integrate mental health with primary care so patients don’t bounce between services. A care coordinator who can stay with a patient across GP visits, community health checks and therapy sessions would reduce fragmentation and delays.

Practical, on-the-ground impact
- In the near term, I’d like to see a ‘local access plan’ for my area with a fixed budget, a bilingual recruitment target, interpreters available at all major touchpoints, and a community advisory group that meets quarterly to review progress and barriers. The goal should be tangible improvements in same-day access and a measurable narrowing of the gaps experienced by marginalised communities.

Overall, timely access can’t be solved by boosting headcount alone or by digital booking alone. It requires targeted, culturally aware, language-accessible services delivered where people live and in ways they can actually use. By funding outreach, interpreters, and culturally competent teams, and by making data-driven decisions with community involvement, we can make timely access a reality for everyone, not just those who already navigate the system with ease.

Investing in co-located community hubs that bring together GP, community and mental health services with social care and VCSE partners would transform local care. It would reduce the fragmentation I see at the moment and mean a patient can get medical advice, social support and a mental health check in one place, with shared records and a single point of access. In practice, this would need robust funding, aligned business cases, and enough staff to avoid long waits. My experience in a mid-tier town is that a patient meeting a GP often has to travel to separate sites for social care or counselling, which can delay urgent needs and discourage people from seeking help.

Evening and weekend clinics, plus guaranteed same-day urgent slots, would be essential for working neighbours and those with intermittent symptoms. I know many who skip care because 9-5 access is the only option. To work, these changes must include flexible transport, accessible locations, and clear, simple referral pathways, plus strong IT links across services to prevent repeating tests or stories. Pilot in a few communities with patient involvement to test appointment flow, data sharing and community linkages.

Timely access is really hit and miss in our area, and I’m not sure there’s a one-size-fits-all fix. I’ve had weeks where I could not get a GP appointment; the first available slot was a week away and sometimes the phone line is constantly busy. A few times last year I tried to get a same-day appointment for a minor issue and ended up going to urgent care because nothing was available. For mental health, a friend waited over a month for talking therapy after reaching out following a stressful period, which felt too long. People I know rely on after-hours or crisis lines, but those aren’t a substitute for regular access. In community health, the nurse visits are irregular and booking a home visit can be a challenge. If there were more staff and clearer triage, plus options like online booking and some walk-in slots, that might help, but I’m not sure what combination would work best here.

Agree. Access to timely GP, nurse and mental health support has become patchy and waiting times are affecting everyday life. To fix this, I support increasing appointment slots and session capacity by hiring more clinicians and expanding session lengths, plus smarter scheduling. Practices could offer longer weekday hours and reliable same‑day or next‑day slots, with a strong triage process so urgent cases are seen quickly and routine checks are still covered. In my area, a small practice added nurse‑led clinics in the late afternoon and a digital booking system with real‑time wait lists, which noticeably reduced no‑shows and improved throughput. Wider adoption of similar approaches, including virtual consultations when appropriate, would help reduce waits. 

On staffing, targeted recruitment and international hiring, with clear incentives, improved pay, flexible working and robust wellbeing support, are essential to grow and retain the workforce. Offering longer contracts, more predictable rotas and generous sickness cover would make a big difference. If local practices can recruit more GPs, nurse practitioners and therapists and give them supportive, sustainable workloads, people won’t feel forced to turn to urgent care or online delays. This combination would steadily improve access over the coming year.

From my perspective living in England and juggling study/work, timely access to GP, community health and mental health services would be helped by a mix of evening/weekend clinics and guaranteed same‑day urgent slots. That would mean two late clinics on weekdays (for example 5–8pm) and one or two weekend mornings, with triage so urgent same‑day appointments aren’t delayed. It’s especially important for mental health triage to offer rapid initial checks within 24 hours rather than letting problems fester.

If traveling or taking time off work is tough, transport, parking and premises can become barriers. I’d support mobile clinics visiting rural villages or town halls monthly, outreach teams in community hubs, telehealth hubs in libraries or community centers, and incentives for practices to run satellite sessions where people actually live. Practical fixes like better bus links, reduced parking costs near clinics, and accessible, step‑free premises would also help those with mobility challenges.

Telehealth can cut travel and waiting times, but we must avoid digital exclusion by keeping in‑person options and offering support for those without devices or reliable internet. Any plan needs adequate funding, committed staffing, and clear targets to avoid pushing patients into longer waiting times. In short, a locally tailored blend of extended hours, mobile/outreach services, and accessible tech could improve timely access without burning out staff.

I welcome this consultation and strongly support actions to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services across Wales. As someone aged 65 and living in Wales, I have seen how even small delays can have a knock-on effect on daily life, independence and peace of mind. The changes I think would make the biggest difference combine targeted, culturally intelligent outreach with real increases in capacity and a sustainable long‑term workforce plan.

First, targeting resources and outreach to reduce gaps in access for deprived, ethnic minority, migrant and marginalised groups is essential. We need more funding for GP practices and community services in areas with higher deprivation and a higher share of people whose first language is not English or Welsh. This should include funding for interpreters and translation services at the point of contact, so a patient can discuss symptoms and concerns without language getting in the way. Culturally competent staff matter too: recruiting and training staff who reflect the communities they serve helps patients feel understood and reduces missed or late appointments.

I have seen how outreach can make a real difference. In our town, there are many older residents from Eastern European communities who often struggle to navigate the system. When there are outreach visits to community hubs, faith groups and sheltered housing with multilingual information and signposting to services, people are more likely to book timely appointments and understand what help is available. A mobile or outreach clinic model, visiting neighbourhoods on a rotating basis with interpreters available, could catch people who would otherwise miss routine checks, vaccines or mental health screening.

Second, expand appointment slots and capacity across GP practices, nursing teams and therapy services. This means hiring more GPs, nurses and mental health therapists, expanding session capacity and optimising scheduling so that same‑day urgent slots and planned follow-ups are readily available. For older patients with complex needs, longer appointment times and a multidisciplinary approach—GPs with nurse prescribers, therapists, social care colleagues—would mean fewer repeat visits and quicker, more holistic care.

In practice, this could look like extended hours at practice hubs, more nurse-led clinics for chronic disease management and quicker access to talking therapies. It should also include robust home-visit options or community-based clinics for people who struggle with travel or transport. While digital booking and telehealth can help, we must maintain real‑world access for those with limited digital literacy or unreliable internet, ensuring a choice between in-person and remote appointments.

Third, I would like to see a strong focus on workforce development that builds capacity for the long term. Increasing the number of training places for GPs, nurses and mental health professionals is vital, as is return‑to‑practice support for those who stepped back from clinical roles and apprenticeships to bring in different routes into primary care. CPD must be accessible and relevant, so staff stay up‑to‑date in primary care, mental health and community health skills. Wales could benefit from regional training hubs that pair clinical practice with community health needs, offering pathways from nursing associates to fully qualified GPs and therapists.

Local success depends on linking training, recruitment and retention with clear career pathways. For example, return‑to‑practice programs supported by mentoring and protected time to update skills can help experienced nurses or therapists rejoin the workforce. Apprenticeships that blend on‑the‑job training with accredited credentials could widen access and bring fresh energy into primary care teams. This must be backed by stable funding, not short‑term pilots, so we can grow a skilled workforce that reflects Wales’ diverse population.

Finally, these changes must be data‑driven and publicly accountable. Local health boards should collect and publish data on wait times by area and by patient group, identify where access is worse for particular communities, and demonstrate how outreach and capacity increases are reducing waits. Patient involvement in planning—through advisory groups or community representatives—will help ensure services meet real local needs.

In short, I support a comprehensive approach: targeted funding for interpreters and culturally competent staff; proactive outreach to marginalised groups; more GP, nurse and therapist appointments and flexible, person‑centred scheduling; and a strong, sustainable pipeline of training, return‑to‑practice and apprenticeship opportunities. With careful sequencing and proper funding, these steps could dramatically improve timely access for everyone in Wales, especially those who need it most.

i strongly believe timely access to GP, community health and mental health services in our area would improve with a mix of capacity expansion, continuity of care and inclusive, flexible access. First, expand appointment slots by hiring more GPs, nurses and therapists and by offering longer sessions for complex or chronic cases. In my community, appointments can be booked weeks out, and longer consultations would cut down on repeated visits and misunderstandings.

Second, protect continuity of care. When possible, see the same clinician and have longer initial assessments and ongoing care plans, so people with long-term conditions aren’t bounced between providers, which often slows progress.

Third, grow online booking and remote care but keep non-digital options. Digital tools speed things up, but not everyone can use them easily—older residents or those with limited data need telephone booking, in-person triage and paper forms, with staff to help navigate digital tools.

Finally, offer flexible access windows and stronger links with community teams. Same-day urgent slots, extended hours for working people, and closer collaboration with schools and local employers on mental health support would catch issues earlier and reduce avoidable visits. These changes together would make timely care more achievable and prevent the cycle of delays and repeat visits!

From our rural community group in England, timely access to GP, community health and mental health services remains hampered by transport gaps, limited parking and ageing premises. In our village the mobile clinic visits fortnightly for a couple of hours, and my mobility‑challenged neighbour relies on it; without it, she would have to travel 20 miles. To change this, I’d prioritise: regular mobile clinics delivering GP checks, nursing visits and mental health support on a parish rota, with clear timetables linked to local bus routes; proactive outreach by district nurses and mental health workers to care homes and housebound residents; telehealth hubs in village halls or libraries with staff to help older users and reliable broadband; transport support such as vouchers or community transport and improved parking and drop-off zones; investment in accessible, modern premises or modular clinics and retention incentives for rural clinicians.

In practice, these changes would reduce waits and keep care closer to home, but telehealth must be reliable, staff must be available to assist with devices and connections, and funding must be sustained and locally accountable.

TIMELY ACCESS TO GP, COMMUNITY HEALTH AND MENTAL HEALTH SERVICES IS CRUCIAL, ESPECIALLY WHEN WORK OR CARING RESPONSIBILITIES MAKE IT HARD TO ATTEND IN PERSON. I WELCOME EXPANDING ONLINE BOOKING, E-CONSULTATIONS AND REMOTE CARE BECAUSE THEY CAN REDUCE WAITING TIMES AND HELP PEOPLE BOOK SLOTS QUICKLY. IN MY PRACTICE, ONLINE BOOKING SOMETIMES SHOWS SAME-DAY SLOTS DURING THE MORNING; A QUICK E-CONSULTATION WITH A NURSE PRACTITIONER HELPED TRIAGE A COUGH AND AVOID A LONG TRIP. FOR MENTAL HEALTH, SHORT VIDEO CHECK-INS HAVE KEPT ME CONNECTED WHEN IN-PERSON APPOINTMENTS ARE SCARCE. HOWEVER, NOT EVERYONE CAN GO DIGITAL: OLDER NEIGHBOURS, LOW-INCOME FAMILIES, OR THOSE WITH LIMITED DATA. TO AVOID EXCLUSION, CLINICS SHOULD KEEP PHONE-BASED BOOKING AND SAME-DAY IN-PERSON OPTIONS, PLUS SUPPORT LIKE GUIDANCE LEAFLETS, INTERPRETER SERVICES, AND DIGITAL ACCESS POINTS IN LIBRARIES OR COMMUNITY HUBS. I’D ALSO LIKE TO SEE BETTER TRIAGE SO URGENT CASES ARE MOVED TO SAME DAY SLOTS, AND CLEARER REMINDERS AND AFTERCARE FOLLOW-UP. FINALLY, INTEGRATION WITH COMMUNITY PHARMACIES AND SOCIAL CARE CAN HELP REDUCE GAPS BETWEEN PRIMARY AND MENTAL HEALTH TEAMS.

I support expanding online booking, e-consultations and remote care, but must provide non-digital options and support (phone access, in-person triage, community hubs) to prevent exclusion of older or disadvantaged patients.

Agree. To improve timely access, prioritise recruitment and retention: international hiring, targeted incentives, competitive pay, flexible shifts, and robust wellbeing support to grow a capable primary care workforce.

Expand online booking and e-consultations while keeping non-digital options; invest in community mental health teams and early intervention; strengthen NHS111, triage, and care navigation to prioritise urgent cases and reduce wasted time, ensuring no one is left behind.

I live in England and am 49, responding as an individual. I don’t think these changes alone will deliver timely access to GP, community health, and mental health services. Expanding multidisciplinary teams with pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates can help treat routine cases, but it risks fragmenting care unless there is clear leadership and someone who knows the patient’s history. In practice I’ve seen people bounce between professionals for the same issue, which just adds waiting time and confusion about who is coordinating care.

Targeted recruitment, international hiring, incentives, pay improvements, flexible working and wellbeing support are essential, yet they won’t fix the core problem if practices are chronically underfunded and overloaded. Staff burnout is real; without sustainable staffing levels and stable schedules, new recruits won’t stay long enough to shift outcomes.

Investing in co-located community hubs sounds good in theory, but they must be truly integrated with IT systems, shared records and strong links to social care and VCSE partners. Otherwise they become new buildings that people can’t reach easily or that don’t connect to the right services when needed.

What would help most is a combination: real same‑day GP access or rapid triage, a credible workforce plan that keeps clinicians healthy and in post, and joined‑up records and pathways across primary, community and mental health, with reliable transport links and clear local access routes.

Agree. I think the changes that would help most are targeting resources to deprived and ethnic minority communities, plus improving NHS111, triage, and care navigation to prioritise urgent needs and smooth patient flow. In my area, interpreters are often unavailable when appointments are booked by phone, which can lead to missed slots or delays for older folk who rely on family members to translate. Increasing funding for interpreters, training staff in cultural competence, and running outreach clinics in community centres would reduce gaps and encourage people to seek help earlier. 

Also, NHS111 and the online booking system should be more robust and patient-friendly: a clear triage path that fast-tracks urgent cases, with a single, easy-to-use booking system across GP practices and community services. Care navigators could guide patients through the system, avoid duplication, and connect mental health referrals quickly. 

With these changes, and regular feedback from patients in disadvantaged areas, timely access to GP, community health and mental health services would become more equitable and simpler for older residents like me to use.

it's outrageous that there are real tensions here in England right now between demand and what the system can deliver, and my experience in everything from GP to mental health services mirrors that gap. In my area, getting timely access to a GP appointment often means waiting longer than I’d consider reasonable for a routine issue. A simple check-up or prescription review can slip into a wait of one to two weeks, and I’ve seen friends struggle to book anything sooner unless it’s urgent. Community physiotherapy or nurse-led clinics sometimes have even longer delays, which makes minor injuries or post‑surgical recovery feel like a longer project than it should be. When it comes to mental health, the delays are more acute: a couple I know had to wait six to eight weeks for an initial IAPT assessment, and then several more weeks for therapy slots. These waits aren’t just frustrating; they can worsen conditions that would have responded well to earlier support and put extra pressure on urgent or emergency services.

What would help substantially is a deliberate expansion of capacity across GP, nurse, and therapist roles, paired with smarter scheduling and pathways so those slots actually get filled by the right person, at the right time. Specifically, I’d like to see:

- More appointment slots through targeted hiring and deployment: increasing the number of GPs and practice nurses, plus expanding the pool of allied health professionals (physiotherapists, occupational therapists, and behavioural health specialists) working in primary and community settings. This should include better retention packages and incentives to work in areas with staffing challenges, rather than relying on short-term locums. In my area, a steadier presence of nurses and therapists would free up GPs to focus on cases that genuinely require physician attention, reducing bottlenecks.

- Expanded session capacity and flexibility: where appropriate, offer longer consultation times for routine checks or complex issues, and create structured group or open-access sessions for common conditions (e.g., back pain education clinics, CBT skills groups). This would help those with chronic or recurring needs, while keeping our individual appointments efficient. I’ve benefited from longer 30-minute GP slots for follow-ups in the past, and I’ve seen how the depth of discussion can prevent repeat visits in a way a 10-minute slot cannot.

- Optimised scheduling and triage: implement robust, data‑driven triage to route people to the most suitable professional or service on day one, reducing wasted slots and the cycle of referrals. A strong triage frontline—via telephone, video consults, or online self‑screeners—could determine whether someone needs urgent attention, a same-day nurse check, a mental health intake, or a community physio. For those with mental health needs, a rapid-access pathway to a therapist or a dedicated IAPT slot would dramatically cut waiting times.

- Better use of digital tools while safeguarding access: flexible online booking, e-consults for simple queries, and remote monitoring for chronic conditions can free up in-person slots for those who truly need them. But we must guard against digital exclusion and ensure that people who lack online access aren’t left behind. A hybrid model, using digital channels while keeping phone access as a core option, would be essential.

- Quality and continuity safeguards: as we expand capacity, we must ensure patients see the most appropriate clinician and maintain continuity where possible. I’m wary of rapid expansion that spreads resources too thin or erodes the patient–clinician relationship. Clear, supportive supervision and training for new staff are vital, as is robust performance monitoring to avoid rush jobs or burnout among already stretched teams.

In practice, I’d like to see a staged rollout: pilot increased GP/nurse capacity and a triage-driven booking system in several trusts, with transparent wait-time dashboards and patient experience feedback. If the pilots show meaningful reductions in routine GP waits, shorter times to mental health intake, and improved outcomes without sacrificing quality, the program should be scaled up nationwide.

Ultimately, timely access matters not just for convenience but for health outcomes and people’s ability to work, study, and care for others. I’m supportive of expanding capacity and reforming scheduling, provided it’s done with staffing stability, patient safety, digital inclusion, and clear governance baked in from the start!

Support widening GP and mental health access by mobile clinics, outreach in rural areas, telehealth hubs, better transport links and parking, plus incentives to keep premises open where transport is tough.

From where I live in Scotland, simply promising more GP, nurse and therapist appointment slots won’t automatically fix access to care. Yes, increasing capacity is essential, but it only works if we fix the underlying staffing problems and the way appointments are scheduled. In my area, routine GP slots vanish quickly and mental health referrals often drag on for months. I’ve had friends who waited weeks for a counselling session only to be told the next available slot was several towns away, adding travel time and cost. Expanding capacity without addressing recruitment, retention, pay, and admin bottlenecks would just shuffle the queue.

I also welcome the idea of multidisciplinary teams, including pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates, to handle routine cases and free GPs for more complex care. But that must come with clear pathways, consistent care plans, and strong information-sharing so patients aren’t passed around without continuity. In rural Scotland, the risk is fragmented care and variable access depending on where you live or broadband availability for virtual slots.

What would help more? sustainable workforce planning with better pay and training pipelines; extended hours and weekend clinics; robust triage and online booking that actually works; and genuinely integrated community hubs that combine mental health, physical health and social support, with transport options for those who need them. Only then will waits shorten in a meaningful way.

I’m responding as a resident of England in my mid-40s, and I’m strongly supportive of changes that would improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services. From my experience and what I’ve observed locally, our main bottleneck is not simply patient demand but the workforce and how we recruit, retain and support the people delivering care. The changes I’d prioritise fall into a few practical areas that work together.

Targeted recruitment and international hiring
- Actively recruit GPs, nurses and allied health professionals from abroad where there are shortages, with clear, streamlined routes for registration and onboarding, plus culturally sensitive orientation and language support where needed.
- Offer attractive relocation packages, mentorship, and fast-track integration into local teams so new clinicians can contribute quickly.
- Encourage practice partnerships to share roles or co-locate teams, which makes transitions smoother for clinicians moving from other areas.
In my area I’ve heard of practices trying international recruitment to plug gaps, but the process can still be slow. A more proactive, well-supported approach could translate into more appointments available sooner rather than later.

Pay improvements and targeted incentives
- Align salaries with the rising cost of living and the workload pressures that come with longer waits for care. Competitive pay helps attract new staff and supports retention, especially in rural or underserved areas.
- Introduce retention bonuses or service-based incentives to reward continuity in primary care teams and reduce churn that disrupts patient care.
- provide relocation and integration grants for those moving to join family practices, which lowers barriers to taking up roles in areas with acute shortages.

Flexible working and workforce models
- Expand flexible working and job-sharing arrangements so more clinicians can fit caring duties around family and other commitments, while maintaining high standards of continuity for patients.
- Create longer, predictable rosters that spread demand more evenly and reduce the heavy peaks that lead to burnout.
- Extend hours where there is demand, including some evenings and Saturdays, but with robust supervision and protected time for professional development and admin.
- Encourage multidisciplinary teams (nurses, pharmacists, physiotherapists, medical associates) to handle routine and chronic-care tasks, freeing GPs to focus on complex cases.

Wellbeing and workload management
- Invest in staff wellbeing as part of workforce planning: protected breaks, access to peer support, and confidential mental health services for clinicians themselves.
- Simplify admin and paperwork where possible, provide efficient IT tools, and ensure that clinical time is protected from non-clinical burdens.
- Normalise reasonable workloads with clear referral pathways, so clinicians aren’t routinely handling overflowing queues that delay care for patients.

Training, career progression and retention
- Expand GP training posts and support for ongoing CPD, especially for early-career clinicians returning after maternity/paternity leave or career breaks.
- Develop clear career ladders for nurse prescribers, physician associates, and allied health professionals to grow within primary care, creating a sense of progression and belonging in local teams.
- Use apprenticeships and funded retraining schemes so existing staff can broaden their skills and stay with their current employers while expanding their contributions.

Digital tools and smarter care pathways
- Improve online triage and e-consults to triage non-urgent issues and book slots more efficiently, while ensuring urgent cases are seen quickly.
- Invest in integrated, user-friendly digital records and scheduling so patients don’t have to repeat information, and clinicians can access the right data at the point of care.
- Expand community hubs where people can access a range of services—mental health support, physical therapy, and social prescribing—reducing the pressure on GP appointments.

Local planning and delivery
- Local health and social care partnerships should use real-time data to shape what services are needed where, including extended-hours clinics in high-demand areas.
- Ensure workforce planning is long-term and funded, with a clear plan for gradually expanding capacity to meet growing demand.

Why these changes matter
- When primary care teams are well-staffed, patients get timely appointments, and mental health services can intervene early, preventing crisis-level care later.
- A diverse, well-supported workforce that can work flexibly adapts to patient needs, reduces backlogs, and improves patient experience.
- Practical investments in recruitment, pay, wellbeing, and flexible working create a virtuous cycle: happier staff deliver better care, which encourages people to seek help earlier rather than delaying until problems worsen.

In short, timely access will improve if we (a) actively recruit and support clinicians from abroad with efficient processes, (b) ensure pay and incentives reflect the workload, (c) give teams flexible, sustainable ways to work, and (d) back this with strong wellbeing, training, and smart digital tools. I’d like to see these elements funded and coordinated at a local level so every patient can get timely help when they need it, rather than waiting weeks for a routine appointment or facing barriers to mental health support.

Improving NHS111 and triage helps, but in Scotland, without co-located community hubs and expanded training for GPs and mental health professionals, timely access won't improve; need integrated local care and robust care navigation to cut duplication.

Yes, I support creating co-located hubs that bring GP, community, mental health and social care together, with VCSE partners, so local services are seamless. Also prioritise interpreters, culturally competent staff and outreach to reach deprived and migrant communities.

absolutely protect continuity of care by offering longer appointment times for complex, chronic and vulnerable patients, which should reduce repeat visits and improve outcomes; but this must be matched with sufficient staffing and funding to keep GP, community and mental health services timely!

I welcome a clear focus on making GP, community health and mental health services more timely and easier to access. From our experience and engagement with local health services across England, the three linked changes below would make the biggest difference in our area: expanding online booking, e-consultations and remote care while safeguarding non-digital options; strengthening community mental health teams and early intervention with robust crisis support and talking therapies; and widening multidisciplinary teams so routine cases can be managed by skilled professionals other than GPs, freeing clinicians to focus on complex care.

Digital access should be expanded not replaced. Online booking and e-consultations can make it much easier for people with busy jobs, carers, or those who struggle to travel to a clinic to get timely advice. In our local projects, online triage and video consultations reduced unnecessary in-person visits and shortened waiting times for non-urgent issues. At the same time, we must keep a real alternative for those who cannot or prefer not to use digital channels: a clear, well-staffed telephone triage line, same-day face-to-face slots when needed, and reliable walk-in or nurse-led clinics. We should also provide practical support: digital access points in community hubs, easy-to-understand guides, and trained staff to help patients navigate the system. For older residents and those with limited digital literacy, proactive outreach and concierge support from care navigators would prevent digital exclusion and ensure no one is left behind.

Stronger community mental health teams and early intervention will deliver tangible benefits in reduced waits and better parity with physical health services. A more integrated, locally based mental health pathway—encompassing urgent crisis response, early intervention teams,ambitious access targets for talking therapies and sustained long-term support—would reduce unnecessary crises and hospital admissions. In practice, this means same-day crisis triage, rapid access to evidence-based talking therapies, and proactive collaboration with primary care to identify risk early. When teams are embedded in the community, people feel supported closer to home, and families avoid the stress of multiple hospital referrals. We have seen that where crisis teams can respond quickly and provide timely talking therapies and support, people recover faster and feel more in control of their mental health.

Expanding multidisciplinary teams will help manage routine cases efficiently and give GPs space to focus on complex or high-risk patients. Integrating pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates into primary care teams can streamline care pathways, improve medication safety, and speed up treatment for common problems such as musculoskeletal issues, minor injuries, dermatology concerns and minor acute illnesses. For example, physiotherapist-led clinics in primary care have successfully managed many MSK conditions, reducing GP workload and improving patient satisfaction. Clinical pharmacists can conduct medicines reviews, reconcile changes after hospital discharge, and alert prescribers to potential interactions, which is crucial as we move to more complex care plans. Paramedics and physician associates can take on triage and routine assessments in urgent care settings, delivering safe, timely care and freeing GPs to concentrate on complex cases. All of this needs clear referrals, strong communication, and shared access to medical records so teams can coordinate effectively.

Implementation must be underpinned by equity and quality assurance. We should track access indicators (wait times, same-day access rates), patient experience, and clinical outcomes to ensure improvements are real and sustainable. Investment should be accompanied by upskilling, robust information governance, and support for frontline staff to work at the top of their training. A phased rollout with local adaptation, plus involvement from patient groups, would help identify unintended consequences early and allow tweaks. We also need to consider long-term funding agreements to maintain the gains once pilots finish.

Overall, I believe these changes—flexible digital and non-digital access, stronger mental health services with early support, and expanded multidisciplinary teams—will deliver timely, equitable care and better health outcomes for residents in our area. I’d welcome a dialogue with policymakers and local providers to translate these principles into practical, funded plans that work in diverse communities across England.

I fully support targeted recruitment, international hiring, better pay, flexible working and wellbeing support to grow and retain primary care staff. Expanding community mental health teams, early intervention and crisis response with talking therapies will reduce waits and improve parity with physical health.

I don’t think simply pushing more online booking and remote consultations will resolve the delays I’m seeing. In my area, someone with a non-digital phone or without reliable internet still struggles to get quick slots; my friend waited three weeks for a mental health appointment after being told to use online triage, which clearly leaves people behind. I do support expanding multidisciplinary teams (pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics, physician associates) to handle routine cases, because it could free GPs for complex care and reduce bottlenecks, but only if it’s properly funded, with clear roles and good handoffs so patients don’t have to repeat their history to several clinicians. 

More visible, local solutions are needed: same-day in-person slots, extended hours, and walk-in clinics in community hubs; plus robust non-digital access like telephone triage and staff-assisted bookings for those who need them. For mental health, short-term crisis slots and community outreach should run in parallel with digital options. Without that balance, the plan risks widening existing inequalities.
Agree. Increasing training places, return-to-practice support, apprenticeships and CPD will sustainably grow GPs, nurses and mental health staff, improving timely access in our area.

From our organisation’s perspective in England, there is a clear tension between keeping care continuous and giving patients timely access. I’d advocate for a two‑track approach: safeguard continuity and lengthen appointment times for those with complex, chronic or vulnerable needs now, while simultaneously building a stronger workforce pipeline to make timely access sustainable in the years ahead. In practice, this means both changing how appointments are scheduled today and investing in the capacity to deliver longer, more holistic care in the future.

First, short term improvements that would have a tangible impact on patients’ experience. Continuity of care is a cornerstone for outcomes, particularly for people with multiple long‑term conditions or social factors that complicate health problems. When a patient can consistently see their named clinician, with access to their history and a shared plan, there are fewer repeat visits, fewer duplicative tests, and better adherence to treatment. Too often, however, patients are shuffled between GPs or have to tell their story repeatedly. A practical change would be to protect the named‑GP model where feasible and ensure robust care coordination when staff need to rotate. 

Alongside continuity, appointment length should reflect patient complexity. 15‑minute slots are rarely enough for someone with chronic disease, mental health concerns, and social determinants all intersecting. In our experience, longer bookings—ideally 20–30 minutes for complex cases—allow clinicians to review medicines, mental health risks, social supports, and prevention goals in one sitting. This reduces the need for follow‑ups and, crucially, supports safer prescribing and better monitoring. We should also pilot same‑day triage with senior clinicians guiding risk stratification, so those in crisis or with rapidly changing symptoms aren’t left waiting for a standard appointment slot.

Better integration with community and mental health services is essential. We’ve seen how gaps between primary and community teams lead to delays and avoidable hospital admissions. A practical model would be multi‑disciplinary same‑day clinics within primary care hubs, including district nurses, social workers, and a community mental health practitioner, to create a rapid, shared plan for patients with complex needs. For patients with mental health concerns, timely access to a clinician who can assess, step‑down from secondary care when appropriate, and coordinate with social supports makes a real difference to outcomes and engagement with treatment.

Second, we must look to the medium and longer term to enlarge the workforce in a sustainable way. The key is to expand the capacity of primary and community teams while maintaining high standards of care. Increasing training places in GP training pathways, expanding return‑to‑practice support for clinicians who have stepped back, and growing apprenticeships for nurses, allied health professionals and mental health staff will help build a resilient workforce. Our area has benefited from return‑to‑practice schemes and practice‑based training hubs, but demand still outstrips supply. More funded slots in medical and nursing schools, targeted incentives for GP partners and practice‑based fellowships, and protected CPD time would help keep skilled clinicians in the system and reduce burnout.

Alongside recruitment, retention matters just as much. Reasonable patient loads, protected time for reflective practice, supervision, and access to allied health professionals within the practice can shorten the path from problem identification to treatment. A team‑based approach—where a GP, a nurse prescriber, a mental health practitioner, and a pharmacist work as a connected unit—can deliver timely care without sacrificing quality.

Practical steps we would like to see include:
- A policy framework that guarantees longer appointment times for patients with complex needs and protects the same‑GP principle where possible.
- Investment in multidisciplinary primary care teams, with routine access to mental health professionals within or adjacent to GP practices.
- Expansion of training places and return‑to‑practice packages, plus intensified CPD funding and administrative support for clinicians re‑entering the workforce.
- Apprenticeships and career pathways for nurses, health coaches, pharmacists, and allied health staff to build a robust, locally rooted workforce.
- Data and IT investments that enable better care coordination across primary, community and mental health services, including shared care plans and timely updates to patients’ records.

These changes won’t be instantaneous, but done together they could shorten waiting times, improve care continuity, and reduce preventable repeat visits. If implemented with stable funding, clear governance, and strong local leadership, this approach can deliver better outcomes for patients with chronic and complex needs while building the workforce we need for the future.

In summary, improving timely access requires both immediate adjustments to appointment length and continuity, and a credible, well‑funded plan to grow the primary and community workforce through training, return‑to‑practice, apprenticeships and professional development. I urge policymakers to pursue this dual track, aligned with local commissioning and integrated care partnerships, to deliver sustainable improvements for patients across GP, community health and mental health services.

I strongly support changes that improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services by expanding online booking and e-consultations, and by integrating remote care into routine practice. In my experience, being able to book appointments online or send a quick e-consult has often meant we get a slot sooner and avoid days of ringing to be told nothing is available. For mental health, quick online triage can help people get the right level of support faster, whether that’s a talking therapy slot or a referral. In my area, I have used online booking to arrange a same-or-next-day GP visit for a teenager’s fever and a quick video consult for prescription renewals, which saved hours on the phone. However, not everyone can use digital tools, especially older neighbours or those without reliable internet. I welcome non-digital alternatives: telephone booking, walk-in slots for urgent needs, and in-practice help to set up digital access. Local libraries or community hubs could offer assisted bookings and digital literacy support. Adequate funding for training staff and ensuring data privacy will be essential to make this inclusive and to reduce avoidable waiting times.

Agree. Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services is essential for people like me, especially as a student and young adult trying to keep on top of things. Right now, GP slots can be hard to book and waiting times for talking therapies can stretch into weeks, which risks problems getting worse. I’d like to see more training places for GPs, nurses and mental health professionals, plus return-to-practice support, apprenticeships and CPD. Building a sustainable workforce now means fewer short-term fixes and quicker access later.

Expanding community mental health teams with stronger early intervention, crisis response and more accessible talking therapies would help people get the right support before issues become emergencies and would improve parity with physical health services. I’ve seen friends struggle to access timely mental health care, so this feels urgently needed.

Transport, parking and premises gaps in rural or mobility-limited areas create real barriers. I back mobile clinics, local outreach, telehealth hubs and incentives for practices to extend hours or open in underserved places. Better transport links and parking near clinics would also make a big difference. These changes would collectively deliver quicker care and better outcomes.

As an organisation representing local health and community services in England, we strongly welcome proposals to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services. Protecting continuity of care is essential for people with complex, chronic conditions and for vulnerable patients; longer appointments enable clinicians to address multiple concerns in one visit, adjust medications safely and reduce the need for repeat trips. We also support increasing appointment slots and session capacity by recruiting more GPs, nurses and therapists, expanding service hours, and using smarter scheduling to prioritise high-need cases. In practice this means more flexible morning and evening slots, longer blocks for long-term care reviews and integrated capacity across primary and community teams. A concrete example from our area shows a patient with diabetes and anxiety who faced multiple separate appointments; a longer, coordinated session would have avoided a further trip and improved safety. We also back expanding online booking, e‑consultations and remote care, provided non‑digital routes remain available for those who need them, including phone access and in-person help for older or digitally uncomfortable users. A blended model with strong digital tools and solid human contact will cut queues, improve outcomes and help people stay independent. We urge rapid rollout with clear performance metrics.

From where I stand, simply adding more GP slots or standalone walk-in clinics won’t reliably improve timely access. The real improvement would come from investing in co‑located community hubs that bring together primary care, community health, mental health services, social care and VCSE partners in one place with integrated records and care planning. In practice, this would reduce chasing staff across sites, cut duplication, and speed up decision-making for people with complex needs. For example, in our area a timely response would have been possible if a hub offered same-day triage with a clinician, social care support and a link to mental health services—without sending families between multiple buildings. The current setup often leaves people waiting when urgent social or mental health support is needed, creating crises that then drive A&E visits.

I also think we must grow the workforce more sustainably: expand training places, return‑to‑practice support and apprenticeships for GPs, nurses and mental health workers so capacity grows long term rather than just patching gaps. And protect continuity of care by longer appointment times for those with complex, chronic or vulnerable needs, which reduces repeat visits and improves outcomes.

The changes must be funded, locally coordinated and routinely evaluated to ensure hubs genuinely connect services and improve timeliness for patients.

From where I live in England, improving timely access to GP, community health and mental health services matters a lot, but I’m wary about making co‑located community hubs the primary solution. The idea of bringing primary care, community teams, mental health services, social care and VCSE partners into one physical space sounds efficient in theory. In practice, though, it risks creating new bottlenecks, formalising complex governance, and pushing patients into a route that isn’t nimble enough to meet urgent needs. If money and time are spent on building hubs rather than fixing core pressures in day‑to‑day delivery, people will still wait for basic access when they need it most.

What makes me cautious
- Timeliness depends on capacity, not just location. Even if a hub exists, if there aren’t enough GPs, nurses, and therapists to see people quickly, patients will still face delays. In my area, urgent same‑day slots are scarce and often booked days in advance; moving to a hub could simply move the problem rather than solve it.
- Complex governance slows things down. Co‑location requires robust data sharing, joint appointment systems and clear leadership across organisations that historically operate on separate budgets and performance targets. Without crystal‑clear governance and agreed pathways, the hub becomes a bureaucratic maze that slows triage and referral rather than accelerating it.
- Access is not only about distance. For many, especially those with work, caring responsibilities, or mobility issues, travelling to a hub can add time and stress. If the hub is not designed with flexibility in mind (for example, co‑located services but still demanding travel to a central site), it can unintentionally widen inequities.
- The hubs risk being slow to deliver tangible gains. Even when established, the real benefits depend on how well the services are integrated and how quickly patients are moved through appropriate pathways. That integration takes time to implement and test; meanwhile, people need help now.

What would actually improve timely access more quickly
- Expand GP capacity and access now. Fund more GP and practice nurse appointments, with options for extended hours, weekend slots, and urgent same‑day care. Increase the use of skilled professionals such as physician associates and nurse practitioners to triage and see a larger share of patients promptly.
- Strengthen digital and navigation tools. A robust, patient‑facing online booking system with reliable same‑day triage, clear indications of what can be treated remotely, and easy referrals to community or mental health teams would help. For people with limited internet access, ensure telephone triage with guaranteed callbacks and in‑person options.
- Create a single point of contact for patients. A dedicated care navigator or link worker who can assess needs and quickly route people to the right service (GP, community nursing, mental health, social care, or VCSE support) would reduce multiple phone calls and delay. This would be especially valuable for people with complex needs.
- Invest in stepped mental health support within primary care. Expand access to low‑intensity psychological therapies and rapid early‑intervention services in GP practices or local community settings. Ensure crisis pathways are clear and accessible, with timely access to specialist mental health when needed.
- Use hubs as a strategic, not solo, fix. If co‑located hubs are pursued, they should be rolled out as targeted pilots in areas with the greatest need, with strong governance, patient involvement, and measurable outcomes. Data sharing agreements, joint performance metrics, and patient representatives must be built in from the start.
- Leverage VCSE and community assets. Keep the voluntary, community and social enterprise sector involved as genuine partners, not just add‑ons. Their local knowledge, social prescribing, befriending services and community outreach can reduce loneliness, prevent crises and improve early‑stage support, which in turn speeds up access to formal care when it’s truly needed.

Personal experience
In my own town, I’ve seen how a lack of GP slots and long wait times for mental health referrals cause real hardship. A relative with anxiety and depression waited months for a response after a referral, while a friend needing urgent GP advice spent days chasing slots or dealing with call queues. A well‑run care navigator could have cut through that maze, guiding us to the right help quickly, whether it was a same‑day GP slot, a nurse‑led triage clinic, or a mental health prompt while a longer‑term plan was arranged.

Bottom line
I’m not opposed to the idea of co‑located hubs, but they shouldn’t be treated as the sole fix for timely access. The fastest, most equitable improvements will come from quickly growing GP capacity, streamlining digital access and triage, and ensuring a capable, well‑coordinated navigation system that can direct people to the right services right away. Hubs could play a valuable longer‑term role if designed with strong governance, real patient involvement, and a clear, evidence‑based plan to deliver tangible benefits without delaying urgent care today.

i strongly believe timely access to GP, community health and mental health services remains uneven where I live in England. A mixed approach seems best: expand multidisciplinary teams to handle routine cases. In our practice, pharmacists and physiotherapists already help triage back pain and medication reviews, freeing GPs for more complex cases. This model could be rolled out more widely, with physician associates and paramedics handling urgent community triage and home visits. 

But there are concrete barriers beyond staffing. Transport, parking and cramped premises persist, especially in rural or mobility-limited areas. I’ve seen a weekly mobile clinic visit to a village hall help those without reliable transport, and a telehealth hub run from the local library cut some waiting times for mental health triage. Incentives for small practices to offer extended hours and outreach would help, as would longer appointment slots for nurse and therapist teams and smarter scheduling to fill gaps. 

Overall, a blended strategy—staff expansion, mobile and telehealth access, and better siting of services—would have the biggest impact, provided it’s funded sustainably and keeps patient‑centered care at the heart!

Thank you for the chance to respond. Our organisation works closely with older residents across England, and we strongly support moves to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services. Too many people experience long waits and fragmented care, which not only worsens health outcomes but adds anxiety and uncertainty for families already juggling multiple appointments and complex needs.

A core priority must be to expand community mental health teams and to strengthen early intervention, crisis response and talking therapies. When mental health support is readily available in people’s communities, and when teams can respond quickly to emerging concerns, crisis points are often avoided and people can stay connected to their routines, families and communities. We would like to see growth in multi-disciplinary teams that include nurses, social workers, psychiatrists and occupational therapists, with a clear pathway from first contact in primary care to specialised or community-based care. In practice, this would translate to more same-day or next-day GP slots for people with emerging distress, rapid non-urgent mental health assessments by community teams, and timely access to evidence-based talking therapies such as CBT and interpersonal therapy.

Crucially, crisis response must be available 24/7 or with reliable after-hours cover, so that people in distress aren’t left waiting. A strong 24/7 crisis line, with capacity to mobilise rapid mobile teams for home or community-based support, would significantly reduce avoidable hospital admissions and help people stay in familiar surroundings when possible. We have seen in our area that when response teams can visit at home or in a community hub, anxiety about presenting at accident and emergency drops, and families feel more confident about seeking help early.

Equity in access is essential. Access gaps persist for deprived communities, ethnic minority groups, migrants and marginalised residents, including many older people who live alone or rely on limited transport. Language barriers, cultural differences, and a lack of interpreters or culturally competent staff are real barriers to timely care. We have witnessed situations where people with limited English could not articulate symptoms clearly, or where mental health concerns were perceived through a biomedical lens rather than a holistic, culturally sensitive lens. We therefore urge targeted resources: long-term funding for interpreters across primary care and mental health services; recruitment and retention of culturally competent clinicians who reflect the communities they serve; and outreach that meets people where they are—community venues, faith groups, libraries and social clubs.

Practical steps should include embedding interpreters in GP reception areas and in mental health triage, commissioning bilingual community health champions who can accompany patients to appointments, and translating patient information into a wider range of languages. Outreach should be supported by trusted local networks and community navigators who can identify early signs of distress and link people to help before crises develop. In our experience, such approaches build trust and reduce the time between first concern and first help, particularly for those who may not self-refer easily to formal services.

We also need to make sure access improvements are inclusive of physical health needs alongside mental health. Co-located services, integrated care plans and shared records where consent is given would mean a patient’s GP, mental health team and social care worker can coordinate around one plan, reducing duplication and miscommunication. Extending hours in GP practices and community clinics, enabling walk-in slots, and making use of social prescribing where appropriate can help older people stay active and engaged while addressing health concerns early.

Finally, these changes must be underpinned by sustainable funding, rigorous workforce planning and robust oversight. We need transparent performance metrics that track waiting times, equity of access, and patient experience, with meaningful involvement of older residents in design and evaluation. Any rollout should begin in areas with the greatest need and be scaled up only once there is evidence of safer, quicker access and improved outcomes.

In summary, expanding community mental health teams, investing in early intervention and crisis response, and ensuring targeted, culturally competent outreach will measurably improve timely access to services. We stand ready to work with commissioners, providers and local communities to turn these principles into practical, effective changes for our older residents and their families.

Urgent changes to NHS111 triage, booking and care navigation in Wales to prioritise urgent cases and cut duplication; alongside expanding community mental health teams, early intervention and crisis services, with better same-day GP slots and digital booking, to ensure parity with physical health.

I support expanding community mental health teams, early intervention, crisis response and talking therapies to bring parity with physical health and cut waiting times. Strengthening NHS111, better clinical triage, streamlined booking and care navigation would prioritise urgent cases and reduce duplication.

Access to GP, community health and mental health services in my area remains inconsistent, and transport and parking constraints make timely visits tough. Buses are infrequent, parking is tight at busy surgeries, and evening slots are hard to come by for shift workers and parents. In my area, a mobile clinic visits once a month, which helps some neighbours but doesn't cover workdays or urgent needs. Providing incentives for practices to extend hours or offer weekend slots could help—but only if capacity and funding grow at the same pace.

A more reliable fix is to increase appointment slots by hiring more GPs, nurses and therapists and by smarter, predictable scheduling to reduce waits. In mental health, appointment access remains the main bottleneck, so more clinicians and group sessions would make a real difference.

I’d also support co-located community hubs that integrate primary care, mental health, social care and VCSE partners. One campus coordinating housing, benefits advice and health would simplify referrals and cut duplication. Any plan must ensure data sharing is secure, funding sustainable and transport remains accessible for those with the least mobility.

Agree. Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services is essential for people like me who juggle work and family responsibilities. I support investing in co-located community hubs that integrate primary care with community and mental health services, social care, and VCSE partners. When these services sit under one roof, it’s easier to triage quickly and stitch together a joined‑up care plan, which saves time and reduces crises.

In my area there’s a hub pilot where a GP, a mental health nurse and a social worker are colocated. During a recent episode, my neighbour could get a same-day slot and leave with a clear plan and linked follow‑ups—meds, social support and rehab all arranged in one go instead of multiple appointments far apart. For complex or chronic cases, protecting continuity of care and lengthening appointment times makes a huge difference; clinicians can review meds, catch interactions, and adjust plans without forcing endless repeat visits.

I also back expanding multidisciplinary teams—pharmacists for med reviews, physiotherapists for rehabilitation, paramedics and physician associates to handle routine checks and urgent care—so GPs can focus on high‑need patients. These changes would improve timeliness, outcomes, and confidence in local services.

Waiting times for GP and mental health care in my area are simply too long. I disagree with ideas that only chase short-term fixes will solve the problem. The changes that would most improve timely access are two linked strands: sustainable workforce growth and immediate capacity expansion. 

First, we must increase training places and support return-to-practice for GPs, nurses and therapists. Apprenticeships and enhanced CPD would create a steady pipeline of capable clinicians and help replace staff who retire or move away. In my neighbourhood I’ve seen local practices struggle when a couple of long‑standing GPs retire and fills remain unfilled for weeks; without long-term planning, waits simply shift from one part of the system to another. 

Second, we must add appointment slots and capacity now: hire more clinicians, expand session lengths where appropriate, and optimise scheduling to spread demand more evenly. In practice this means longer opening hours, protected clinics for complex cases, and more robust triage so patients are directed to the right professional first time. It would also help to bolster reception/admin and digital signposting so people aren’t left waiting on phone lines. 

In short, I support a two-pronged approach, but only if there is honest investment now and a clear retention plan; otherwise waits will simply get worse and more people will drift away from seeking timely care.

Online booking and e-consultations can offer convenience, but I strongly disagree with making digital access the default route for GP, community health and mental health services. In our area many older residents and neighbours struggle with online systems: my neighbour with arthritis can't navigate the portal, my sister has dementia and struggles with passwords, and broadband in our village is unreliable. The hike in automated phone lines merely adds to frustration. When urgent issues arise, I fear people delay help or end up at overcrowded urgent care because non-digital options are too hard to find or too slow. We need clear, reliable non-digital routes alongside digital ones: longer, well-staffed phone lines, in-person same-day triage, pop-up clinics in community halls, and patient advocates to help with bookings.

Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services is essential for people trying to work, care for family and stay well in busy lives.
