This could streamline referrals, support self‑care and provide social support in one place. In my experience, neighbours benefit from a hub that includes a district nurse, a mental health link worker, and access to a social prescriber within walking distance.

Delivery will hinge on adequate staffing, sustainable funding and clear IT and data‑sharing pathways with consent. Pilots in a few sites with robust evaluation would help refine hours, appointment lengths and hub configurations before wider rollout.

I disagree with expanding short slots; protect continuity of care by longer appointment times for complex, chronic and vulnerable patients, which improves outcomes and reduces repeat visits, ultimately supporting timely access.

Expand online booking and e-consults, but preserve non-digital options (phone, in-person slots, community hubs) and practical support for older or less tech-savvy patients to safeguard timely GP, community and mental health access.

Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services remains uneven in my area. I think the changes most likely to help are investing in co-located community hubs that bring primary care, district nursing, mental health teams and social care around one building, with input from voluntary, community and social enterprise (VCSE) partners. Such hubs could streamline referrals, share records (with robust consent) and offer same-day triage. For example, if a patient can see a GP and quickly access a mental health worker or health visitor in one place, waits would drop and people wouldn’t bounce between services. However, I’m concerned about funding stability and IT integration. Co-located hubs require secure data-sharing, cross-training and long-term staffing commitments; without that they risk fragmenting care again if a single programme ends. 

I also welcome expansion of community mental health teams, early intervention and crisis response, plus more talking therapies. In practice this could mean crisis teams that respond within hours, clearer referral pathways, and expanded waiting-time targets to parity with physical health. In my experience, a friend waited weeks for counselling after housing stress triggered anxiety; quicker access could have prevented escalation. Local investment should involve patients and VCSEs in design and measured pilots, with transparent reporting.

I'm worried that the main changes proposed – broadening training places, return-to-practice support, apprenticeships and CPD, upgrading NHS111/triage, and simply 'more appointment slots' – won't deliver timely access quickly enough.

Long waits for GP slots persisted here last winter; a local practice had just two same-day slots and many cancelled appointments; training takes years to produce new fully competent clinicians. In the meantime patients with real urgent needs end up in ED or in prolonged limbo. Mental health referrals linger for months; waiting times for talking therapies remain unacceptable.

NHS111 and care navigation can help, but only if triage is clinically led and avoids routing people away from in-person contact when needed. Too often, call-centre triage adds steps and delays. We need more front-line clinicians involved in triage within primary care, with clear escalation to GPs when red flags appear, and better record-sharing to avoid repeating questions.

Increasing capacity must be practical now: extend hours at existing hubs, incentivise flexible shifts, and use non-GP clinicians (nurses, pharmacists, therapists) to handle routine and mild cases. Expand same-day slots, group CBT sessions for suitable patients, and stand-up additional urgent-care slots in community sites to reduce waits.

In short, short-term, tangible capacity and smarter routing matter as much as long-term workforce growth.

Living as a young adult in England, I see how delays in GP and mental health care affect daily life. I strongly support changes to expand community mental health teams, increase early intervention options, and boost crisis response and talking therapies. If specialist teams could respond quickly—ideally within days—people would get timely assessments, urgent support, and ongoing therapy without spiralling waits. In my area, CAMHS and adult mental health services sometimes mean waiting weeks for an appointment; stronger crisis lines and quicker access to talking therapies would keep people safer and functioning at school or work.

On the workforce side, I back more training places, return-to-practice support, apprenticeships and CPD to grow GPs, nurses and mental health professionals long-term. I’ve heard from friends who paused NHS training due to costs or caring responsibilities; clearer, funded routes back into practice would bring talent back sooner. Expanding apprenticeships and funded CPD would also help staff stay up to date and motivated. With a steadier, larger workforce, same-day GP slots and timely mental health help would become the norm, matching the parity we expect with physical health services.

Access to GP, community health and mental health services in our area is too slow for too many people, and that delay isn’t just a line on a waiting list – it translates into worse health and greater stress for families trying to plan work, schooling and caring responsibilities. In my experience, appointment slots for GPs and nurses often feel almost ceremonial rather than responsive: when you call for a same-week issue you’re told the next available slot is in two or more weeks, and for mental health support the bottleneck is even more acute. People I know have had to navigate multiple phone triages or put off appointments altogether, which then shows up later as more serious problems. I’d like to see changes that tackle capacity and scheduling directly, not just promises about “digital access” alone.

First, we need to increase the actual capacity of the workforce and the way appointments are run. This means hiring more GPs, practice nurses and therapists, and expanding the length and variety of sessions where appropriate. For example, longer in-person appointments for complex cases, and the option of structured group sessions for chronic conditions like diabetes and COPD, could free up one‑to‑one slots for those who need them most. It also means smarter scheduling: protected time for ongoing care plans, more predictable weekly rosters, and robust backfill to avoid a day’s worth of slots disappearing because someone’s off sick. In practice this could look like a mix of standard daytime appointments plus a pool of pre-bookable slots that are held specifically for complex cases, so a patient doesn’t have to start from scratch every time.

Second, there should be real provision for evening and weekend clinics and guaranteed same-day urgent slots. People work, have school runs, or rely on carers, and a limited weekday-only system excludes a large part of the population from timely care. I’d support at least two reasonably staffed evening clinics each week and a regularly available Saturday morning slot in every area, with a guaranteed same-day urgent slot for non-emergency but urgent health issues (and a transparent pathway to escalation if a mental health crisis is identified). This isn’t about creating a separate “secondary” service; it’s about ensuring primary care is accessible when people have work and caring responsibilities, and when problems arise that can’t wait two or three weeks for a preliminary triage call.

Third, I’d like to see targeted work to close access gaps for deprived, ethnic minority, migrant and marginalised groups. In practice that means better interpreters and culturally competent staff across GP surgeries and community hubs, plus proactive outreach to local communities. I’ve seen long waits for someone with limited English who doesn’t have family nearby to translate; practical steps like on-site interpreters, multilingual appointment reminders, and clear information about where to go for non-emergency mental health support can make a real difference. Outreach shouldn’t be a one‑off event; it needs ongoing presence in community centres, schools, religious groups and local employers, with co-produced services that reflect the needs of different communities.

A few concrete examples from my own experience underscore why these changes are needed and how they could work:
- A relative had to wait nearly a month for a GP appointment for a new chronic symptom; the delay led to a more alarming issue that required urgent care rather than routine management. If there were guaranteed same-day urgent slots and more flexible scheduling, the issue could have been addressed earlier and more effectively.
- A friend who works shifts found it almost impossible to attend a daytime mental health assessment. An evening clinic option would have allowed access without risking job security or childcare arrangements.
- In our area, there’s a sizeable non‑English-speaking community. When appointments are only offered in daytime hours with limited interpreter support, people skip care or rely on emergency services. Systematic interpretation, culturally appropriate staff training, and active outreach would reduce avoidable crises and build trust with health services.

If these changes are to be credible, they must be supported by clear performance targets and accountability. Data on wait times, appointment mix (face-to-face vs. telephone vs. virtual), and patient experience by ethnicity, language and deprivation level should be published and used to adjust staffing and outreach. Digital tools can help with scheduling and triage, but there must be inclusive options for those who can’t use or access online systems.

Overall, I support a multi-pronged approach that expands capacity, broadens access with after-hours options, and centres on reducing disparities through interpreters, culturally competent staff and sustained community outreach. Done well, these changes could shorten waits, improve the quality of care, and build more resilient, trustful relationships between health services and the communities they serve.

From where I live in Scotland, timely access to GP, community health and mental health services would improve with a balanced package of digital and non-digital options, plus well‑integrated local hubs. Expanding online booking, e-consultations and remote care can save time—triage calls that point you to a GP slot or mental health worker, and virtual follow‑ups after hospital discharge. Yet many neighbours, especially the elderly, have limited internet or find digital systems confusing. Therefore, we must preserve phone lines, paper referrals, home visits and staffed walk‑in slots, with clear, simple help to get online when possible. Local drop‑in digital clinics and volunteer “tech buddies” could support people to book and use e‑services.

Investing in co‑located community hubs that bring primary care, district nursing, mental health teams, social care and VCSE partners under one roof would cut duplication and speed up referrals. For example, a single hub could arrange a same‑day GP slot, a mental‑health check, and social‑care advice in one visit, with coordinated follow‑ups. In rural parts, reliable transport and online access must be paired with strong phone access and outreach. I’d welcome pilots and monitoring to ensure no one is left behind.

absolutely we need more GP, nurse, and therapist slots and better appointment capacity, plus funded interpreters and culturally competent staff. Prioritise outreach to deprived and minority communities to close access gaps, with sustainable funding and scheduling that won’t compromise care quality!

As an older resident in England, I’m finding it harder to get timely GP, community health and mental health support. In my area, same-day GP slots are often unavailable, the phone queue is long, and when I or neighbours need home visits the wait can be days. A relative’s mental health care required weeks before any clinician could assess them, even after contacting crisis lines. The changes that would help most are practical, funded steps to grow and retain primary care staff.

- Targeted recruitment: long-term campaigns in high-need towns, clearer routes to partnership for nurses and GPs, and supported return-to-practice for those who’ve stepped back.
- International recruitment: welcome skilled clinicians with robust language training and induction, plus ethical visa and integration pathways that don’t override local training standards.
- Pay and incentives: improved pay bands, retention bonuses, and pension terms to attract and keep experienced clinicians.
- Flexible working and wellbeing: more part-time and job-share posts, protected admin/cover time, and robust wellbeing support to reduce burnout.
- Local integration: a community-hub model where GP, physiotherapy and mental health staff share space and triage to speed referrals.

These require proper funding and governance, but without them access will only worsen and place added strain on older neighbours who need continuity and reliability.

i really think i welcome the proposals to improve timely access to general practice, community health and mental health services. As someone in their mid-sixties living in England, I’ve seen how important it is for people with long‑term conditions or caring responsibilities to have steady, reliable access to the same clinician and to be able to get help when it’s really needed. The changes I’d like to see would, I believe, reduce unnecessary trips back to the surgery and improve outcomes for vulnerable patients.

First, protecting continuity of care and lengthening appointment times for complex, chronic and vulnerable patients would make a real difference. When you’re managing several conditions—blood pressure, diabetes, arthritis, and medication reviews—short 5– to 10‑minute slots don’t give enough space to review symptoms, adjust medications safely, and check for side‑effects. I’ve had experiences where I saw different GPs over a few weeks and the transitions felt rushed; important information was missed and I ended up needing another appointment soon after. Longer, better‑paced appointments (around 20–30 minutes for those with complex needs) would help the clinician see the whole picture, ensure medicines are appropriate, and improve adherence. Keeping the same GP or care team whenever possible also builds trust and reduces the chance of conflicting advice, which in turn reduces repeat visits and hospital admissions down the line.

Second, expanding online booking, e‑consultations and remote care, while ensuring non‑digital options, would make access easier for many. I value being able to book online or submit a quick message for non‑urgent follow‑ups, because it saves time and can prevent unnecessary trips. For some people my age, a virtual review of blood pressure readings, chat about symptoms, or remote monitoring can be very convenient. At the same time, we must not leave behind those who struggle with digital tools or who live alone. Non‑digital routes—telephone triage, simple paper forms, and in‑person booking assistance at the surgery or local libraries—need to be available and actively offered. Providing staff to guide people through online systems and offering printed summaries after consultations would help ensure no one is excluded by technology.

Third, evening and weekend clinics and guaranteed same‑day urgent slots would improve access for working people and those with urgent non‑emergency needs. Many in my community work daytime hours and cannot easily take time off for medical appointments. Evening clinics would allow people to attend after work without risking medical need turning into a crisis. Guaranteed same‑day urgent slots are vital for symptoms that can escalate quickly, such as chest discomfort, severe infections, or anxiety spikes that threaten safety. A clear, predictable urgent‑care pathway would reduce the fear of waiting too long and encourage people to seek help earlier when it could prevent more serious problems.

Mental health services also need to be embedded more closely with primary care. Quick access to talking therapies, same‑day triage for crisis situations, and a stronger link between GP practices and community mental health teams would prevent deterioration and support families who are trying to cope at home. For example, a same‑week appointment with a mental health professional, or a same‑day phone check‑in when someone is anxious or distressed, can make a big difference to stability and may avert the need for emergency care.

All of these changes require investment in staffing and training, plus reliable digital‑skills support for older patients. Additional general practice capacity, longer appointment times for complex cases, and well‑resourced remote and in‑person options would together reduce delays, improve safety, and—crucially—protect the continuity of care that so many of us rely on.

In short, I’d like to see a system that makes it easier to book and attend appointments with the same clinician, offers longer appointments for those with complex needs, provides flexible online and offline access, and guarantees urgent slots and after‑hours options. If done thoughtfully, these steps will save time, reduce anxiety, and improve health outcomes for people in the community who need it most!

it's outrageous that from living in England and being in the 18–24 age group, I think the biggest gains would come from protecting continuity of care and lengthening appointment times for complex or vulnerable patients. When people can see the same GP over time, diagnoses are more accurate and care plans safer, which reduces repeat visits and hospital admissions. For someone juggling chronic conditions and study, a 10– to 15‑minute slot often isn’t enough. Longer appointments (25–30 minutes) or structured multi‑disciplinary reviews with a GP, nurse and pharmacist would make management easier and safer, and would improve medication reviews and referrals. It would also help with follow‑ups and more reliable triage, and making some slots available in evenings or weekends would assist students and shift workers who can’t attend during the day. 

On mental health and community services, expanding teams and offering early intervention, crisis response and talking therapies could reduce waits and improve parity with physical health. But I’d want clear recruitment targets, culturally sensitive services and genuinely integrated care, so someone in crisis isn’t shuttled between services. A same‑day triage option alongside ongoing talking therapies would feel more dependable and keep people out of crisis as much as possible!

I support expanding multidisciplinary teams (pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics, physician associates) to handle routine cases, freeing GPs for complex care. Improving NHS111, triage and booking systems will prioritise urgent needs, reduce duplication and simplify access for older residents.

I strongly support changes that improve timely access by protecting continuity of care and lengthening appointment times for complex, chronic and vulnerable patients. In my area, the pressure of short slots means clinicians rush through visits, leaving symptoms under-explored and care fragmented, which drives repeat visits and anxiety. For example, a relative dealing with asthma, diabetes and depression would benefit from a 30-minute slot to review meds, check inhaler technique, assess mental health and social needs in one go, which could reduce hospital visits and crises.

Expanding multidisciplinary teams would also make a big difference. If pharmacists take on routine med reviews and minor interactions, and physiotherapists triage back and joint pain, GPs would have more capacity for complex cases. Paramedics and physician associates could handle home visits and routine follow-ups, freeing GPs to focus on continuity of care. In mental health, quicker access to MDT pathways—supported by talking therapies or behavioural support—could prevent deterioration and avoid urgent crises.

To make this work, there must be robust IT sharing and stable funding so patient records are accessible to all team members and MDTs are properly staffed to meet demand, ensuring reliable, timely care for those who need it most.

I welcome moves to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services in our area. As someone who works full-time and tries to juggle family life, I know how hard it can be to get timely care if clinics only run within standard office hours. The idea of evening and weekend clinics, alongside guaranteed same-day urgent slots, would make a real practical difference for working people and for urgent non-emergency needs that can’t wait. When you’re managing flu-like symptoms, a stubborn pain that’s not clearly serious but worrying, or a child’s fever after school, being able to book something the same day, even outside the usual hours, would reduce anxiety and prevent problems from escalating. I’ve seen friends and colleagues miss work to attend midweek slots, which simply isn’t sustainable for many families; a predictable service that runs into the evening or weekends would help many of us stay in work and still get decent, timely care. It would also align with the reality that people go out to work in the day and often rely on after-hours support to avoid taking more unpaid time off.

Coupled with urgent same-day access, continuing to protect continuity of care is essential. For people with complex, chronic conditions or vulnerabilities, seeing the same clinician over time builds trust and leads to better outcomes. I’ve seen how fast-moving health issues can slip through the cracks when you’re handed a different GP every visit; the medication changes aren’t always reconciled, and important social factors can be overlooked. Longer appointment times for those patients would mean clinicians can review multiple conditions, medications, and social determinants of health in one sitting, reducing the need for repeated visits and minimising hospital trips. In my experience with a close family member who lives with diabetes and mild anxiety, the benefits of continuity were clear: consistent guidance, a shared plan, and an opportunity to flag concerns early before they became crises. Extending appointment times from the standard 10–15 minutes to 20–30 minutes for complex cases would translate into more accurate diagnoses and safer care, and it would also reduce patient frustration and repeated calls or visits.

Mental health services are a particular area where timely access and continuity matter. Waiting weeks for an initial appointment can lead to deterioration, making it harder to engage in therapy or follow a self-management plan. If urgent slots could be guaranteed on the same day for escalating concerns, and if a trusted clinician could follow people through the early stages of treatment, the system would be more responsive and supportive. I’ve witnessed the relief of someone who finally spoke to a familiar practitioner after a downturn, who could tailor cognitive-behavioural strategies to their daily routine and coordinate with community support services. In practice, this would mean structured triage with options for same-day slots when red flags appear, quick rebooking within the same care team, and more robust pathways between GP practices, community nursing, and mental health teams so people don’t fall through the gaps.

To make this work, I’d prioritise investment in workforce and local planning. Sufficient GP and nurse practitioner capacity, well-resourced call handling, and virtual triage that still routes people to a real clinician the same day are essential. We also need a clear commitment to continuity—systems that flag and retain the same clinician for long-term or complex care, with longer appointments where needed. This would not only improve patient satisfaction but should reduce avoidable hospital visits and improve overall outcomes. In short, more flexible hours, guaranteed urgent access, and sustained continuity of care are the practical levers that will help our area turn timely access into real, lasting health gains for people who work, families, and those with chronic or mental health needs.

I support evening and weekend clinics with guaranteed same-day urgent slots, which would help working people and urgent non-emergency needs. Also, increasing GP, nurse and therapist appointment slots and expanding multidisciplinary teams would reduce waits and free GPs for complex care.

I’m supportive of the changes proposed to improve timely access to GP services, community health and mental health care. In my area I’ve seen how waiting times and fragmented care can bite, especially for people juggling work, family and long-term health needs. I believe a balanced mix of digital and non-digital options is the way forward, so no one is left behind.

Expanded online booking, e-consults and remote care can make a real difference. Being able to book appointments online, submit a quick symptom check or have a short video or phone consultation has already helped me avoid unnecessary trips and get advice sooner. For example, when I had a persistent skin issue, an online triage flagged it as non-urgent but needing follow-up. I received guidance within 24 hours and a same-day teleconsult was offered, which meant I could be seen quickly without waiting weeks for an in-person slot. Remote care also supports ongoing management of chronic conditions; for my family member with a long-term health issue, home blood pressure monitoring combined with virtual check-ins has helped keep track of symptoms without constant clinic visits.

That said, digital access must not become a barrier. Many friends and neighbours still find online forms and video calls confusing, and some in our community lack reliable internet or devices. We need robust non-digital routes: a responsive phone line with extended hours, straightforward in‑person booking, and clear support at local libraries or community hubs to help people book or use online tools. Practices could offer low-tech onboarding sessions, and translators or carers should be able to assist with digital access where needed. I’d also welcome a simple, consistent alternative to e-consults for those who prefer speaking to a clinician directly, including more same-day phone triage when digital isn’t practical.

Continuity of care and adequately long appointments for complex or vulnerable patients are crucial for better outcomes. Short slots often lead to repeated visits or fragmented care, which isn’t efficient for anyone. I’d like to see a named clinician for those with long-term or complex needs and longer appointment times (for example 20 minutes as a standard, with 30 minutes or more for multi-morbidity or social risk factors). When clinicians know a patient’s history, symptoms can be interpreted more quickly, appropriate tests ordered sooner and care plans coordinated with pharmacists, nurses and mental health teams. In practice, maintaining stronger continuity reduces avoidable hospital visits and improves safety and trust in the system.

To support this long-term, we need to grow the workforce responsibly. Increasing training places, return‑to‑practice support, apprenticeships and CPD is essential if we want sustainable access. In recent years, staffing gaps have limited capacity; more funded places for GPs, practice nurses and mental health professionals, plus structured induction and mentorship, would help retain staff and reduce burnout. Returning clinicians could be offered tailored refreshers and supervised practice to re‑establish confidence quickly, ensuring skills match current guidelines.

Mental health access also needs to be front and centre. Timely access to community mental health teams, timely counselling or talking therapies, and closer integration with primary care can prevent crises. I’ve seen how convenient it is when a GP can quickly refer to a community mental health worker who understands the patient’s history and can coordinate with social care if needed. Digital options for CBT or guided self-help can be useful, but there must be ready non-digital equivalents (face-to-face sessions, telephone support) for those who prefer or need them.

If these changes are implemented, I’d expect to see fewer delays, more people getting early advice and treatment, and better outcomes for people with long-term or complex needs. The right balance between digital innovation and human touch is essential to make timely access a reality for everyone, including the elderly and those with limited digital skills.

In short: expand flexible digital access where appropriate, pair it with strong non-digital routes, protect longer appointment times for complex needs, and invest in training and support to grow our healthcare workforce for the long term. That combination would make a tangible difference in my area.

In my experience, timely access would improve most if we bring services closer to people and speed up triage. I would support expanding community mental health teams, with stronger emphasis on early intervention, crisis response and talking therapies, so people don’t wait weeks for help and so mental health care becomes as much of a priority as physical health. In my area, GP slots are often full and the car park at the health centre is crowded; transport is challenging for those with mobility issues. I’d like to see mobile clinics visiting village halls on a regular rota, outreach workers who can coordinate with GPs and district nurses, and telehealth hubs in local libraries or surgeries to reduce unnecessary journeys. Incentives to recruit and retain staff in rural areas, plus better premises and flexible hours, would also help. In short, more local, visible services, faster triage, and community-based access before crisis point would make a real difference.

Agree. In Scotland, I’ve seen how delays for mental health support can leave people – especially young adults like me – feeling alone and overwhelmed. Expanding community mental health teams and early intervention would change this quickly: clinics and teams in local hubs with youth specialists who can spot issues early and offer structured, short-term therapies before things spiral. Crisis response must be able to act fast, with mobile teams available 24/7 to visit people at home or meet in community centres, so nobody has to wait days for help. We also need more capacity for talking therapies, including CBT and guided self-help, with smoother GP referral pathways so people aren’t stuck waiting months. Practical changes would include wider GP hours, same-day or next-day mental health triage in practices, and better digital access for booking and remote consultations, especially in rural areas. Transparent wait-time data would help families and individuals plan and feel confident about care. Overall, these steps would bring mental health care closer to physical health in a fair, timely way and reduce needless distress for young people here.

To improve timely access, I think we need a two-pronged approach: invest in the workforce pipeline and redesign access windows for patients who work or have urgent needs. First, increasing training places for GPs, nurses and mental health professionals, plus structured return-to-practice support, apprenticeships and ongoing CPD, would help grow a sustainable frontline workforce. In my area I see colleagues retiring faster than retraining permits fill, leading to bottlenecks when someone needs a diabetes check or mental health input. If trusts could offer funded return-to-practice placements and clear CPD routes, more clinicians would stay in frontline care. Apprenticeships for nurse associates and physician associates could widen entry routes and bring practical experience. Second, practical access reforms: evening and weekend clinics, plus guaranteed same-day urgent slots. My work schedule means weekday mornings are the only realistic window for me; if there were evening clinics I could be seen the same day for urgent symptoms, rather than waiting days. A simple same-day urgent slot policy, with triage by phone or online, would reduce avoidable attendances and ease pressure. Strong GP and community mental health integration would also help with quicker referrals and shorter waiting times.

There's real value in expanding online booking, e-consultations and remote care. In my experience, online slots can be quicker for simple check-ins, prescription renewals, or triage for a minor issue, and they save time on travel. However, my neighbour's elderly parent struggles with apps and my local practice still requires many to call long lines, which risks delaying care. So I’d support expanding digital access alongside non-digital routes: a robust phone triage line, same-day in-person slots when needed, and clear guidance on when remote care is suitable. Also invest in digital support at the practice: drop-in sessions, translators, accessible interfaces, and options to use staff-assisted booking.

For mental health, more online therapies and rapid digital triage would help reduce bottlenecks, but must be paired with face-to-face options and crisis support. In primary care, addressing workforce is crucial: increase training places, backfill for return-to-practice, and expand apprenticeships and CPD with NHS partners and local universities to grow GPs, nurses and therapists long-term. My town’s GP recruitment has been slow, and we see longer waits; sustained investment is essential, with monitoring to ensure equity across all communities.

I believe the changes that would most improve timely access fall into two linked strands: expanding multidisciplinary teams to handle routine care, and removing practical barriers that stop people from reaching services quickly, especially in rural or mobility‑challenged areas.

First, I’m broadly supportive of expanding multidisciplinary teams within primary care. If pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics, physician associates and mental health workers can manage everyday concerns under appropriate supervision, it frees GPs to focus on more complex cases and safeguarding issues. In practice, this could mean same‑day or next‑day access to a physiotherapist for back or joint pain, a pharmacist for medicine reviews and minor ailments, or a mental health practitioner for mild to moderate concerns, all within the same practice or local hubs. Shared clinical records and clear referral pathways would be essential so patients don’t have to repeat information and can move smoothly between professionals.

I’ve seen how a well‑coordinated team can improve outcomes. For example, a recent knee niggle that might have led to a GP appointment sooner could have been managed by a physiotherapist with a follow‑up plan, while a medication review by a pharmacist could prevent adverse effects or duplications. When these professionals are available locally, patients aren’t left waiting weeks for a GP appointment for issues that could be resolved more quickly and safely elsewhere. The key is strong governance, appropriate supervision, and training to ensure high quality care and patient safety, with patients always informed about options and free to choose the path that suits them.

Second, on access barriers: transport, parking and premises deficits are real brakes on timely care, and they hit rural and mobility‑impaired residents hardest. I’d support a mix of mobile clinics and outreach, telehealth hubs, and incentives to attract staff to underserved areas, coupled with practical measures to make existing premises easier to reach.

- Mobile clinics and outreach: rotating services that visit villages or neighbourhoods on a predictable schedule would bring GP, nurse, and allied health appointments closer to people who can’t easily travel. In my county, a fixed central clinic means hours and travel times are a real barrier for older residents with limited transport.
- Telehealth hubs and digital inclusion: establishing staffed telehealth hubs in community venues (libraries, community centres) with free Wi‑Fi and staff guidance helps those who can’t access digital care at home. It’s useful for triage, mental health support, and follow‑ups, but we must recognise that not everyone has a home internet connection or the confidence to use new tech.
- Transport and parking: better bus routes to health centres, safer and more accessible parking, and, where possible, partnerships with community transport services for medical appointments would make a real difference. For those with long journeys or sensory/mobility needs, even small improvements in access can shave days off waiting times and reduce no‑shows.
- Premises and environment: waiting areas that are accessible, comfortable, and easy to navigate, with clear wayfinding, improve the experience for patients who have to attend frequent appointments. Longer opening hours or weekend slots could also reduce waits for carers or shift workers.
- Incentives to work in rural or mobility‑restricted areas: targeted recruitment and retention packages—relocation allowances, training bursaries, and workforce supplementation during peak demand—could help build stable teams in areas that struggle to recruit.

From a personal perspective, I’d like to see a two‑tier approach work together: (1) a grown‑up, well‑funded expansion of multidisciplinary teams in localities where demand is high, and (2) practical access measures that ensure people can actually reach the services they’re offered. I’ve heard neighbours in rural parts express frustration at long travel times and limited appointment windows; I’ve also met patients who benefited from pharmacist or physiotherapist input when GP pages were full. Neither strategy works in isolation.

Implementation matters. I’d want pilots with clear evaluation—tracking wait times, patient satisfaction, clinical outcomes, and equity of access across age groups and disability. Any expansion must protect patient choice, ensure safety nets for complex cases, and maintain data privacy. The aim should be a more responsive primary care system where people can get appropriate help quickly, without unnecessary travel or delay, while GPs retain capacity for those genuinely needing their expertise.

Overall, I’m cautiously optimistic. With careful planning, sufficient funding, and a strong emphasis on integration and accessibility, these changes could deliver timely GP, community health, and mental health care that better reflects people’s real lives and needs.

I’m worried that the emphasis on online booking and e-consultations will widen gaps rather than close them. While digital tools can help, many people in my area still face barriers: older residents with limited tech skills, households without reliable broadband, and those who don’t speak English as a first language. A friend missed a same-day GP slot because the online system was slow and the phone line was busy; another neighbour struggled to navigate the app and then received a reminder by post only days later. We need robust non-digital options alongside any digital push: a clear, freephone service with real human triage during evenings and weekends, walk-in slots, and in-person help to book appointments at every practice or hub for those who need it. 

We also need to expand community mental health teams, early intervention, crisis response and talking therapies to reduce waits and achieve parity with physical health. In my area CAMHS waits are long and crisis support can feel under-resourced; timely early support could prevent crises, but only if funded and staffed properly. 

Finally, targeted outreach and language support are essential. We must fund interpreters, employ culturally competent staff, and run community outreach in deprived and migrant communities to close access gaps, not widen them. A balanced mix of digital and non-digital routes, with concrete support for those who need it, is essential for real improvement.

I welcome the proposals to improve timely access to GP, community and mental health services. In our rural area, transport is limited, parking is tight, and getting to appointments can take hours. Mobile clinics visiting village halls and GP outreach teams would make a big difference for older people and those with mobility issues. Telehealth hubs in local community centres, with staff to help people use the tech, would cut waiting times and spare me long journeys. It would help if there were incentives—travel allowances, flexible hours and longer-term contracts—to attract doctors and nurses to rural posts.

Another important change is a network of co‑located community hubs that bring together primary care, district nursing, mental health teams, social care and VCSE partners. When my neighbour was unwell, having a single hub with GP advice, mental health support and social services under one roof saved us trips and worry, and would improve continuity of care.

Finally, NHS111, clinical triage, booking systems and care navigation should prioritise urgent cases and reduce duplication. A clear, one‑path system for urgent access and a smoother flow from triage to appointment would be a real relief.

Expanding online booking, e-consultations and remote care would significantly improve how quickly people in my area can access GP, community health and mental health services. Online booking is convenient for both urgent and routine visits, and a quick e-consult can triage symptoms so clinicians can prioritise and reduce delays. Remote appointments suit those who travel long distances or have mobility issues; a short video or phone check can monitor blood pressure, adjust medications or provide mental health support without a hospital trip.

That said, digital tools must be matched with non-digital options to avoid excluding older or less tech‑savvy patients. A simple phone line, in-person booking at a local practice, and walk-in clinics remain essential. Local digital‑support sessions at libraries or community centres, with volunteers to help complete online forms, would be invaluable. In my street, a neighbour used a one‑hour library session to learn to book online and then had a same‑day appointment when they felt unwell. A hybrid system—more digital access with robust human support—would bring timely help to everyone.

Living in Scotland, I want to see tangible changes that make timely access to GP, community health and mental health services real, not just promised. In practice, a lot of the delay and confusion comes from a patchwork of NHS111/triage processes, separate booking systems and referrals, and a lack of clear navigation through the system. If we could sort that out, the demand pressures on primary care and community teams would feel more manageable, and people would get help before problems escalate.

First, streamline the front door. A single, region-wide digital triage and booking platform would let people describe urgency once, and then be directed to appropriate slots—same-day GP access for urgent symptoms, rapid routes into mental health support, and clear next steps when more time is needed. This should sit with real-time visibility so patients know where their referral stands rather than repeating calls and emails. Clinically trained staff should be able to triage, but there must be a guaranteed, transparent pathway for urgent cases that actually delivers timely appointments, rather than bouncing people from pillar to post.

Second, invest in care navigation and joined-up pathways. For patients with complex needs—older people, those with chronic conditions, or people juggling multiple services—a care navigator could coordinate appointments, prescriptions, and community supports. A practical idea is a patient-held ‘care passport’ (with consent) that travels with you across services, so every clinician sees your medications, allergies, and crisis plan without re-entering forms. This would cut duplication and reduce the risk of conflicting advice or missed follow-ups. It would also help a lot with carers who often feel they’re the ones chasing everyone.

Third, close gaps for deprived, ethnic minority, migrant and marginalised groups. We need more interpreters and multilingual information, and staff who understand different cultural expectations around care and mental health. Outreach in communities—through local libraries, community centres, faith groups and schools—can raise awareness of what’s available and how to access it. Practical steps include multilingual booking lines, easy-to-read appointment reminders, and targeted contact in areas with lower access. The goal is not to lower standards but to make the system feel trustworthy and reachable for everyone, especially where language and distrust of services can get in the way.

Fourth, expand community mental health teams and early intervention, with strong crisis response and accessible talking therapies. Mental health must have parity with physical health in terms of speed and quality of care. Expanding teams in the community—so people can be seen locally rather than traveling long distances or facing long waits—would help, as would urgent crisis support that can respond within hours rather than days. Quick access to talking therapies, including CBT or other evidence-based options, should be available soon after a referral. I’ve seen how a timely community mental health response can keep a family out of crisis and out of hospital, but it’s still inconsistent region to region.

Finally, these changes must be funded and designed with safeguards. We need more GPs and practice nurses, longer appointment times for complex cases, and flexible options (in-person and telehealth) so people who work shifts or who have caring responsibilities aren’t excluded. Any digital system must protect privacy and be inclusive of those less comfortable with technology—phone lines and face-to-face options must remain robust. Pilots should be evaluated for equity: do they actually reduce wait times for the most deprived areas? Do interpreters arrive in time for urgent cases?

If implemented with stable funding, strong governance, and genuine involvement from local communities, these changes could reduce waits, simplify patient flow, and bring mental and physical health care closer together in Scotland. My experience suggests that when triage is sensible, navigation clearer, and outreach targeted, people feel respected and are more likely to seek help early—which in turn reduces downstream pressure on the system.

Yes, I strongly support measures to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services. In our area waits for routine GP appointments can be lengthy, and when my neighbour needed a mental health check, the slot was often a month away. Expanding GP, nurse and therapist capacity by recruiting more staff, extending session lengths where appropriate and smarter scheduling would make a real difference. I welcome the growth of community mental health teams, with stronger early intervention, crisis response and talking therapies, so people get help before problems escalate and to bring parity with physical health services. For me, timely access to talking therapies has helped when available promptly, but delays are common. Expanding online booking and e-consultations is helpful, yet we must keep non-digital options for older or less tech‑savvy patients: telephone triage, paper forms, and in‑person clinics in local community venues, with home visits where appropriate. The mix of more slots, integrated teams and flexible access channels would reduce waits, help people stay independent and lessen unnecessary hospital visits.

Access to timely GP, community health and mental health care in our rural area remains hampered by transport, parking and premises deficits. The distance to the main surgery, infrequent bus services and crowded car parks mean people skip appointments or arrive late. My mother-in-law recently missed a follow-up because there was no suitable parking. To fix this, I support deploying mobile clinics that visit villages on a predictable schedule with a GP, nurse and pharmacist on board to handle routine reviews and triage mental health concerns. Outreach teams could perform home visits or run drop-in clinics in village halls, especially for those with limited mobility. Telehealth hubs in local libraries or community centres would enable quick video or phone consultations when a trip to town isn’t feasible. We also need incentives for clinicians to work in rural posts—longer contracts, housing assistance and dedicated capital funding to upgrade premises—so services can be reliable and consistent. In my experience a mental health video consult was much easier than navigating a town centre; expanding such options would materially improve timeliness for many neighbours.

Access to GP, community health and mental health services would improve most if we strengthened continuity of care and allowed longer appointment times for those with complex, chronic or vulnerable needs. In my area, a neighbour with diabetes, COPD and limited mobility has waited weeks to see the same clinician, and such delays can worsen conditions and spark unnecessary trips to urgent care. When the same GP follows a patient, they can adjust medications, review care plans and spot social needs early, reducing avoidable visits to hospital or the out-of-hours service. Longer appointment slots would let clinicians address multiple issues in one sitting and prevent the cycle of repeat check-ins just to reset a plan. 

I would also back a named-GP approach supported by a robust care-coordination team—practice nurses, therapists and mental health workers who know the patient, with shared notes to avoid fragmentation. For mental health and community care, closer integration with local teams and appropriate home visits would help frail or isolated patients; telehealth is useful but must not replace personal contact. In short, protect continuity, invest in longer slots, and build integrated teams so patients aren’t shuffled from pillar to post.

Access to GP, community health and mental health services should be timely, especially for frail, long-term conditions. In our area, waiting times for GP appointments can stretch to a week or more; elderly patients struggle with transport and parking, and many premises are not fully accessible. I welcome moves to recruit and retain staff: targeted recruitment, expanding international GP recruitment with settlement support, better pay, flexible working patterns, and wellbeing resources. These measures are essential to stabilise staffing; without a reliable workforce, proposed telehealth or mobile clinics won’t reach those most in need.

Additionally, addressing distance and access deficits is vital. Mobile clinics visiting villages, outreach workers, and telehealth hubs in community venues could reduce unnecessary travel for routine checks and mental-health follow-ups. In rural and mobility-limited areas, incentives to practice and to keep longer appointment times for complex cases would improve outcomes and reduce repeat visits.

Continuity matters: longer, consistent appointments for chronic patients, with a named clinician or care team, would prevent deterioration and hospital visits. Investments to improve premises and parking, plus accessible transport links, are no longer optional.

Overall, a coordinated package combining workforce, flexible delivery, and patient-centred continuity would deliver timely care and better outcomes.

Agree. Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services in Wales would be greatly improved by growing and stabilising the workforce and by protecting continuity of care for those with complex needs. This means a real push on recruitment and retention, including international hires, better pay, and flexible working with strong wellbeing support.

- Targeted recruitment and international hiring: expand training places, fast‑track overseas clinicians, and offer incentives to work in rural or underserved areas. In my area, gaps often appear when locums rotate; a steady, local team would mean fewer delays for appointments.
- Pay and incentives: higher salaries, student loan relief, relocation/housing support for posts in harder‑to-staff locations.
- Flexible working and wellbeing: more flexible hours, sustainable rotas, protected admin/triage time, and accessible staff wellbeing services so teams aren’t burnout and can stay in place.
- Continuity of care and appointment length: longer slots for complex, chronic or vulnerable patients (ideally 15–20 minutes), and efforts to see the same clinician when possible to improve outcomes and reduce repeat visits.
- Additional: better digital triage and online booking, plus stronger integration with community teams and mental health services to speed up referrals and follow‑ups.

These changes would help me and others get seen sooner and feel confident in ongoing support.

Our organisation works with people across Scotland who rely on timely GP, community health and mental health services. From what we’re hearing on the ground, the changes most likely to improve access in the long term depend on growing the workforce in a sustainable, well-supported way. That said, we are sceptical that simply increasing training places or expanding CPD, return‑to‑practice supports and apprenticeships will deliver meaningful relief to patients quickly unless paired with substantial reform to funding, working conditions and service design.

First, the core problem is chronic workforce shortages and retention, not a lack of training opportunities alone. Training pipelines take years to bear fruit, particularly in rural and remote parts of Scotland where vacancies sit unfilled for longer and the demand for urgent GP and mental health support remains high. We need a credible, adequately funded multi‑year plan that links medical schools, GP specialty training, nursing places and allied health professional routes with real, local job opportunities and clear progression paths. Without that, increases in training capacity will not translate into more timely access for people locally.

Second, return‑to‑practice schemes are essential, but they must be properly supported. People hesitate to re‑enter practice if supervision is thin, if revalidation feels punitive, or if their previous, valuable clinical skills cannot be refreshed quickly. We would like to see funded, flexible return‑to‑practice pathways that include mentoring, protected time, and a staged load so clinicians can re‑establish confidence while delivering care. In our area, a number of qualified professionals have held back from returning because the practical barriers – time away from family, travel costs, and insufficient supervision – are too high. That must change.

Third, apprenticeships and CPD should help build career ladders rather than serve as transient fixes. There is real potential in expanding nursing associate routes, mental health support worker apprenticeships and new roles within primary care teams. However, these must offer genuine progression to degree-level qualifications and sustainable pay, so people are not leaving once they hit the first rung. We also need to ensure apprenticeships are accessible to people in all parts of Scotland, including rural communities, with regional training hubs and funded travel supports where necessary.

Fourth, the design of care itself must evolve. Timely access is not just about more clinicians; it’s about how care is delivered. Multidisciplinary, team‑based primary care hubs that include GPs, practice nurses, pharmacists, mental health professionals, physiotherapists and social care staff, with shared digital records and clear triage pathways, can frequently resolve issues without a long wait for a GP appointment. This requires investment in integrated care models, extended hours where feasible, and better use of telemedicine and remote monitoring to manage routine problems and free up clinicians for the most complex cases.

Concrete steps we would want to see include:
- A credible, ring-fenced, multi‑year plan for increasing GP and nursing training places in Scotland, with clear targets, regional distribution and links to rural deployment incentives.
- Expanded and funded return‑to‑practice routes with protected time, mentorship, and streamlined revalidation processes; incentives to attract people back from retirement or different sectors.
- Broadening and funding apprenticeships in primary care and mental health, ensuring real career progression, integrated with degree programs and sufficient clinical supervision.
- Protected time and high‑quality CPD that is tightly aligned with service needs, not generic modules; embedding CPD within work hours and ensuring practical skills reflect current practice and digital tools.
- Immediate improvements to care pathways: more same‑day triage slots, enhanced digital triage and scheduling, and the creation of local, multidisciplinary hubs that can manage a larger share of low‑to‑moderate‑need cases without long waits for a GP.
- Targeted measures for rural and island communities, including selective recruitment, regional training placements, and enhanced remote or outreach services to prevent geographic inequities in access.

We recognise that many people in Scotland experience delays now, and any long‑term workforce strategy must come with near‑term measures to stabilise access. However, the real, durable improvement will come from a comprehensive approach to grow the workforce in a way that is sustainable, well supported and locally responsive. Without that, patients will continue to face unnecessary waiting times, and staff will confront burnout rather than a healthy, resilient system.

In summary, our stance is that boosting training places, return‑to‑practice pathways, apprenticeships and CPD is essential but only if tied to robust funding, meaningful career progression, and a redesigned service model that makes best use of a multidisciplinary, digitally enabled primary care system. If the government can commit to that long‑term framework, we would be more optimistic about the prospects for timely access across GP, community health and mental health services across Scotland.

it's outrageous that agree. Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services in rural and mobility‑limited areas will only improve if transport, parking and premises deficits are addressed alongside smarter service delivery. My organisation has observed patients missing urgent GP check‑ins because the last bus home is early or parking is full when clinics run late.

I would prioritise: mobile clinics delivering GP, district nursing and counselling in villages on a predictable rota; outreach teams who call high‑risk patients ahead of time; and telehealth hubs set up in libraries or community centres with private booths and staff to help bookings and tech.

Incentives for practices to offer local access: better funding for rural patients, grants to share premises or co‑locate services, and support for longer appointment blocks in community venues to reduce travel.

Premises and transport: ensure accessible parking near venues, clear signage, safe drop‑off points and coordination with local transport with timetables aligned to clinic hours. Use flexible, temporary spaces in schools, halls or GP trailers during peaks.

These changes, backed by reliable funding, would cut delays and keep people – especially those with mental health concerns – connected to timely care. We have seen improvements when mobile and telehealth options are funded consistently rather than as pilots!

Access to GP, community health and mental health services remains patchy in my area. I would welcome investment in co‑located community hubs that bring primary care, district nursing, mental health teams, social care and VCSE partners under one roof. In practice, that could cut duplication, speed triage and improve holistic care, provided it is funded for sustainable staffing, clear governance and kept close to patients' needs rather than as a centralised rebuild that may disrupt existing relationships. A risk is that hubs could become uneven if some areas struggle to recruit staff or tie up with adult social care quickly; we would need local buy‑in and flexible models that preserve choice and continuity with familiar clinicians.

On transport and premises deficits: where people cannot easily reach appointments, mobile clinics visiting village halls and GP practice car parks, outreach workers, and telehealth hubs in libraries or community centres could help. In our village, a monthly mobile clinic made a real difference for older residents who can't travel, and telehealth has helped with follow‑ups for mental health support, though not everyone can use video due to digital exclusion; therefore, we need both phone triage and in-person slots. Incentives to run services in rural or mobility‑limited areas – funding for travel time, staff rotations, and shared premises – would also help. Finally, any expansion should be evaluated for impact on waiting times, patient satisfaction, and equity between towns.

From my experience in England, timely access to GP and mental health services needs two things: continuity of care for complex cases, and a smarter use of the broader health team for routine issues. Extending appointment times for those with chronic or vulnerable conditions would improve outcomes and reduce repeat visits. For example, my parent with diabetes and arthritis would benefit from a 25- or 30-minute slot with a named clinician and an updated care plan, rather than several short appointments that miss the bigger picture.

I also welcome expanding multidisciplinary teams—pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates—to handle routine concerns and triage, freeing GPs to focus on complex care. In local pilots, a physiotherapist and a pharmacist supporting primary care cut unnecessary GP contacts and speed up help, but only if communication and shared records are strong.

On mental health, faster access through a coordinated team and clear referral routes matters. The risk is fragmentation if teams aren’t integrated or funded properly. My view is conditional: I support these changes where funding, IT, and governance ensure teams work as one system rather than competing priorities.

Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services is crucial for families like mine. I strongly support measures to sustainably grow the workforce and make services more accessible. Increasing training places, return‑to‑practice schemes, apprenticeships and continuous professional development will help address shortages in the long term and reduce pressure on current staff. For example, funded return‑to‑practice programmes for former GPs and nurses would quickly bring skilled clinicians back into front‑line care, while expanding nursing and psychology/therapy training slots would boost capacity over the next few years. 

I also welcome targeted resources to close gaps for deprived and ethnic minority communities. Providing interpreters, culturally competent staff and outreach in local communities would help people know where to get care and feel understood when they ask for help. 

Finally, expanding appointment slots and session capacity by hiring more clinicians, extending hours and improving scheduling systems would cut waits. In my area, even a same‑day slot or a longer early‑evening appointment would make a real difference for working families and those with limited daytime options.

Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services is a real concern in our area. Expanding multidisciplinary teams could genuinely free GPs to focus on complex cases, while routine problems are managed by professionals like pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates in local hubs. For example, a physio-led triage for persistent back pain, a pharmacist doing medication reviews after a minor infection, or a paramedic-led home visit for a simple assessment could shorten waits and reduce unnecessary GP appointments. In practice, where this has been piloted, wait times for routine issues shortened and patients reported clearer, quicker pathways. 

That said, it only works with robust governance: clear scopes of practice, shared digital records, and explicit accountability so patient safety isn’t compromised. Without strong coordination, we risk fragmented care and missed warning signs.

On NHS111, clinical triage, booking systems and care navigation, I’d welcome improvements that prioritise urgent cases and cut duplication. My experience is variable: some NHS111 encounters fast-tracked urgent needs, others sent me along longer routes for non-urgent issues. A streamlined digital system showing real-time availability, plus care navigators who can steer people to the right service, would help mental health and urgent care alike. Any changes must ensure equity across urban and rural areas and protect continuity where people value it most.

Like many of my fellow pensioners, I have experienced delays in getting GP appointments and in accessing community and mental health support in my town. I welcome proposals to grow the workforce long term by increasing training places, return-to-practice support, apprenticeships and CPD. In practice, more medical school places and expanded GP training would steadily replenish the clinicians we rely on, rather than scrambling for locums. Return-to-practice schemes for nurses and allied health professionals who paused work would help them rejoin safely, bringing valuable experience back into the patient journey. Apprenticeships for healthcare assistants and nurse associates offer a clear route into frontline roles, enabling quicker local cover and smoother triage. Sustained CPD funding ensures staff keep up with chronic disease management, mental health guidelines and new digital tools, so they can see patients earlier rather than firefighting late referrals.

For my area, a regional training hub and funded mentorship would reduce delays and improve continuity of care. Please back long-term investment in training and workforce planning; it will pay off in fewer urgent calls and better well-being for us all.

From our organisation representing community groups across England, we strongly support changes to NHS111, clinical triage, and booking systems to prioritise urgent cases and streamline patient flow. Too many people experience delays reaching a GP appointment or mental health support, and information is duplicated between NHS111, reception staff and out-of-hours services. A consistent, clinically guided triage system with clear escalation pathways would direct patients to the right service first time, reducing unnecessary A&E visits and saving time for patients and clinicians.

Key changes we would welcome: expanding NHS111 to provide reliable, evidence-based triage with fast paths to urgent GP, mental health or community-based care; modernising online booking so same-day slots are visible and reservable; and employing care navigators who can review a patient’s history and coordinate care across GP, pharmacy, mental health teams and social care. In practice, this would cut duplication of calls and repeated symptom explanations, helping an older resident with a new health concern get timely access to the appropriate clinician rather than waiting days.

Together, these steps would improve timely access while easing pressure on frontline staff.

I believe timely access to GP, community health and mental health services is a priority, especially for people with mobility issues or who rely on public transport. In my area, buses run infrequently and parking at the main clinic is limited, so people miss appointments or have to travel long distances. Changes like mobile clinics visiting villages on a rotating schedule would remove a lot of friction. A GP van could offer daytime and early evening slots at local community halls, closer to people’s homes. Outreach workers could identify those with chronic conditions and help organise follow-ups in person or through home visits when needed.

I’d also support telehealth hubs in libraries or community centres, with quiet private rooms and staff to help people use the tech. That would make it easier for students and working people to access urgent mental health triage quickly without long waits, while still offering in-person options when needed. And practical incentives to recruit and retain GPs, nurses and mental health staff in rural areas—like financial rewards, additional training opportunities and funded transport subsidies for patients—would make services more stable.

From my own experience, urgent care would have saved hours of travel and stress if a mobile clinic had been available. A mix of on-site mobile presence, user-friendly telehealth and sensible incentives would make timely, local care a real possibility for everyone.

Agree. In my area I see GP and mental health delays that disproportionately affect deprived and ethnic minority communities, often because language, trust and navigation are barriers. The changes that would help most are:

- Targeted resources: fund community health workers from local communities, provide guaranteed interpreters across GP, hospital and mental health services, and ensure ongoing cultural competence training for all front-line staff.

- Outreach and navigation: multilingual information about access pathways, simpler booking systems with bilingual staff, and outreach sessions in community hubs (libraries, places of worship) to explain how to get timely appointments.

- Access design: extended hours, same-day triage, flexible modalities (phone, video) with language support, and walk-in slots where appropriate.

- Integrated mental health pathways: colocated mental health teams in primary care, fast-track referrals, and dedicated support lines with interpreter options.

- Accountability: track access by language, ethnicity and deprivation, publish quarterly progress, and adjust funding where gaps persist.

From a neighbour’s experience, a local community worker helped them register and secure a GP slot within two days; similar outreach in mental health would prevent delays and reduce crisis care.

Strengthen NHS111 and clinical triage, improve booking and care navigation to prioritise urgent cases and cut duplication, while safeguarding continuity of care and longer slots for complex patients; invest in co-located hubs uniting primary, community and mental health with social care.

I live in Wales and I welcome proposals to improve timel access to GP, community health and mental health services. Expanding multidisciplinar teams makes sense. A clearer path—triage to the right professional, better online booking, and a practice care navigator guiding us to the right appointment—would save time and ease pressure on everyone. These changes would help me stay independent and safer in my own home.

Prioritise urgent cases via better NHS111 triage and simpler booking, with improved care navigation to cut duplication. At the same time, address staffing by targeted recruitment, flexible hours and wellbeing support to recruit and retain GPs, community health teams and mental health staff.

absolutely from my perspective as a pensioner in England, the most important change to improve timely access is to protect continuity of care and to lengthen appointment times for those with complex, chronic conditions. When I needed ongoing support for a long-standing heart issue, a 10-minute slot was never enough; longer consultations reduce the need for repeat visits and help clinicians spot problems early. I’d support a policy that guarantees longer appointments for vulnerable patients and ensures consistent care across teams. Finally, targeted resources are essential: interpreters, culturally competent staff and outreach to deprived and ethnic minority communities. Translated information, community health champions, and extended hours in local hubs would reduce gaps and improve uptake and outcomes!

To improve timely access, the most impactful changes would be to expand appointment capacity across GP, nurse and therapist services by hiring more clinicians and expanding session lengths, plus smarter scheduling. In my area, I’ve experienced GP delays when trying to book same-week slots; if practices could guarantee same-day triage and offer a mix of in-person and video slots, that would cut waits. Hiring additional GPs and nurse prescribers, with extended hours to evenings and Saturdays, would help working families. For mental health, increasing the number of talking therapies and reducing waiting lists by employing more CBT therapists and counsellors, plus offering group sessions for common concerns, would be transformative. On community health, we need more district nursing and rehab slots, especially post-hospital discharge, with predictable follow-ups through a digital scheduling system and proactive reminders. In practice, a model where practices pool locum support, implement protected appointment slots for vulnerable patients, and run 1-day-a-week urgent care clinics would reduce bottlenecks. I’ve seen how even small increases in slots dramatically cut wait times and improve wellbeing.

Living in England and trying to use GP, community health and mental health services, I’ve seen how waits drain time and frustration from both patients and staff. The single most impactful change would be to increase appointment slots and overall session capacity across primary care, community services and talking therapies. This isn’t just about more hours on the clock, but about hiring the right people, expanding how long certain sessions run, and building smarter ways to schedule care so people aren’t left waiting for days or weeks for something that should be routine.

What I’d like to see put into place
- Hire and retain more frontline clinicians and support staff
  - Recruit more GPs, nurse practitioners, physiotherapists and therapists, with a clear roadmap and competitive retention packages to stop churn. A funded plan to reduce reliance on locums would stabilise access and improve continuity of care.
  - Build multidisciplinary teams in which nurses, pharmacists and therapists share responsibility for follow-ups and routine checks. This would free GPs to see patients with more complex needs while still giving timely attention to others.
- Expand sessions and adjust delivery models
  - Increase the number of appointment slots each practice can offer, including longer blocks for chronic disease management and mental health intake. For example, where a 10–15 minute slot used to suffice for simple concerns, many patients with multiple conditions would benefit from 20–30 minute appointments.
  - Create more extended, local community clinics for physio, district nursing and mental health support, ideally in easily reachable hubs. Weekend or evening slots would help working people who struggle to attend during the day.
  - Invest in scalable therapy capacity: more slots for talking therapies, group sessions where appropriate, and stepped-care approaches so people move quickly to the level of care they need without long waiting lists.
- Optimise scheduling to match demand
  - Implement stronger triage at the front door (phone or online) to direct people to the right professional and to urgent slots when needed. This would ensure someone isn’t stuck waiting in a general queue when their issue would be better addressed by a nurse, a pharmacist-led clinic, or a mental health worker.
  - Reserve predictable same-day or next-day slots for urgent concerns and create clear pathways so people know when a slot will become available. Use data to forecast demand by time of day, day of week and by community needs, then align staffing and room capacity accordingly.
  - Improve digital booking while protecting those without online access: a straightforward online system with SMS reminders, while keeping a non-digital option for people who rely on phone access or who need interpreter support.
- Ensure space and support keep up with staffing
  - Increased staffing must come with better space planning: more consultation rooms, efficient use of clinics, and mobile units if needed in rural areas. Without space, even more staff won’t translate into real-world access.
- Keep equity and patient safety at the centre
  - Ensure digital access doesn’t widen gaps for older people or those with limited internet. Maintain walk-in access or assisted bookings for those who need it.
  - Monitor wait times publicly and hold practices to targets, with support and intervention where patient outcomes are affected by delays.
