It also depends on transport, childcare, and how easy it is to navigate booking systems. For instance, when I tried to book a GP appointment last month, the earliest in-person slot was two weeks away; online booking sometimes showed shorter waits, but you still need a slot that fits work and school pick-ups. In mental health, referral delays can stretch to weeks before any face-to-face contact, and after-hours support is patchy. That said, I can see why some would argue for more extended hours or more same-day triage. The risk is burning out staff if we push too hard without solving underlying recruitment and retention. A balanced path might include: improved local hubs with flexible access (evenings and weekends) linked to robust telehealth; better transport and childcare support near clinics; clearer wait-time information; and sustained investment to grow the workforce rather than quick, isolated fixes. I’m unsure which combination would work best here without a detailed local plan. Some of these considerations, like how schools and employers support time off for medical appointments, matter almost as much as the clinical changes.

Yes, I strongly support changes to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services. In my area, evenings and weekend clinics would make a big difference for people who work or care for others, and I think guaranteeing same-day urgent slots would prevent deterioration while waiting. For example, when my neighbour had a sudden respiratory flare-up last winter, the daytime surgery was booked for two weeks ahead; if there had been evening slots, they might not have needed to go to urgent care. For mental health and non-emergency needs, flexible access matters.

Transport and parking are constant hurdles, especially in rural or suburban areas. Mobile clinics delivering GP checks, vaccinations and blood tests to village halls or community centres on Saturday mornings would cut travel. Outreach nurses and telehealth hubs in libraries or council buildings would help mobility-limited residents stay connected. Incentives to practices—funding for extended hours, improved premises, and better appointment triage—would reinforce these gains. Overall, these changes would deliver timely care and reduce stress.

We fully support targeted changes to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services in our area. People deserve quick, clear routes to care, and the system should prevent duplication and patient confusion. Doing so will reduce pressure on urgent services and help people stay well at home where possible.

NHS111, clinical triage, booking systems and care navigation
- Strengthen NHS111 with robust clinical triage that reliably directs people to the right service first time. A clear, ethically sound triage path should prioritise urgent cases while still routing non-urgent needs efficiently to the appropriate care channel. Integrating triage decisions with real-time GP and community-slot availability would reduce unnecessary contact and repeated explanations of symptoms.
- Move toward a single, interoperable view of a patient’s needs so care navigators can guide people through the system without requiring repeated hand-offs. For example, someone presenting with chest discomfort should be fast-tracked into an urgent assessment rather than being bounced between call handlers.
- Simplify booking flows so outcomes of triage can directly reserve an appropriate slot (same-day GP or nurse appointment, urgent care slot, or specific mental health support) with clear expectations and follow-up steps. Real-time reminders and self-service updates would further reduce the need for multiple calls or visits.
- In practice, local feedback shows that people often have to repeat information to different operators and wait longer than necessary to secure appropriate appointments. A streamlined, digitally linked NHS111–booking system would cut duplication, speed access, and improve patient confidence in the pathway to care.

Co-located community hubs with integrated services
- Invest in hubs that bring together primary care, community health, mental health services, social care and VCSE partners in one place (physically or as a tightly integrated network). The aim is to offer a seamless local care journey, with a shared care plan and common referral pathways. Such hubs would make it easier for residents to access multiple services in one visit, reducing travel, missed appointments and fragmented care.
- Local pilots have shown how co-location can shorten referral times and improve patient experience, by allowing rapid access to physiotherapy, counselling, district nursing and social support in a single setting. We advocate expanding these models, with flexible hours to reach people who work, have mobility challenges, or live in rural parts of the area. VCSE partners are essential for addressing social determinants of health and for delivering timely preventive support alongside clinical care.
- Key features should include alimented digital records, standardised referral criteria, and care coordinators who can navigate patients through the hub and ensure timely follow-up. This approach helps especially older residents who often juggle multiple needs and may otherwise fall through gaps between services.

Increased appointment capacity and smarter scheduling
- Increase the number of GP, nurse and therapist slots by recruiting additional clinicians and expanding session capacity. We should also extend hours (evenings, weekends) and implement extended clinics where demand justifies it. Flexible scheduling, paired with efficient rostering and workload management, will help reduce wait times for routine and urgent appointments alike.
- Expand session formats, including group therapy or education sessions for common conditions, to improve throughput while maintaining quality of care. Telehealth where appropriate can also widen access without compromising the patient experience.
- In our experience, waiting times in some practices remain a barrier to timely care. A targeted recruitment drive for GPs, practice nurses and allied health professionals, coupled with smarter scheduling and workload-sharing across networks, can stabilise capacity across peak periods and lessen avoidable delays.

Overall, these measures would create a clearer, faster and more person-centred pathway to care. By improving triage accuracy, building integrated hubs and expanding capacity, we can deliver timelier support for urgent needs and ongoing conditions, reduce unnecessary journeys, and support people to stay healthier in their communities.

As an organisation representing older residents in England, we welcome proposals to create co-located community hubs that bring together GP, district nursing, mental health teams, social care and VCSE partners. In our area, a pilot hub with a shared workspace and integrated care plan has reduced duplicate referrals and cut the time to arrange social support for a frail neighbour’s husband, but it needs reliable IT sharing and protected funding. Expanding multidisciplinary teams is essential: a pharmacist or physiotherapist in a practice can triage minor musculoskeletal issues and medications, freeing GPs to focus on complex cases. Paramedics and physician associates can carry out home visits for routine follow-ups, preventing emergency attendances. However, these roles require clear scopes of practice, robust supervision, and training to avoid fragmentation. We also strongly support protecting continuity of care and longer appointment times for patients with chronic or vulnerable conditions; this reduces repeat visits and improves outcomes, yet it needs sustainable funding and time-slot allocation. In short, local co-location plus diverse teams, backed by trusted data sharing and consistent funding, could significantly improve timely access.

Agree. To improve timely access, resources should be targeted to the groups most affected—deprived communities, ethnic minorities and migrants—by ensuring interpreters, culturally competent staff and active outreach are standard across GP, community health and mental health services. In my arra, language barrirrs have slowe care, especially for newcomers and low‑income residents. A local practice now offers on‑site interpreters and a bilingual receptionist, plus one evening clinic, which has cut late cancellations and helped people book promptly. But this needss to be rolled out more broadly. I’d like to see several changes funded consistently: dedicated interpreter hours across all sites; hiring and retaining staff with cultural competence; mandatory training on inclusive, stigma‑free care; and proactive outreach through community groups, colleges and faith networks to explain how to access services, what help is available, and how to book. Also important: more access points—mobil GP clinics on housing estates, extended hours, same‑day urgent slots, and a multilingual online booking system. Mental health services should include therapies delivered in community venues and crisis lines in multiple languages. Clear information in several languages about navigating the systrm would help too. If these steps are put in place, timely access should improve for everyone, particularly those most marginalised, and trust in services will grow.

Access to GP, community health and mental health services in my rural area is hampered by patchy transport, limited parking at clinics, and buildings that feel hard to reach. In my village, the monthly mobile clinic has helped, but cancellations and timing still complicate visits for families with kids and shift workers. To improve timely access we should roll out mobile clinics that visit village halls, schools and care homes on a predictable schedule, with adequate parking and pre-bookable slots. Outreach teams could do home visits for the elderly, disabled and those with irregular work patterns.

Create telehealth hubs in existing community spaces—libraries, parish halls and leisure centres—staffed to help people sign in, book slots and use simple devices. These hubs could host same-day mental health triage and quick GP video appointments, reducing long journeys for families.

Offer incentives to rural clinicians: housing allowances, student loan relief, and protected admin time to reduce burnout. Invest in safe, accessible premises with clear transport links and sufficient parking; central funding for upgrades is essential. A simple online booking platform and occasional mobile phlebotomy clinics would keep care timely for those living far from the nearest practice.

Thank you for the chance to feed in on this. I strongly support the proposed changes to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services in our area. For families and workers trying to juggle responsibilities, delays turn small health concerns into bigger problems, so making access quicker and smoother is essential. 

First, expanding the workforce in a sustainable way is crucial. Increasing training places for GPs and nurses, boosting return-to-practice support, expanding apprenticeships and investing in CPD will help us build a steady, skilled workforce for the long term. In our area, GP appointment slots are already tight and waiting times have grown, especially for same-day or early-evening access. By growing the pipeline—more GP trainees, more nurse practitioners, and more therapists—we can reduce those waits across primary and community care. Support for clinicians returning after a career break or caring responsibilities, plus clear pathways for ongoing professional development, will help retain staff and keep services available where people live and work.

Second, I’d like to see targeted resources for those who face the greatest barriers. Interpreters and multilingual staff must be available where needed, and information about services should be translated into common community languages with plain-English options as well. Culturally competent staff who understand different backgrounds can make care feel safer and more accessible, which is especially important for deprived, ethnic minority, migrant and marginalised groups. Practical outreach—working with local schools, faith groups, community organisations and housing associations—helps people know what’s available and how to access it without fear of discrimination or confusion. In practice, this could mean multilingual outreach workers visiting communities, clearer appointment reminders in different languages, and cancelled-appointment data reviewed with a view to reducing language-related no-shows.

Third, co-locating services into community hubs could transform how local care is delivered. A hub that brings together primary care, community health, mental health services, social care and VCSE partners (voluntary, community and social enterprise) creates a single front door for people and a unified care plan. This reduces the need for multiple visits to different sites, speeds up referrals, and enables quicker, more holistic support. In our area, people often have to navigate several organisations to get what they need—physically travelling between sites, waiting, repeating information, and not always getting a coordinated plan. A co-located hub would mean a patient can see a GP, start assessment for mental health services, and receive social support or housing advice in one place, with a named care coordinator to track progress.

Practically, this could be supported by 1) dedicated funding to establish and run local hubs, with shared IT and data systems so records follow the patient safely across teams; 2) extended hours—including evenings and some weekends—so people who work can access care without taking time off; 3) streamlined triage so those with urgent needs are seen the same day while those with less urgent issues are scheduled in a timely way; 4) integration with social care and VCSE partners to address wider determinants of health—housing, benefits, transport, social isolation—at the point of care.

Overall, these changes are interconnected: more training and return-to-practice support will grow capacity; targeted, culturally competent outreach ensures people aren’t excluded; and co-located hubs will knit everything together into a seamless local system. With stable funding and local leadership to implement them, we can achieve timely access that reflects the needs of our diverse community and reduces avoidable health crises. I’m confident these steps would deliver better health outcomes and a fairer, more accessible service for everyone in our area.

Living in England, I support expanding online booking, e-consultations and remote care, as they can speed up access while keeping care convenient. I recently booked a same-day GP chat via the online portal, which avoided a long phone queue and gave me a clear plan quickly. For ongoing mental health support, brief video check-ins have helped manage symptoms while I waited for in-person slots, and I’d welcome more of this option. 

That said, we must avoid leaving anyone behind. Non-digital options are essential: robust phone access, in-person appointments, and local hubs where staff can help people book and navigate the system. 

To improve timeliness and reduce duplication, NHS111 and clinical triage should prioritise urgent cases and guide patients to the right service first time. A single care-navigation touchpoint that can book GP, nurse, or mental health slots and share notes would simplify patient flow. Real-time slot availability and clearer triage criteria would cut delays and wasted trips. All changes should come with adequate support and training to protect and assist older or digitally-anxious patients while maintaining high standards of safety.

From our organisation’s perspective serving communities across rural England, timely access to GP, community health and mental health services remains hampered by transport gaps, scarce parking and cramped premises. For mobility‑limited residents, a 60‑minute round trip to a GP that isn’t near a bus route is common, and parking costs deter attendance. We need pragmatic fixes beyond bigger buildings.

Concrete steps:
- deploy mobile clinics and outreach teams that visit villages on regular cycles, with simple online booking and protected appointment slots for urgent concerns.
- extend telehealth hubs in libraries or community centres, including same‑day video slots for triage and follow‑ups.
- incentivise primary and mental health staff to work in rural/marginalised areas through conditional bursaries, rota relief and flexible hours.
- invest in co‑located community hubs that bring together GP, district nursing, psychology, social care and VCSE partners, so referrals are seamless and there’s a single point of contact.
- prioritise interpreters, multilingual staff and targeted outreach for deprived ethnic minority, migrant and marginalised groups, with culturally competent training and partnerships with faith groups and community organisations.

We should pilot these with robust evaluation and patient involvement. However, any plan must be funded, co‑produced with local communities and monitored with accessible metrics to avoid repeating past gaps.

Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services in my area feels uneven, with real gains possible but also practical pitfalls that need careful design. I think changes could work, but they must be built around people who are not always easy to reach or willing to press for help. 

Expanding community mental health teams and improving early intervention and crisis response would likely reduce waits and help mental health parity with physical health. In my experience, when someone can access a community mental health nurse or worker quickly, they stay out of crisis and get better outcomes sooner. Universities and student services could benefit from more staffed, integrated teams that can respond within days rather than weeks, offering talking therapies such as CBT or ACT earlier and with clearer referral routes. This would also help people who fall through the cracks after a GP visit but before therapy starts. I would welcome a model where primary care teams work hand in hand with mental health specialists, with shared care plans and rapid access slots for urgent needs. 

However, I am concerned about NHS111 and the clinical triage and booking systems. There have been times when NHS111 has led to a detour, sending someone to a service that was not the most appropriate, or not available when a crisis loomed. A more reliable, clinically led triage with clear escalation criteria for urgent mental health issues would reduce delays and duplication. Reducing repeated information requests and ensuring seamless handoffs between NHS111, GP practices and urgent care would help people get the right help on the first call. 

On digital access, I see real benefits from online booking, e-consultations and remote care for routine issues and follow ups. They can save time and make it easier to manage appointments around lectures or work. But there is a real risk that online systems exclude those without good broadband or smartphones, or those who are not confident with digital tools, including some older students or people in more deprived areas. In my city, there are blocks with poor mobile signal and data limits, which makes online booking and video consults frustrating or impossible. Any plan to expand digital access must go hand in hand with non-digital options: a reliable telephone line, walk-in slots, in-clinic booking support, and dedicated staff like care navigators who can guide people through the system, explain options in plain language, and help book urgent care when needed. 

Practical steps I would like to see include: funded expansion of community mental health teams with clear targets for response times; same-day or next-day GP and mental health triage slots for urgent cases; a merged digital and non-digital booking system with visible urgent pathways; care navigators or patient representatives within GP practices to help people understand options and coordinate across services; and a clear, publishable policy on parity between mental and physical health care with monitoring to prevent long wait times for mental health referrals. It would also help if crisis response could reach people quickly, for example within a few hours in urban areas, with options to connect with in-person or remote support as soon as a crisis is identified. 

Overall, I support a balanced approach that improves accessibility without leaving anyone behind through digital-only solutions. If implemented with strong equity checks, real staff capacity, and robust patient feedback loops, these changes could meaningfully shorten waits and make care feel more connected across GP, community and mental health services.

As an organisation supporting health services across England, we strongly agree that timely access to GP, community health and mental health services must be improved through a holistic workforce strategy. Central to this is targeted recruitment and international hiring, backed by clear registration pathways, visa support and welcome packages, plus incentives such as sign-on bonuses and relocation assistance, to attract practitioners to hard-to-fill areas. Flexible working is essential: offer part-time and job-share GP roles, more flexible rosters, remote triage, and late-evening or weekend clinics to spread demand and fit staff lives. Paired with this, pay improvements and transparent career progression will help retain staff long-term and reduce churn. Robust wellbeing support is non-negotiable—protected time, confidential coaching, burnout prevention and peer supervision so teams stay resilient.

In our network we’ve piloted overseas GP and nurse practitioner recruitment with streamlined induction and flexible rotas; early feedback shows expanded appointment slots and higher patient satisfaction. We also advocate sustained investment in community health teams and mental health services, including integrated digital triage, stronger linkages with social prescribing, and embedded IAPT/CAMHS capacity. With coordinated funding and simpler processes, these measures can deliver quicker, local access and better outcomes for patients.

Thank you for the opportunity to respond. From our perspective as an organisation representing people across England, the drive to expand online booking, e-consultations and remote care must not come at the expense of those who rely on non-digital routes. In many communities, especially where transport is poor, where people are older or less digitally confident, and where physical premises are already stretched, a digital-first approach risks widening health inequalities and delaying timely access rather than improving it.

Digital tools can be part of the solution, but only if there is a genuine, well-funded safety net of non-digital options. In practice, we see patients who cannot or will not use online systems for reasons of age, disability, language, data costs or lack of digital literacy. In our area, a sizeable proportion of residents struggle with online booking or teleconsultations: some lack devices, others have unreliable internet, and several have difficulty communicating without a clinician present. There have also been cases where important information is lost in translation or miscommunicated in a remote setting, leading to repeat calls or visits that clog the system rather than ease it. Therefore, any expansion of digital access must be accompanied by robust, easy-to-use non-digital routes – including telephone triage with clear pathways, walk-in slots for urgent concerns, and in-person visits where needed. A “true end-to-end” option that allows a patient to choose online, phone or in-person without being funnelled into a single channel would be the minimum requirement.

Continuity of care and adequate time for complex cases must be core to any reform. Shortening appointment times to push people through quicker will not improve outcomes for those with long-standing or multiple conditions. We routinely see patients with chronic illness and frailty who need longer appointments, careful review of medications, and a consistent clinician who knows their history. Our evidence to date suggests that when practices shorten first or follow-up appointments for complex patients, this leads to more repeated calls, more missed issues and ultimately higher use of urgent care or hospital services. What would help is longer initial assessments for high-need patients, a named or small team of clinicians for continuity, and protected clinic time for reviews and care planning. More effective management of chronic and mental health conditions should be about stable, ongoing relationships rather than rapid triage via digital channels.

Transport, parking and premises limitations are tangible barriers that reduce timely access, especially in rural and mobility-impaired communities. We know people who cannot reasonably travel to a clinic in a timely way, or who risk losing work and paying high travel costs for frequent visits. Practical responses that have shown promise include mobile outreach clinics visiting villages or community hubs, extended hours (including evenings and Saturdays) to accommodate working people, and co-located or linked services in familiar community venues such as libraries or community centres. Telehealth hubs hosted in local venues with staff support can also help those who lack private spaces at home or who need help with setup and privacy. Incentives for practices to run regular outreach sessions, paired with funding for mobile equipment and transport, would make a real difference. In one local area, a weekly nurse-led outreach clinic in a village hall cut the need for several long journeys and reduced non-attendance by offering convenient, familiar settings. We should scale such approaches where appropriate rather than relying solely on digital access.

In short, the most effective changes to improve timely access will be blended: expand digital access where appropriate, but preserve and fund strong non-digital routes; lengthen appointment times for complex and vulnerable patients and ensure continuity of care; and actively address transport and premises barriers with mobile clinics, outreach, telehealth hubs and incentivised outreach partnerships. Any national direction must come with adequate funding and a clear equality impact assessment to prevent the very groups we are meant to serve from being left behind. We want a system that offers choice, supports clinicians, and delivers timely, high-quality care for everyone who needs it.

Living in England, I see that timely access to GP, community health and mental health services can still be patchy in my area. I would welcome a broad package of changes that targets both short-term access and long-term resilience.

First, expand the workforce: increase training places for GPs, nurses and therapists, support return-to-practice for those who have paused, and widen apprenticeships and funded CPD. In my experience, a local practice could raise capacity if there were more graduate-entry programmes and ongoing training funded centrally.

Second, tackle transport, parking and premises deficits: use mobile clinics and outreach teams to reach rural and mobility-impaired residents; establish telehealth hubs in community venues; provide incentives to attract clinicians to underserved areas, such as travel allowances or housing support.

Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services is vital for someone like me who balances work and caring responsibilities, especially where language or culture can slow things down.
