Language, disability access and interpreters should be built in so no one is excluded.

A key caveat is funding and workforce planning. If more slots are created without a sustainable workforce and funding model, we risk burnout and erosion of care quality. Also, while digital solutions can help, we must avoid widening the gap for those who aren’t online or who struggle with technology.

Overall, I support the intent and think a multi-pronged approach—more staff, smarter scheduling, extended hours, better hubs, and stronger mental health integration—could make a real difference. The crucial thing is a credible implementation plan: clear timelines, local accountability, and safeguards to protect continuity of care and patient experience while we scale up.

it's outrageous that i live in England and, as someone in my early sixties, I rely on timely GP, community health and mental health services to manage my health and that of my family. I believe the changes proposed would make a real difference to everyday life and to how long people wait for essential care. In practice, the biggest gains come from expanding capacity and improving how we book and access services, while still keeping non-digital options for those who need them.

What would help most:

- Increase appointment slots and expand session capacity by hiring and extending services: GP, nurse and therapist slots need to grow to match demand. A practical step would be to fund more nurse-led clinics for chronic conditions, more mental health practitioners in or linked to primary care, and longer, more flexible GP slots for complex issues. In my local area, we’ve seen a few extra GP slots and a new nurse practitioner, which shortened some routine waits, but we still have a backlog for people with multi-factor illnesses or mental health concerns. Allocating more resources to cover peak times, and offering longer appointment times for new or complex cases, would reduce the risk of delayed treatment turning into bigger problems later.

- Optimised scheduling and front-end triage: A more efficient, data-driven scheduling approach can cut waiting times dramatically. This could include same-day triage to identify urgent needs, smarter allocation of slots based on typical case length, and better reminders to reduce no-shows. In addition, clinics could run structured same-day “urgent care” blocks and evening sessions a couple of days a week so people who work or have carer responsibilities can access help without taking a whole day off.

- Expand online booking, e-consults and remote care, with non-digital support: Online booking and video or phone consultations are a real help for people with mobility constraints, childcare responsibilities, or limited time. For many routine enquiries, a brief e-consult followed by a short follow-up can be enough and avoids long phone queues. I’ve seen a neighbour use an online appointment for a mental health check and secure a timely referral; it cut out days of trying to reach someone by phone. It’s essential, however, to keep non-digital routes—such as telephone bookings and in-person visits—so those without internet access or who are not comfortable with digital tools aren’t left behind. Practices could offer help desks, hardship-friendly tutorials, or staff-assisted bookings at certain hours in the week. 

- Bring remote care into everyday life without leaving anyone behind: Remote care should be more than a convenience; it should be integrated with the patient’s normal routine. For example, sharing simple self-management checklists for chronic conditions, or short therapist sessions via video during the week, can prevent deterioration and reduce the need for urgent care. Yet it’s important to provide alternatives like home visits for those who can’t travel, or a phone-based option when video isn’t possible.

- Concrete examples from my experience: Last winter I waited a couple of weeks for a GP appointment for a persistent cough and fatigue. Then a minor expansion of slots in my practice made it easier to book within a week, which reduced anxiety and kept me from needing urgent care services. My spouse benefited from an online triage that led to a mental health referral within days rather than weeks. And a local community hub now hosts weekly drop-in sessions to help older residents navigate booking systems and use digital tools, which has helped several neighbours who felt overwhelmed by online platforms.

- What this would mean day to day: quicker access to GP or nurse advice for everything from infections to ongoing symptoms, faster mental health support to prevent crises, and better continuity of care for long-term conditions. It would also reduce the burden on urgent and emergency services, since people can get timely advice or treatment in primary care when it’s appropriate.

In short, boosting capacity (staff and slots), refining scheduling, and combining digital convenience with robust non-digital options would make timely access to GP, community health and mental health services much more achievable for people in my area, including those who are older or less able to use digital tools. I believe these changes would pay dividends in health outcomes and in the relief they would bring to families who often juggle work, caregiving, and health together!

I’ve read the aims about improving timely access to GP, community health and mental health services with more MDTs, longer appointments for complex cases, and greater use of online and remote care. I’m not convinced these changes, as currently proposed, will reliably deliver faster or fairer access in my area. They may help in principle, but without careful design and proper funding they risk just shifting bottlenecks or leaving some groups behind.

First, expanding multidisciplinary teams to treat routine cases so GPs can focus on complex care sounds sensible in theory. The idea is to free up doctors and speed things up. In practice, it requires seamless IT integration, shared records, and clear referral paths. In my town there was a trial where pharmacists and physiotherapists started handling some routine checks. While there were quick wins for medication reviews, there were also delays and confusion because patient notes didn’t always transfer cleanly between teams. People value seeing the same clinician who knows their history. If you can’t maintain continuity and you create a rotating cast of faces handling routine issues, patients may feel less secure and appointments may take longer as staff chase up information. If MDTs are to work, you need robust data sharing, rigorous training, clear accountability, and funding to ensure these teams can function like a single unit, not a loose collaboration that diverts capacity without improving flow.

Second, there’s real merit in protecting continuity of care and offering longer appointment times for those with complex, chronic or vulnerable needs. The outcome data suggests better management when the same clinician follows a patient over time. But extending the length of every appointment without expanding overall capacity simply moves the bottleneck. If a GP appointment becomes longer but there aren’t enough slots to accommodate everyone, patients with simple concerns may wait longer, or more calls are triaged to non-GP clinicians who may not be able to resolve issues promptly. In my experience, my family’s chronic conditions have benefited from longer, dedicated slots, but there are weeks when even a 20– or 30-minute slot is hard to secure. Any plan should guarantee a named clinician for continuity and reserve sufficient slots to prevent new delays; otherwise, extending time for some becomes a new barrier for others.

Third, expanding online booking, e-consults and remote care can be a real timesaver for many, but it isn’t a universal fix. For able-bodied and digitally confident people, it can speed things up. For older residents, those with limited data access, or people who struggle with digital platforms, it can actually slow things or exclude them entirely if non-digital routes aren’t equally strong. In our area, the online system works well on some days but, if the line is busy, there’s little transparency about why a request hasn’t been answered. I’m worried that reliance on remote pathways without guaranteed non-digital alternatives will widen inequities. A blended approach is essential: continue phone triage, walk-in slots, and home visits for those who can’t or won’t use online services, plus community-led digital literacy support and clear guidance on how to access non-digital options when needed.

Overall, I don’t oppose reform, but I do oppose assuming the proposed changes will automatically improve timely access. The reforms need to be paired with sustained investment in staffing, better IT that truly links MDTs to a single patient record, and a governance framework that protects continuity of care. Pilots should be accompanied by clear performance metrics, rigorous evaluation and a commitment to retain low-tech access points. If governments and NHS providers want faster, fairer access, they must ensure: named clinicians for complex patients, flexible scheduling that preserves routine access, comprehensive digital and non-digital routes, and a plan to prevent new bottlenecks as services evolve. Without that, the changes risk rearranging the queue rather than shortening it, and that won’t help people in real life.

Timely access to GP services, community health and mental health support matters a lot for people my age and in our community. I’m not against using online tools, but I’m worried that pushing digital-only solutions will leave people behind, especially those who aren’t comfortable with tech, don’t have reliable internet, or rely on someone else to help them. In my area I’ve seen both sides: online booking can make it easier to grab a slot between lectures, but when a family member tried to use e-consultations for a sudden health concern, the system was slow, the questions felt irrelevant to urgent issues, and there wasn’t a straightforward way to switch to a phone call or in-person check if needed. That kind of friction can cost time and, worse, health.

What would most realistically improve timely access is a well-balanced, two-track system that expands online capabilities while guaranteeing robust non-digital alternatives and support. Here’s what that could look like in practice:

- Keep and expand online booking, e‑consultations and remote care, but with clear safeguards. Users should be able to book same-day or next-day slots digitally if they want, and remote triage should guide people to the right level of care quickly. At the same time, clinics must guarantee that if online options aren’t working—whether due to device issues, complex symptoms, or just preference—patients can pick up the phone or walk into a reception and be helped immediately.
- Strengthen phone-based access with reliable, shorter hold times and a proactive call-back service. In our town, the phone lines often clog up for hours, and people without smartphones or data plans miss out. A dedicated urgent-appointment line with promised call-backs within a few hours would prevent delays for sore throats turning into longer infections or mental health concerns escalating while people wait online.
- Guarantee in-person triage and same-day appointments as a default option. Digital tools should route people to appropriate care, but not replace the option to see a clinician face-to-face on the day it’s needed. For mental health especially, I’ve heard from peers that quick, in-person assessments can be the difference between someone reaching out or withdrawing. 
- Improve access points in the community. Mobile clinics, GP nurse outreach, and clinics in libraries or student unions could deliver quick checks, vaccinations, blood pressure checks, and mental health drop-ins without people having to travel far or worry about booking windows. In my campus area, a weekly mobile clinic near the student centre made a real difference during exam season when people felt more stressed and anxious.
- Provide non-digital support and upskilling. Not everyone is comfortable with online forms or apps. Clinics should offer on-site help with booking at reception, and perhaps quick “how to use the system” sessions at libraries or community hubs. Providing access to loaner devices or Wi‑Fi in the clinic lobby could also help those who can’t buy or borrow a device last-minute.
- Transparent wait times and clear pathways. Real-time or daily posted wait times for GP, community health, and mental health slots would help people decide when to seek care and reduce unnecessary calling or visiting. A simple, published pathway showing when to use urgent care versus routine care would also cut down on confusion.
- Strengthen mental health access specifically. Digital options can be a bridge, but they must be complemented by scalable in-person crisis support, school-based counselling, and rapid access to a clinician. For example, timely same-day online triage should always be paired with a guaranteed in-person follow-up if the patient requests it, and crisis lines should be clearly advertised in student services and community centres.
- Data and listening as a core part of implementation. Regular reviews of who is being left behind by digital changes, and adjustments to outreach where digital gaps are found, are essential. If a policy rollout doesn’t monitor these gaps, it will fail the people who need it most.

Bottom line: I’m not against digital enhancements; I’m against digital enhancements that substitute for real access. The changes that would most improve timely access in our area are those that keep online channels open and efficient while ensuring non-digital routes are fast, friendly, and fully capable of meeting urgent needs. When people can choose the path that suits them—online, phone, or in person—and can move quickly through the system, we’ll see real improvements in how quickly we get the care we need, when we need it.

Changes that would most improve timely access in my area would be to protect continuity of care and lengthen appointment times for complex, chronic and vulnerable patients, and to expand mental health services in parallel. The benefit of continuity is clear: patients with long-term conditions often see multiple providers, repeat histories and carry avoidable distress when care is fragmented. A named GP with 20–30 minute slots for complex cases would enable one consultation to cover medication reviews, psychosocial needs and care planning, reducing repeat visits and hospital admissions. 

On the mental health side, we need stronger community teams, earlier intervention, robust crisis response and access to talking therapies to achieve parity with physical health. In practice, waits for counselling or psychology can stretch to months; early intervention in primary care could catch issues before crisis point. Embedding mental health professionals in primary care, plus 24/7 crisis support and digital self-help options, would help. 

Caveats: this requires sustainable funding, adequate recruitment, and rural/remote access. I would support these changes if rolled out with clear targets, improvements in workforce planning, and ongoing outcomes monitoring.

I appreciate the aim to speed up access, but I disagree that simply ramping up GP, nurse and therapist slots or extending hours will fix the problem - what a surprise. The core issue is sustainable staffing and funding. Without addressing pay, workload and training, more appointments will just fill and professionals burn out, leading to more cancellations and longer waits in practice. In my area, routine GP appointments can be booked two weeks ahead, and therapy referrals often take 6–8 weeks to start. Even with the promise of same‑day urgent slots, those slots disappear quickly, and genuinely urgent cases can still slip through the cracks without better triage. 

Evening and weekend clinics sound helpful for working people, but they require reliable staffing, childcare support, and safe transport options for staff and patients alike; otherwise many can’t use them. Instead of adding hours that may become unsustainable, I’d favour a sustained workforce strategy: longer‑term investment in training posts, retention bonuses, and international recruitment; more nurse‑led and digital triage to free doctors for complex cases; and integrated urgent care hubs that bring GP, mental health and social care under one roof. If we invest in those, we’ll see real reductions in waits rather than temporary shifts in timing.

To improve timely access, I would push for targeted resources in areas with high deprivation and diverse communities, plus practical measures that come from lived experience in our town. Ensure funded interpreters and multilingual information across GP, community health and mental health services, so families where English isn't first language can book and understand care quickly. I've seen neighbours miss GP slots or delay care because interpreters weren't available or information wasn't in their language. Hire and train more staff who reflect the local communities and are trained in cultural competence and trauma-informed care; this helps patients feel understood and reduces miscommunication. Strengthen outreach by employing community hralth workers and setting up drop-in clinics in familiar places—faith centres, community halls, organised workplaces—so people know where to turn and can access appointments more quickly. Extend hours and offer same-day slots, particularly for mental health triage, and improve digital booking with language options and transparent wait times. In practice, these changes would cut delays for migrants and marginalised groups who often face the longest waits, and would make the system easier to navigate for everyone in our area.

I welcome changes that make GP, community health and mental health services more timely by combining mobile clinics, outreach, telehealth hubs and sensible incentives. In our rural area, buses are infrequent, parking is limited and the main surgery can be hard to reach. A timetable of mobile clinics visiting village halls or care homes would bring urgent checks and follow‑ups closer to home, reducing travel and missed appointments. Telehealth hubs in libraries or community centres, with friendly staff to help older patients use the tech, would cut travel and waiting times while keeping good care. Incentives for clinicians to work in hard‑to-reach areas—housing support, travel allowances and protected time—would help recruit and retain skilled staff.

Targeted resources for interpreters, culturally competent staff and outreach to deprived, ethnic minority, migrant and marginalised groups are essential to close gaps in access. Quick language help and culturally sensitive care would prevent avoidable trips and miscommunication, especially for complex conditions. For those with chronic or vulnerable needs, preserving continuity of care and lengthening appointment times makes a real difference; 30 minutes rather than 10–15 allows proper assessment and reduces repeat visits.

From my experience, longer, consistent appointments and a local mobile or tele‑option when travelling is difficult lead to better outcomes and less stress for patients and families.

From my experience living in England and using GP and mental health services, I think the changes that would most improve timely access are those that focus on targeted resources for deprived and ethnic minority communities, and robust staffing strategies. Relying on generic digital improvements or morning appointments won't close the gaps. In my community, significant delays for non-English speakers happen because interpreters are scarce and booked late; outreach via trusted local groups has helped only when funded properly. I would prioritise guaranteed interpreters in common community languages, proactive outreach clinics in housing estates with high migrant populations, and culturally competent staff who understand barriers like work schedules and stigma around mental health. On staffing, we need not just more GPs, but targeted recruitment—including international hires with streamlined credential recognition, better pay, flexible hours, and wellbeing support—to attract stable teams. I’ve seen practices rely on short-term locums; patients notice the inconsistency in care. If policy leans on general capacity increases without all these targeted measures, timely access will remain poor for marginalised groups.

I live in Wales and see that timely access to GP, community health and mental health services in my area remains inconsistent, particularly for those in more deprived or marginalised communities. To really improve things, we need targeted resources for groups most affected: multilingual interpreters and culturally competent staff, plus Outreach that reaches ethnic minority, migrant and marginalised residents. For example, funded community health workers who visit schools, workplaces and local hubs to explain services and help people register with a GP would remove a lot of barriers.

We also need more capacity. That means recruiting more GPs, nurses and therapists and expanding session lengths where appropriate, plus flexible scheduling—evenings and weekend slots and rapid same-day triage. Local pilots like weekend GP clinics or after-hours mental health triage have shown how waits can fall when capacity is boosted and booking systems are well designed. Better digital booking, reminders and prioritised same-day access would help; funding must be ongoing and tied to real improvements in access for deprived and minority communities, not just overall wait times.

While digital tools can help, I don’t believe expanding online booking, e-consults and remote care alone will fix access issues. It risks leaving behind older or less IT-literate patients. In our area, since the practice moved to more online booking, my elderly neighbour struggled to secure a same-week appointment and often had to chase repeated phone calls; some people simply can't use the system. There should be strong non-digital options: a well-staffed phone line with trained call handlers, dedicated same-day triage slots, and regular in-person clinics at predictable times. We also need more appointment slots overall: recruit more GPs, nurses and therapists, expand session lengths to avoid rushed visits, and optimise scheduling to reduce gaps and patient dead time. This will require funds and retention strategies; simply expanding e-consults won't deliver timely care if capacity isn't increased. I’d also push for more training places, return-to-practice support, apprenticeships and CPD so the workforce grows sustainably. Finally, ensure digital access support is available: digital champions in practices and alternative booking routes for those who need them. Timeliness depends on both digital and human capacity.

I disagree with policies that push for shorter, more fragmented access at the expense of continuity of care. The changes that would most effectively improve timely access are ones that protect a named clinician or stable care team, and that give complex and vulnerable patients longer appointments to address multiple needs in one go.

- Guarantee a named GP or stable team for patients with chronic conditions so they see the same clinician each time; this builds knowledge of long-term history and reduces miscommunications.
- Extend appointment lengths for adults with complex needs or mental health concerns (around 20 minutes for initial reviews and 15–20 minutes for follow-ups) to prevent rushed, incomplete assessments and fewer repeat visits.
- Invest in integrated community health teams and care coordinators who manage long-term plans, medications and referrals, so patients aren’t shuffled between services.
- Keep a robust urgent-access pathway, but use it to support continuity—same-day triage followed by follow-up with the same clinician whenever possible.
- Combine digital triage with genuine human review, ensuring patients can still access in-person care when it’s needed.

Personal experience: last winter my partner, who has COPD and anxiety, waited weeks for a mental health referral. We saw different clinicians repeatedly, and important details were missed, delaying treatment and risking a crisis. A stable clinician and longer consults would have caught issues earlier and reduced repeats.

In short, timely access should not come at the cost of continuity or the quality of assessments; longer, linked appointments with a consistent clinician will actually reduce delays and crises.

I strongly welcome practical changes to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services in our area. In rural and mobility‑limited communities there are real barriers: transport, scarce parking and overfull premises. I’d back mobile clinics that rotate through village halls, outreach teams visiting care homes, and pop‑up clinics in community centres to bring care closer to people. Telehealth hubs in libraries or GP surgery rooms could handle routine follow‑ups and many mental health check‑ins without long journeys. Where possible, weekend and evening appointments, same‑day triage, and longer slots would reduce waits and fit around work and carers. We also need to recruit more GPs, nurses and therapists and expand session capacity, including group sessions where appropriate, with smarter scheduling to use existing staff efficiently. Practical incentives to attract staff to rural areas and improved parking and clear signage at premises would help. In my experience, a telehealth follow‑up saved a long round trip last month, and a mobile clinic would have helped during winter when buses were infrequent.

Agree. Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services in rural and mobility‑limited areas will improve if we combine mobile clinics, outreach teams, telehealth hubs and sensible incentives. In our region a weekly mobile GP van and district nurse visits to village halls or care homes would cut travel burdens for families and older residents, enabling same‑day urgent slots, vaccinations and routine reviews. Pairing this with targeted outreach to schools, workplaces and sheltered housing helps people stay connected with care. Telehealth hubs in libraries or community centres, staffed to assist with booking and tech use, would unlock video or telephone consultations for those who otherwise struggle to get to appointments. We also need practical fixes to transport and parking: free or discounted parking for booked visits and a coordinated community transport offer to bridge gaps on evenings and weekends. Sustained incentives for GP recruitment and retention in rural posts, plus small premises upgrades and flexible hours (including Saturdays) would attract and keep staff where they are most needed. Together, these changes create a more joined‑up, patient‑centred system that reduces delays and supports better health outcomes for rural communities.

From my perspective living in England, I disagree with approaches that assume universal improvements alone will close timing gaps in GP, community health or mental health access. The changes that would move the dial most are targeted resources to address language, culture and trust, especially for deprived, ethnic minority, migrant and marginalised groups.

In my area, GP appointment slots are often available, but many people cannot use them promptly because there is little interpreter coverage or staff with cultural competence. I have seen families delay follow-ups because phone interpreters fail or staff cannot explain medications clearly. Outreach to non-English speaking communities is often ad hoc, with clinics few and far between in estate areas or faith centres.

What would help: guaranteed funding for interpreters across all services, including mental health assessments; recruitment or retention of bilingual clinicians and trained cultural liaison staff; regular, visible outreach in community venues, supported by multilingual information and flexible hours to accommodate shift workers; and simple data dashboards showing access gaps by language, ethnicity and deprivation to target resources. Without targeted, sustained investment, broader reforms won’t reach the people who need care most.

Living in England and juggling work and family commitments, I see timely access to GP, community health and mental health services as essential to staying well and productive. I strongly support a package of changes that would make responsive care a normal part of the system, not a rare exception.

First, expanding multidisciplinary teams in primary care would make a real difference for routine problems and help GPs concentrate on patients with complex needs. In my local practice, patients with minor ailments or medication reviews often wait longer than they should. If pharmacists were co-located with GP teams, they could handle common issues like minor infections, repeat contraception prescriptions, and chronic disease medication reviews, freeing GPs to focus on people with multiple conditions or complex care plans. I’ve known colleagues who benefited from physiotherapists within the GP setting for musculoskeletal problems, which meant quicker access to therapy and faster relief. Paramedics and physician associates integrated into the primary care team could triage and manage routine appointments or home visits, reducing pressure on daytime GP slots. My own experience with a back pain flare showed how a prompt physio assessment could prevent escalation and keep me at work, rather than sitting in a waiting room for weeks. A more flexible, varied team would also improve continuity of care and make better use of everyone’s skills.

Second, extending access outside the usual 9–5 would be transformative for working people and those with urgent but non-emergency needs. Evening and weekend clinics, plus guaranteed same-day urgent slots, would stop so many issues from accumulating into bigger problems. I’ve met colleagues and neighbours who struggle to get an appointment during the week due to work hours, only to end up using NHS 111 or urgent care far from home. If practices offered predictable evening clinics and reserved same-day urgent slots, people could get timely advice, speak to someone who knows their history, and avoid unnecessary trips to emergency departments. A streamlined triage system, including digital booking and same-day escalation for urgent cases, would make it far easier to secure care when illness or injury strikes outside regular hours.

Third, expanding community mental health teams and investing in early intervention, crisis response, and talking therapies is vital for parity with physical health. Waiting lists for talking therapies and for CAMHS (child and adolescent mental health services) can be frustrating and harmful when early help could prevent deterioration. A more robust community mental health footprint would bring services closer to home, with early intervention for anxiety, depression and emerging psychosis, alongside more accessible crisis response that can support people at their most vulnerable—before situations escalate to crisis admissions. I’m encouraged by the potential of integrated talking therapies (such as IAPT) to reduce overall waiting times and to support people with longer-term mental health needs alongside physical health care. In my circle, timely support could mean earlier return to work, steadier mood, and better management of long-standing stressors that otherwise spill over into physical health.

To make this work, I’d like to see sustained investment in workforce development, clear role definitions, and flexible funding that enables practices to recruit pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates as standard members of the care team. Digital tools should support online triage, robust appointment systems, and shared records so that patients aren’t repeating histories or navigating multiple pathways. The goal should be simpler access, more proactive care, and treatment that happens close to home—so people don’t have to travel far or wait unnecessarily for help.

In short, expanding multidisciplinary primary care, offering evening/weekend access with guaranteed same-day urgent slots, and strengthening community mental health services with early intervention and crisis support would deliver quicker, fairer care for everyone. I’d welcome a practical plan to implement these changes in my area, with clear milestones and accountability, so we see real improvements in people’s health and daily lives.

From my experience living in England, continuity of care makes a real difference. When people with complex, chronic, or vulnerable needs see the same GP and have longer appointment times, issues are spotted early and management plans are clearer, which reduces repeat visits and avoids unnecessary hospital trips. I would support changes that protect continuity of care and lengthen appointment times for these patients.

For example, a neighbour with COPD and anxiety benefited from a 40-minute GP appointment that covered inhaler technique, breathing exercises, and signposting to social support. Since that longer slot, hospital admissions dropped and conversations with the care team felt more coherent. In mental health, longer initial assessments and follow-ups with a trusted clinician help build trust, stabilise medication, and prevent crises.

However, this must be funded with additional staff and flexible delivery models. We need protected time for complex caseloads, without making routine access harder for others. A mix of in-person and supported telehealth, plus integrated community nurses and pharmacists, would help maintain access in rural and urban areas alike.

Responding on behalf of an organisation representing young people across England, we welcome the focus on improving timely access to GP, community health and mental health services. From our perspective, the aim is achievable but must be framed around real-world barriers that many mobility‑limited and rural residents experience: transport gaps, limited parking, and premises that feel inaccessible or unsuitable. We advocate a mixed model of mobile, digital and locally embedded care, combined with a strong, well-supported workforce strategy and genuinely co‑ordinated services with social care and VCSE partners.

What would make the biggest difference, in our view, is a combination of the following, with a focus on local delivery and measurable improvements in access for all ages, including younger people who often face unique barriers to timely care:

- Mobile clinics, outreach and telehealth hubs: Establish regular, well-advertised mobile GP and nurse clinics that visit rural villages and wards with limited primary care access, including evening slots to fit work or study schedules. Pair these with targeted mental health outreach teams that visit schools, student unions and community centres. Complement this with telehealth hubs located in easily reachable community spaces such as libraries or youth hubs, equipped with private booths and user-friendly tech. These must include guidance for digital literacy and access to devices, so no one is left behind by tech gaps.
- Co-located community hubs: Invest in multi‑service hubs that bring primary care, mental health services, social care, and VCSE partners under one roof or within a shared network of services. A single point of access, with triage on site, can reduce duplication and ensure urgent social needs (housing, payments, carers’ support) are addressed alongside health care. In practice, a hub that includes a GP, a nurse, a counsellor or psychologist, a social worker, and a voluntary sector link worker can shorten waits, improve adherence to treatment plans and enable smoother referrals.
- Transport, parking and premises: Address practical barriers by offering parked and accessible sites, subsidised or organised transport to appointments, and flexible premises arrangements (for example after-hours clinics in community centres). Where possible, use mobile or pop-up spaces to avoid people needing to travel long distances. Clear signage, inclusive access and reasonable waiting areas are essential to create welcoming environments.
- Workforce development: Secure longer‑term improvements through increasing training places, return‑to‑practice support, apprenticeships and CPD for GPs, nurses and mental health professionals. We need visible career paths that young people can aspire to, including GP fellowships in hospital-to-community practice, nurse practitioner pipelines, and mental health practitioner apprenticeships linked to local universities. Streamlined re‑entry pathways for those who paused clinical work will be crucial to stabilise the workforce. In the near term, more flexible working patterns and reduced admin burdens would help retain staff and improve timely access.
- Local co-ordination and governance: Create formal partnerships between health services, social care, schools, universities and VCSE groups with locally accountable plans for access. Data sharing (with consent) across providers, common appointment systems and shared care plans should be prioritised to avoid fragmentation and duplication.
- Digital inclusion and safeguarding: While telehealth is essential, we must guard against widening inequalities. Invest in digital inclusion programmes (training, devices, affordable connectivity) and ensure multilingual support and culturally competent care. Privacy considerations must be explicit in any telehealth hub model, especially for mental health services.
- Short-term wins and monitoring: Set clear, achievable targets for 6–12 months—for instance, monthly mobile clinic slots in identified gaps, telehealth hubs in five community locations, the launch of two co‑located hubs with basic joint referral pathways, and 500 new training or return‑to‑practice places. Track impact with time-to-appointment metrics, patient satisfaction, and equity indicators across rural and mobility‑limited populations.

From our experience, the most successful models blend convenience with quality and trust. A local resident who cannot drive, or who cannot reliably attend a fixed clinic, benefits from a mobile clinic that visits their community and from a trusted hub where mental health support, social care and primary care feel connected. Co‑location and co‑ordination help reduce the sense that “care is out of reach” and can deliver more holistic support, including social prescribing where appropriate.

In conclusion, we support a policy direction that expands mobile and telehealth access while investing in co‑located, well‑governed community hubs and a robust workforce pipeline. The emphasis must be on practical delivery, local adaptability and real-time evaluation to ensure improvements in timely access are felt by young people and other mobility‑limited residents alike.

While I understand the aim behind speeding up access to GP, nurse and therapist care, I remain unconvinced these changes will help in Wales. In my area, GP shortages aren’t solved by promises of more slots; recruitment across rural practices is a years‑long challenge and patients wait weeks for routine appointments. Expanding capacity on paper without reliable staffing simply shifts the bottleneck. 

The idea of bigger multidisciplinary teams could help with routine tasks, but in small communities it risks fragmenting care and eroding continuity. People value familiar clinicians; handing routine checks to pharmacists, physiotherapists, or paramedics is useful only if there are clear, safe pathways and enough supervision. Otherwise, patients may be bounced around and lose the sense of who is managing their overall health. 

I welcome longer‑term plans for training and return‑to‑practice, but the benefit will be felt only after a long horizon. It will require protected posts, apprenticeship routes and robust supervision in place now. 

My priority would be strengthening retention, better local scheduling, reliable transport to larger hubs, and targeted CPD for current staff. Any rollout should be carefully piloted with transparent evaluation before broad adoption.

Blended, blended is the word: expand online booking, e-consultations and remote care, but back it up with clear non-digital routes so no-one is left behind. In my Welsh town, online booking is handy for routine things and prescription renewals, yet my elderly neighbour found it confusing and slow to get a real appointment because of patchy broadband and clunky security prompts. A recent attempt to get a same-day GP slot online ended in a system crash and I had to phone—only to face long waits and fewer open slots that day. 

What would help most: more same-day slots and later hours, especially for mental health and for families juggling work, school and shifts. Invest in nurse-led triage clinics to handle non-urgent cases quickly, with rapid referrals if something flags up. Digital tools should be user-friendly, with simple guides and options for video, chat or phone—plus a robust support plan for those who struggle online. Put digital champions in community hubs and libraries to help people book, fill forms and access e-mental health tools. Crucially, keep non-digital access: longer phone lines, walk-in clinics, and home visits for those who can’t travel or can’t use tech.

With better-coordinated digital and non-digital channels and appropriate privacy safeguards, services can be faster without leaving vulnerable residents behind.

I strongly agree that the most effective way to improve timely accesss to GP, community health and mental hralth services is to invest in co-located community hubs. These would bringg together primary care, district nursing, community health teams, mental health services, social care and VCSE partners under one roof, enabling quicker triage, smoother referrals and a shared care plan so people don’t have to repeat their story to multipl teams. In my area, families wait too long for GP appointments and those needing mental health support often bounce between services. A hub with several disciplines in one place would reduce red tape and keep people safer, with ongoing coordination across services. I’v seen a local pilot where a GP, a mental health clinician and a social worker share weekly drop-in sessions; it cut avoidable crises and helped carers feel their loved ones were being looked after holistically. To tackle transport and premises gaps, mobile clinics and outreach are vital—nursing or mental health vans visiting village halls, plus telehealth hubs in libraries or community centres. Incentives to recruit staff for rural sites and better parking at existing practices would also make timely access more realistic for everyone.

Living in Scotland, I often see how delays in GP, community health and mental health services ripple through families. I’m supportive of strengthening NHS111, clinical triage, booking systems and care navigation to prioritise urgent cases, reduce duplication and simplify patient flow. Real-world tweaks could make a big difference without compromising safety.

If NHS111 triage could access up-to-date patient records and local service availability, a caller with red-flag symptoms could be fast-tracked to urgent slots or same-day teleconsultations, rather than sitting in a general queue. A more integrated booking system that shows urgent slots across GP practices, district nurses and community mental health teams would cut duplicated calls and repeated history taking. A single care navigator role—someone trained to assess needs, book follow-ups and coordinate between primary care, social care and psychology services—would help households juggling multiple health issues and reduce unnecessary referrals.

I’d also value clear performance data and guarantees that rural users aren’t disadvantaged, plus robust privacy safeguards for digital triage. Overall, with proper staffing and local flexibility, these changes could shorten waiting times and improve fairness, while still protecting patient choice and safety.

I understand the aim of reducing waits, but I don’t think simply expanding community mental health teams, increasing training places, or pushing more GP and therapist slots will deliver timely access in practice. In my area, CAMHS wait times remain lengthy even after new staff were advertised; GPs can squeeze in more slots, yet real urgent care capacity still feels stretched. The bottleneck is often the systems around patients: unreliable booking, insufficient out-of-hours coverage, and fragmented records between NHS, local authorities and third parties. To fix this, we need immediate, navigable pathways: a same-day triage system with guaranteed slots for urgent mental health needs; 24/7 crisis hubs that can accept referrals within 24 hours; and a unified IT platform so a patient’s history, referrals and wait times are visible across services. Long-term, yes to training and workforce, but with secure, protected funding and retention plans, otherwise expansions will fade. Personal experience shows that promises of ‘more staff later’ translate into more adverts rather than real, timely help now. We need measurable targets, transparent wait-time reporting and flexible staffing tied to demand, not just headcount.

I live in England and I value timely access to GP, community health and mental health services. I strongly support proposals to increase training places, return-to-practice support, apprenticeships and CPD as a long-term solution to grow GPs, nurses and mental health professionals. In my area, wait times have grown as retirements outpace new recruits; a friend’s parent struggled to get a mental health appointment, and delays meant symptoms worsened. Expanding undergraduate and GP specialty training places would help build a locally rooted workforce. Return-to-practice schemes supported by light-touch revalidation and flexible routes can bring experienced staff back after career breaks, reducing gaps faster. Apprenticeships for health care assistants and practice managers would create career pathways for local people and support teams on the ground. Continuous professional development funded and easy to access keeps skills up-to-date and improves patient confidence. I’d like to see regions funded to plan workforce with GPs and psychiatrists co-locating with community services so patients can get holistic care quickly.

I welcome the plan to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services. In my area, older residents and those from deprived or ethnic minority backgrounds still face delays and barriers. Targeted resources for interpreters and culturally competent staff are essential so people feel listened to and understood. Clinics should offer multilingual receptionists, interpreter services, and outreach workers who can guide patients through bookings and follow-up care. Outreach through faith groups, community centres and mobile clinics would help migrants and marginalised residents who struggle with forms or digital booking.

Expanding multidisciplinary teams would also help. If pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates handle routine concerns such as medication reviews, back and joint pain, minor infections and home visits, they free GPs to care for complex cases. I have seen physio led care reduce GP visits for chronic back pain in our neighbourhood. For mental health, integrated community teams with culturally sensitive therapists, with in person and supported digital options, would make help more accessible.

It is important not to abandon in person access for older people who have limited technology. Adequate funding and local accountability will make these changes real.

From my perspective as a patient in England, timely access to GP, community health and mental health services often depends on whether a clinician has time to look beyond the surface. I would welcome changes that protect continuity of care and lengthen appointment times for complex, chronic and vulnerable patients. Longer slots allow us to review multiple conditions in one visit, agree pragmatic care plans and reduce the need for repeat visits in a few weeks. For instance, my neighbour with COPD benefited from a 30‑minute GP appointment where we adjusted inhalers and set up home monitoring; since then hospital visits have reduced. Conversely, when GP lists are stretched and same-day slots vanish, a relative waits weeks for a mental health referral, which only adds to distress and risk.

Looking ahead, I think expanding training places, return‑to‑practice support, apprenticeships and CPD is essential to sustainably grow GPs, nurses and mental health professionals. A local practice could recruit more practice nurses or counsellors if there were clear pathways and funded training. In the meantime, stronger triage, integrated community teams and longer initial assessments for those with complex needs would help deliver safer, more equitable care. Any changes must preserve continuity and be available to all, not just some.

I support expanding community mental health teams, early intervention, crisis response and talking therapies, while protecting continuity of care with longer appointments for complex cases, and providing evening/weekend clinics with guaranteed same-day urgent slots.

Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services would improve most if resources were targeted to those most marginalised, with interpreters and culturally competent staff at the core, plus proactive outreach into communities that often fall between the cracks. I’d prioritise: 1) ring-fenced funding to expand GP slots and mobile or pop-up clinics in deprived neighbourhoods, including some same‑day appointments and extended hours so people don’t have to miss work. 2) Interpreters and language access as a standard service: on-site interpreters where possible, and a robust, fast telephone interpreting option across common community languages, with privacy guaranteed. 3) Culturally competent staff: mandatory training for all frontline workers and recruitment of more diverse clinicians and peer support workers who share lived experience with local communities. 4) Outreach and partnerships: link workers based in trusted community venues, schools, faith groups and charities to help people register, navigate services and attend appointments; translated materials and community events to raise awareness of what’s available. 5) Data and monitoring: routinely collect language and deprivation indicators and publish wait times by group to ensure progress isn’t just claimed but measured. My experience in a migrant-heavy area shows that delays and missed appointments often stem from language barriers and a lack of culturally aware staff, not from patient willingness to seek help.

I disagree that simply expanding daytime GP slots will fix access; we need targeted resources for interpreters, culturally competent staff and outreach to deprived, ethnic minority and marginalised communities, plus evening/weekend clinics and guaranteed same-day urgent slots for working people.

Yes, creating co-located hubs that bring primary care, mental health, social care, and VCSE partners together will speed up access locally. Expanding teams with pharmacists, physios, paramedics, and physician associates will handle routine cases, freeing GPs for complex care.

it's outrageous that timely access to GP, nurse and mental health services in my area remains a frequent problem. The change that would have the biggest impact is increasing appointment slots and capacity by hiring more clinicians and expanding session lengths, combined with smarter scheduling. If a practice could recruit two GPs, two nurse practitioners and three therapists, and offer a mix of same-day triage plus longer follow-up slots, waits would shorten noticeably. In my experience last winter I had to wait a week for a routine GP appointment, and a family member waited over six weeks for an initial mental health session; each stage required multiple calls to get a slot. 

Alongside capacity, we need smarter scheduling: same-day triage by phone or online that routes people to the right professional, protected slots for urgent mental health checks, and longer blocks for complex cases to reduce repeat visits. Data-informed forecasting should guide staffing and hours, including more out-of-hours options. 

Funding and staff wellbeing must be safeguarded to keep these improvements sustainable!

it's outrageous that yes, longer appointments for complex patients to protect continuity, and expand teams with pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates to handle routine care, freeing GPs for complex cases, subject to adequate funding!

i really think access to timely GP, community health and mental health services would be greatly improved by evening/weekend clinics with guaranteed same-day urgent slots, plus stronger multidisciplinary teams and co-located community hubs. As someone who works during the day, I've struggled to get a same-day appointment for urgent non-emergency issues. Extending hours, including Saturday mornings, would allow people to be seen promptly without taking time off. A guaranteed urgent slot would also reduce pressure on A&E. Second, expanding multidisciplinary teams—pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates—embedded in GP practices would handle routine problems, meds reviews and minor illnesses, freeing GPs for complex care. I've seen how quick physio input prevents a GP visit turning into weeks of discomfort. Third, investing in co-located hubs that integrate primary care with mental health, social care and VCSE partners would make referrals smoother and care more seamless. In our town, a hub with a GP, counselor and social worker on one site cut missed follow-ups and improved continuity. With digital triage and shared records, timely access would become routine, not a postcode lottery!

I think the most reliable way to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services is to grow the workforce from within. That means more training places for GPs, nurses and mental health professionals, strong return-to-practice support, and expanded apprenticeships and CPD to sustain skills long term. In my area, GP appointments can be hard to come by and community teams feel stretched; boosting training places would start to ease these pressures within a few years. A formal return-to-practice pathway with up-to-date refresher modules, supervised placements and flexible hours would bring back experienced clinicians who paused their careers. Apprenticeships for healthcare assistants, nursing associates and peer-support workers would create clear career ladders and help staff clinics and mental health services to cope with demand. Paired with ongoing CPD funding and digital skills training, teams stay current and confident in early intervention. By investing in local training pipelines and flexible career routes, we can deliver timely, high-quality care rather than relying on reactive short-term fixes.

Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services remains uneven in our area, with long waits for those with complex needs and for people from deprived or migrant backgrounds. I’ve seen neighbours struggle to get interpreter support when urgent symptoms arise, and in my own experience, it can be weeks before a GP appointment is available for non-urgent concerns, leading to repeated calls and avoidable stress.

I would support targeted investment to reduce gaps: more multilingual interpreters and cultural competence training; outreach workers who understand local communities; and mobile or after-hours clinics in neighbourhood hubs, especially where public transport is poor.

We also need to grow and retain the workforce. This means targeted recruitment, including international hires, clearer incentives, better pay, flexible working patterns, and strong wellbeing support so staff are not burnt out and can stay in jobs that deliver continuity.

Crucially, protect continuity of care and lengthen appointment times for complex or vulnerable patients, so clinicians can develop fuller understanding and avoid repeat visits. Longer mental health assessments and a named care team by default would help.

Overall, a joined-up plan that couples staffing improvements with targeted outreach and longer, continuous care would improve timely access for all, especially the most marginalised.

Thank you for the opportunity to respond. I live in England and, at my age, timely access to GP services, community health and mental health care matters daily to how I manage my health and stay independent - what a surprise. I want to see a system that recognises the realities of transport limitations, parking pressures, and the challenges of premises in rural and mobility‑impaired areas, while also benefiting from more multi‑disciplinary support for routine issues so GPs can devote time to complex care.

From a practical standpoint, I would strongly back a package of changes that tackles the whole journey a patient takes to access care. First, transport and premises: in my village there is one small GP practice and a bus service that runs only a few times a day. If appointments fall at inconvenient times, or if the car park is full or unfriendly for older people with mobility aids, people give up waiting. A solution would be to deploy mobile clinics that rotate to village halls or community centres on set days (for example, a morning clinic in the village hall one day a week and a mid‑week pop‑up in the next village). These would be designed for routine, low‑complex visits—routine blood pressure checks, repeat prescriptions, minor skin concerns, and triage for mental health early steps. The same footprint should support outreach to housebound patients with home visits by trained nurses supported by pharmacists for medication reviews. In addition, telehealth hubs located in libraries or community centres, staffed by volunteers with basic digital guidance, would offer video consultations for those who find travel difficult. It’s essential these hubs are staffed with real people to help those who are not confident with technology, to safeguard equity and prevent digital exclusion.

Second, incentives and premises: I would back incentives to attract GPs and other clinicians to rural posts—enhanced salaries, relative‑to‑cost housing supports, protected time for training and mentoring, and improved funding for practice premises that include accessible parking, step‑free entrances and appropriate space for MDTs. In many small practices, space is a squeeze; retrofitting spaces and sharing facilities with allied health professionals could unlock more timely access for a broader range of services without demanding patients to travel long distances.

Third, expanding multidisciplinary teams in primary care to handle routine problems and free GPs for complex care. I have seen how much time is spent in clinics on repeating minor issues that a pharmacist, physiotherapist or paramedic could handle after brief triage. A model where a pharmacist conducts medication reviews, a physiotherapist runs musculoskeletal clinics, a paramedic or physician associate can manage urgent but non‑complex presenting problems, and a mental health nurse or practitioner provides early intervention would free GPs to focus on those patients with more complex or multi‑morbid needs. This is especially valuable in mental health care, where timely access can be life‑changing: a dedicated mental health practitioner embedded in a primary care setting can offer brief CBT‑informed sessions, crisis triage, and rapid referral pathways to CAMHS or adult services when needed.

There are practical considerations to get this right. IT systems must allow seamless sharing of notes and care plans across MDT members; patients must retain a clear, single care plan so the experience doesn’t feel fragmented. Training and supervision are essential to ensure non‑GP clinicians are working within safe, evidence‑based boundaries, and patients should always have a clear route back to a GP if symptoms worsen or red flags appear. For older people, continuity matters: so while expanding teams, we must preserve personal relationships with clinicians who know our history.

Finally, I would want to see a phased rollout with monitoring. Start with high‑need rural pockets, measure impact on waiting times and patient satisfaction, then scale up. The fund­ing must be predictable and long‑term; piecemeal pilots that disappear when political cycles shift won’t deliver lasting improvements. And we must ensure options exist for those who prefer in‑person appointments, with clear information about how to book and what alternatives are available.

In summary, I am supportive of a combined approach: extend mobile and outreach services to improve physical access; build telehealth hubs as a supplement rather than a substitute; provide incentives to improve rural access; and empower multidisciplinary teams to manage routine care efficiently. If designed with strong governance, clear clinical roles, good IT support, and a focus on equity, these changes could meaningfully shorten waiting times, reduce avoidable trips to hospital, and help people like me stay healthy and independent in our own communities.

Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services is fundamental to people’s wellbeing here in Scotland. We welcome the focus on strengthening NHS111, clinical triage, booking systems and care navigation to prioritise urgent cases, cut duplication and simplify patient flow. In our experience, the current bottlenecks tend to compound when people are shuffled between services or forced to repeat information. Getting the first point of contact right—whether that’s NHS111, a GP line, or a community nursing team—can dramatically shorten the time to an appropriate intervention and prevent unnecessary escalation.

What we think would most improve access, with a few practical examples drawn from community experience:

- NHS111 and clinical triage: Increase access to trained clinical staff who can perform robust triage 24/7, with clear escalation pathways to same-day GP slots, urgent care and mental health crisis services. Triage should be evidence-based, language-accessible, and capable of linking directly to the patient’s preferred practices so that once triage determines urgency, an appointment can be booked without the patient having to repeat information. In practice, we hear about times when NHS111 directs someone to book an appointment—but the earliest slot is days away. A more integrated triage workflow would couple triage decisions with immediate booking options and a visible estimate of wait times.

- Booking systems that work for real people: We need a single, real-time booking system that spans GP practices, out-of-hours, community nursing, urgent care centres and mental health services. It should be accessible by app, website and phone, including for those with limited digital access. The system should enable same-day urgent bookings, automatic reminders, and easy rescheduling. In rural communities, where transport and connectivity can be barriers, a reliable phone-based pathway is essential.

- Care navigation as a core service: Invest in trained care navigators who can guide patients through the system, explain options, and help overcome practical barriers (transport, language, carer responsibilities). Navigators should sit at the heart of the care pathway, not as an afterthought, helping families determine whether a GP, community nurse, mental health service, or pharmacy-led service is most appropriate. Local care navigation hubs in communities, libraries, or pharmacies could act as supportive touchpoints, especially for vulnerable groups.

- Reducing duplication and sharing information safely: A shared patient record across GP, community teams and mental health services is vital. With consent, clinicians should be able to see what assessments have already been done, what tests were ordered, and what actions were taken, so we avoid repeating triage steps and duplicate referrals. Standardised referral pathways will help ensure that patients enter the correct service first time and stay on a clear, coordinated treatment plan.

- Streamlined patient flow and urgent pathways: Create fast-track routes for urgent problems—such as chest pain, acute mental health concerns, or high-risk scenarios in children—so people aren’t bounced between services. Co-located or tightly integrated urgent care hubs that bring GP, district nursing, and mental health teams together can reduce handoffs and delays. This requires practical scheduling, predictable staffing, and a governance framework that keeps flow smooth even during winter pressures.

- Governance, evaluation and workforce resilience: Any reform must come with robust performance data, transparent reporting and patient feedback loops. Publish wait-time targets, booking success rates, and patient experience metrics so communities can see progress and hold teams to account. Adequate staffing, training, and wellbeing support are essential to prevent burnout and sustain improvements over the longer term. We should pilot changes in representative areas, evaluate them, and scale what works.

- Inclusion and diversity considerations: Ensure digital solutions do not widen disparities. Maintain accessible alternatives (phone, in-person help) and ensure interpreters and culturally appropriate information are available. Rural, remote and economically vulnerable groups must not be left behind as systems digitalise.

If implemented with the right resourcing, clear data sharing, strong governance and user-friendly design, these changes could noticeably reduce time to care, lower unnecessary hospital visits and improve patient confidence in the system. At their best, NHS111 becomes a precise, compassionate gateway that directs people to the right service at the right time, with minimal friction and duplication. We are ready to support pilots, share practical feedback from frontline staff, and help monitor outcomes to ensure these reforms deliver real improvements for people across Scotland.

I support growing primary care capacity with competitive pay, flexible hours and wellbeing support, including international recruitment and incentives; plus interpreters and outreach to marginalised groups. Ensure funding to hire GPs, nurses and therapists and smarter scheduling to reduce waits.

Digital improvements can help, but not at the expense of the elderly or financially stretched families. In my area, online booking is a lifeline for some, yet my 78-year-old neighbour struggles with portals and loses appointments because the phone line is busy and the portal keeps timing out. I would hate to see others like him excluded. Therefore I urge a dual path: expand online booking and e-consults, and invest in non-digital routes—a dedicated phone line with longer hours, in-surgery kiosks, and staff to assist patients in registering for digital tools. Provide clear same-day urgent slots and guaranteed evening/weekend clinics to help working people manage urgent non-emergency needs and reduce emergency visits. For mental health, offer rapid access slots and crisis drop-ins, plus community-based support to bridge gaps while people wait for longer-term therapy. Also ensure outreach clinics in underserved neighbourhoods so people aren’t forced to travel far. If we narrow options to online bookings alone, inequalities will widen.

From my experience here in England, the problem with access isn’t simply a lack of evening slots but a steady erosion of staffing for GP, community and mental health teams. I cannot support plans that chase more clinics and guaranteed same‑day urgent slots without first fixing the workforce. In our area, routine appointments are routinely scheduled weeks ahead, and urgent slots disappear quickly once lists fill. Extending hours would simply push overworked clinicians to burnout unless we recruit and retain staff properly.

A credible path would include targeted recruitment, including international hiring where appropriate, accompanied by incentives and pay improvements, flexible working patterns and strong wellbeing support. Such measures are essential to grow a stable primary care team that can staff longer hours and new out‑of‑hours slots without compromising quality or continuity of care. Concrete examples from neighbours show that without a sufficient workforce, even 'same‑day' promises become hollow. So I urge Ministers to prioritise staffing reform — not just more appointment slots — before expanding hours or guaranteeing urgent access.

Access to timely GP, community health and mental health services would be greatly improved by targeted changes that tackle transport, parking and premises deficits. I support mobile clinics, outreach, telehealth hubs and incentives to attract staff to rural and mobility‑limited areas. In our village, irregular bus services and limited parking mean many people miss or delay appointments. A weekly mobile GP van visiting the parish hall or the market day could make routine checks feasible for those who cannot travel easily. Telehealth hubs at the library or community centre would help with follow‑ups and mental health check‑ins without long journeys. Regular outreach teams visiting schools, care homes and workplaces would catch issues early and reduce crises. Financial incentives—student loan forgiveness, retention payments and funded practice expansion—would help recruit and retain clinicians in rural posts. If these measures are funded and coordinated with flexible hours, we’d see shorter waits, better appointment adherence and fewer avoidable trips to A&E, improving overall wellbeing in our community.

i really think from my experience living in England, timely access to GPs, community health and mental health services varies a lot by area. In our rural/peri-urban patch, GP appointments are often hard to come by because premises are limited and transport links poor. A mobile GP clinic visiting weekly, outreach sessions in local halls, and a telehealth hub in the village library would help those who can’t travel easily. Practical tweaks like reserved parking, better signage, and extending hours into evenings and weekends would also stop people from delaying care.

Staffing is the real bottleneck. We need flexible working, stronger wellbeing support, and proactive recruitment. That should include targeted initiatives and international hiring where appropriate, with clear career paths and competitive pay to attract and retain clinicians. If we can offer flexible shifts and robust supervision, practices may keep skilled staff rather than lose them to busier urban posts.

On mental health, waits remain unacceptably long. Expanding community mental health teams, boosting early intervention, crisis response, and talking therapies would improve parity with physical health. In my area, CAMHS waits and adults in crisis rely on stretched services; coordinating care through a dedicated navigator and 24/7 crisis access, plus digital self-management tools with timely professional support, would make a meaningful difference.

Overall, a funded, locally tailored plan with measurable progress would genuinely improve timely access!

Agree. Longer appointments for complex cases protect continuity of care and reduce repeat visits; use mobile clinics and telehealth to address transport and premises gaps; expand training and CPD to sustainably grow GPs, nurses and mental health staff.

I welcome and strongly support steps to improve timely access to GP,, community health and mental health services. To reduce gaps for deprived, ethnic minority, migrant and marginalised groups, I think we need targete resources, interpreters, and culturally competent staff, plus active outreach in local communities. While I understand the idea behind co-located hubs, I think investing in them as the main way to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services won't deliver quick, local improvements for people like me. My area already has long GP wait times; I've waited over a week for a same-day appointment and heard friends describe calling early and still missing slots. A big build of hubs would take years and huge funding; meanwhile people slip through the cracks. Instead, we should push practical, short-term changes: more GP appointments offered in evenings and weekends; improved online booking and triage with nurse-led first contact; urgent mental health support with same-day access through primary care and improved liaison psychiatry; extended phone/video triage.

I do support closer working with social care and VCSE partners, but not only by creating new shared buildings. Those partners can be embedded in existing practices or delivered via mobile hubs, pop-up clinics, or satellite clinics in schools or community centres so travel is minimized. A pilot with robust data should test what works locally, before committing to a network of new co-located hubs. We need faster access now, not a long-term reorganisation.

I understand the aim to improve timeliness, but I must express clear opposition to leaning on online booking and e‑consultations as the main fix. In Wales, especially here in rural and coastal areas and for the 65+ cohort, digital access is not universal. Last winter, a neighbour waited three weeks for a GP appointment; the online system wouldn’t show available slots and the phone line was congested. Many friends in our community lack reliable broadband or feel uneasy with apps, so online‑only approaches risk excluding vulnerable patients and widening gaps in care. Remote consultations can help some, but they cannot replace the need for physical assessments, house visits, or timely in‑person advice when symptoms are urgent.

Longer‑term, the priority should be expanding training places, return‑to‑practice support, apprenticeships and CPD so that GPs, nurses and mental health staff are available in adequate numbers and with up‑to‑date skills. This is the sustainable solution to reducing waits. If digital tools are used, they must be offered with non‑digital routes: telephone triage, in‑person clinics, and assistance to use online systems, with staff and community hubs providing support. In my experience, a balanced mix works best.

I want changes that genuinely improve timely access, but I’m not convinced the current focus will deliver. In my rural England village the problem isn’t just more staff; it’s patients slipping through because appointment slots are too short and transport is poor.

I support targeted recruitment, including international hiring and pay incentives, but it won’t fix continuity if patients keep getting a different clinician each week. We need longer appointments for complex cases and vulnerable patients to avoid repeat visits and worse outcomes. For example, my relative with COPD had a 10‑minute slot recently; there’s no time to adjust meds and we ended up returning. A stable GP with longer slots would have helped.

Transport and premises matter too: limited parking and irregular local bus routes deter people, especially the elderly. Mobile clinics in village halls and reliable telehealth hubs on tough days would help, provided there’s privacy and good IT. We also need investment in premises so clinics aren’t cramped or unsafe and staff have decent space to work.

In short, pair sustainable workforce strategies with better access to transport, longer visits, and continuity of care. Without those, timely access will stay uneven and health outcomes will suffer.

absolutely access to GP, community health and mental health services would improve most if we expanded community mental health teams, introduced stronger early intervention, 24/7 crisis response, and more talking therapies, and ensured parity with physical health. In my area, GP slots can be hard to come by, and mental health referrals sometimes wait weeks. I’ve seen a friend wait two months for counselling through IAPT, while a physical health appointment could be booked sooner. Expanding community mental health teams to include psychologists, psychiatrists, social workers and MH nurses based in local hubs would mean quicker triage, same-day or next-day contacts, and better coordination with GPs.
