- Longer‑term workforce growth: There’s a real need to grow the workforce sustainably. Increasing training places, return‑to‑practice schemes for those who’ve paused their clinical work, apprenticeships, and ongoing CPD would help us avoid repeating cycles of shortages. In the meantime, better career pathways and flexible working conditions could make roles more attractive to young clinicians and keep people from leaving the profession. I’ve heard from friends in training that more funded places and clear progression routes can change the outlook for staying in care long‑term.
- Data, pilots and evaluation: Any changes should be rolled out with proper pilots, local data, and a clear plan to scale what works. I’d want monitoring on patient experience, wait times, equity of access (including for those who are digitally excluded) and the impact on clinicians’ workload and wellbeing.

My experience is that digital tools can speed things up and reduce pressure on GPs, but they only help if they’re used as part of a broader, people‑centred system. If you roll out online booking and e‑consultations, make sure non‑digital routes are equally fast and reliable, and integrate MDTs so people with routine needs aren’t stuck waiting weeks for an appointment. With thoughtful implementation and ongoing support for training, I think these changes could meaningfully improve timely access rather than simply shifting the bottleneck elsewhere.

In summary: expand digital access while protecting non‑digital options; empower multidisciplinary teams to handle routine care; invest in the workforce for the long term; and govern the changes with strong evaluation to ensure equity and quality for everyone, including those who are less tech‑savvy or on low incomes.

As someone living in England and navigating the health system as a young person, I wholeheartedly support proposals to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services by growing the workforce in sensible, long‑term ways. In my area I’ve seen how a lack of clinicians can push people to wait longer for appointments, which then affects study, work and overall wellbeing. If we want quicker, reliable access now and a sustainable system for the future, expanding training places, return‑to‑practice support, apprenticeships and CPD is the right path.

First, increasing training places for GPs, nurses and mental health professionals is essential. If universities, NHS trusts and clinical placements are expanded together, we could create a steady pipeline so new recruits don’t have to wait years for a post. In practice, this could mean more undergraduate medical student places, more GP specialty training posts and more nursing and psychology/mental health training places in local hospitals and community services. A few additional trainees in a cluster of practices could transform local access, especially if paired with protected supervision time and clear progression routes. I’ve heard from peers that even small delays in securing a GP appointment ripple into larger problems—missed lectures, late assignments, or delayed treatment for anxiety or mood issues. Increasing training places would help prevent those pinch points before they start.

Second, return‑to‑practice support is vital. People step away from care for many reasons—care responsibilities, burnout, or re‑training needs—and some could rejoin sooner with the right package. I’d like to see structured return‑to‑practice schemes that offer updated clinical competencies, mentored placements, and flexible hours to fit people back into work without losing their confidence. If a nurse or a therapist can return with a short bridging course and a buddy mentor, we gain experienced clinicians who already know their local community and can start helping patients again faster.

Third, apprenticeships should be a real part of the long‑term workforce strategy. Apprenticeships create clear routes into nursing, therapy support and even some GP roles, pulling in people from the local area who might not have followed traditional routes. For example, an apprenticeship pathway for nursing associates or mental health support workers could lead straight into more senior posts as skills grow. This also helps with retention because people build a career here rather than moving away to find a better job elsewhere. In our area, I’ve seen students who would have pursued healthcare careers if there were accessible work‑based routes alongside academic study; expanding these programs would open doors for them and strengthen local services.

Fourth, continuing professional development must be well funded and easy to access. CPD should be practical, bite‑sized and delivered in a way that fits the realities of student life and part‑time work. For example, funded online modules, weekend workshops and short refreshers on digital tools used in GP and community care would keep skills current without pulling staff away from patients for long periods. When clinicians feel they're continually learning and supported, they’re more likely to stay in local practices, which reduces churn and keeps appointment slots available.

In terms of delivery, I’d like to see local bodies coordinate with universities and NHS partners to create apprenticeship hubs tied to actual staffing needs. Clear timelines for expanding training places, combined with return‑to‑practice programs and CPD funding, would give young people confidence that a career in primary and community care is viable in their hometown and that it will stay strong for years to come. It would also be helpful to pilot these changes in a few trusted local sites, with transparent reporting on wait times, appointment availability and staff numbers, so we can learn and adjust quickly.

Ultimately, better access is not just about more staff; it’s about a system that trains and retains the right people in the right places. If we invest now in training, return‑to‑practice support, apprenticeships and ongoing professional development, we’ll see more timely GP and mental health appointments, stronger community health teams, and a healthier generation who can focus on study, work and everyday life instead of worrying about when they’ll get seen.

From my perspective living in rural England, the biggest barrier to timely GP and mental health care is not a lack of digital tools but the everyday realities of travel, parking and the suitability of premises. I live about 15 miles from the nearest GP, and the bus only comes twice a day on weekdays; parking at the clinic is cramped and the front entrance is hard to reach for someone with mobility issues. In winter, this means I often miss slots or have to cancel. I do not think more online booking alone will fix this.

What would help: mobile clinics that visit parish halls or community centres on a regular timetable; same-day triage by outreach nurses; mental health practitioners visiting care homes and supporting carers; telehealth hubs at accessible local venues with trained volunteers to assist older people to use the tech. We also need robust transport solutions: subsidised travel to appointments, better parking and safer disabled access at all sites.

For staffing, the region needs targeted recruitment, international hires where appropriate, pay rises, flexible hours and wellbeing support to keep doctors and nurses from burning out. If these measures aren’t backed with on-ground services, timely access will not improve.

TIMELY ACCESS TO GP, COMMUNITY HEALTH AND MENTAL HEALTH SERVICES WOULD IMPROVE IF PRIMARY CARE EXPANDS MULTIDISCIPLINARY TEAMS TO HANDLE ROUTINE MATTERS, FREEING GPS FOR MORE COMPLEX CASES. EMBEDDING PHARMACISTS, PHYSIOTHERAPISTS, PARAMEDICS AND PHYSICIAN ASSOCIATES IN GP PRACTICES, WITH ROBUST TRIAGE AND CLEAR HANDOFFS, WOULD ALLOW MANY COMMON ISSUES TO BE RESOLVED QUICKLY AND LOCALLY. FOR INSTANCE, A MINOR INFECTION, A MEDICATION REVIEW, BACK OR KNEE PAIN, OR A MENTAL WELL-BEING CHECK COULD BE ADDRESSED BY THE APPROPRIATE PROFESSIONAL, REDUCING DELAYS AND THE NEED FOR URGENT CARE APPOINTMENTS.

IN MY EXPERIENCE, WAITING WEEKS FOR A GP FOR A ROUTINE CONCERN OFTEN COMPELS PEOPLE TO SEEK URGENT CARE OR ENDURE SYMPTOMS LONGER THAN NECESSARY. A WELL-DESIGNED MDT WITH SHARED RECORDS AND DEFINED SCOPES WOULD KEEP CARE COHERENT AND SAFE. I RECOGNISE THE BENEFITS, BUT IT MUST COME WITH PROPER FUNDING FOR RECRUITMENT, SUPERVISION, AND TRAINING, PLUS GOVERNANCE TO PREVENT FRAGMENTATION AND ENSURE PATIENTS KNOW WHO IS RESPONSIBLE FOR THEIR ONGOING CARE. IF DONE WELL, THIS COULD IMPROVE ACCESS WITHOUT COMPROMISING QUALITY.

From a 65+ resident in Wales, I don’t think simply stacking co-located hubs will swiftly improve timely access. In practice, we already have local primary, community and mental health teams, but when the GP is stretched or staff are off, same‑day slots vanish. A new hub could help, but only if there is real staff equity, reliable transport for older people, and clear, sustained funding across organisations. Without that, it risks being another layer of admin that delays care.

Increasing training places and return‑to‑practice support is welcome for long‑term resilience, but it won’t fix this winter’s bottlenecks. We need immediate recruitment and retention incentives for GPs, nurses and therapists, simpler admin, fair pay in Wales, and flexible hours that suit pensioners and carers. Apprenticeships are fine in principle, but we must ensure they deliver experienced clinicians fast enough to relieve pressure.

Protecting continuity of care and longer appointments for those with complex or vulnerable needs is essential. But longer slots must not come at the expense of everyone else’s access. A practical approach would be targeted longer slots for complex cases, plus robust case management and better transport to hubs, so people aren’t left waiting or travelling long distances for care.

I welcome proposals to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services. In our area, both adults and families often face long waits for GP appointments, limited same-day options, and delays when trying to access mental health support. I think the changes you’re proposing could make a real difference if they are properly funded, well planned and closely tied to the needs of local communities. First, we need a stronger, more resilient primary care workforce. Targeted recruitment and international hiring should play a bigger part, with streamlined routes for qualified clinicians who want to settle here long term. It isn’t just about growing numbers; it’s about creatin a supportive environment that makes people want to stay. That means competitive pay, clear career progression, and flexible working patterns so staff can balance shift work with family life and wellbeing. For example, job-sharing and extended hours in safer, well-managed clinics can help cover evenings and weekends when people are most likely to need access after work. Importantly, there must be robustt wellbeing support for staff—supervision, mental health resources, decen staffing levels, and manageable workloads—so wr don’t end up with burnout and high turnover that undermine access in the long run. Second, we need targeted support to close access gaps for deprived communities, ethnic minorities, migrants and marginalised groups. The NHS has to reflect the diversity it serves, which means investing in interpreters and culturally competent staff as a standard part of every practice and service. It isn’t enough to have translation on call; we need interpreters embedded in the system and staff trained in cultural competence so that people feel understood and respected from the first contact. Practical steps could include outreach teams that work directly with community groups, faith organisations and schools to raise awareness about what services are available and how to accesss them. In my experience, loca outreach and trusted community links reduce missed appointments and improv engagement with screenings and preventive care. Flexible payment options for patients who can’ navigate complex systems would also help remove barriers. Third, expand multidisciplinary teams so routinr cases are treated by a wider range of professionals, freeing GPs to focus on complex or chronically ill patients. Pharmacists can conduct full medication reviews, identify drug interactions, and run adherence clinics; physiotherapists can manage back and joint problems early, reducing GP referrals and helping people stayy active; paramedics and physician associates can carry out triage, home visits and simple urgent care tasks, and then escalate when necessary. In practice, this means more clinic slots for new and ongoing issues without waiting weeks for a GP appointment I’ve heard from colleagues about pilot pharmacist-led clinics that successfully managed stable conditions and gave GPs more time for complex cases—and the positive impact on patient flow was clear. Our local practices could scale this up with proper funding and standardised pathways. Fourth, we should ensure that these reforms are backed by accessible digital and physical access points. Online booking, remote triage, and timely patient communication channels reduce unnecessary trips to a practice while preserving a warm, human touch in care. Equally we should offer flexible locations—extendedd hours, walk-in slots, and pop-up sessions in community hubs or care homes—so people who work, carers or those without reliable transport can still get timely help. Finally, any plan must be closely monitored with meaningful targets, patient representatives, and local clinicians at the table. Funding should be long-term and predictable, not piecemeal, with transparent progress metrics on wait times, appointment availability, and the impact on hralth outcomes. It’s crucial that communities feel ownership of these changes and see that improvements are rral, not just promises. If these ideas are pursued with urgencyy and kindness toward staff and patients alike, we can make timely accrss to GP, community health and mental health services a genuine reality for more people in England. I’m supportive of this approach and keen to see practical steps and funded pilots rolled out in my area so we can learn and scale what works best.

I strongly agree that changes to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services are needed, and I think the plan should focus on growing the workforce as well as expanding flexible, accessible care. To do this, we need targeted recruitment, including international hiring, with incentives and pay improvements, plus flexible working and robust wellbeing support so staff stay in primary care. In our area, waiting times have grown as GP numbers fell; when the practice offered longer hours and recruited clinicians from abroad, some of those delays reduced. Continuing with similar recruitment drives and fair pay would help stabilise services.

Equally important is widening access through online booking, e‑consultations and remote care, but never at the expense of those who are less digitally able. I use online booking for routine visits, which is very convenient, yet many elderly neighbours rely on phone lines or help from carers. Practices must maintain phone triage, longer dedicated phone lines, and in‑person slots with staff to assist less‑affluent or less‑digital patients. For mental health and community services, same‑day access and integrated teams with social care, plus clear reminders and occasional outreach clinics, would make timely help much more likely. The overall aim should be a genuinely flexible system that works for everyone, not just those who are comfortable online.

Agree. To improve timely access, support mobile clinics, outreach and telehealth hubs to reach rural and mobility‑limited residents; develop co‑located community hubs linking primary, mental health, social care and VCSE partners; expand community mental health teams, early intervention, crisis response and talking therapies to cut waits.

absolutely thank you for inviting input on how to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services. Our organisation recognises the scale of the challenge and welcomes a multi‑pronged approach that combines better initial triage, smarter booking, and more targeted outreach. At the same time, we think any reform must be locally adaptable, data‑driven and sensitive to the realities of transport, digital access and language needs. In short, the changes should get people to the right care, first time, with as little friction as possible.

To that end, key improvements should include:

- NHS111 and clinical triage: Invest in robust clinical triage led by qualified clinicians who can accurately assess urgency and safer alternatives. When a call is triaged as urgent, there should be a clear, rapid route to appropriate care – whether a same‑day GP appointment, a mental health crisis service, or a community nurse. Ensure reasonable call‑back targets and a transparent escalation process so patients aren’t shuttled unnecessarily between services. Where appropriate, offer an immediate link to booking instead of multiple handoffs.

- Booking systems and care navigation: Create interoperable, patient‑facing booking channels across GP practices, community services and mental health providers. A single, user‑friendly portal (and NHS App integration) should support same‑day urgent slots, with options to book by phone for those who prefer it. A trained care navigator should accompany patients through the system, helping them understand pathways, complete referrals and minimise duplication of information requests. This would reduce the current churn where patients repeatedly repeat details to different teams.

- Targeted outreach and culturally competent provision: To close gaps for deprived, ethnic minority, migrant and marginalised groups, increase interpreters, bilingual staff and culturally competent training for frontline teams. Deliver outreach through trusted community organisations, faith groups and local networks to raise awareness of available services, how to access them and what to expect from triage. Flexible appointment options (evenings, weekends) and clear multilingual information will help those who face work, caring responsibilities or stigma barriers.

- Transport, premises, and access in rural or mobility‑limited areas: Address physical and logistical barriers directly. In rural or mobility‑restricted communities, mobile clinics and outreach presences in community hubs can bring care closer to people who cannot easily travel. Invest in telehealth hubs in libraries or community centres with appropriate privacy and staff support to help patients use remote consultations. Where feasible, expand home visiting where clinically appropriate. Improve car parking, step‑free access and clear way‑finding at existing premises to reduce unnecessary delays and confusion.

- Telehealth and digital inclusion: Support a network of telehealth hubs and remote monitoring where they genuinely reduce wait times and improve outcomes. This should be accompanied by a rapid assessment of digital exclusion and alternatives for those without reliable internet or devices. Any telehealth expansion must preserve the human element that many patients rely on, including the ability to speak to a real clinician when needed.

- Incentives and shared governance: Provide incentives for practices to extend opening hours and to participate in integrated care models, with clear accountability for improving access metrics in deprived and rural communities. Encourage joint planning across primary, community and mental health services so that resource allocation aligns with local need and capacity.

- Data, monitoring and accountability: Build in robust monitoring of access for different groups, including wait times, no‑show rates and patient experience indicators. Regular public reporting at regional or local level will help identify where gaps persist and whether targeted interventions are working. This should be complemented by patient involvement in redesign to ensure solutions meet real-world needs.

In my experience, even well‑intentioned reforms can falter if they rely on a single solution. For example, where NHS111 triage has improved clarity but is not linked to an easy booking route, patients end up waiting or seeking A&E as a default. Conversely, streamlined booking is undermined if interpreters are unavailable or if outreach is not culturally sensitive. The most effective approach I’ve observed combines strong triage with practical navigation and a visible commitment to reducing transport barriers, particularly for older residents and those without reliable transport.

Ultimately, timelier access depends on ensuring that people can navigate the system quickly, understand what care they need, and receive care in a setting that suits their circumstances. A blend of improved triage, smarter booking, targeted outreach, and mobility‑friendly delivery models—supported by good data and genuine local collaboration—offers the best chance of delivering faster, fairer access for GP, community health and mental health services.

I disagree with the proposal to tackle timely access purely by extending hours into evenings and weekends and by guaranteeing same-day urgent slots. While I appreciate the aim to help working people, such changes would put additional strain on already stretched GP practices and their staff, risking burnout and lower quality of care. It would also be costly and may not reach those most in need if transport, carer support, and information about the new slots are not consistently available.

In my experience in this area, longer hours do not automatically translate into shorter waits; I have spoken with several patients who value continuity with their own GP and fear that weekend clinics would be staffed by temporary teams with limited knowledge of their histories. A guaranteed same-day urgent slot could shift attention from primary prevention and chronic care management to a rush for urgent care, potentially compromising safety.

Better options would include sustained investment to grow the workforce (more GPs, practice nurses, mental health staff), improved digital triage linked to local clinics, and closer integration of community health and social care. And crucially, making any changes alongside transport support and clear, local communication so older residents can actually access them.

As a resident of England in the 25-34 age group, I find that simply increasing overall capacity won't reliably improve timely access. Language barriers, cultural gaps and staff shortages in deprived and ethnic minority communities persist far too long. What would help most is targeted resources and robust interpreters across GP surgeries and community services, plus outreach into trusted local venues to guide people through registration and appointment booking. In my area I’ve seen people miss care because there was no interpreter available, and I’ve had to wait weeks for mental health referrals when a culturally competent clinician could have helped sooner. Continuity matters: longer appointments for complex and vulnerable patients (30 minutes instead of 10–15) and keeping the same GP for ongoing issues would cut repeat visits and delays. On the workforce side, we need clear incentives, targeted international recruitment, flexible hours and genuinely funded wellbeing support to attract and retain primary care staff; otherwise longer wait times simply shift the burden onto patients who are already struggling to navigate systems. If reforms ignore outreach, language access and continuity, timeliness will not improve in practice.

Disagree that simply adding slots will fix access—what's needed is bold workforce reform: targeted recruitment and international hires, better pay, flexible working, wellbeing support, and expanded session capacity to actually reduce waits.

I’m concerned that expanding online booking, e-consultations and remote care alone will widen inequality and leave vulnerable people behind. Timely access won’t improve if you can’t use the system from the start.

A balanced approach would be to keep digital options alongside robust non-digital routes: preserved telephone triage with clear, short wait times; same-day in-person appointments; and walk-in hubs in every borough. In our area, the online slot search can be unreliable and I’ve had to chase calls for days when a flare-up of back pain felt urgent. My neighbour without reliable broadband gives up trying and just waits, risking deterioration.

For complex, chronic, or vulnerable patients, we must protect continuity of care. Longer, coordinated appointments and a dedicated care plan reduce follow-ups and hospital visits. The same principle applies to mental health: rapid access matters, but video calls aren’t suitable for everyone due to privacy, connectivity or preference. Some people engage better face-to-face or via a confidential phone line.

Invest in more staff, longer appointment times, and clear guidance on how to access the right pathway. Digital tools should enhance, not replace, the human connection and must be accompanied by real-world options for those who need them.

I strongly support expanding multidisciplinary teams in primary care to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services. In my area, patients still face long waits for routine appointments while GPs carry heavy caseloads. If pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates could manage routine cases—triage, minor wound care, injections, simple infections, medication reviews and early rehab—GPs would have more capacity to focus on complex or high-risk cases. Last year I had a knee problem; a physiotherapist from the local community service assessed me and prescribed exercises the same week, which stopped it getting worse and meant I didn’t need a GP visit. A pharmacist-led medication review could catch drug interactions and simplify regimens for those with several prescriptions. Paramedics could visit patients at home for simple chronic condition checks, preventing unnecessary hospital visits. For mental health, integrated practitioners within primary care could offer timely brief support and fast referral if escalation is needed.

To deliver this, I’d back funded MDT expansion, shared digital records, clear escalation pathways and extended triage hours to secure same-day access.

To improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services in my area, I think a blended strategy works best: grow the workforce for the long term while expanding flexible access now, with safeguards for those less digitally connected.
- Long-term workforce: more training places for GPs, district nurses and mental health professionals; expanded return-to-practice schemes, apprenticeships and CPD; local training hubs near universities to keep talent in the area; reduced admin load so clinicians can see patients more quickly.
- Short-term and digital access: expand online booking and e-consultations, with clear non-digital options (phone lines with extended hours, in-person triage) to avoid excluding older or financially vulnerable patients; robust triage to direct patients to the right service; guarantee same-day urgent GP or mental health slots where possible.
- Flexible hours: offer evening and weekend clinics and ensure urgent care and mental health crisis services are accessible outside core hours.
- Equity and support: provide help to navigate online services, translations, and accessibility; ensure digital options supplement but do not replace in-person care.
In my circles, quicker access to urgent mental health support would have reduced stress during exams and study periods.
As someone in my sixties, I worry about housing quality and energy costs driving ill health; better homes would lessen pressure on GP and mrntal health services, even if access reforms fall short.

I support practical, well‑funded steps to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services, especially in rural and mobility‑restricted areas. In our village and surrounding parishes I’ve seen how a lack of suitable transport, limited parking at clinics and outdated premises can make already fragile access even worse. Small changes can add up to real improvements for families who juggle work, caring responsibilities and long journeys to reach care.

A core part of the answer is bringing services closer to people who can’t easily travel. Mobile clinics and regular outreach visits would make a real difference. For example, a monthly GP and nurse mobile clinic that visits each village on a predictable timetable would cut out the need for cross‑county journeys for routine check‑ups, blood pressure reviews and vaccinations. In between visits, trained community health workers could use outreach sessions in village halls or libraries to triage concerns and signpost to the mobile clinic or local services. For people with chronic conditions who find it hard to travel, home visits or short‑notice telephone/video triage supported by a nurse could maintain continuity of care.

Premises and parking are tangible barriers. I’d like to see co‑located, multi‑discipline hubs in accessible locations with adequate parking and clear disability access. If a single site can host GP services, mental health professionals, a district nurse, pharmacy and social care, it would be easier for patients to stack appointments in a single trip and for staff to coordinate care. Where travel remains necessary, reliable local transport options or smart parking incentives near clinics would help, as would dedicated telehealth hubs in community venues. A well‑equipped telehealth hub with private rooms, digital devices and trained staff could enable video consultations, remote monitoring and self‑management support for conditions like hypertension, diabetes and anxiety, reducing the need for repeat physical visits while still delivering high‑quality care.

Technology can extend reach without replacing the value of human contact. Telehealth hubs should be paired with digital literacy support for older or less confident patients, equipment loans, and simple, secure online triage. Regular virtual clinics with primary care staff and practice nurses, plus integrated mental health check‑ins, could help in‑between physical appointments. Community hubs could also host drop‑in sessions for mental health work‑ups and early intervention, so people don’t have to wait until a crisis to get help.

To make these changes sustainable, we need a strong pipeline of trained staff. Increasing training places for GPs, nurses and mental health professionals, alongside return‑to‑practice support and CPD, is essential. Rural placements during training nurture relationships with local communities and reduce recruitment challenges after qualification. Apprenticeships for practice nursing and allied health roles would create a smoother pathway into primary care roles for local people. Financially, targeted recruitment and retention packages—international recruitment where needed, streamlined visa routes, higher pay bands, flexible working options, and wellbeing support—will help grow and keep the workforce in the areas that need it most.

Flexible working patterns are particularly important for work‑life balance and retention. Job sharing, part‑time roles with clear progression, and supportive management culture can reduce burnout and improve patient continuity. Wellbeing programmes for staff—mental health support, adequate downtime after demanding shifts, safe handling of clinical workload and reduced administrative burdens—will translate into more stable and available teams for patients.

In practice, these measures must be funded and planned as a coherent, long‑term strategy with local co‑design. I’d welcome pilots in a few rural districts to test mobile clinics, telehealth hub operations and integrated hubs, with clear metrics on wait times, appointment adherence and patient experience. The goal isn’t quick fixes but sustained, people‑centred access that recognises transport limitations, the value of face‑to‑face care where needed, and the role technology can play to extend reach. If implemented thoughtfully, these changes would make timely care a reality for more people in our area and beyond.

I strongly support a plan that combines growing the workforce with targeted outreach to those who often miss or delay care. Increasing training places and providing return‑to‑practice support, together with apprenticeships and ongoing CPD, is essential to sustainably grow GPs, nurses and mental health professionals over the coming years. In my area, waiting times are worsened when staff leave or are redeployed; more local clinicians and longer, more predictable hours would cut unnecessary delays and improve continuity of care. 

Equally important is targeted resource allocation to close access gaps for deprived, ethnic minority, migrant and marginalised communities. This means more interpreters and culturally competent staff, plus proactive outreach through community centres, schools and faith organisations so people know what help is available and how to book it. For example, having interpreters at GP and mental health appointments and outreach workers visiting local hubs could transform appointment uptake and early intervention. 

If these investments are properly funded and planned with workforce data, they would deliver timely access, reduce avoidable hospital visits and support families in our communities more effectively.

I understand the goal of expanding online booking, e‑consultations and remote care, but I strongly disagree that this alone will improve timely access for GP, community health and mental health services in Scotland. Many in my area face digital exclusion: students without quiet space or reliable data, older neighbours without smartphones, and people who simply struggle with the tech. A GP online triage can reduce some delays, but it also risks hiding people who need in-person assessment. For example, last winter a library near our town lost a week of service when broadband failed; meanwhile bus timetables to the clinic are infrequent and parking is scarce and expensive, making same-day in-person visits a challenge for mobility-impaired individuals. What would help: keep robust non-digital channels (free phone lines with prompt callbacks, in-person reception, walk-in slots) and provide digital literacy and device support; fund mobile clinics to reach rural villages; outreach teams for mental health in schools and community centres; telehealth hubs in libraries or GP practices with trained staff; incentives to clinicians to offer flexible hours; transport vouchers or community transport schemes to get people to appointments. A mixed model is essential to prevent anyone being left behind while we catch up with tech.

I support strengthening NHS111 triage and booking systems to prioritise urgent cases and reduce duplication. Evening/weekend clinics and guaranteed same-day urgent slots would help working people, while expanding multidisciplinary teams would free GPs for complex care.

Agree. The changes that would most improve timely access in my area are a mix of more flexible clinic hours and strengthened digital options—with real non‑digital support to avoid leaving some people behind. 

- Evening and weekend GP clinics with guaranteed same‑day urgent slots: as someone with a part‑time job, weekday mornings are hard. Last month I needed quick medical advice after a late shift and the earliest GP slot was two days away. A guaranteed same‑day urgent slot would have prevented a minor issue from turning into something bigger and saved me from extra stress.
- Expanded online booking, e‑consultations and remote care, plus non‑digital options: using online booking and quick e‑consults saves hours on travel and waiting. For mental health, short remote check‑ins could bridge gaps between talks or counselling slots. But not everyone can use digital tools, especially older relatives. We should keep telephone triage, walk‑in help at local hubs, and paper booking forms so no one is excluded.
- Real‑world examples: a friend waited weeks for counselling; quicker online triage could have connected them sooner, and my mum’s elderly neighbour struggles with forms, so clear support is essential.

If these developments are funded and well‑coordinated, they would make timely access feasible for students, workers and those who rely on public transport, without compromising safety or inclusivity.

I support expanding community mental health teams, early intervention, crisis response and talking therapies to reduce waits and improve parity with physical health, and I back targeted recruitment, international hiring, pay improvements, flexible working and wellbeing support to grow and retain primary care staff.

I would strongly support changes that sharpen NHS111 and the clinical triage system, streamline booking and navigation, and promote robust outreach so urgent cases are prioritised and patients are not bounced between services. In practice, that means NHS111 operators with better access to up-to-date GP and community team capacity, improved triage protocols that reliably identify red-flag mental health crises, and a single, transparent booking flow that shows urgent slots across GP, out-of-hours, and community links. Reducing duplication by sharing summaries and care plans between services would also free up capacity and cut time wasted on repeating questions. I have seen how interpreters, culturally competent staff, and targeted outreach in deprived and ethnic minority neighbourhoods can close access gaps: multilingual receptionists, interpreter lines, and community health workers visiting schools, mosques and community centres make a real difference. Also, expanding online booking and e-consults helps many, but keeping non-digital options and support for older or digitally-excluded patients is essential Obviously.... Flexible hours, mobile clinics, and home visits would help my area reach those in need quickly.

From my position as a longer-standing resident in England, the changes that would most improve timely access are not purely digital. I support efforts to improve NHS111, clinical triage, and booking systems, but I strongly disagree with relying mainly on online tools to prioritise urgent cases. In practice, many elderly neighbours struggle with apps and websites; when NHS111 directs to a phone call that becomes a week later, the gap between services creates delays and duplication. A single, well-resourced care navigation hub linked to GP practices, community health teams and mental health services would help more, with real-time, standardised appointment slots and clear pathways to urgent same-day or home visits. We need to reduce duplication by sharing records and aligned assessments, so a patient is not asked for the same history twice. Also, keep non-digital channels open: walk-in clinics or phone access with trained staff who can triage and book on the day. True progress means faster access without leaving older people behind.

I'm in England and in my early 20s, and I think timely access isn’t just about picking an appointment window—it’s about how the whole system works for someone my age. When I tried to book a GP visit this term, the earliest slot was two weeks away, which feels far too long when you’re dealing with a sudden cold, anxiety, or a flare-up of something you’ve been managing. A friend in another town booked online and saw a time, only for a call-back to never arrive and the slot to vanish. It makes me wonder if the bottlenecks aren’t just queues, but the way care is designed for younger people who juggle study, part-time work, and transport. I’d value more youth-friendly options: extended hours, same-day triage that actually leads to advice or a quick check-in, and mental-health support with shorter waits. Schools and universities could help by offering on-site clinics or walk-in mental-health drop-ins and clearer guidance on what to do when GP access is delayed. Better, more flexible out-of-hours services would reduce pressure on urgent care and feel fairer to people my age with busy schedules.

Evening/weekend clinics may help some, but they would overburden staff and disrupt continuity. I’d prefer more GPs, better daytime access, and reliable home visits and community support for older residents.

Access to GP, community health and mental health services in Wales is uneven, and the gaps are most visible in deprived areas and where language support is needed. To improve timely access, I’d push for targeted resources: permanently funded interpreters and bilingual staff, plus cultural competence training for front‑line staff and triage teams. Proactive outreach through community centres, schools and faith groups would also help reach marginalised groups who don’t routinely engage with clinics and often wait longer for care.

On the workforce side, we need to grow and sustain primary care by targeted recruitment, flexible working and wellbeing support. This could mean incentives for roles in high‑need areas, fair pay, and possibilities for international recruitment with strong induction and mentoring, coupled with safe visa paths. Flexible appointments (early morning, evenings, weekends) and better telehealth options with language support would reduce barriers.

In my experience, a local practice has tried on‑demand interpreting, but delays persist; mobile clinics and outreach days would make a real difference. Crucially, we must collect clear data on wait times, interpreter use and mental health referrals so progress can be monitored and reported transparently. Funding and careful implementation are essential to avoid unintended downsides.

I support expanding online booking, e-consults and remote care, while keeping non-digital options for older or disadvantaged patients; plus evening/weekend clinics and guaranteed same-day urgent slots would improve timely access.

Plans must go beyond general access boosts: target resources to deprived and minority groups, provide interpreters, longer appointments for complex patients, and expand multidisciplinary teams to free GPs for urgent cases and reduce repeat visits.

As an organisation, we support increasing GP, nurse and therapist slots through extra staff, expanded sessions and smarter scheduling to reduce waits; crucial to fund training, retain staff, and ensure equitable access across areas, including urgent mental health pathways and out-of-hours options.

absolutely as a pensioner living in England with several long‑standing conditions, timely access to GP, community health and mental health services would be improved most if we protect continuity of care and lengthen appointment times for complex, chronic and vulnerable patients. Too often I have found myself telling the same story to a succession of clinicians who do not share notes or history, leaving decisions rushed and medications unsettled. When a clinician who knows my case can review everything in one session, outcomes improve, and I make fewer repeat visits. A longer appointment is not a luxury; it is a safety measure for people like me and my peers who live with several conditions at once and rely on a small, coherent care team.

To make this possible, I would suggest the following changes:

- Guarantee a named clinician or small continuity team: Every patient should have a named GP or a stable team who coordinates across GP, district nursing, pharmacy and, when needed, mental health services. That team would write and regularly update a concise, shared care plan that travels with the patient between services.

- Lengthen appointments for complex cases: Ensure a minimum slot length for chronic disease reviews and multi‑problem care. I would push for at least 25–30 minutes for an initial review of a complex condition, with 15–20 minutes for straightforward issues. Mental health assessments should be allocated 30 minutes when necessary.

- Introduce dedicated care coordinators and home visits: Fund care coordinators to manage people with multiple conditions, including post‑discharge follow‑ups and regular check‑ins for those living alone or with cognitive impairment. When mobility or frailty makes clinic visits difficult, home visits should be available as part of the standard package of care.

- Strengthen integration with community services: Create an integrated care pathway where primary care, district nursing, social care and community mental health teams share a single, updatable care plan (with consent). Regular case conferences and easy information sharing would reduce duplicated questions and tests and speed up decisions.

- Maintain accessible and flexible access channels: Keep a mix of in‑person, telephone and digital options. For the oldest or most vulnerable, staff should offer straightforward telephone triage and the option for a timely appointment with someone who knows their history, not just a generic clinician.

- Improve mental health access within primary care: Hire or colocate mental health professionals in practices to offer rapid triage and short‑term therapy where appropriate, with stepped care that directs people to the right level of support. Reducing waiting times for talking therapies would prevent crises and unnecessary hospital visits.

- Workforce planning and sustainable funding: The changes require sustained investment in GPs, nurses, allied health professionals and social care, plus flexible working arrangements to reduce burnout and turnover. Longer appointment times will increase demand for staff but should reduce downstream pressures by preventing avoidable hospital admissions and repeated visits.

- Transparent performance and patient feedback: Publish waiting time data by area, and collect regular patient experience feedback focused on continuity and the usefulness of care plans. Use these findings to adjust staffing and appointment models.

Overall, delivering these changes would not only improve health outcomes for older residents but also reduce the stress and cost of unmanaged chronic and mental health issues. It will require a long‑term, adequately funded plan and a commitment to putting the patient’s ongoing relationship with a known clinician at the centre of primary care!

From where I live in England, timely access to GP, community health and mental health services still feels uneven. NHS111 and clinical triage often act as bottlenecks, with urgent concerns sometimes treated like routine queries. A clearer, better-prioritised single-entry triage that flags red-risk symptoms and escalates quickly to the right clinician would help massively, as would a streamlined flow that avoids asking the same questions multiple times and shares a clear outcome with the patient’s GP or community team. This would cut duplication and move people to the right service faster. 

On capacity, I’d support expanding GP, nurse and therapist slots through targeted recruitment and longer appointment times for complex cases, plus more flexible hours and weekend slots so people can book without taking time off work. In my area, waiting 2-4 weeks for a GP and 6-12 weeks for therapy isn’t uncommon, which can have real consequences. 

Digital and non-digital options must go hand in hand. Online booking and e-consults are useful, but we must keep phone lines and in-person options, plus digital support for those who need it—through local libraries, community hubs, or trained volunteers—so no one is left behind. A joined-up care-navigation service would also help people move smoothly between GP, community health and mental health services.

I STRONGLY SUPPORT CHANGES TO IMPROVE TIMELY ACCESS TO GP, COMMUNITY HEALTH AND MENTAL HEALTH SERVICES BY STRENGTHENING NHS111 AND CLINICAL TRIAGE, SMARTER BOOKING SYSTEMS AND EFFECTIVE CARE NAVIGATION. THE GOAL SHOULD BE TO ASSESS URGENCY QUICKLY, DIRECT PEOPLE TO THE RIGHT SERVICE FIRST TIME, AND PROVIDE DIRECT ACCESS TO URGENT GP OR NURSE APPOINTMENTS WHERE APPROPRIATE, WHILE REDUCING DUPLICATION OF CALLS AND REPEATS OF INFORMATION.

TO TACKLE TRANSPORT AND PREMISES DEFICITS, I’D LIKE TO SEE MOBILE CLINICS IN RURAL VILLAGES, REGULAR OUTREACH TO WORKPLACES AND SCHOOLS, AND TELEHEALTH HUBS IN COMMUNITY VENUES. IMPROVING PARKING, QUEUE MANAGEMENT AND THE USABILITY OF DIGITAL SYSTEMS AT CLINICS WILL HELP THOSE WHO RELY ON PUBLIC TRANSPORT OR HAVE LIMITED MOBILITY. FLEXIBLE HOURS AND A FEW STREAMING APPOINTMENT SLOTS COULD ALSO HELP SHIFT WORKERS.

ON MENTAL HEALTH, EXPANDING COMMUNITY MENTAL HEALTH TEAMS, EARLY INTERVENTION, CRISIS RESPONSE AND TALKING THERAPIES IS ESSENTIAL TO REDUCE WAITS AND ACHIEVE PARITY WITH PHYSICAL HEALTH. IN PRACTICE, MORE AFTER-HOURS OPTIONS, RAPID ACCESS TO CBT AND DIGITAL THERAPY WOULD MAKE A REAL DIFFERENCE FOR FRIENDS AND COLLEAGUES WHO STRUGGLE TO GET TIMELY SUPPORT. A CLEAR, JOINED-UP CARE-NAVIGATION PATH WOULD HELP PEOPLE MOVE BETWEEN SERVICES WITHOUT GETTING LOST.

Increase training places and return-to-practice schemes to sustainably grow GPs, nurses and mental health staff, with targeted recruitment, flexible working and wellbeing support to attract/retain staff; and modernise NHS111, triage and booking to prioritise urgent care and reduce duplication.

Based on what I’ve seen locally, the quickest wins aren’t more rapid, generic access channels but protecting continuity of care and giving clinicians adequate time for complex cases. Longer, planned appointments with a stable GP would help people with chronic conditions manage their health and reduce repeat visits later on. When a patient has diabetes or heart issues, rushing them through a 10-minute slot often leads to missed warnings and worse outcomes. If you want timely access, you need to keep the same clinician or team responsible for a patient’s care over time, with slots long enough to address multiple needs in one go.

I also think targeted resources are essential for deprived and ethnic minority communities. Funded interpreters and staff who understand different cultures, plus proactive outreach through trusted community groups, would close access gaps far more effectively than broad digital campaigns alone. In my area language barriers slow initial assessments and create delays, and interpreters during intake cut miscommunication and wasted appointments.

For mental health, early, joined-up care with longer initial assessments and clear pathways to ongoing support would prevent crises and reduce emergency referrals. Telehealth has its place, but it must not erode in-person continuity for vulnerable patients who rely on trust and nuanced conversations.

I disagree with pushing digital-first access alone; it risks excluding the elderly and disadvantaged. Prioritise urgent cases through robust triage, but ensure evening/weekend clinics, guaranteed same-day urgent slots, and non-digital booking options.

absolutely timely access to GP, community health and mental health services in my area is hampered by transport, parking and premises deficits, especially for those with limited mobility. I’d back mobile clinics that rotate through villages, regular outreach in schools, workplaces and community centres, and extended hours on evenings and Saturdays so people don’t have to travel far for simple issues. Telehealth hubs in libraries or community venues, staffed to help patients set up video calls, could reduce unnecessary journeys. Incentives for GP practices to run satellite clinics or co‑locate with pharmacists, plus transport vouchers, would also help.

There’s also a case for expanding community mental health teams, early intervention, crisis response and talking therapies to reduce waits and improve parity with physical care. But these must be well integrated into primary care and adequately funded to prevent bottlenecks.

Online booking and e‑consultations have promise, yet I’d avoid digital exclusion. Non‑digital routes should stay: telephone triage, walk‑in slots, and clear paper alternatives; plus simple digital tools with support and digital literacy programs for older or less tech‑savvy residents. In practice, I’ve seen relatives miss timely care when online‑only systems were used; that risk must be mitigated!

I’m a pensioner living in rurall Wales, and I’m replying as an individual who relies on local GP and community health services. I understand the goal of improving timely access—making it easier to see a GP, a nurse, or a therapist when we need to. But I don’t think simply increasing slots and rushing to expand sessions will by itself sort out the problems we face in everyda life. First, the obvious issue is not just the number of appointments but where and when they’re available. In my area, the majority of extra GP slots end up concentrated in the main town, which is difficult to reach for many of us with limited public transport or who don’t drive. If a patient in a village branch can only get to a weeklyy clinic, and it’s booked a month ahead, the practical benefit is small. Increasing capacity in a few places without reliable, accessible covrrage across the county just redistributes the bottleneck rather than removing it. Second, there’s the matter of transport, mobility, and sensible scheduling. An exhausted bus timetable, a rough road, or a patient who needs a carer to accompany them means a 60–90 minute journey for a 10-minute appointment is simply not timely care. I’ve had neighbours who missed slot because travel was impractical or thr carer wasn’t available. More slots won’t help if people can’t physically reach them, or if the system assumes people can arrive for conventional midday sessions when many of us live far from health hubs. Third, the quality and length of appointments matter Many of us deal with multiple ongoing conditions, medications, and social issues. A 10– or 15-minute GP slot is rarely enough to cover everything a patient needs to discuss, let alone review medicines, talk through side effects, or arrange social support. Expanding the number of slots is not the same as expanding the capacity for thoughtful,, patient-centred care. We need longer, more flexible appointments for complex cases, with time to coordinate care across GPs, nurses, pharmacists, and social services. Fourth, the nurse and therapist workforce is stretched too. When I’ve needed a therapist or a mental health professional, the waits have been long and the pathways feel fragmented. Expanding slots without ensuring hteere are enough trained therapists, counsellors, and allied health professionals to fill them would just push people into long queues elsewhere, including out-of-area pathways or over-reliance on crisis services, which is a poor use of NHS resources and not good for patients. Fifth, digital access and triage must be handled carefully. Booking by phone can be a slog, and not everyone has reliable internet or feels comfortable with online systems. If we push for more slots but neglect the basics—friendly, patient-focused telephone triage, clear information about where to go for urgen issues, and options for in-personn visit for older patients—some people will still be left waiting when there are urgent needs. Finally, we should not treat increased appointment slots as a stand-alone cure. We need a holistic plan that also addresses workforce recruitment and retention, sustainable funding, and better integration with second-tier services and social care. It should include: - A truly county-wide spread of accessible clinics, with flexible hours including evenings and weekends where needed, and reliable transport support. - Longer and more flexible appointment times for patients with chronic conditions or complex needs. - A broader, well-supported multi-disciplinary approach in communities, so patient can see thee right professional in the right setting withoutt endless referrals. - Investment in home visits and community outreach to reduce unnecessary travel for frail or mobility-impaired patients. - A clear, patient-friendly triage system that directs people to the most appropriate care promptly, whether that’s GP, nurse, therapist, or community support, and that keeps older people out of crowded waiting rooms whenn a home visit or telecare would be safer and more convenient. - Practical support forr digital access, such as helplines with real people who understand local geography, and assistance with booking for those who struggle with online systems. I want to see a plan that recognises the lived realities in Wales—the hills, the farms, the villages, the towns—and that places patients at the centre. Increasing slots in a few places, without addressing transport, appointmrnt length, workforce, and care integration, risks simply moving the bottleneck rather than removing it. I’d like to see a system that guarantees timely access in practical ways—where I can reasonably expect to be seen when I need to be, with proper attention to the breadth of my health and social needs.

Expanding multidisciplinary teams within primary care could improve timely access, as routine conditions are handled by pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates, freeing GPs to focus on complex or risk-related cases. In my area, back and joint pain often means long waits for physio or an unsatisfactory GP appointment; seeing a physiotherapist or trained pharmacist for triage would have saved weeks and reduced unnecessary prescriptions. I welcome the idea of co-located teams and clearer referral pathways, with shared patient records so care remains continuous across providers. However, there are caveats: we need robust governance, clear triage criteria, and guaranteed patient choice about who they see. Training and supervision must be consistent to avoid variability in care; funding must be long-term and not tied to short-term pilots. We should also ensure mental health access is integrated, with quick warm-handovers to psychologists or counsellors when needed, and that rural patients aren’t left with longer journeys. Overall, a well-funded, opt-in model with strong data sharing and performance monitoring could help markedly, provided safeguards are in place.

There are several changes that would make a real difference to how quickly people can get GP, community health and mental health support in our area, and I think the best approach is to combine smarter digital systems with more flexible, people‑centred services on the ground. From my own experience as a young person juggling studies and part‑time work, I’ve twice felt the frustration of being stuck in a loop: calling NHS111 or a GP line, getting given vague waiting times, and eventually needing to go somewhere in person but not being sure what service is truly urgent or where the simplest route to help lies. A package of improvements that prioritises urgent cases, reduces duplication and eases transport barriers would help a lot for people like me and for families with mobility challenges or who don’t drive.

First, modernising NHS111 and clinical triage would be a game changer. If NHS111 could consistently connect people to a clinician who can triage over the phone or via video on the same day, and then quickly route them to the right service, that would save everyone time and prevent unnecessary trips. I’d like to see a system where if a clinician assesses a potential urgent issue, they can immediately book the next available urgent GP slot, mental health same‑day assessment, or community nurse visit, rather than leaving people to chase appointments themselves. A more predictable, real‑time triage process would also help reduce the current churn when people get passed between departments without a clear plan. In my experience, a few extra minutes of trained triage can save days of waiting later on.

Second, booking systems and care navigation need to be streamlined and integrated. A single, user‑friendly online platform that shows real‑time appointment availability across GP practices, community health teams and mental health services would be transformative. If I could see the next available slots for a GP, a nurse practitioner, or a mental health worker in one place and receive proactive reminders, I’d be far less likely to use multiple phone calls and multiple apps. This should be paired with a trusted care navigator who can help me choose the most appropriate service for my symptoms and urgency level, explain what to expect, and provide clear instructions on what to do if I feel worse. The aim is to avoid duplicating consultations for the same issue and to prevent people from having to repeat their story to different staff members. For students and young people who often have irregular schedules, weekend or evening triage and booking windows would also help keep care accessible.

In practice, I’ve seen how confusing it can be when you’re told to call NHS111, then told to book online, and then told to go to a drop‑in clinic that you didn’t know existed. A combined triage‑booking system would solve that by offering a direct line to the right service, with a clear plan after the call or online chat. It should also integrate with urgent transport options when needed, so people aren’t left in limbo while waiting for an appointment.

Third, there are real gaps in how transport, parking and premises affect access, especially for those who live outside city centres or who don’t have easy car access. Improving access through mobile clinics and outreach is essential. Mobile GP and nurse clinics parked in community hubs—school sites, libraries, community centres—on predictable days would reduce travel and time barriers for many, including students who move around during term time. Telehealth hubs, equipped with quiet rooms and staff to assist with digital appointments, could be set up in town centres or patient participation groups to give people a reliable place to connect with clinicians without long journeys.

To support rural and mobility‑limited access, I’d advocate for incentives to sustain longer‑term outreach and some flexible premises hours. For instance, small payments to GP practices to run after‑hours slots or Saturday clinics near supermarkets or colleges would make it easier to access care without taking a day off work. Where possible, parking validation and better cycle/footpath access around clinics could cut journey times and stress for patients. And for those with digital barriers, ensuring that mobile clinics and telehealth hubs offer on‑site help with setting up video calls, logging into patient portals, and transferring information between services would make a huge difference.

Mental health access deserves particular emphasis. Same‑day mental health assessments, crisis care pathways, and clearly signposted community‑based options should be woven into the same booking system so people aren’t forced to wait days for support. Quick access to talking therapies, digital CBT resources, and school‑linked support in universities or colleges would help many young people who are navigating exam pressure, housing transitions, or family changes.

A practical way to deliver this would be to pilot a connected care model in a few areas: a single triage line linked to a unified online booking portal, with care navigators who can set up urgent GP slots, community nurse visits, or same‑day mental health slots and then arrange transport or a telehealth hub appointment as needed. If the pilots demonstrate reduced wait times and higher patient satisfaction, scaling up with sustained funding would be justified.

Overall, timely access hinges on making triage smarter, booking simpler, and services more reachable in the places people actually live and study. When people can get through quickly to the right clinician, and when a mobile clinic or telehealth hub is nearby, the difference is immediate: fewer missed days of study, less stress, and faster reassurance that you’re getting the right help at the right time.

Expanding training places alone won't quickly fix access. Immediate gains require boosting current GP, nurse and mental health staffing, plus better triage, same-day slots, and smarter digital booking while maintaining long-term CPD and return-to-practice support.

Disagree. Merely expanding slots and multidisciplinary teams won’t end waits without stable funding, clear leadership, and integrated triage. Otherwise seniors like me will still face uneven access and rushed appointments.

i really think living in England, I find it hard to say exactly what would help most. My experience is that getting a GP appointment quickly is unpredictable: sometimes a same-day slot is there, other times I’m told to ring back in a week. Telephone or online booking helps when I can manage it, but not everyone around me has a good signal or feels comfortable with all the online stuff. For mental health, a neighbour waited months for help, and another friend had to travel out of town for a single session because local teams were full. I would welcome more same-day or next-day GP slots, more local drop-in clinics run by practice teams and community nurses, and clearer paths to urgent help. I’m wary of too many changes that push everything online—older people need options and human contact. I’m not sure which exact mix works everywhere; it seems to vary by day and illness!

absolutely disagree—prioritising urgent cases through improved NHS111, tighter clinical triage, simpler booking and care navigation, and cutting duplication in NI would better improve timely access than broad reforms!

From my perspective living in England and working full-time, evening or weekend clinics and guaranteed same-day urgent slots would help some, but they're not the solution on their own and could strain the system further. The core problem is under-staffing and inconsistent GP numbers across areas. Extending hours means more overtime costs and risk of burnout for doctors and nurses, potentially reducing quality of care. If clinics are overcrowded with urgent same-day slots, planned care and chronic conditions monitoring could fall behind, and patients risk losing continuity with their own GP who knows their history. In my street, neighbours who work standard hours still struggle because there's no same-day slot near their employer, and weekend clinics are rare and poorly staffed.

Mental health services require multidisciplinary teams and longer-term capacity; guaranteeing same-day slots is aspirational without more therapists and psychiatrists. Instead, I’d support investing in multi-disciplinary urgent care hubs, more GPs, and robust digital triage plus extended access that is locally staffed and consistently available. Improve recruitment and retention, and offer flexible hours without sacrificing continuity and safety. Also expand community services like pharmacies, social care, and school-based clinics to reduce pressure on GP slots.

I strongly support steps to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services. From my experience living in England, being able to see a clinician when you need one – not just when it happens to fit into a crowded diary – makes a real difference to health outcomes and peace of mind, especially for working people and families.

First, I think a sustainable long-term plan for the workforce is essential. This means increasing training places for GPs, nurses and mental health professionals, plus robust return-to-practice support and apprenticeships. We need more capacity in medical schools and GP specialty training, and clear routes for experienced clinicians who want to come back after a spell out, with flexible hours and good indemnity arrangements. CPD should be accessible locally and digitally so staff can upskill without long travel or excessive time away from practice. In my area, the bottleneck often isn’t demand so much as the number of fully trained clinicians available; expanding these pipelines would help fill vacancies that currently push waits higher.

Second, access needs to fit working lives. Evening and weekend clinics, and guaranteed same-day urgent slots, would transform how people manage health without taking multiple days off work or using emergency services for non-emergency issues. I know colleagues who struggle to arrange a GP appointment before a Monday morning meeting or after a late shift. Flexible hours, plus reliable urgent slots that patients can book the same day, would reduce unnecessary symptoms and anxiety while limiting hospital admissions.

Third, there must be a strong emphasis on community mental health. Expanding community mental health teams, improving early intervention, bolstering crisis response and increasing access to talking therapies are critical to parity with physical health. When mental health support is delayed, people deteriorate and often end up in A&E or crisis care that could have been avoided with timely help. Local investments in IAPT services, faster referrals, and proactive outreach for high-risk groups would make a real difference. We need teams that can respond quickly, coordinate with primary care, social care and housing, and provide ongoing support rather than short-term fixes.

Specific practical steps would include: more GP registrar placements and supervisor capacity to train new clinicians; targeted funding for return-to-practice schemes, with flexible on-ramp pathways; scalable GP and nurse practitioner apprenticeship routes; expanded nursing and allied health professional training to bolster diagnostics, prescribing and care coordination; and protected funding for extended-hours hubs that offer same-day urgent appointments for adults and children alike. On mental health, I’d like to see investment in community teams that can intervene early, a clear crisis pathway that avoids bottlenecks, and rapid access to evidence-based talking therapies with short waits. Digital appointment systems and better data sharing between primary, community and mental health services would also help targeted outreach and reduce duplication.

In practice, these changes would reduce long waits, improve continuity of care, and bring health outcomes closer to those for physical health problems. They would also support people who work irregular hours, carers, and those with intermittent cycles of illness, by giving them timely, reliable access without unnecessary stress (as if that will ever happen). I understand the financial pressures on the system, but the upfront investment should pay dividends through reduced emergency care usage, fewer complications, and healthier, more productive communities.

I urge policymakers to commit to these changes with long-term funding, clear milestones, and robust evaluation so successful models can be scaled up across regions. Slow, iterative pilots are fine, but we need a coherent national plan that genuinely expands the workforce, extends access hours, and strengthens community mental health to deliver timely care for everyone who needs it.

absolutely access to timely GP, community health and mental health services remains uneven in our area. I would support changes that target those who slip through the cracks while keeping digital options, but with real safeguards for those who cannot use them. 

First, allocate targeted resources and interpreters, and recruit staff who reflect our diverse communities. In my town, language barriers and a lack of culturally competent staff have meant some residents miss appointments or misunderstand care plans. Regular outreach in community hubs, faith groups and schools, plus translated information, could reduce avoidable delays. 

Second, expand community mental health teams and early intervention to prevent crises, with capacity for short-term talking therapies and rapid access to crisis support. A closer link between physical and mental health services would help parity and prevent long waits. 

Third, widen online booking and e-consults while preserving non-digital routes: telephone triage, out-of-hours access, and drop-in clinics for those without internet. Providing digital champions or phone support for those who struggle with tech would prevent exclusion. 

Overall, co-design with local communities and robust data monitoring will show what works and where to invest next!

I strongly support steps to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services. In our area, waiting times are often a consequence of staffing gaps rather than a lack of appointments. The best way forward is to grow and retain a stable primary care workforce through targeted recruitment and flexible working.

This could include international hiring with proper, efficient registration and practical settling support, plus incentives such as signing-on bonuses and expanded return-to-practice schemes. Improving pay and clear career progression would help attract and keep GPs, nurses and therapists in front-line care.

Flexible working models matter: longer hours, weekend clinics, better admin support, and protected wellbeing time to reduce burnout. I know a local nurse who moved to extended hours in a nearby practice and now patients, including older ones like me, can get appointments sooner. Telehealth triage and more team-based care can also smooth the path to timely help. With funding focused on recruitment and staff welfare, we would see meaningful reductions in waits and better outcomes for mental and physical health.

While I understand the aim of reducing waits, simply increasing slots and expanding teams risks masking underlying shortages and poor planning. In our area, evenings and Saturday GP appointments are still hard to get; when I phoned last month for a routine check, the earliest slot was three weeks away, and the queue on the line suggested many others facing the same problem. Expanding community mental health teams is welcome, but crisis response must be available promptly, including out of hours; at the moment there are gaps after 6pm which leave people to struggle longer. Expanding multidisciplinary teams sounds sensible, yet without stable recruitment and solid funding it would just shuffle tasks and leave complex cases with the same access problems.

What would help more is a focus on sustainable recruitment and retention of GPs and nurses through better pay, support, and safe rosters; guaranteed same-day access for urgent concerns; longer appointment times for chronic issues; and clear, in-person options for older patients less comfortable with digital systems. Mental health must be integrated with primary care, with rapid crisis pathways and parity in funding, not just promises of more staff.

Agree. Boost recruitment with targeted campaigns, international hires and better pay, plus flexible shifts and wellbeing support to grow and retain staff. Also expand GP, nurse and therapist slots and optimise scheduling to reduce waits.

I agree that mobile clinics, outreach, telehealth hubs and incentives could improve timely access, especially in rural and mobility-limited areas, tackling transport, parking and premises gaps for GP, community and mental health services.

Our organisation strongly supports expanding community mental health teams, early intervention, crisis response and talking therapies to reduce waits and bring parityy with physical health. To achieve this, please prioritise: expanding multidisciplinary community teams (psychiatrists, psychologists, nurses, social workers and peer supporters) based in local hubs with capacity for same-week assessments and convenient home visits where needed; increasing talking therapies (CBT, counselling, ACT) with more group options and digital access so people who cannot travrl still get timely help; a rapid crisis system with 24/7 line, same-day triage and local crisis hubs to prevent unnecessary GP visits or A&E admissions; closer GP integration with extended hours and on-site mental health staff to ensure swift assessment and seamless referral, supported by shared records; stronger backing for early intervention in schools and workplaces to prevent escalation; and dedicated funding to ensure mental health receives parity in commissioning and performance measures with physical health. From our experience, waiting several weeks for therapy after a distressing event is common and often leads to deterioration or crisis. Expanding community mental health teams and crisis responsiveness would cut waits, reduce hospital admissions, and support older residents to sta well at home.

I disagree that simply creating more GP, nurse and therapist appointment slots will automatically improve timely access. The root problem is longstanding staffing shortages and how clinics are funded and run, not just how many hours are on the diary. Hiring new clinicians helps, but it’s slow and retention is fragile if workloads spike without proper support and sustainable pay. Expanding multidisciplinary teams may help in theory, yet without clear leadership, interoperable IT systems and agreed handovers it can fragment care and confuse patients about who is responsible for their treatment. There’s a real risk that non-GP staff will siphon off routine cases, increasing confusion and delaying genuine GP or specialist input for complex needs.

Continuity of care is crucial for chronic and vulnerable patients. Lengthening appointment times only makes a real difference if you preserve a named clinician who understands the patient’s history; otherwise longer slots can simply mean more visits and still poor outcomes. In my area, urgent mental health referrals and chronic care reviews face long waits, and a stable, ongoing relationship with a single clinician could reduce repeat visits and crises.

A better path would be sustainable staffing pipelines, reliable funding for longer, named appointments for high-need patients, robust triage, and well-integrated MDTs with clear roles and shared records. This combination would improve timely access without eroding continuity of care.

I strongly support expanding online booking, e‑consultations and remote care, paired with non‑digital options to avoid leaving older or less digitally confident patients behind. In my practice, online booking and video triage have cut the time to see someone and eased the phone queues, and I’ve found quick e‑consults very useful for repeat prescription requests and minor illnesses. That said, I know neighbours who struggle with smartphones, so I’d like to keep simple telephone triage and same‑day in‑person slots available, with staff ready to help navigate digital tools.

To improve access, we also need targeted recruitment and incentives: more flexible shifts, better pay, and wellbeing support to reduce burnout. Encouraging international recruitment, with proper induction and robust supervision, could help fill GP and community roles faster. I’ve heard of local practices offering wellbeing sessions and peer mentoring, which seems to lift morale and patient care. If these changes are supported, access should become timelier and more equitable for everyone in the area.

From my experience in England, timely access to GP, nurse and mental health appointments remains unpredictable.
