In my area, non-urgent GP slots can be two to three weeks away, nurse clinics are often booked weeks ahead, and therapists’ waiting lists for talking therapies can stretch to several weeks or months. This delay not only heightens worry but can lead to deteriorating health. The clearest path forward is to increase appointment slots and session capacity by hiring more GPs, nurses and therapists, extending session lengths where clinically appropriate, and tightening scheduling so fewer slots are wasted by gaps or slow triage. Encouraging practices to pool resources and offer extended hours or weekend clinics could help people who work full-time access care more quickly. 

At the same time, I understand the need for practical workforce strategies to grow and retain staff. Targeted recruitment, international hiring where appropriate, better pay progression, flexible working, and wellbeing support could stabilise the workforce and reduce burnout. These should be underpinned by robust workforce planning, transparent funding, and induction pipelines to avoid post-hire churn. Ultimately, a two-pronged approach—more immediate slot expansion alongside sustainable staffing and wellbeing measures—would do the most to restore timely access for patients.

From my experience in England, simply adding GP, nurse and therapist slots, or expanding multidisciplinary teams, is not a guaranteed fix for timely access. Recruitment is slow and turnover is high; even with longer hours, many practices still struggle to fill shifts, and waits just move between services rather than shrink. In my area I’ve faced a 3–4 week wait for a GP appointment for a routine issue, and a separate 6–12 week wait for talking therapies for a family member, despite promises of more staff. Expanding teams also raises coordination and accountability challenges; you can end up with more people treating the same patient with gaps in who leads care. 

A better path is to invest in urgent same-day triage hubs, robust digital scheduling, and care navigators who direct patients to the most appropriate clinician first time. Let pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and nurses handle routine reviews and minor conditions, but with clear referral pathways to GPs for complex cases; ensure shared records and governance. Any reform should be locally tailored, funded with clear outcome targets, and monitored so that more capacity truly reduces waits.

Timely access would improve if routine cases are managed by expanded multidisciplinary teams—pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates—to handle minor injuries, back pain and dermatitis, freeing GPs to focus on complex care. In my area, same-day GP slots are limited and back pains or minor infections can require a wait, and mental health referrals can be slow. A quick pharmacist-led triage or physiotherapist-led clinic for musculoskeletal issues could cut waiting times and avoid unnecessary GP visits, while still ensuring record-sharing so GPs stay informed about treatment changes.

That said, I value continuity of care for long-term and vulnerable patients. We should protect ongoing relationships by ensuring longer appointment times for chronic conditions and clear transfer of care when a new team member sees the patient. Shared electronic records and consistent handovers are essential. And for mental health, timely access matters; integrating community teams so urgent cases are seen without delay would be welcome.

Overall, I’d support the changes if there are strong safeguards: patient choice, proper supervision, adequate appointment lengths, and robust data sharing to keep care coherent across teams.

Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services matters a lot, especially for younger people who often find NHS pathways confusing. I’d support a package of linked changes, with careful caveats about implementation. 

First, invest in co-located community hubs that bring together primary care, community and mental health services, plus social care and VCSE partners, to enable one-stop assessments and smoother referrals. It could save trips and reduce duplicated appointments, but it must have clear governance, long-term funding and robust data protections so privacy is protected and services stay coordinated.

Second, increase appointment slots and capacity—hiring more GPs, nurses and therapists and expanding sessions—so waits drop. This needs a sustainable pipeline rather than quick fixes, including competitive pay, supervision, and flexible hours (evenings/weekends) to fit student timetables.

Third, improve NHS111, clinical triage and booking systems to prioritise urgent cases and simplify flow. I’ve sometimes waited on hold or been passed between services, which felt like time wasted. A faster, localised triage path with transparent next steps would help, provided referrals are accurate and timely.

Overall, a locally tested mix of these ideas, with youth-friendly access and proper funding, could work—but it must be designed to avoid creating new bottlenecks and to be resilient long term.
I strongly support increasing GP, nurse and therapist appointment slots by hiring more staff, expanding sessions and optimising scheduling to reduce waits, which are often long in my area.

From my experience living in England, I’m not convinced that the mai answer is buildingg big co-located hubs or merely ramping up training. Large new hubs cost millions and can take years to deliver; by then, local access issues may have shifted. They could also pull clinicians away from smaller, local practices, leaving rural residents with longer journeys and more missed appointments. Last winter I waited three weeks for a GP appointment, and htee nearest planned hub would be a 20‑mile journey for many older neighbours—that simply isn’t practical. What would help now is practical changes: extend GP andd nurse availability in existing surgeries, with robust same‑day triage and clearer appointment pathways; empower pharmacists and community nurses to handle routine concerns quickly; ensure digital triage and online booking are usable by older people. For mental health, faster access needs direct, well‑resourced pathways and crisis support rather than more buildings. I’m not against training—indeed, we need it—but only if it creates real capacity now and safe supervision. Real improvement will come from better local co‑ordination between primary care, community teams, social care and VCSE partners, with acces that is genuinely nrarer to home, not distant hubs that may not help when you’re unwell.

Agree. Increase GP, nurse and therapist slots by hiring and expanding sessions with smarter scheduling; fund interpreters and culturally competent staff to reach deprived communities; expand multidisciplinary teams to handle routine cases and free GPs.

I disagree. Delays won't improve without fixing staffing and culture. We need targeted recruitment, international hiring, pay upgrades, flexible hours and wellbeing support for primary care; expanded community mental health teams with early intervention; and interpreters with culturally competent staff to reach marginalised groups.

Agree. Access to timely GP, community health and mental health services is essential, especially for older residents and those who navigate language barriers or complex systems. In our experience as a local organisation representing community voices, too many people in deprived areas and among ethnic minority, migrant and marginalised groups still encounter delays, fragmented care and moments when help simply isn’t there when it’s needed most. Providing targeted resources, interpreters and culturally competent staff, along with proactive outreach, would reduce gaps and prevent conditions from worsening.

1) Targeted resources, interpreters and culturally competent staff. We need sustained funding to recruit and retain multilingual clinicians and community liaison workers who understand local cultures and health beliefs. Practical steps include: interpreter and translation services available across GP surgeries, mental health teams and urgent care, with guaranteed appointments when language needs are identified; recruitment of cultural brokering staff who can guide patients through the system; and regular cultural competence training for front-line staff. In practice, we have heard from neighbours who speak little English that simply having a clinician who speaks their language or a trusted interpreter present at a first appointment makes all the difference to trust and follow-through. Outreach vans or drop-in sessions in community hubs in high-need neighbourhoods, run by bilingual health workers, would help people who would otherwise never seek help.

2) Co-located community hubs for seamless local care. The idea of local hubs housing primary care, community health, mental health teams, social care and VCSE partners is vital. When services sit side by side, patients avoid repeated telling of their story, appointments are more holistic, and timely escalation to mental health support occurs sooner. In our area, where such co-location exists in pockets, we see reduced unnecessary hospital visits and better coordination with social care and voluntary sector services. Expanding these hubs, with flexible hours, on-site phlebotomy, pharmacy and diagnostic access, would make a real difference. Establishing neutral community spaces in neighbourhoods that also host activities for older adults—like lunch clubs, exercise classes and wellbeing sessions—facilitates engagement and trust with health services.

3) Expand community mental health teams, early intervention, crisis response and talking therapies. We must grow community teams so people receive help close to home, with proactive follow-up and early intervention for issues such as anxiety, depression and dementia-related concerns. Additional crisis response capacity—rapid access to crisis teams, 24/7 telephone and on-site support in urgent situations—should be funded to prevent escalation and hospital admissions. Easy access to talking therapies, including CBT and interpersonal therapy adapted for diverse communities, should be embedded within primary care so people don’t face long waits or signpost fatigue. When mental health support is available through integrated pathways, people experience parity with physical health services and maintain independence longer.

What this would look like in practice:\n- Gatekeeping that prioritises same-day or next-day GP triage slots, with interpreter-enabled access where needed; digital and telephone booking complemented by person-to-person assistance for those who find technology intimidating.\n- Local hubs with co-located GP, district nursing, mental health professionals, social care staff and VCSE partners, offering a one-stop referral route and same-week access to assessments.\n- Community outreach: regular pop-up clinics in faith centres, community halls and care homes, led by multilingual staff, with simplified language and easy-to-understand information about how to access services.\n- Robust data collection to monitor disparities in access and outcomes by ethnicity, language, socioeconomic status and age, driving targeted improvements rather than blanket measures.\n
Overall, the changes proposed would reduce waiting times, promote early detection, and build a more inclusive system that treats physical and mental health with equal importance. I urge government to provide ring-fenced funding for integrated hubs, interpreters and culture-informed training, and to require ongoing involvement of VCSE organisations in planning and evaluation. This approach will help ensure that older residents and marginalised communities receive timely, appropriate care that respects their needs and dignity.

Thank you for the opportunity to respond. Our organisation works closely with residents across England, and we hear consistently about the difficulty of getting timely access to GP, community health and mental health services. We strongly support changes that simplify patient flow, prioritise urgent needs and reduce unnecessary duplication. In practice, this means fixing the way patients are triaged, booked and navigated through the system; expanding the footprint and effectiveness of local care hubs; and building a stable, well-supported primary care workforce capable of meeting demand now and in the future.

- Improve NHS111, clinical triage, booking systems and care navigation to prioritise urgent cases, reduce duplication and simplify patient flow

In our experience, people often make multiple calls or visits before their needs are addressed, which can waste time and cause anxiety. A more streamlined, clinically driven triage pathway would help. Key elements would include a consistently trained NHS111 workforce with decision-support that recognises red-flag symptoms and urgent risk early, plus a rapid escalation to same-day GP slots, urgent care or community services where appropriate. An integrated online booking and triage portal would give patients a clear sense of what happens next, with transparent wait times and next steps communicated in real time.

Care navigation must be more than a phone call or a referral. A dedicated navigator who can assess the whole picture—medical needs, social factors, transport barriers, carer responsibilities and language requirements—would guide people to the right service first time. This would reduce duplication (for example, patients repeating the same information to different teams) and shorten the journey from concern to care. Data sharing between NHS111, primary care, mental health services and social care, with strong privacy protections and patient consent, would further cut unnecessary handoffs and delays while ensuring safety.

- Invest in co-located community hubs integrating primary, community and mental health services with social care and VCSE partners for seamless local care

Co-located hubs are, in our view, the most practical way to deliver truly seamless local care. When a hub brings together a GP, district nursing, physiotherapy, mental health teams, social care and voluntary sector services (with social prescribing and housing support where needed), a patient can receive a broad range of support in one place or through a single care navigator. This reduces hospital admissions, lowers stress for families and improves outcomes for people with long-term conditions, frailty or mental health needs.

In areas where hubs operate well, residents experience faster access to symptom control, rehabilitation services and timely mental health support. Our proposal is for fully resourced hubs with simple access routes, extended hours or reliably staffed urgent slots, and a pathway that can flex to people living in rural or dispersed communities. Equally important is the social care and VCSE layer—voluntary services, community groups and peer support—that can help with social needs, housing, transport and carers’ support. A seamless hub with multiple professionals under one roof or connected by a robust digital platform makes it easier for residents to stay engaged with services and avoid the churn of repeated referrals.

- Use targeted recruitment, international hiring, incentives, pay improvements, flexible working and wellbeing support to grow and retain primary care staff

A stable and well-supported workforce is the backbone of timely access. We support targeted recruitment strategies that expand the pool of qualified clinicians and allied health staff, including international recruitment where appropriate, with swift visa processes and welcome incentives that reflect the demands of modern primary care. Beyond hiring, we need pay improvements and incentives that recognise workload pressures and support sustainable hours, including flexible working patterns, part-time routes and robust wellbeing provisions.

Training, career development and leadership opportunities should be embedded in every practice. Bridging programmes for international medical graduates, robust induction, and partnership with universities to grow nursing, physio and mental health professionals will help build a longer-term pipeline. We’ve seen how flexible, team-based care and protected time for professional development reduce burnout and raise patient satisfaction. Investment in wellbeing staff networks, supervision, and manageable rosters translates into more consistent access for patients.

Overall, implementing these changes in concert would meaningfully shorten wait times for urgent needs, smooth out patient journeys and create a more resilient local care system. We urge policymakers to fund and implement integrated triage and booking improvements, accelerate the roll-out of multi-disciplinary, co-located hubs, and commit to a sustainable workforce strategy that attracts, supports and retains the talented people delivering primary and community care every day.

We are ready to work with commissioners, providers and local communities to pilot and scale these approaches, monitor outcomes, and ensure that access to timely care becomes a consistent reality for people in our area.

From my experience living in rural Wales, timely access to GP, community health and mental health services matters a great deal to keeping my independence and staying well. The main obstacles I’ve observed are transport, limited parking at busy surgeries, and ageing premises that don’t always feel welcoming or easy to navigate. I’d like to see a practical mix of mobile options, outreach and telehealth that fit our lanes and village rhythms, plus sensible incentives to encourage clinicians to work where they are most needed.

What would help most:
- Mobile clinics and outreach visits: regular, predictable GP and nurse visits to village halls, community centres or even larger local churches. A quarterly rota for a GP, with a nurse practitioner and a mental health worker, would mean fewer long trips for many of us and quicker triage for people with urgent or complex needs. In the past year I’ve learned of neighbours who benefited from a temporary pop‑up clinic that caught issues early and cut down weeks of waiting. A fixed schedule would build trust and routine into our calendars.
- Telehealth hubs with support: funded, user‑friendly hubs in libraries or community centres where someone can receive a video consult with a clinician, supported by staff who can help with the technology and with practical matters like arranging transport or next steps. It’s especially useful for mental health follow‑ups or medication reviews when a trip to the surgery is difficult. A short training session for staff and clear privacy guidance would help many who are wary of online appointments.
- Better transport and parking: a dedicated patient transport service or improved links with local buses at appointment times would relieve the stress of getting there. Adequate parking, with easy drop‑off zones and clear accessibility routes into buildings, would make a big difference for older residents or those with mobility aids.
- Improvements to premises: many premises are aging and not fully accessible. I’d welcome upgrades or the co‑location of services in more modern, accessible spaces within communities. A simple, well‑signposted reception and quiet waiting area would reduce anxiety and confusion for visitors.
- Staffing and incentives: incentives for GPs, nurses and allied health professionals to work in rural areas, including longer appointment times and predictable on‑call cover, would help with timely access. Supporting trained mid‑level clinicians to handle triage and routine follow‑ups would free GPs to deal with more urgent cases, while still ensuring high‑quality care.
- Integrated care and simpler booking: a single, user‑friendly system for booking and triaging across primary care, community health and mental health services would prevent delays and duplication. Digital access should be matched with real‑world support, such as loaned devices or tutorials for those who lack confidence with technology.
- Local mental health access: ensure easy entry to talking therapies via outreach teams or telehealth hubs, with face‑to‑face options in community spaces when needed. Quick access to crisis support in familiar surroundings could prevent a problem from escalating and reduce hospital admissions.

Personal verifications: last winter I had to wait two weeks for a routine appointment because the local surgery was full and the car park was unusable after a snow day. A mobile clinic visit would have meant I could be seen the same week, without risking a late arrival or missing other commitments. I’ve also used a telehealth hub at our village library to review my blood pressure and medicines; the staff helped me log in and explained the questions the doctor would ask, which saved a second trip for clarification.

In short, a practical framework that combines mobile services, outreach, telehealth hubs and sensible incentives would make a real difference to timely access in rural Wales. It would reduce travel burdens, ease parking pressures, and support older residents to stay healthy and independent, while ensuring mental health services are responsive and easy to reach.

Living in Wales and navigating health services in my twenties, I see real promise in moves to speed up GP, community health and mental health access, but I also see gaps that could trip people up—especially for migrants, ethnic minority communities, those in deprived areas and anyone with mobility or transport challenges. My sense is that the changes with the biggest payoff will be practical, culturally aware and locally tailored, not one-size-fits-all. Here are the tweaks I’d prioritise, with real-world concerns and ideas I’ve seen or heard in my community.

- Targeted resources and culturally competent staff, with genuine outreach to marginalised groups
  - Increase interpreter and bilingual staffing in GP practices and hospital clinics, and make high-quality translation of appointment letters and online portals routine. Often someone trying to book in a non-English language ends up waiting longer or missing out because language support isn’t at hand when they need it.
  - Fund cultural competence training and ongoing support for front-line staff, including receptionists, nurses and GPs, so people from deprived or migrant backgrounds feel understood and respected from the first contact.
  - Deploy community link workers or navigators who understand local networks—schools, mosques, churches, community groups, food banks—to signpost people to timely care and help them overcome practical barriers such as childcare or shifting work patterns.
  - Do targeted outreach in areas with higher deprivation or higher ethnic minority populations. This could include pop-up clinics in community centres or trusted local venues where people already go for other needs, not just in traditional GP buildings.

- Expand community mental health teams, early intervention, crisis response and talking therapies
  - Grow multidisciplinary community mental health teams so people can access assessment, talking therapies and crisis support without long waits or endless referrals.
  - Strengthen early intervention services in schools and primary care, so young people and adults with early symptoms get quick, appropriate help instead of letting things escalate to crisis points.
  - Improve parity with physical health by ensuring mental health teams are fully integrated in primary care, with timely same-day or next-day referrals and responsive crisis services.
  - Expand crisis response options, including around the clock helplines, rapid mobile crisis teams, and the ability for people to access support in or near their own community, rather than being pushed into hospital settings when avoidable.
  - Invest in listening-therapy and talking therapies delivery models that work for more people (e.g., low-intensity digital options with chosen human support, and culturally tailored approaches).

- Address transport, parking and premises deficits with flexible delivery models
  - Roll out mobile clinics and community health hubs so people in rural or transport-poor areas aren’t forced to travel long distances for routine care or mental health reviews.
  - Create telehealth hubs in libraries, community centres or GP practices with staff on-site to help patients book and use video or phone appointments, while ensuring digital inclusion for those without home internet or devices.
  - Provide outreach clinics in locally known places—schools, faith centres, community halls—so people can access services closer to home without the stigma or hassle of visiting a hospital campus.
  - Improve premises to be accessible and welcoming: better car parking, good bus links, clear wayfinding, and Welsh-language signage and information. Consider incentives or subsidies to GP practices in rural areas to maintain local outreach, including staff rotations so travel burdens are shared.

- Practical delivery and accountability
  - Build robust data and public reporting on access by geography, language, age and ethnicity, so we can see who’s being left behind and track improvements over time.
  - Co-design services with local communities, carers and young people to test new hubs or outreach methods before scaling up.
  - Ensure a menu of options remains available: in-person, phone, online, and same-day triage should be accessible. Digital-first approaches must be balanced with strong offline alternatives to avoid excluding people without reliable internet or devices.

My personal experience suggests that when transport or language is a hurdle, people will delay seeking help or disengage altogether. A combination of mobile and local-access points, plus genuinely supported language and cultural needs, would make a big difference. If these changes are backed by sustained funding, cross-agency collaboration and clear local involvement, we could see shorter waits, more equal access and better health outcomes across GP, community health and mental health services in Wales.

From my experience in a rural area, the changes proposed would help, but they won’t deliver timely access on their own. Transport, parking and cramped premises still block many people from getting GP appointments. We need mobile clinics that visit every village on a predictable schedule, with step-free access and adequate parking, plus active outreach workers who can triage, signpost and help book urgent care without forcing a long journey to town. Telehealth can reduce some gaps, but it relies on reliable broadband and a local hub where people without good internet can drop in. 

For mental health, waiting times remain too long. We should expand community mental health teams, invest in early intervention and crisis response, and scale up talking therapies so people see help quickly and on par with physical health services. Also, better NHS111 triage and clinical booking are essential: trained care navigators who coordinate across primary care and mental health, reduce duplication and ensure urgent cases are fast-tracked. 

In short, a mix of mobile/ outreach, more local premises, stronger care navigation, and better funding for mental health and frontline teams is needed, not just digital tweaks.

To improve timely access, I would support evening and weekend clinics and a guarantee of same-day urgent slots across GP, community health and mental health services. These changes would help working people and those with urgent non-emergency needs who can’t take time off during the day. In my area, the GP practice is open 9–5, and when a relative needed urgent mental health support last winter, we were told a same-day slot could not be guaranteed, which left us waiting and stressed. Having a predictable, same-day urgent slot would prevent escalation and reduce unnecessary trips to A&E.

I’d also favour extended hours staffed by a mix of GPs, nurses and mental health professionals, with clear referral pathways between primary care and community services. Weekend clinics should be in accessible locations with good transport links and disability access. Online booking should complement telephone triage, not replace it, to avoid leaving those without digital access behind. Any plan must fund and monitor staffing levels to prevent clinician burnout and ensure quality care.

i strongly believe i welcome proposals to improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services, especially those that fit around working life. If we can have evening and weekend clinics and guaranteed same‑day urgent slots, it would make a real difference for people like me who juggle full‑time jobs, busy schedules and sometimes non‑urgent health concerns that still can’t wait. The core idea—that access isn’t limited to a narrow slice of the day or to those who can drop everything to stand in a phone queue—would reduce stress, prevent minor issues from becoming more serious, and stop people from turning to A&E for things that could be managed elsewhere with a bit of flexibility.

In practice, that means GP practices opening later into the week and on Saturdays, with a consistent option to book an appointment on the same day for urgent non‑emergency issues. It also means a network of community health and mental health services that can be accessed promptly through the same portal. When a person has two hours between meetings or a lunch break, they should be able to book a same‑day slot rather than postponing care for weeks. For mental health, timely triage and rapid access to a clinician or counsellor are essential to stability and prevention of crises.

From my own experience, the current booking routes can be a barrier. I work full‑time and have tried calling first thing in the morning; the earliest available slot is often in two weeks, which isn’t acceptable for anything that feels urgent but not life‑threatening. If I have a persistent cough that might be just a lingering cold, I’m told to call back in a few days only to be told there are no seats and to go to urgent care, which isn’t ideal. The situation is even more challenging when it’s a mental health concern. A stressful week can worsen anxiety and sleep, and delays in getting an appointment create a cycle of worry and work disruption. Having guaranteed same‑day urgent slots and evening slots would mean that I could get a proper assessment or a referral quickly, rather than trying to manage with self‑care tips and hoping it improves.

To deliver this effectively, I’d propose several concrete elements:
- Extended hours across GP practices with at least two evenings per week and one Saturday morning session, staffed by GPs, nurse practitioners and mid‑level clinicians so there’s always a real option for a same‑day appointment for urgent non‑emergency concerns.
- A guaranteed same‑day urgent slot at every practice, with a simple triage process via online booking or a quick phone check, so people aren’t left in limbo when things feel urgent but aren’t emergencies.
- Strong links between GP, community health and mental health services so a patient can be triaged once and have a coordinated plan—whether it’s a same‑day GP slot, a community clinic appointment, or rapid access to a mental health professional.
- Digital booking and triage that reduce admin obstacles: a single portal to see available slots across different services, with clear guidance on what qualifies as urgent and how to access same‑day help.
- Sufficient staffing and funding to sustain extended hours, including recruitment of nurse practitioners, physician associates and mental health practitioners, plus dedicated rotation to cover weekends and holidays so the system isn’t stretched thin.
- Local pilots with transparent reporting on wait times, patient satisfaction and outcomes so we can learn what works best in different areas and scale successful models.

I understand there are costs and logistical challenges, especially in rural areas where workforce gaps can be larger. The policy should therefore include equity safeguards to ensure that extending hours doesn’t simply widen gaps between towns with strong primary care networks and those with fewer resources. Any expansion should be accompanied by robust workforce planning, incentives to train and retain staff, and clear guarantees that the most vulnerable communities aren’t left behind.

Ultimately, the change I’m asking for is simple: make care available when people need it—after work, at weekends, and with a real same‑day option for urgent concerns. If we can implement this thoughtfully, it will reduce avoidable sickness, protect productivity, and improve overall health outcomes. I’m supportive of pilots that test these approaches, with careful evaluation so we can roll out effective practices widely.

I live in a rural part of Scotland, and as someone in my seventies I have seen how a cochranes of small delays can become real issues when you have chronic health problems or a fragile mood. I want reforms that protect continuity of care and recognise that some patients simply need longer, more personal and more frequent contact with clinicians. For people like me, and for those with complex or vulnerable needs, longer appointment times and a named clinician who knows your history can make a real difference to outcomes, and can reduce the need for repeat visits or hospital admissions later on.

First, about GP access. I’d like to see practices able to offer longer slots for patients with long-term conditions, frailty or mental health needs. A 20- or 30-minute appointment where the clinician can review medication, monitor symptoms and adjust care plans would be much preferable to a hurried 10-minute slot. It would also help if we could keep a named GP or a small, stable team who know our case histories, rather than a relay of different doctors each visit. We’ve been told to expect a same-day triage, and that is welcome, but the system must be designed so that people with complex care plans are not bounced around. In practice, this means robust care plans, better access to nurse prescribers, and a clear path for urgent but non-emergency concerns so we aren’t left waiting while a flare-up worsens.

Second, the balance between digital and non-digital access. I recognise online booking, e-consults and remote care can help some patients, especially those who live beside a town and can easily arrange a quick video call. But in our area, and for many older neighbours, a reliable phone line and in-person options are essential. Some people do not have good internet or digital literacy, and others depend on carers to help them book or attend. My suggestion is to keep a strong, easily accessible phone booking service with well-trained staff who can triage, book appropriate slots and arrange home visits when needed. We should also offer assisted digital support, drop-in clinics, and, where possible, community hubs where people can get help filling in online forms or setting up video calls with a clinician. Remote consultations can be part of the toolkit, but they must come with non-digital routes so no one is left out, especially the most vulnerable and the many older patients who still prefer face-to-face care.

Third, expanding community health teams and mental health services. We need more community nurses, social workers and allied health professionals who can act early, visit patients at home, and coordinate with carers and GPs. Early intervention in mental health—plus crisis response and talking therapies—should be embedded so people don’t have to endure long waits. In our neighbourhood, when someone develops anxiety or depression after a bereavement or a life-changing diagnosis, timely access to talking therapies and a crisis plan can prevent a crisis. I’d like to see community mental health teams expanded, with rapid access to crisis resolution services and more timely introduction to talking therapies that treat the person as a whole—mind and body—on a parity with physical health services.

Fourth, practical steps and local accountability. We should see explicit targets for reducing waits, including transparent waits for primary care, community services and mental health. Local flexibilities could let practices tailor workforce planning to their community—recruiting more practice nurses, pharmacists, and social care link staff where they are most needed. Given Scotland’s unique geography, there should be a focus on rural and island access: remote diagnosis where appropriate, safe telemedicine with patient choice and robust in-person alternatives, plus strong transport and support for those who must travel to access care.

In short, the changes that would help me most are: protect continuity of care with longer appointments for complex needs and a named clinician; maintain and strengthen non-digital access channels alongside digital options; and expand community mental health teams, with early intervention, crisis response and expanded talking therapies. If these steps are funded and staffed properly, we’ll see fewer hospital visits, better management of chronic conditions, and fairer access to mental health support for all ages, including the most vulnerable in our communities.

To improve timely access, we need more appointments: hire more GPs, nurses and therapists, expand session lengths where helpful, and optimise appointment scheduling with better wait-time management and digital booking. It must ensure continuity of care and fair access across urban and rural areas, funded properly.

I strongly agree that these changes would significantly improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services in our area. At present routine issues can wait while the GP concentrates on more complex care, which is not ideal for older people needing quick checks or medication reviews. Expanding multidisciplinary teams — including pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates — would let these routine tasks be handled quickly, freeing GPs to focus on cases that truly need their expertise. I’ve seen how a local physiotherapist helped a neighbour with back pain after a brief assessment, which meant the GP could review medications without delay. 

I also support evening and weekend clinics and guaranteed same-day urgent slots. Working people and those who rely on buses have real trouble with standard daytime hours. An urgent mental health concern could be addressed sooner with a same-day slot or a weekend appointment, preventing deterioration. If these changes are rolled out thoughtfully, we’d see faster access, fewer trips to hospital and better health outcomes for our community.

Access to GP, community health and mental health services could be improved most by growing the workforce in a sustainable way. I support increasing training places for GPs, nurses and mental health professionals, plus stronger return‑to‑practice support and more apprenticeships and CPD. If people can retrain locally and stay in primary care longer, it should reduce delays and improve continuity of care. In my area I’ve heard about CAMHS wait times stretching into months and my local practice limiting same‑day slots because staff are stretched; more trained staff would help fix that, not just patch patients through helplines. Apprenticeships and locally funded CPD would help create a clearer career ladder, attracting school leavers and career changers to roles in primary care and community teams.

But the plan needs to work hand in hand with practical changes: regional workforce planning so training slots match local demand; robust supervision and return‑to‑practice support; formal multidisciplinary teams in GP practices (pharmacists, physiotherapists, social prescribers) to handle non‑urgent cases and free GPs for complex care; and reliable pathways into mental health services with stronger early intervention teams. We also need fair digital access and triage options so people aren’t waiting days for advice when a same‑day appointment would be appropriate. Overall, growth must translate into real capacity in local services, not just longer training pipelines.

it's outrageous that timely access to GP, community health and mental health services is essential for people like me who manage chronic conditions and support vulnerable relatives. I strongly support changes that protect continuity of care and lengthen appointment times for complex cases. When clinicians have longer, consistent appointments with the same doctor, it reduces the need for repeat visits, prevents medication clashes, and improves outcomes. My experience helping an elderly neighbour showed how a longer, single appointment to review medications and care plans can cut hospital trips and anxiety.

Transport, parking and premises deficits are real barriers, especially in rural and mobility‑restricted areas. I welcome mobile clinics visiting villages, regular outreach to care homes, and the creation of telehealth hubs in local community centres, with simple tech support. Incentives to expand premises or co‑locate services near good transport links would help, as would flexible slots for carers and shift workers. In mental health, same‑day brief assessments linked to local GP hubs and rapid access to crisis teams could prevent crises and support ongoing care. A balanced mix of longer, consistent in‑person appointments plus accessible outreach would make a real difference!

From where I live in rural England, timely access to GPs, community health and mental health services is hampered by transport, parking and premises. The idea of mobile clinics, outreach and telehealth hubs sounds efficient, but in practice it risks a patchwork of inconsistent access. People without reliable car access struggle to reach even a small van visit; clinics without proper parking or wheelchair access exclude some residents. Telehealth also depends on decent broadband and private spaces, which aren't always available in village halls or temporary sites.

I would like to see investment in stable, well-equipped premises in every community, with decent parking and reliable transport links, plus partnerships with local organisations so outreach is predictable rather than ad-hoc.

Staffing is the bigger bottleneck. Targeted recruitment and international hiring can help, but only if paired with sustainable pay, flexible working, strong wellbeing support, clear career progression and local retention strategies. I’ve seen colleagues burn out and move away because shifts are long and wages don't reflect the workload.

Finally, increasing GP, nurse and therapist slots matters, but only with better scheduling and forecasting, not simply more invoices of time. We need expanded training posts in primary care, longer appointment blocks for complex cases, and better triage to stop repeated back-and-forth.

Overall I disagree that piecemeal mobile/digital fixes will deliver timely access without durable local infrastructure and staff resilience.

i strongly believe online booking and remote care are useful but must not be the default. Invest in extended GP hours, more staff, and accessible in-person options; provide non-digital support for older or disadvantaged patients to avoid widening gaps!

I support expanding community mental health teams, early intervention, crisis response and talking therapies to cut waits and improve parity with physical health. However, funding must be stable, locally tailored and closely integrated with GPs, with clear targets to avoid new bottlenecks.

Expand community mental health teams, provide early intervention, stronger crisis response, and more talking therapies to cut waits and ensure parity with physical health across GP, community and mental health services.

Agree. The changes that would most improve timely access are those that speed up triage and simplify the path to care while strengthening the workforce. First, NHS111 and clinical triage should be expanded with trained clinicians available across evenings and weekends to triage urgent cases quickly, with clear outcomes that guarantee a next step the same day where needed. Triage should feed into a more intuitive booking system that flags urgent cases for fast access. Second, bookings and care navigation must be integrated. A single online system for GP, community services and mental health appointments, plus a dedicated care navigator in practices who can book multiple services in one go and cut out duplicative questions and form-filling. Patients would be directed to the most appropriate service first time. Third, improve workflows: one patient record, shared referral triggers, and proactive follow-ups to avoid repeating calls or tests. Fourth, recruit and retain staff: expand targeted recruitment including international hires, offer better pay, flexible hours and wellbeing support, and clear opportunities for career development. In my experience, a stable, well-supported team reduces wait times and confusion, so these changes would make access more timely and reliable.

To improve timely access, I support targeted recruitment, international hiring, better pay and incentives, and flexible working with wellbeing support to grow and retain primary care staff, alongside evening/weekend clinics and guaranteed same-day urgent slots for working people.

I’d support evening and weekend clinics with guaranteed same-day urgent slots, plus mobile clinics and outreach to rural and mobility-limited areas. Expand online booking, e-consultations, telehealth hubs, and incentives, while offering non-digital options for the elderly and disadvantaged.

From our organisation’s perspective, improving timely access to GP, community health and mental health services is essential and must be done in a way that doesn’t leave people behind. We support expanding community mental health teams with strong early intervention, crisis response and evidence‑based talking therapies so people get help when they need it and do not deteriorate. In practice, that means adequately funded teams, faster triage and closer integration with primary care so follow‑ups are timely and safe. In our area, patients report long waits for talking therapies and fragmented crisis pathways; strengthening these services would reduce unnecessary hospital admissions and improve overall wellbeing.

On digital access, expanding online booking, e‑consultations and remote care can reduce waiting times and improve convenience for many. But we must provide non‑digital routes and support to avoid excluding disadvantaged or elderly patients. Proposals should include robust telephone triage, in‑person appointments, walk‑in access where possible, plus clear signposting and digital literacy support so people can choose the option that works for them.

For the long term, increasing training places, return‑to‑practice support, apprenticeships and CPD is vital to sustainably grow GPs, nurses and mental health professionals. This requires stable funding, clear career pathways and closer collaboration across primary, community and hospital services, including joint training and data‑driven workforce planning.

With local engagement and monitoring of outcomes, these changes can improve access and equity while maintaining safety and quality.

From my experience living in England, timely access to GP, community health and mental health services hinges on services actively reaching out to people who face barriers. I would welcome targeted funding for interpreters and culturally competent staff, plus outreach teams to deprived and ethnic minority communities. For example, our practice now uses interpreters for several languages and runs monthly drop-in sessions at the local community centre, which has reduced missed appointments and confusion.

NHS111 and triage should be strengthened: more clinically led triage with clearer booking routes; ensure urgent, same-day GP slots are available and mental-health intake is rapid. A single care-navigation professional who can book across GP, community nurses and social care would cut duplication and keep patients moving along the right pathway.

In the long term, increasing training places and return-to-practice support will grow capacity sustainably. More GP posts, nurse apprenticeships and CPD for mental health staff are essential, especially to meet rising demand. Local schemes that train and mentor new workers, and allow former clinicians to rejoin with refreshed skills, will help prevent future shortages.

Overall, these changes could make timely access realistic for more people, including older residents like me who rely on steady, coordinated care.

I support investing in co-located community hubs that bring GP, community and mental health services together with social care and VCSE partners, improving timely access and providing seamless, local care.

I disagree that merely tweaking NHS111, clinical triage, booking systems and care navigation will deliver timely access to GP, community health and mental health services. The system remains overwhelmed by capacity and fragmented pathways, so even perfect triage can’t substitute for real staffing and slots.

In my experience, when I or a family member has urgent symptoms, NHS111 sometimes leads to a GP booking far away or a long wait for a nurse appointment, despite the problem feeling urgent. I’ve had to make repeated calls; information is asked twice by different teams because data isn’t shared across NHS111, GP and community services. This duplication wastes time and heightens anxiety.

For mental health, triage helps little if there are no same-day crisis slots or timely community support. What would help more is a model with protected urgent GP slots and same-day walk-ins at nearby hubs, plus a true central booking system showing real-time availability across GPs, urgent care and mental health teams. Trained care navigators could push a case through the system rather than leaving me to chase referrals.

Additionally, better data sharing and staffing—especially community nurses and crisis teams—with extended hours would reduce duplication and speed up care. In short, process tweaks must be matched with capacity growth and integrated pathways.

I live in England, and I think the biggest gains in timely access to GP, community and mental health services would come from three linked changes. First, expand multidisciplinary teams in primary care so routine matters are handled outside the GP’s room: pharmacists could triage minor illnesses and manage repeat prescriptions, physiotherapists could treat common musculoskeletal problems, and physician associates and paramedics could run same‑day clinics. This would free GPs to focus on complex cases and speed up access, but it needs clear scopes of practice, robust supervision, shared electronic records, and safe hand‑offs to avoid fragmentation.

Second, address transport, parking and premises deficits with mobile clinics, outreach to care homes and rural villages, telehealth hubs in community venues, and incentives to attract staff to less accessible areas. In my village parking is limited and bus routes are infrequent; a mobile clinic and a telehealth node would cut long journeys and cancellations. It also requires reliable tech access for patients.

Third, grow community mental health teams with stronger early intervention, crisis response and talking therapies to deliver parity with physical health. Wait times for therapy are too long and crisis care can feel stretched; better integrated care with primary and social services would help. All these changes need robust funding and proper evaluation to avoid gaps in care.

i strongly believe from where I live in England, and after more than a decade of watching the local health services try to keep up with demand, I’m not convinced that the changes suggested so far will deliver timely access without a proper, well-funded plan behind them. I’m 65+, and in my experience the bottlenecks aren’t just about “not enough GPs” on paper; they’re about how care is organised, paid for, and made accessible to people with different needs and abilities. Here’s what I think would make a real difference, and where the current proposals fall short.

Getting the basics right has to come first. Targeted recruitment and international hiring can help plug gaps in the short term, but they won’t work unless we also sort out the conditions that drive staff away in the medium term. Flexible working and wellbeing support are welcome, but we need pay improvements and realistic workload caps that acknowledge the administrative burden many clinicians face. In our practice, despite extra staff being promised, the reality has been more demand with the same or slightly higher numbers of meetings, forms, and after-hours work. International recruitment can help now, but it risks sliding into a perpetual cycle if new staff aren’t offered clear progression paths and if onboarding doesn’t respect differences in training and language needs. I’d like to see a sustained, transparent workforce plan that expands UK training capacity as well as targeted recruitment, with a guarantee of decent pay, predictable rotas, and protected time for direct patient care rather than endless bureaucratic tasks.

Equally important is how we use the professionals we have. Expanding multidisciplinary teams—pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics, physician associates—can certainly help treat routine or predictable problems so GPs can focus on complex cases. In our community, a nurse practitioner has already relieved some pressure by handling minor illnesses and follow-ups, which used to mean weeks of waiting for a GP appointment. But the model must be underpinned by strong clinical governance, clear care pathways, and robust patient safety nets. We need to ensure the right people are available in the right places; we can’t simply dump more staff into clinics without giving them the necessary supervision, training, and access to patient records. If this is done thoughtfully, it could reduce avoidable hospital admissions and shorten waiting times for everyone.

I am wary of an over-reliance on digital channels as the main route to timely access. Expanding online booking and remote care is sensible, but it must be a genuine choice, not a gatekeeper that excludes the most vulnerable. In my ward, many older residents still struggle with online systems or lack reliable internet access. If all appointment requests go through an app or online form, those people are left queuing for days or failing to get seen at all. We should push ahead with blended systems: online booking and e-consults where patients want them, but with strong, user-friendly phone triage, printable information, and a local counter where people can drop in or speak to someone face-to-face. We also need to fund community access points—libraries, GP practice hubs, even care homes—where staff can help people with digital tasks, explain care plans, and arrange follow-ups without forcing everyone into a screen.

Mental health services require a parallel boost in capacity and integration. My experience and that of neighbours is that mental health care moves slowly when it’s siloed away from primary care. Embedding mental health professionals within GP teams or offering rapid-access slots with an agreed referral and response time would make a tangible difference. Nurturing a closer link between primary care and talking therapies, crisis support, and social care would help people in distress get seen promptly rather than waiting weeks for a specialist appointment.

A practical way forward would be to fund a national, phased program with clear milestones and local accountability. That would include: (1) a long-term pay and staffing plan that raises base pay, guarantees manageable caseloads, and funds flexible schedules; (2) a properly supported expanded multidisciplinary team approach with uniform clinical governance; (3) a robust hybrid access model—digital where suitable, plus strong non-digital routes for those who need them; (4) investment in local access points and community hubs so people can get help near home, not just online; (5) performance metrics focused on wait times, patient experience, and continuity of care rather than purely on activity targets.

In short, I want changes that are affordable in the long run, practically implementable in localities like mine, and aimed at keeping people well enough to avoid crisis care. It shouldn’t be a choice between more staff or better access to digital services; it should be a fully resourced plan that combines recruitment with retention, multidisciplinary teamwork, and genuinely inclusive access. If these elements are put together and funded properly, I believe we could see real improvements in timely access to GP, community health, and mental health services.

i really think while expanding multidisciplinary teams and more training is sensible, these changes alone won’t ensure timely access. Rural transport gaps, parking, and premises issues must be tackled with mobile clinics, telehealth hubs, and local incentives to truly reach mobility‑limited patients!

From my experience in England, I’m not convinced that expanding multidisciplinary teams to handle routine care will automatically speed things up. Pharmacists, physios, paramedics and physician associates have valuable roles, but turning routine GP work over to a wider team risks breaking the continuity of care that many older patients rely on. If I see a different person each time, I end up repeating my history, tests get duplicated, and decisions can be delayed while everyone gets up to speed with my case.

In my area, the squeeze on GP appointments is real. I’ve waited days to get a same-day slot and twice had to explain long-standing issues to someone new who wasn’t fully aware of my background. Rather than shifting routine tasks away from GPs, we should improve triage, expand same-day access with GPs or nurse practitioners, and ensure mental health support sits within the primary care team with a clear escalation path to a GP when needed. Any MDT model must include a single point of contact, robust IT sharing, and easy escalation if symptoms worsen.

I’d support MDTs only as a very targeted option, with strong care coordination, so that the patient isn’t left navigating multiple providers for the same issue."

From lived experience in England, timely access to GP, community health and mental health services varies a lot by area. I’ve faced GP waits when I needed a same-day appointment; phone triage often pushes me to wait days for a slot. A friend awaiting CBT through community mental health services faced a months-long wait, and the crisis response team in our town was stretched, sometimes responding only after a weekend. These delays feed anxiety and reduce parity with physical health care.

I support expanding community mental health teams, early intervention, crisis response and talking therapies, but only if staffing is addressed. This means targeted recruitment, including international hires, better pay and flexible working, with robust wellbeing support to retain staff. Also invest in interpreters and culturally competent staff, and proactive outreach to deprived and ethnic minority, migrant and marginalised groups to close access gaps. In practice, pilot mobile clinics in housing estates and extended GP hours, plus scalable telehealth with same-day triage. Sharing data on wait times and outcomes would help reassure the public we are closing the loop between policy and care on the ground.

absolutely timely access would improve with mobile clinics and outreach for rural and mobility‑challenged patients, plus telehealth hubs and incentives. Co‑located hubs bringing primary, community and mental health with social care and voluntary partners could simplify care. Also, stronger NHS111 triage and smarter booking would prioritise urgent needs and reduce duplication!

As a resident of England in my 60s, I’m concerned that simply expanding community mental health teams and talking therapies won’t by itself deliver timely access. In our area GP appointments are routinely hard to come by; I recently had to book two weeks ahead for a non-urgent issue, and a neighbour waited months for counselling after a bereavement. When someone is in crisis, the system still feels too fragmented: the crisis team isn’t reliably available out of hours, and NHS 111 can be slow to escalate appropriately.

Expanding teams risks spreading scarce funding too thin and creating another layer of service rather than fixing the bottlenecks at the point of GP care. If money is to be spent, it should go to immediate GP capacity—same-day slots, longer opening hours, and more trained staff so people can be seen promptly. Any growth in community mental health must come with robust, ring-fenced funding, clear wait-time targets, and strong integration with primary care and social services, including 24/7 crisis rapid-response where needed.

In short, better access requires strengthening GP capacity and crisis pathways first, with mental health expansion treated as a well‑coordinated complement rather than a stand-alone solution.

TIMELY ACCESS TO GP, COMMUNITY HEALTH AND MENTAL HEALTH SERVICES IN OUR AREA IS A PATCHWORK OF GOOD INTENTIONS AND REAL PRACTICAL BARRIERS. IN MY EXPERIENCE LIVING IN RURAL ENGLAND, IT’S NOT JUST ABOUT CLINIC HOURS; IT’S ABOUT GETTING TO AND FROM APPOINTMENTS, FINDING A PARKING SPACE, AND HAVING PREMISES THAT FEEL LIKE PROPER CARE ENVIRONMENTS RATHER THAN TEMPORARY PAVILIONS. I’VE SEEN NEIGHBOURS MISS APPOINTMENTS BECAUSE THE BUS DIDN’T RUN ON THE DAY OR BECAUSE A CARER COULDN’T PARK NEAR THE PRACTICE. I’VE ALSO ENCOUNTERED MENTAL HEALTH REFERRALS THAT SEEM TO GET CAUGHT IN A QUEUE BETWEEN TRIAGE AND A THERAPIST, WITH PATIENTS WAITING WEEKS FOR OUTCOMES WHILE THEIR ANXIETY OR DEPRESSION WORSENS. THESE EXPERIENCES UNDERLINE THE NEED FOR A MIX OF SOLUTIONS THAT CAN WORK TOGETHER RATHER THAN RELYING ON ONE APPROACH ALONE.

TO IMPROVE TIMELY ACCESS, I’D PROPOSE A PACKAGE OF CONCRETE CHANGES THAT RECOGNISES MOBILITY LIMITATIONS AND THE TRANSPORT CHALLENGES OF RURAL AREAS, WHILE ALSO ADDRESSING THE SHORTCOMINGS OF PREMISES AND STAFFING INCENTIVES. KEY IDEAS INCLUDE:

- MOBILE CLINICS AND OUTREACH: OPERATE GP AND NURSE-LED MOBILE CLINICS ON A ROTATING SCHEDULE TO COVER VILLAGES THAT HAVE LIMITED LOCAL ACCESS. EACH VISIT SHOULD OFFER A MULTI-DISCIPLINARY CHECK (NURSE, GP WITH LIMITED-HOURS CAPABILITY, AND WHERE POSSIBLE A PHARMACIST OR MENTAL HEALTH LINKWORKER) AND INCLUDE BASIC DIAGNOSTICS. PRIVACY AND CONFIDENTIALITY MUST BE GUARANTEED INSIDE THESE MOBILE UNITS, WITH A CLEAR BOOKING SYSTEM AND THE OPTION FOR URGENT SAME-DAY SLOTS WHEN SOMEONE IS ACUTELY UNWELL. REGULAR COMMUNITY OUTREACH BY HEALTH VISITORS AND CARE COORDINATORS WOULD HELP IN IDENTIFYING THOSE MOST AT RISK OF FALLING THROUGH THE CRACKS, SUCH AS OLDER RESIDENTS OR CARERS WITH TIME CONSTRAINTS.

- TELEHEALTH HUBS IN LOCAL COMMUNITY SPACES: SET UP PATIENT-FRIENDLY TELEHEALTH HUBS IN LIBRARIES, VILLAGE HALLS OR COMMUNITY CENTRES WITH SECURE VIDEO LINKS TO GPS AND MENTAL HEALTH PROFESSIONALS. PROVIDE STAFF ON-SITE TO HELP WITH BOOKING, BASIC DIGITAL LITERACY, AND TRIAGE. ENSURE ACCESS TO DEVICES, RELIABLE BROADBAND AND LANGUAGE/NEEDS SUPPORT SO THAT PEOPLE WHO ARE NOT TECH-SAVVY ARE NOT LEFT BEHIND. TELEMEDICINE SHOULD COMPLEMENT, NOT REPLACE, FACE-TO-FACE CARE WHERE PHYSICAL EXAMINATION OR RAPPORT IS ESSENTIAL.

- TRANSPORT AND PARKING SOLUTIONS: CREATE PRACTICAL ROUTES FOR PATIENTS TO REACH APPOINTMENTS, INCLUDING SUBSIDISED OR DEMAND-RESPONSIVE TRANSPORT FOR RURAL RESIDENTS AND THOSE WITH MOBILITY ISSUES. ALIGN GP, PHARMACY AND SOCIAL CARE VISITS WHERE POSSIBLE TO REDUCE MULTIPLE TRIPS. IMPROVE PARKING AT EXISTING PREMISES WITH CLEAR DISABLED ACCESS AND SAFE DROP-OFF ZONES. WHERE PARKING REMAINS SCARCE, MOBILE AND TELEHEALTH OPTIONS CAN REDUCE THE FREQUENCY OF TRAVEL WHILE MAINTAINING TIMELY ACCESS TO ROUTINE CARE.

- PREMISES INVESTMENT AND CO-LOCATION: MODERNISE AND EXPAND PREMISES TO CREATE SAFE, ACCESSIBLE ENVIRONMENTS WITH ADEQUATE PARKING, DISABLED ACCESS, AND PRIVATE CONSULTATION ROOMS. CO-LOCATING GP SERVICES WITH COMMUNITY NURSING, DISTRICT NURSING, AND MENTAL HEALTH TEAMS CAN SHORTEN WAITING TIMES AND IMPROVE INFORMATION FLOW BETWEEN TEAMS, MAKING IT EASIER TO COORDINATE SAME-DAY CARE WHEN NEEDED.

- INCENTIVES TO RECRUIT AND RETAIN STAFF IN RURAL AND MOBILITY‑LIMITED AREAS: OFFER TARGETED RECRUITMENT AND RETENTION PACKAGES FOR GPS, NURSES AND THERAPISTS WILLING TO WORK IN RURAL SETTINGS, INCLUDING HOUSING ALLOWANCES, FLEXIBLE/FAMILY-FRIENDLY ROTAS, LOCUM SUPPORT, AND FINANCIAL INCENTIVES TIED TO LOCAL ACCESS OUTCOMES. SUPPORT FOR MULTI-SKILLING SO STAFF CAN MANAGE A BROADER RANGE OF NEEDS IN ONE LOCATION, REDUCING THE NEED FOR PATIENTS TO TRAVEL ELSEWHERE.

- PATIENT-CENTRIC DESIGN AND MONITORING: ESTABLISH LOCAL DASHBOARDS TO MONITOR WAITING TIMES, CANCELLATION RATES, AND TRANSPORT-RELATED DELAYS. REGULAR PATIENT FEEDBACK CHANNELS SHOULD BE AVAILABLE TO IDENTIFY BOTTLENECKS AND ADJUST ROUTES, HOURS AND HUB AVAILABILITY ACCORDINGLY. PILOT PROJECTS IN THREE DIFFERENT VILLAGE CLUSTERS COULD TEST THE MIX OF MOBILE, TELEHEALTH AND OUTREACH COMPONENTS BEFORE WIDER ROLLOUT.

I RECOGNISE THAT DIGITAL SOLUTIONS CANNOT FULLY REPLACE IN-PERSON CARE, ESPECIALLY FOR COMPLEX MENTAL HEALTH OR PHYSICAL HEALTH ASSESSMENTS. ANY PROGRAMME MUST PRESERVE CLINICAL SAFETY, PROTECT PRIVACY, AND AVOID WIDENING INEQUALITY FOR THOSE WITHOUT DIGITAL ACCESS. THE MOST SUCCESSFUL APPROACH WILL BE LOCAL, WELL-FUNDED AND CO-DESIGNED WITH PATIENTS AND CARERS, BALANCING MODERN TECHNOLOGY WITH THE HUMAN TOUCH THAT MAKES PRIMARY CARE WORK.

IF THESE ELEMENTS ARE FUNDED AND IMPLEMENTED TOGETHER WITH ROBUST PERFORMANCE MONITORING AND COMMUNITY INVOLVEMENT, WE SHOULD SEE REDUCTIONS IN UNNECESSARY TRAVEL, SHORTER WAITS FOR ASSESSMENTS, AND EARLIER INTERVENTIONS ACROSS GP, COMMUNITY HEALTH AND MENTAL HEALTH SERVICES.

Thank you for the opportunity to respond. I would strongly support changes that make access to GP, community health and mental health services timelier and easier for people in our area. In my experience, when people can get a same‑day urgent slot or an appointment in the evenings or at weekends, problems can be addressed before they get worse, and overall health remains better; this is particularly important for older residents who may have mobility limits or rely on family members to help with travel.

Evening and weekend clinics would make a real difference to working carers and retirees alike. Our local practice runs most appointments during weekday mornings, which can be difficult for those who still help with grandchildren, or for people who want to avoid taking time off work during the week. A regular evening clinic, perhaps once or twice a week, and a Saturday morning slot for urgent non‑emergency needs would reduce the need to wait days for a basic check or symptom review. I have seen neighbours delay seeking care because the only available slots are during the middle of the day; extending hours would keep people healthier and reduce the risk of complications that require hospital care later on.

Similarly, guaranteed same‑day urgent slots for GP or nurse‑led access are essential. If someone has a sudden rise in blood pressure readings, chest discomfort, or a worrying mental health concern, waiting a day or two can be too long. A robust triage system that guarantees a same‑day slot with a clinician who can assess needs, arrange referrals if required, or offer appropriate quick interventions would provide reassurance and prevent deterioration. In practice, I’d like to see streamlined processes where a nurse triage can initiate a same‑day review, with clear options for in‑person, video, or phone contact depending on the situation.

Investing in co‑located community hubs that bring primary care, community services and mental health support under one roof—alongside social care and VCSE partners—would vastly improve our local care experience. Right now, people often must navigate several buildings and different teams to get help with physical health, social needs, and mental wellbeing. A single hub would offer a one‑stop point of contact, easier access for people with mobility issues, and better care coordination. For example, imagine a local centre where a patient could have a GP appointment, see a district nurse, access mental health support, and talk to a social care adviser or a voluntary sector worker in the same place. A co‑located hub also makes it simpler to arrange practical assistance—like transport to appointments, home adaptations, or social activities—that can prevent loneliness and help people stay independent longer.

In my own community, I have seen the benefits of this integrated approach when services are aligned and co‑funded with local charities and community groups. The reality is that when services are separated, people fall through gaps, miss follow‑ups, or struggle with the navigation process. A well‑designed hub, with accessible booking systems (online and phone), clear pathways, and strong links to social care and VCSE partners, would make timely access more than a promise—it would be a reality for many local people.

I know it will require sustainable funding, smart workforce planning, and ongoing involvement from patients and carers to tailor the hubs to local needs. But with reliable funding, clear referral pathways, and effective digital and community partnerships, these changes could shorten waiting times, improve patient experience, and reduce avoidable hospital visits. Please prioritise evening/weekend access, guaranteed same‑day urgent slots, and the development of co‑located community hubs as central to improving timely care in our area.

To improve timely access, we must expand community mental health teams and intensify early intervention, crisis support and talking therapies, connected to GPs to deliver parity with physical health. In my area, I’ve heard stories of people waiting many weeks for talking therapies after a referral, and crisis support that isn’t reliably available outside office hours. Expanding CMHTs with multidisciplinary staff—psychologists, psychiatrists, social workers and nurses—based in local hubs attached to GP practices would create clearer, faster pathways from referral to treatment. An effective early-intervention offer should be available promptly for common conditions, with CBT and other talking therapies available within a couple of weeks, not months. Crisis response should be 24/7 and mobile to reach people at home, reducing escalations and hospital admissions. Parity with physical health requires ring-fenced funding, equitable appointment timetables and shared digital records so clinicians can monitor mental and physical health together, not in silos. Concrete steps: recruit and retain staff; extend therapy slots (including evenings and weekends); and integrate mental health triage into GP services so nobody falls through the cracks.

I live in Wales and I want to see timely access to GP services, community health and mental health care improved so people can get the right help quickly, close to home. I support changes that streamline how people move through the system, reduce unnecessary steps and grow the workforce so we don’t wait weeks for a simple appointment or a mental health check-in. There are practical steps that could make a real difference in our communities.

NHS111, clinical triage, booking systems and care navigation
- Modernise NHS111 so it acts as a real gatekeeper that directs urgent cases to the right local service without delays. That means robust clinical triage with clear decision support, so someone with potentially urgent chest pain or signs of a mental health crisis can be booked for same-day assessment when needed.
- Make online and telephone booking channels user-friendly and interoperable with GP practices, community clinics and mental health teams. People should be able to see available slots, choose the most convenient location and have their information automatically shared across services so they don’t have to repeat symptoms or repeated histories.
- Expand care navigation roles in primary care and community settings. A trained navigator can help people understand what level of care they need, book appointments, organise social and transport support if necessary, and follow up to ensure people don’t fall through the cracks. In my experience, a single point of contact who follows a patient through the system reduces duplication and confusion.
- Improve integration between urgent care, primary care and community services. When a routine issue becomes more complex, the pathway should flex without forcing the patient to restart the process at every step. Clear handovers and shared care plans would save time and improve safety.

Workforce development for sustainable capacity
- Increase training places for GPs, nurses and mental health professionals in Wales, with clear ladders for progression. More medical and nursing school places, plus targeted incentives for working in under-resourced areas, would help grow the workforce where it’s most needed.
- Support return-to-practice and CPD for experienced clinicians. A well-structured return-to-practice pathway can reduce the time it takes for skilled clinicians to re-enter patient care after a break, which is vital for stability in general practice and community teams.
- Expand apprenticeships and training pipelines across primary care. Offering routes from school or college into primary care roles—pharmacists, nurses, physician associates, and allied health professionals—helps build a broader, more adaptable workforce.
- Prioritise rural and coastal areas with tailored recruitment and retention packages. In Wales, access can be uneven; targeted support to recruit locally and retain staff will keep services responsive to local needs.

Multidisciplinary teams to manage routine cases
- Extend multidisciplinary teams in primary care to handle routine and ongoing care. Pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates can manage many common issues, freeing GPs to focus on complex or high-risk patients.
- Embed mental health professionals within GP practices or community hubs. A timely, integrated mental health check, brief therapy sessions or crisis support can prevent deterioration and reduce long waiting lists for specialist services.
- Use pharmacist-led clinics for medication reviews, chronic disease monitoring and minor ailments. This not only improves safety and adherence but also reduces unnecessary GP appointments.
- Encourage joint working with community nursing, social care and voluntary sector partners. A coordinated approach means people receive help for housing, welfare and social needs alongside health care, which often speeds up recovery and prevents readmission.

Personal experience and practical implications
- In our area, a family member waited too long for a mental health assessment after routine signs of anxiety escalated. If there had been a faster, integrated pathway with a navigator and a mental health professional in the local GP practice, that person could have started support sooner and avoided a crisis.
- I’ve also encountered delays when trying to book a same-day appointment for a dependent relative. A more straightforward, unified booking system and clearer triage would have saved time and reduced stress for everyone involved.
- Conversely, I’ve seen benefits when clinics use physiotherapists and pharmacists more actively for knee and back pain. Those clinic slots filled quickly, patients gained timely relief, and GPs could focus on more complex cases.

Conclusion
Overall, I warmly support reforms that strengthen NHS111 and triage, reform booking and care navigation, invest in training and return-to-practice, and expand multidisciplinary teams. The goal is simple: ensure timely, safe access to the right care, in the right setting, with less duplication and smoother patient flow. If these changes are implemented thoughtfully—with local flexibility to meet community needs in Wales—they can deliver faster access, better outcomes and a more sustainable NHS for the future.

I welcome measures to improve timely access by expanding online booking, e-consultations and remote care, provided there is a safety net for those who cannot or prefer not to go digital. In my practice, online triage and video quick chats have sometimes reduced unnecessary trips and helped squeeze in urgent requests the same week. I recently used an online booking to secure a same-day appointment for a flare-up, and an e-consult to renew a repeat prescription without a long phone call. But we must not leave behind older neighbours who struggle with smartphones or broadband; there must be clear non-digital options—telephone bookings, walk-in slots, home visits where appropriate, and on-site help with digital access in libraries or community centres. From where I live in England, simply widening GP hours into evenings and weekends or guaranteeing same-day urgent slots would not by itself deliver timely access. On several occasions, I’ve waited weeks for a GP appointment that was supposed to be same-day, and when I did get in the clinician was rushed and didn’t address all concerns. For many people with urgent non-emergency needs, an extended-slot doesn’t help if you can't get to the surgery or if there isn’t space to see you.

What would help more is a dual approach: mobile clinics that visit housing estates, workplaces and rural hubs during evenings/weekends; outreach workers who triage and signpost to the right service; telehealth hubs that provide rapid digital triage plus link-ups with mental health crisis teams and community physio; and real incentives to attract practitioners to rural and mobility-restricted areas. In short, hours alone won’t fix the problem; we need place-based delivery, flexible models and investment in infrastructure.
