Examples from our area: a neighbour with diabetes and anxiety struggled with very short GP slots; longer appointments would have enabled integrated care. Mental health waits, especially for CAMHS and IAPT, are too long—expansion and timely crisis support would make a real difference. These changes must be backed by funding, workforce planning and clear success metrics.

Agree. For rural and mobility-limited residents like many of us, timely GP and mental health care would improvr with mobile clinics and outreach, telehealth hubs, better transport and parking, and incentives to attract staff to underserved areas.

I’m writing to push back on the idea that simply expandin online booking, e‑consultations and remote care will automatically deliver quicker, better access to GPs, nurses, therapists and community health teams Yes, technology can help in some cases, but I’m worried it will exclude and confuse a lot of people if it isn’t paired with strong non‑digital options and real, on‑thr‑ground support. First, digital access is not universal. In my community, plenty of people struggle with online systems or don’t have reliable internet, a suitable device, or the data to use apps for bookings or video appointments. I’ve seen neighbours' parents get frustrated trying to book online only to be told to “book through the portal” when their phone line is busy or the portal keeps timing out. I’ve also heard of patients who are very anxious about their data security and would rather speak to a real person than chat through an online form. If you push digital‑first without guaranteeing a non‑digital route, you’ll just push people further up the waiting list or push them away altogether. Second, remote care can be convenient but it isn’t a universal remedy, especially for mental health and certain physical problems. I’ve had friends who felt a teleconsult missed important non‑verba cues, or who needed a physical check (palpation, listening to lungs, or a careful eye exam) that simpl can’t be done well over video or phone. In mental health, there’s real value in building trust and rapport in person, and some situations require a face‑to‑face assessment, a safe space, or in‑clinic escalation if risk factors are present. Remote triage or quick “check‑in” calls can be better than nothing, but they often end up delaying proper assessment or breaking continuity of care when patient cycle through multiple providers or digital channels. Third, expanding appointment slots is not a silver bullet unless you also invest in the workforce and the scheduling systems that actually deliver them. You can open more slots on paper, but if there aren’t enough GPs, nurses, therapists, and suppor staff those slots won’t materialise in a meaningful way. i strongly believe from my situation as a pensioner living in a small town in England, I’ve seen how delays in GP, community health and mental health appointments ripple through families and everyday life. When you’re managing long‑term conditions or supporting a partner who needs regular check‑ups, even a few extra days of waiting can mean symptoms worsen or crises arise. I’m therefore strongly in favour of changes that would increase appointment slots, expand session capacity and optimise scheduling. In practice, that means more clinicians, longer or more flexible appointment times, and smarter booking systems that actually reflect people’s real needs.

First, widening clinical capacity is essential. Our GP practices already juggle high demand with stable staff numbers, but I’ve noticed longer waits for routine appointments, and urgent same‑day slots fill up quickly. Hiring more GPs and expanding the roles of nurse practitioners, physiotherapists and counsellors would free GPs to handle complex cases, while nurses and therapists can see patients earlier for chronic disease reviews, fall-prevention checks, wound care, and mental health assessments. In my area, I would welcome more evening and weekend clinics so carers and retired residents who cannot take time off work or who struggle with daytime transport can still access care without rushing or missing doses of daily medications.

Session length matters, too. For those with multiple conditions, 10‑minute slots simply aren’t enough. Longer appointments—15 to 20 minutes for seniors with multimorbidity and medication reviews—would lead to more accurate assessments, reduce the need for repeat visits, and help prevent adverse interactions. Expanding session capacity could also mean more joint clinics across disciplines, for example a combined GP, nurse, physiotherapist and pharmacist slot to review a patient’s medications and mobility in one visit. I’ve benefited from longer appointment times when visiting a clinic that runs holistic reviews; it saves time overall and gives people confidence in the plan.

Optimised scheduling should be at the heart of any reform. A triage‑driven system that uses careful telephone or online triage to sort urgent from routine cases can get people seen sooner. My experience shows that a well‑run online booking portal, with real‑time visibility of available slots across a local hub of practices, reduces the back‑and‑forth and the frustration of calling repeatedly. Even better would be a shared appointment model across several nearby practices so patients can be slotted into the next available appropriate clinician without having to travel to a specific site. And for those with memory issues or mobility challenges, having a clear option for home visits or community clinic drop‑ins would be life‑changing.

Mental health access is a particular worry. Waiting weeks or months for therapy or counselling often leads to deterioration. Increased capacity could include more cognitive behavioral therapists, counsellors and agreed pathways for early intervention, crisis support and stepped care. It would help to offer flexible formats—phone or video sessions where appropriate, with in‑person options for more severe or complex cases—to reduce no‑shows and support continuity of care. In my neighbourhood, even a modest expansion—an additional weekly mental health clinic or more weekend slots—could prevent admissions to hospital or A&E by catching problems early when they’re manageable.

I also think technology and data can help. A unified, user‑friendly booking system with reminders, the ability to reschedule easily, and transparent wait times at practice level would empower patients. Real‑time dashboards for practice staff to monitor capacity, plus administrative support to handle bookings and follow‑ups, would keep flows smooth and prevent bottlenecks. For those who rely on public transport or have mobility issues, partnerships with community transport and home‑visit schemes should be funded and expanded.

In short, a multi‑faceted approach—more clinicians, longer and more flexible appointment slots, better scheduling and shared access across providers, plus strengthened community and mental health services—would deliver timely access for many people like me. It would also ease pressure on urgent care and help people stay independent longer, which I believe is good value for the NHS and for the communities it serves. Implemented thoughtfully, these changes could transform everyday life for older residents and their carers, reducing stress and keeping people healthier at home.

it's outrageous that timely access to GP, community health and mental health services would improve if resources were targeted where gaps are widest and language and cultural support were routine, not an afterthought. In my area, people who don’t speak English or who come from deprived or migrant backgrounds face real delays and confusion when trying to book or navigate care. My suggestions: 

- Interpreters and language access: ring-fenced funding for in-person and remote interpreters across GP, urgent care and mental health services; ensure booking systems flag language needs and offer translations of key forms and information in common community languages; extend hours so interpreters are available for evening appointments.
- Culturally competent staff: recruit staff from diverse backgrounds and provide ongoing cultural competence training; involve community voices in service design to reduce miscommunication and build trust.
- Outreach and service delivery: deploy mobile clinics in housing estates and at community centres; run targeted outreach with trusted community organisations, faith groups and migrant networks, including evenings and weekends; create simple, multilingual materials on how to access help and what to expect; offer drop-in mental health sessions with translators.
- Data and accountability: monitor access by ethnicity and deprivation, publish annual progress, and adjust funding to areas where gaps persist.

Sustainable funding and strong partnerships are essential. I’ve seen pilots fade when backing isn’t long-term—please commit to ongoing support and clear performance measures!

Invest in mobile clinics and telehealth hubs, with outreach and better transport access, plus co-located community hubs; recruit internationally and improve pay and wellbeing to sustain staff, ensuring timely GP, community and mental health care.

I understand the aim of making GP, community health and mental health services more timely, but I’m not convinced the current proposals will reliably improve access in my area. Expanding community mental health teams, boosting early intervention and crisis response, and widening talking therapies all sound sensible in principle, yet without careful integration with existing GP and social care networks, they risk adding layers rather than reducing waits. People needing urgent mental health support often fall through the gaps between different services, and the reality on the ground is that delays in getting through to an initial clinician are still too common. If we’re serious about parity with physical health, then mental health must be treated as urgent, with predictable pathways and timely assessments, not a lottery of where you live or which waiting list your local coordinator happens to manage.

Recruitment and workforce planning are another sticking point. The idea of targeted recruitment, international hiring, incentives and flexible working may help fill gaps, but it also raises concerns I’ve heard from residents and carers about continuity of care and turnover. International staff bring valuable skills, but frequent changes in clinicians can Fragment patients’ sense of who is looking after them, and lead to repeated handovers for individuals with complex needs. Pay improvements and wellbeing support are welcome, but they must be paired with reliable staffing levels, safe-to-work rotas and guaranteed in-person availability where needed. Flexible working is fine in principle, yet it should not come at the expense of predictability for patients who rely on routine appointments and home visits.

Transport, parking and premises remain endemic hurdles in rural and mobility-limited areas. Even when the idea of mobile clinics or outreach hubs is appealing, they are not a substitute for stable, well-located services that people can access without long journeys. Telehealth hubs can help, but many older residents face digital barriers—poor connectivity, unfamiliar devices, or a lack of on-site assistance to use them. I’ve seen neighbours miss appointments because travel to the town centre was too difficult or parking was impossible, and I’ve heard of people delaying care because they couldn’t navigate a new telehealth platform. Any plan must include a robust digital inclusion strategy, plus high-quality in-person options for those who can’t, or won’t, use technology.

In practice, a few concrete changes would help more than broad promises:
- Ensure same-day GP access and accurate triage, with clear, predictable pathways into mental health care so people aren’t waiting weeks for a first appointment. This could involve extended hours, more nurse prescribers and clinician-led triage that feeds directly into timely mental health or social care follow-up.
- Build stable, locally rooted recruitment pipelines: invest in training locally, offer clear career progression, and ensure staffing levels are maintained during transitions between teams. Retaining staff should be a condition of any expansion so patients don’t feel they’re handed from one new team to another.
- Invest in transport and premises with a balanced mix of in-person and supported digital options. Mobile clinics and community outreach are valuable adjuncts, but not a replacement for accessible, well-equipped local clinics with parking, disabled access and flexible appointment slots.
- Prioritise digital inclusion alongside telehealth. Provide on-site support at libraries or community hubs, loan devices where feasible, and offer straightforward, telephone-based options for those who prefer it.
- Publish transparent local performance metrics so residents can see whether waits have shortened and whether referrals to urgent care are being acted upon promptly.

From personal experience in this area, the best improvements come from coupling stronger mental health pathways with reliable primary care access and practical, locally tailored transport solutions. If the plan truly wants to reduce waits and deliver parity with physical health, it must be implemented with emphasis on continuity, local capability, and genuine accessibility for the elderly and those with limited mobility. Otherwise we’ll end up with more teams on paper but little real, timely help for the people who need it most.

Timely access to GP, community health and mental health services would be most improved by two changes: protect continuity of care and lengthen appointment times for complex, chronic and vulnerable patients. When my family member with long‑term conditions can see the same GP or a small, stable team, the clinician knows the history, current medications and triggers. That avoids duplicated tests, reduces confusion and cuts down on repeat visits. 

Key changes I would support:
- Guarantee named clinicians or small care teams with shared, up-to-date care plans across primary and community services so information follows the patient.
- Extend consultation times for complex cases to 20–30 minutes, with longer slots for mental health reviews or polypharmacy reviews.
- Increase multidisciplinary capacity in practices and community hubs (nurses, health visitors, psychologists, social workers) and provide clear, well-supported same-day triage routes to maintain continuity.
- Use digital tools to support, not replace, in-person continuity, ensuring notes and treatment plans are accessible to the whole team.

Pilots to test these approaches should be funded, with outcomes monitored (patient satisfaction, hospital admissions, adherence). In practice, these changes would reduce follow-ups and improve outcomes for those with chronic conditions and mental health needs.

I strongly support changes that would improve timely access to GP, community health and mental health services, with a clear focus on expanding community mental health teams, early intervention, crisis response and talking therapies. In my experience and from talking to friends and colleagues in England, the delays between needing help and getting the right support can be long, and that gap often worsens crises that could have been prevented with earlier, more integrated care.

First, expand community mental health teams so people can get help close to home and before problems escalate. CMHTs that include psychologists, nurses, social workers, occupational therapists and peer support, working alongside GP practices and local community hubs, would mean people don’t have to navigate multiple doors to get help. When someone presents with early warning signs—low mood, anxiety, sleep disruption or problematic thoughts—a well-resourced CMHT could offer triage within days, provide home visits if needed, and coordinate with primary care to ensure smooth referral to talking therapies or crisis support. In our area, the lack of co-ordinated teams often means people bounce between services, and the first sustained intervention arrives only after a crisis; expanding CMHTs would help prevent that cycle.

Second, prioritise early intervention. The sooner someone receives targeted support, the better outcomes tend to be. That means rapid access to evidence-based options like specialised early intervention for psychosis, but also timely help for anxiety, depression and stress-related conditions that are common in young adults. Local models that co-locate mental health staff in GP practices or university health services, with clear pathways to psychologists and counsellors, would make a real difference. I’ve seen people in their 20s struggle with long wait times after referral for talking therapies, losing motivation and missing work or study. If we can shorten the window from concern to sustained support—often through Step 2/3 therapies and stepped-care approaches—we reduce the chance of escalation and promote better long-term resilience.

Third, strengthen crisis response. A timely, compassionate crisis service can prevent people from reaching breaking point or ending up in A&E. I’d like to see 24/7 crisis lines with rapid, mobile crisis teams who can visit people at home, assess risk, and provide short-term stabilization and a direct handover to ongoing CMHT support when needed. Crisis cafés or brief crisis beds in communities can serve as humane, less-stressful stops on the way to longer-term care. In practice, that means funding to guarantee prompt responses (ideally within hours) and to prevent avoidable admissions, especially for people in rural areas where access can be even more challenging.

Fourth, expand access to talking therapies while widening the range of options. IAPT has shown what can be possible when mental health care is more accessible, but too many people still wait weeks or months for an initial contact, and later sessions can be scarce. We should aim to meet demand with more therapists, offer a broader menu of therapies (CBT, ACT, IPT, EMDR where appropriate), and ensure flexible delivery—face-to-face, video, phone—and group formats for those who prefer them. It’s also important to integrate talking therapies with practical supports—employment, housing, and social connection—to sustain improvements after therapy ends.

Finally, give mental health parity with physical health. This means funding and staffing levels that reflect the true need, clear national targets for waiting times, transparent performance data at local level, and joint pathways so a patient’s care plan follows them across GP, CMHTs, community services and hospital teams. Co-funded, no-wrong-door approaches, and shared electronic records, would remove needless repetitions and speed up care.

What would most improve timely access in my area is a package that combines: more community mental health staffing and colocations; proactive early-intervention pathways; a robust 24/7 crisis response; expanded talking-therapy capacity with flexible delivery; and stronger parity with physical health funding and governance. If implemented, these changes would reduce waits, cut unnecessary crises, and help young adults like me stay well and able to work or study with less disruption.

Access to timely GP, community health and mental health services in my area is uneven, especially for those who cannot drive and for people living in rural pockets. To improve this, I think we need a combined approach.

First, practical fixes on the ground: mobile clinics stationed in village halls and market squares on rotation, with daytime and evening slots, would reduce the need to travel long distances. Regular outreach to care homes and school-linked health workers can catch people earlier. Establish telehealth hubs in community venues (libraries, GP practices) with trained staff to assist using devices, not just as software. Improve premises and parking at existing sites and create co-located services so people can see multiple professionals in one trip. Offer incentives to attract GPs, nurses and mental health workers to rural and mobility-limited areas, and support flexible contracts.

Second, while expanding online booking and e-consultations can help, we must provide non-digital alternatives. My 70-year-old neighbour relies on a phone appointment system—an online-only model would exclude him. A hybrid approach with robust phone triage, walk-in slots, and in-person clinics alongside digital options is essential.

Third, to sustain these gains long-term, increase training places, return-to-practice support, apprenticeships and CPD for GPs, nurses and mental health professionals. In our area, stronger training pipelines could prevent repeated staff shortages.

Overall, a mixed, well funded strategy focused on transport, human support, and workforce growth would improve timely access.

Timely access to GP and community services remains uneven in my area. I would support expanding capacity: more GP, nurse and therapist appointment slots by recruiting staff and extending session lengths where appropriate, plus smarter scheduling to reduce gaps. In practice, a longer evenings and weekend slots would help busy families. For mental health, increasing therapist numbers and stepping-up outreach would cut waits and prevent crises.

However, transport and access in rural-like parts create real barriers. Buses are infrequent and parking is tight at our village clinic. I’d welcome mobile clinics that visit rural hamlets, plus outreach teams to check on people with mobility limits. Telehealth hubs in local libraries or community centres could also bridge the gap, provided they offer private, easy-to-use tech and clear referral pathways.

I also think expanding multidisciplinary teams—pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates—could handle routine checks and rehabilitation, freeing GPs to focus on complex cases. The key would be robust governance, clear triage, and consistent funding so these changes are joined up and sustainable.
